# PREFACE

->I.<-

The *Works of Descartes* were published several times during the 17th century, both during the philosopher’s lifetime and after his death, but these were issued separately from one another, as will be seen in the specific discussion of each work. Even the Blaeu edition in Holland, which is moreover in Latin <note>original: "en latin"</note> (9 volumes, in-quarto <note>A book size where each printed sheet is folded twice to create four leaves.</note>, 1682-1701), does not offer a true sense of unity; it was only after the fact, in 1692, that a catalog of the nine combined volumes appeared, as if their publication had been conceived according to a methodical plan. The Company of Booksellers <note>original: "La Compagnie des Libraires," a powerful guild of publishers in Paris.</note> in Paris issued a small edition from 1723 to 1729 which—with the exception of the Latin text of a few letters for which only translations had previously existed, and some French versions of Latin letters—is merely a reprint. Only the six volumes of *Letters* (1724-1725) offer sequential volume numbering; the seven other volumes, containing the rest of the *Works*, have only artificial volume numbering <note>Volumes grouped together by a binder or collector that were not originally printed as a matching set.</note>. It is therefore to Victor Cousin (as he rightly took pride in) that France owes an edition of the *Complete Works* of Descartes (11 volumes in-octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves.</note>, Paris, Levrault, 1824-1826). However, in the first place, this edition is entirely in French; furthermore, the requirements of critical analysis, as well as the progress of scholarship, soon made even the editor himself recognize (as he gracefully admitted at the end of his life) that his work needed to be undertaken anew. Joseph Millet, author of a *History of Descartes before 1637* (Paris, Didier, 1867), and *after 1637* <note>1637 is a pivotal year in philosophy, marking the publication of Descartes' "Discourse on the Method."</note> (Paris, Dumoulin, 1870),

...was conscientiously preparing for this task, and even published a prospectus <note>A printed document describing a forthcoming book to attract subscribers.</note> for a first volume at the beginning of his second work; but war broke out, followed by the author's premature death in October 1870, and his project was abandoned. Shortly thereafter, the studies of Mr. Louis Liard on Cartesian philosophy <note>The philosophy of René Descartes, named after the Latinized version of his name, "Cartesius."</note>, while he was a professor at the Faculty of Letters in Bordeaux (1874-1880), convinced him more than anyone of the necessity of a new edition, and in concert with Mr. Paul Tannery, then an engineer in Bordeaux, he considered producing it: the *Descartes* that he published in 1882 remains a lasting testament to these early labors. But starting in 1884, the Directorate of Higher Education at the Ministry of Public Instruction <note>The French government body overseeing schools and universities.</note> imposed other duties upon Mr. Liard, and from then on he devoted himself entirely to bringing the great work to which he was dedicated to fruition: the reorganization of the Universities in France.

However, the third centenary <note>The 300th anniversary of his birth (1596–1896).</note> of the birth of Descartes was approaching; it could be celebrated no better than by an edition of his *Works*. Mr. Émile Boutroux announced this in the *Review of Metaphysics and Morals* <note>original: "Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale"</note> on May 15, 1894; and the zealous Director of this *Review*, Mr. Xavier Léon, immediately became the project's promoter. Mr. Paul Tannery was increasingly the designated collaborator, especially for the scientific portion: the new edition of the *Works of Fermat* <note>Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665), a French mathematician famous for his work in number theory.</note>, to which he had just attached his name along with Mr. Charles Henry, had notably engaged him in deep research regarding the *Correspondence* of Descartes and that of Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk and mathematician who acted as the central hub for scientific correspondence in Europe during Descartes' time.</note>. Mr. Charles Adam, after more than ten years of study on the history of philosophy in France in the first half of the 17th century, was well acquainted with the philosophical portion of Descartes’ *Works*. He spent part of the year 1894 conducting research, under an official mission, in the libraries of the Netherlands and Hanover, and he returned with numerous and important finds. In the month of November, a Committee was

From the very first meeting, Mr. Adam presented a *Project for the Edition*, which was examined, discussed, and approved in principle. In the following sessions, spaced throughout the year 1895, various questions were settled: the spelling to be followed, the format of the volumes, the choice of typefaces, etc., and finally, in January 1896, a contract was signed with the firm Cerf and Co., to whom the edition was entrusted.

The third centenary of the birth of Descartes was celebrated at the Sorbonne <note>The historic seat of the University of Paris.</note> on March 31, 1896, among philosophers and...

...scholars, under the presidency of Mr. Liard. After an address by the president, the floor was given to the two collaborators: to Mr. Tannery, for a reading on "*Descartes as Physicist*", and to Mr. Adam, for a lecture entitled "*In Search of Descartes' Papers*".

Similar ceremonies were celebrated in Rio de Janeiro, Moscow, Prague, etc.

Soon Mr. Léon had gathered, thanks to the publicity in his *Review*, a sufficient number of subscribers for the upcoming edition. The Ministry subscribed for 200 copies. On July 15, 1896, the *Review of Metaphysics and Morals* <note>original: "Revue de Métaphysique et de Morale"; a highly influential French philosophy journal founded by Xavier Léon.</note> issued, as a bonus to subscribers, a fascicle dedicated entirely to Descartes; to clearly highlight the international character of the subscription, Mr. Léon had invited foreign scholars and philosophers to collaborate on this exceptional issue. Thus, the names of Messrs. Natorp and Schwartz for Germany, Gibson for England, Korteweg for Holland, and Tocco for Italy, were associated with those of Messrs. Boutroux, Brochard, Lanson, Hannequin, Blondel, Berthet, Tannery, and Adam for France. Finally, a Committee comprising no fewer than sixty-four names, all drawn from Philosophy and Science, sponsored the subscription not only in France but throughout Europe (Germany, England, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Holland, Italy, Russia, Sweden, Switzerland), and even as far as America ¹.

# XII
# PREFACE.

...a quantity of notes that would initially overwhelm the space reserved for Descartes' own text. This new difficulty is resolved by dividing the notes into several categories in the following manner:

1. For the letters found *without a name or date*, the information required for these two points is placed at the beginning in a *Prolegomenon* <term>Prolegomenon: A formal introductory essay or preliminary set of remarks.</term>.

2. A good number of details throughout each letter require *clarifications*: these are facts mentioned by Descartes, or perhaps responses to objections that had to be located elsewhere. The necessary information is moved to the end of the letter, each marked with the corresponding page and line numbers; the reader, while moving through the text, is alerted by an *asterisk* that they will find a *clarification* further on.

3. At the bottom of the pages, in the usual place for notes, we have been content to provide *brief notes* <note>original: "notules"</note> (the title of a cited work, the name of an author for whom we only had an initial or an imperfect designation, references to preceding or following letters, etc.). Above all, we have arranged the *variants* of the text in two columns whenever they exist: for several letters, indeed, we have two versions, both by Descartes: the text of the *draft* <term>Minute: The preliminary draft of a letter or document kept by the sender for their own records.</term> preserved by him and printed by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the primary editor and publisher of Descartes' posthumous works and letters.</note>, and the text of the *original* found in a recovered autograph <term>Autograph: A manuscript written in the author's own handwriting.</term>. — At the top of each page, two numbers indicate the volume and page of the Clerselier edition for the letter below: the pagination is the same for all editions of volumes II and III; for volume I, it changes from the first to the second edition: we provide the numbering for the second and third editions; a vertical bar within the text indicates the start of each page in Clerselier’s edition.

# XIII
# PREFACE.

names reappear quite often; it would therefore be necessary each time to refer back to the note placed at the bottom of the first letter where the name occurs. What a mess of cross-references and what a complication! We decided to gather all these proper names into a sort of *Biographical Dictionary*, published separately, where the reader will find the information they desire on each one.

Presented in this way, the *Correspondence of Descartes* will be easy to read, offering all the advantages of a scholarly edition without the general appearance of the text losing any of its beauty. Messrs. Cerf and Co. <note>MM. Cerf et Cie was the publishing house responsible for this monumental edition.</note>, responding indeed to the wish of the Ministry of Public Instruction, have neglected and spared nothing so that France may display, at the Universal Exhibition of 1900 <note>The 1900 Paris Exposition was a massive world's fair intended to celebrate the achievements of the past century and accelerate development into the next.</note>, an edition of its philosopher worthy of her and worthy of him.

# INTRODUCTION

## TO DESCARTES’S CORRESPONDENCE

I. The Clerselier Edition (1657–1659–1667).
II. Legrand’s Editorial Project and the La Hire Collection (1675–1704). The Classification by Poirier or Arbogast (1793–1803).
III. The Victor Cousin Edition (1824–1826).
IV. Autograph Letters and Manuscript Copies.

### I.

### THE CLERSELIER EDITION.

->(1657–1659–1667.)<-

The first edition of *Descartes’s Letters* is that produced by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s friend and literary executor, responsible for preserving much of his work</note>, in three <term>quarto</term> <note>a book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to form four leaves</note> volumes, published in Paris by Charles Angot in 1657, 1659, and 1667. However, several letters had already been printed separately; the following describes the circumstances.

In 1638, Plemp <note>Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius (1601–1671)</note> (*Plempius*), Professor of Medicine at the University of Louvain, who had twice raised objections against Descartes, summarized the philosopher’s two responses in a first edition of *On the Foundations of Medicine* <note>original: "De Fundamentis Medicinæ"</note> (1638). Henry de Roy (*Regius*) <note>Hendrik de Roy (1598–1679), a Dutch physician and early follower of Descartes who later broke away from him</note>, of the University of Utrecht, found the summary inaccurate and complained about it in public theses in 1640; Plemp therefore printed the full text of the two

Descartes’s letters in a second edition of the ***Foundations of Medicine*** <note>original: "Fundamenta Medicinae"</note> in 1644. That same year, a physician from Dordrecht named Beverwick requested these same two responses from the philosopher, and Descartes sent him the drafts <note>original: "minutes"; the preliminary versions or personal copies kept by the author</note> he had kept: they appeared in Beverwick's (*Beverovicius*) ***Epistolary Questions*** <note>original: "Quaestiones epistolicae"</note>, a small <term>duodecimo</term> <note>original: "in-12"; a book size where each sheet of paper is folded to create twelve leaves, resulting in a small, pocket-sized book</note> printed in Rotterdam in 1644. Clerselier would only make use of this last work, in which the two letters are incomplete and lack dates.

In 1653, Pierre Borel, "Physician to the King," published in his ***Summary of the Life of René Descartes*** <note>original: "Compendium vitae Renati Cartesii"</note> (a small duodecimo of only 55 pages, printed in Castres), a Latin translation of several letters or fragments of letters (eleven items in total) that were then circulating in copy form. These included, among others, two letters to Princess Elisabeth dated May 7 and June 28, 1643. Borel nearly always provided the precise date of the pieces he published; however, Clerselier was either unaware of this publication or, at the very least, took no account of it—though he could have used it to date certain pieces of Descartes’s Correspondence.

Finally, in 1656, there appeared in Amsterdam, under the title ***The Great Descartes’s Spirit Defended by Himself, or the Honorable René Descartes’s Apologetic Complaint*** <note>original: "Magni Cartesii Manes ab ipsomet defensi, sive N. V. Renati Des-Cartes Querela apologetica"</note>, the philosopher’s long defensive letter to the City Council <note>original: "Vroedschap"; the Dutch municipal administrative body</note> of Utrecht. Descartes appears to have written this short work himself in both French and Latin. It was the Latin text that was published in Amsterdam in 1656; Clerselier would provide the French text in the third volume of his edition in 1667.

Regarding the materials he had at his disposal, Clerselier himself recounts this in the ***Preface*** of his first volume. He possessed Descartes’s manuscripts—which is to say, not the letters actually sent by the philosopher, but the drafts <term>minutes</term> <note>from the French "minutes," referring to the original drafts retained by the sender for their own records</note> that he had preserved for a good number of them. These drafts were found among other papers brought from Holland to Sweden. In the inventory drawn up on February 14, 1650, three days after Descartes’s death—of which a manuscript copy by Clerselier himself is now held at the National Library <note>original: "Bibliothèque Nationale"</note> (fr. 13262),

In short, two-thirds and nearly three-quarters of each volume offer an order that is easy to follow, and Clerselier seems to have been troubled only by a small number of letters that he threw together at the end of his volumes, despairing of finding for each one, not the date—which mattered little to him—but the name of the recipient. Even then, he hardly bothered with it: the essential thing for him was the very substance of each letter, or the subject it treated; the rest seemed to him only an accessory that could be removed without much loss—small pieces of news with which the letter was sprinkled, or polite phrases at the beginning and the end. "As for what

> concerns," he says, "the order and the sequence of the letters in general,
> as it often mattered very little which one was placed
> first, each almost dealing with different questions
> which do not depend on one another, I did not
> dwell much upon it; but as for the arrangement and
> structure <note>original: "œconomie" — meaning the internal organization or "economy" of the argument.</note> of each letter in particular, since it is the
> work of a master, one will see the same order and the same
> distribution as in all his other writings." One will

understand better how Clerselier proceeded and what services his edition can still provide by studying the three volumes one after the other.

Clerselier had skillfully chosen the letters for this volume: though professional mathematicians did not find what they were looking for—as Christiaan Huygens wrote on March 2, 1657—on the other hand, the public, which takes more interest in questions of ethics, physics, and even medicine, found much to satisfy them. Furthermore, the names of Queen Christina and Princess Elizabeth—both still living—as well as Balzac, not to mention that English gentleman, Mr. More <note>Henry More, the Cambridge Platonist.</note>, and a certain nobleman whose name was not mentioned, were bound to attract attention and bring honor to the philosopher who had been in correspondence with such eminent figures. The book's success was guaranteed; two years later, when Clerselier published his second volume, he noted in the *Preface* that the first was already "entirely sold out."

In the 17th century, when an author's ideas were valued above all else, one might have been satisfied with this edition. But we have become more demanding; we ask at least two things of a collection of correspondence: first, that it be complete—that is, two-sided, including the letters from the correspondents as well as those of the author; second, that the whole be arranged in chronological order. Now, these two elements are sorely lacking in Clerselier's edition; they even seem to have been the least of his concerns.

In France, however, he did obtain from J.-B. Morin <note>Jean-Baptiste Morin, a professor of mathematics and a critic of Descartes.</note>, Professor at the Royal College <note>Now the Collège de France.</note>, the communication of several letters written to Descartes as well as the replies. Even so, of the seven pieces in this correspondence, the first (Letter 57), written long before the others, is not dated; but one then finds several...

dates, February 22 and July 13, 1638 for LVIII, LIX, and LX; August 12 of the same year for LXI; and nothing for LXII and LXIII.

Here is another correspondence that Clerselier could have easily completed and dated: he concerned himself with it even less. Chanut <note>Pierre Chanut (1601–1662) was a French diplomat and a close friend to both Descartes and Queen Christina of Sweden.</note> kept a *memento* <note>original: "memento"; a record or logbook of correspondence.</note> of the letters he wrote or received; Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, Descartes's first major biographer.</note> and Legrand would later use it to establish several dates. Chanut had also recovered his letters upon the philosopher's death, and Baillet would provide long passages from them in the *Life of Descartes*. Yet Clerselier made no use of these family papers. Perhaps he had to contend with the modesty of his brother-in-law <note>Chanut was Clerselier's brother-in-law.</note>, to which he pays tribute in the dedication of his first volume: Chanut had not even permitted this dedication to be printed in 1657, and it was necessary to wait until after his death in 1662 to provide it to the public in the second edition of 1663. Perhaps, also, the dictates of propriety stood in the way of publishing letters in which an ambassador spoke freely of the Queen to whom he was accredited, and while she was still living (Christina did not die until 1689). — These same reasons, added to a sense of reserve quite natural for a woman, explain why Clerselier could not surrender the letters of Princess Elizabeth <note>Princess Elizabeth of the Palatinate, a brilliant student and long-term correspondent of Descartes.</note> to public curiosity: she had requested them back immediately upon Descartes's death; Chanut returned them to her, and the Princess, says Baillet (vol. II, p. 428), "*would not permit any of them to be printed alongside those of the philosopher*." However, she did allow copies to be taken, and it was in this way that they were later rediscovered and published in 1879 by Foucher de Careil.

Always through a similar excess of modesty, Clerselier—who printed three responses made to him at the end of the first volume—did not simultaneously provide his own letters to which Descartes was responding. And by the same negligence or perhaps indifference, he did not date these three responses.

Finally, the three letters to Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac, a famous French writer known for his influence on the French language.</note> (C, CI, and CII) have no date; it was easy, however, to date at least the last two...

the latter, by interspersing among them a letter to Descartes, dated April 25, 1631, which was printed as early as 1636 in the *Second Part of the Letters of Mr. de Balzac* <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654) was a famous French author known for reforming French prose; his letters were widely read as models of style.</note>, and reprinted in 1637, 1641, etc. For the first, there was also a response, dated March 30, 1628, and printed in 1657, 1664, etc., in private editions of the *Christian Socrates by the Lord of Balzac* <note>original: "Socrate chrestien par le Sr de Balzac"</note> and other works by the same Author. Finally, another letter from Descartes to Balzac—or rather a copy of a letter—dated June 14, 1637, was discovered among the papers of Conrart <note>Valentin Conrart (1603–1675), the first secretary of the Académie Française.</note> at the Arsenal Library. However, in 1691, Baillet, regarding Descartes’s letters to Balzac, would place this note in the margin of volume I, page 401: <margin>“they are mostly lost.”</margin>

Meanwhile, Clerselier had written from Paris on December 12, 1654, specifically “to Mr. More, an English gentleman” <note>original: "Henricus Morus"; Henry More (1614–1687) was a prominent Cambridge Platonist philosopher.</note>, and the latter had replied from Cambridge on May 14, 1655. These two letters, LXIV and LXV, undoubtedly provided us with the dates for those that follow: LXVI and LXVII, December 11, 1648, and February 5, 1649; LXVIII and LXIX, March 5 and April 15 (LXX is undated); and LXXI, October 21. Finally, LXXII is merely a draft of a letter, also undated. But More had altered something in his letters before sending them to Clerselier; they are, therefore, no longer exactly what Descartes had received. This was the risk one faced when addressing the philosopher's correspondents after the fact: would they always provide the faithful text of what they had written? On the other hand, possessing Descartes's original drafts <note>original: "minutes"; the retained copies or rough drafts kept by the author.</note> gave Clerselier an advantage: he found there, for instance, letter LXXII, which was a final reply that had never actually been sent.

But since Clerselier was writing to England, why did he not inquire after that nobleman to whom Descartes had addressed at least three letters, LII, LIII, and LIV? This was the Marquis of Newcastle <note>William Cavendish, 1st Duke of Newcastle (1592–1676), a Royalist commander and polymath.</note>, the brother of another of Descartes’s correspondents, Charles Cavendish; and while the latter had died in 1652, his elder brother lived until 1676.

It also highlights his failure to contact living correspondents like the Marquis of Newcastle to complete the collection.</summary>

<page-num>XXIV</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

The first volume also contains letters from Descartes and correspondents in the Netherlands. These are, first, letters LV and LVI, objections from a Reverend Jesuit Father with the responses. Clerselier could have known (as Descartes himself says in other letters) that this Jesuit was Father Ciermans, from the University of Louvain, who died in 1648. He could have also known—as we saw on the first page of this study—that the Physician from Louvain who made objections to which Descartes responded (letters LXXVII–LXXX) was Professor Plemp (*Plempius*), from the same University.

Finally, in the Netherlands, there still lived Henry de Roy (*Regius*), a Professor at the University of Utrecht. He was a great friend of Descartes between 1638 and 1646, but later became his enemy. Clerselier had a copy of Regius's letters in his hands; however, he did not publish them in 1657, even though doing so would have greatly helped in understanding Descartes’s responses—or rather, fragments of responses—in which far too many gaps are found. In the form they were published, they displeased Regius, and one of his friends complained in a book that “*these responses from Descartes were things contrived and made to please*” <note>Meaning the friend accused Clerselier or Descartes of fabricating or doctoring the letters to favor Descartes’s arguments.</note>. To justify himself, Clerselier then thought of publishing the actual letters from Regius to which Descartes was responding in the second edition of 1663. “*But*,” he says (p. 8 of his *Preface to the Treatise on Man*, 1664), “*having written to Mr. de Roy, so as to do nothing except in cooperation with him, he would not allow it.*” The second edition therefore appeared without Regius’s letters, and once again with Descartes’s letters truncated and mutilated, as Clerselier had discreetly complained as early as 1657 at the end of one of them (LXXXIV in the first edition, LXXXVII in the second): “*The rest is missing. And if Mr. Regius wishes to act candidly and generously, he will supply it.*” <note>original Latin: “Deest reliquum. Et si candidè et generosè D. Regius velit agere, illud supplebit.”</note> This was both a direct appeal to Regius to share the originals of the letters Descartes had written to him, and an allusion to the motto, *candidly and generously* <note>original: “candidè et generosè”</note>, which Regius himself had placed on his portrait at the beginning—

of the *Foundations of Physics* <note>original: *Fundamenta Physices*</note> (1646). Certainly Clerselier could not have done better in this instance.
There remain some letters to Mersenne, numbered LXXIII and LXXIV, CXI and CXII, or to the Jesuits, CXIII-CXVI, and eight letters without name or date, CIII-CX, except for CVI, which was addressed to Mr. de Zuylichem <note>This refers to Constantin Huygens, a prominent Dutch diplomat and father of the scientist Christiaan Huygens</note>.
Doubtless, if Clerselier had asked him (Constantin Huygens, the father), or perhaps Mr. de Pollot, with whom he was moreover in correspondence, he would have obtained the name of the recipient as well as the date for several of them: letter CVII, for example (a letter of consolation "on the death of a brother"), is addressed to Alphonse de Pollot, whose brother Jean-Baptiste had died at The Hague on January 14, 1641, etc. If, therefore, thanks to Clerselier, Descartes's letters were saved from total destruction, he nevertheless did not fully fulfill his duty as an editor; or rather, he understood it in the fashion of the 17th century, being uniquely preoccupied with the subjects treated in this correspondence, and indifferent to accessory matters of time, person, or place.

### VOLUME II.

The second volume appeared in 1659 with this title: *Letters of Mr. DESCARTES in which several fine difficulties regarding his other Works are explained. Second volume: Paris, Charles Angot, Saint-Jacques Street, at the Sign of the City of Leiden (printing completed May 28, 1659)*. It was reprinted, without any changes, in 1666 (printing completed January 2). A remarkable peculiarity of this second volume is that one no longer finds any Latin in it: all the Latin letters, twenty-two in total, are translated into French <note>For this English edition, all such letters are rendered in English</note>. Readers had complained about those in the first volume; Clerselier therefore had the others translated by his young son as a form of exercise; he himself recounts this fact, partly in the *Preface* of this second volume (1659) and at length in the preface to the *Treatise on Man* (1664). The title was: **Letters of René DESCARTES, partly written by the author in the Latin language, partly translated from French, etc.** <note>original: *Renati DESCARTES Epistolæ, partim ab auctore latino sermone conscriptæ, partim ex gallico translatæ, etc.*</note> (2 volumes in quarto). However, a question arises regarding at least 22 letters in the second volume: is the Latin text provided by the Dutch edition the original, or merely a Latin version of what was already, in Clerselier's edition, only a French version? This is especially pressing since this Dutch edition provides all the letters in Latin without specifying which ones are merely translations and which are the originals.

Certain clues, however, allow this problem to be solved. Letter IX, to Plempius <note>Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius was a professor of medicine at Leuven who engaged in a famous debate with Descartes regarding the circulation of blood</note>, dated December 20, 1637, provides an entire sentence in the Latin text that is missing in the French version; where else would the editors have found this sentence if they did not have the original before their eyes? Furthermore, one finds several dates in the Dutch edition that are missing in Clerselier, and these are dates of Latin letters: for example, for letters LXXV and LXXVI of the first volume, June 10 and July 5, 1643; for the letter from Mersenne to Voët <note>Gisbertus Voetius, a Dutch theologian and a fierce opponent of Descartes</note>, which serves as a foreword to the second volume, *the Ides of December 1642* <note>original: *Idibus Decemb. 1642*; this refers to December 13</note>; for letter IV, *June 4, 1648* <note>original: *4 Iunij 1648*</note>; for letters VII and VIII, *the 5th nones of October 1637* <note>original: *5 nonas octobris 1637*; this refers to October 3</note>. Let us add that for these last two, a manuscript copy of the original was found in the Huygens collection at the Leiden University Library, and, with rare exceptions—which are more likely simple variations—the text of this copy is the same as the Latin text printed by Raei and Schooten. The latter therefore took the trouble to seek out Descartes's originals and publish them, at least for the Latin letters. Finally, in his first volume of 1657, Clerselier provided two Latin letters, LV and LVI, of which only a French version can be found in the second edition of 1663. Clerselier seems to have intended only to collect a certain number of objections along with Descartes's replies. Most of these objections (this being perhaps the only unity to be found there) came from the Netherlands, except for two letters from Arnauld, III and V, and two other letters sent from France: Letter XIII from Mr. Le Conte—to whom Abbé Picot and Clerselier had already replied—and Letter XV from that unknown individual who has been called the *hyperaspistès* <note>original: "hyperaspistès"; from the Greek for "shield-bearer" or "defender," referring to an anonymous critic who challenged Descartes's *Meditations*</note>.

Letters X, XI, and XII have this in common: they are all addressed to correspondents in Dordrecht: Mr. de Buitendijk, whom Clerselier names, and Isaac Beeckman, whom he does not name. Letter XVIII presents a mystery, but one with clues that will allow it to be solved (specifically, the title of a printed work and the date of February 1646).

The following four letters, XIX and XX, then XXI and XXII, relate to Descartes’s disputes with the University of Leiden; here again, Clerselier might have obtained the full dossier from the Professors if he had requested it. The two letters from Descartes, XXI and XXII, dated May 27, 1647, are not the only ones he wrote on this occasion; a very long initial letter from May 4, 1647, can be found in the *Registry of the Curators of the University of Leiden*, not to mention the philosopher's petition to the ambassador Abel Servien, which Baillet would later print in the *Life of Descartes* (Vol. II, p. 318), and not counting a note to Heereboord <note>Adrian Heereboord, a philosophy professor at Leiden who supported Descartes</note> from April 19, 1647, which is now in Paris at the Victor Cousin Library.

The two letters XXIII and XXIV, which conclude Series A, remain mysteries to this day.

The two series B and C, which we have since distinguished, offer a much more satisfactory order, especially if they are transposed, with series C (LXI–XCVIII) being placed before series B (XXV–LX). This results in an uninterrupted sequence of letters running from 1630 to 1639, then from 1639 to 1642. Most are addressed to Father Mersenne, and a few to others; however, these latter letters are always inserted chronologically between the former. Clerselier seems to have possessed two bundles of letters here, arranged in chronological order, which likely did not suffer from the shipwreck in the Seine nor from their time at the bottom of the water <note>In 1653, the chest containing Descartes’s papers fell into the river Seine near Paris during transport. The papers remained submerged for three days before being recovered and dried on lines like laundry.</note>. ->TO THE CORRESPONDENCE OF DESCARTES. XXXI<-

We see all that we owe to Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s friend and literary executor who edited the first collection of his letters.</note> for the 41 letters of this series (letters LXXV, LXXX, and LXXXI counting as two). Without him—that is to say, without the <term>drafts<note>original: "minutes," referring to the file copies or rough notes Descartes kept for himself before sending the final versions.</note></term> that he published—we would have only 7 letters to Mersenne (LXVI, LXXV, LXXVII, XCI, XCII, XCVI, and XCVII), and 4 letters (LXX, LXXXI, LXXXII, and LXXXVI) to Golius, Renery, Huygens, and Pollot <note>These men were prominent intellectuals: Jacob Golius was a mathematician and orientalist; Henri Renery was a philosopher and Descartes's first follower; Constantijn Huygens was a diplomat and scientist; and Alphonse Pollot was a soldier and courtier.</note>. In addition, we have 18 drafts of letters to Mersenne and 12 drafts of letters to various others, totaling 30 items.

And the old edition <note>Referring to Clerselier’s original 17th-century edition of the letters.</note> gives us here not only letters that we otherwise would not have, but also the order in which these letters follow one another chronologically. Let us take, for example, the dates we know today from the <term>autographs<note>The original documents written in the author's own hand.</note></term> as reference points: February 2, 1632; July 22, 1633; and August 14, 1634 (letters LXX, LXXV, and LXXVII). If we assume that the letters placed between them were indeed written during the intervals of those dates, the assumption is proven correct in a marvelous way. For example, letter LXXV comprises two drafts: one from July 22, 1633, as the original attests, and the other from the end of November, as we learn from a subsequent letter. This second draft is very precious, for the original was lost in transit (Descartes always believed it had been stolen); it is precisely the letter where, alarmed by the condemnation of Galileo <note>In 1633, the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo Galilei for advocating the heliocentric view that the Earth moves around the Sun. Descartes, who held similar views, famously suppressed his own scientific treatise, "The World," out of caution.</note>—which he had only just learned of—he declares that for a long time he will publish nothing. As for letter LXX, of which we have the autograph addressed to Golius from February 2, 1632, it is also very precious when compared to the 68th letter (which can be dated with certainty to October–November 1631, as it announces Renery’s departure for Deventer, where he had been appointed professor on October 4, 1631, and where he began his teaching on November 28). These two letters, in effect, simultaneously provide the approximate dates for several others that precede or follow them, as Descartes had hurried to join his friend in Deventer, where he remained until December 1633.

<page-num>XXXII</page-num>

# INTRODUCTION

Letters LXXVIII–XCVIII <note>Letters 78 to 98.</note> form a series that is even easier to reconstruct, thanks to the fixed dates of six of them: October 5, 1637; February 12, July 13, and November 15, 1638; and January 9 and February 9, 1639. A simple reading of the others suggests that they were indeed printed in chronological order. One can therefore, without too much risk, leave Letter XC <note>Letter 90.</note> in its place, for example, between LXXXIX and XCI (July 13 and October 11, 1638), and likewise Letter XCIII between XCII and XCIV (November 15 and December 1638). However, one cannot rely absolutely on the order followed by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes’s friend and the first editor of his letters.</note> for this series, known as Series C: if Descartes's papers had been perfectly in order, Letter LXVII should have immediately followed LXXII; furthermore, under each of the two numbers LXXX and LXXXI, Clerselier combined two letters of different dates, neither of which is in its proper place.

But if we now return to Series B (XXV–LX), we will see that the chronological order is followed more faithfully there. It follows immediately after the series we have just examined, with the last letter of Series C being dated February 20, 1639, and the first of Series B being dated April 30, 1639. Out of these 36 letters (or rather 35, as XXVIII and XXIX count as only one), 27 are addressed to <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a Minim friar who served as the central hub for scientific and philosophical correspondence in Europe.</note> Mersenne. Of these 27, we have the original handwritten copies of 14, which have fixed dates; Clerselier therefore provides us with an additional 13 <term>drafts<note>original: "minutes"; these were the preliminary versions or file copies Descartes kept for his own records.</note></term> whose originals have disappeared. By the very position they occupy, he also gives us the approximate date for each of them; for he undoubtedly placed them in the volume as he found them in Descartes’s bundles, and the drafts appear to have been arranged here one after another as the letters were being sent out, judging by the alignment of the two series of drafts XXXIX to XLIV and numbers 30 to 37. Consequently, Letter XXXI, for example, being printed between two letters to Mersenne with fixed dates (27 August and 16 October 1639), one is authorized, it seems, to give it an intermediate date of September–October 1639. Here is another draft, Letter XXXIII to Mersenne, found between two letters dated 16 October and 25 December 1639 (numbers 26 and 27 in the La Hire inventory): there is indeed room between these two dates for another letter, likely written in November; the original must have been lost, and we should be grateful that Clerselier [preserved it for] us.

### ON DESCARTES'S CORRESPONDENCE.

The confusion is all the greater because on several occasions—up to eight times (CIII, CV, CVIII, CIX, CX, CXII, CXV, and CXVI)—two letters are found sewn together, as has been confirmed, for most of them, by comparing them with the originals.

To now unravel this chaos, let us first make two divisions: those of <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a monk and a central figure in the European "Republic of Letters," acting as a primary correspondent for Descartes and other great thinkers.</note> Mersenne and those of the other correspondents.

The letters to Mersenne are categorized fairly well into two small series, which are, moreover, entangled with one another; the first from 1629 to 1636, the second from 1642 to 1643. This second series is established without difficulty using the numbers from <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718) was a mathematician who produced an inventory of Descartes's papers after the philosopher's death.</note> La Hire.

This is the assessment of this second volume, so precious to us because of the two series, C and B, in the middle (61–98 and 25–60), which together form a whole—not complete, certainly, but nonetheless compact and solid, with parts that follow one another logically and hold together. Series A, although less well-ordered, still consists of parts whose destination and date can be determined. Finally, although Series D is the most flawed of the four, initially offering only confusion and obscurity, we have seen that it was not entirely impossible to find one's way through it.

### VOLUME III.

The third volume appeared late, in 1667, ten years after the first. It consists, for the most part, of scientific questions: <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s friend and the dedicated editor who spent decades publishing his remains.</note> Clerselier informs the reader of this with this explicit title: *LETTERS OF M<gloss>r</gloss> DESCARTES, where he responds to several difficulties proposed to him regarding Optics, Geometry, & several other subjects.*

The *Preface* to this third volume (written in 1666, since the <term>printing completion notice</term> <note>original: "l'achevé d'imprimer"; a legal statement at the end of a book indicating when printing was finished.</note> is dated September 7, 1666) should be compared with the one that Clerselier had already placed two years earlier at the beginning of the *Treatise on Man*, 1664. Both are clearly apologetic <note>In this context, "apologetic" means a formal defense of a person's opinions or conduct.</note> in nature. Descartes's philosophy, if not the man himself, was under attack: Clerselier defends them. In 1664, he protests against the reproach of irreligion and publishes the

But in 1666, Rome placed Descartes’s books on the Index <note>The *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, the list of books forbidden by the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, and the Jesuits had not been strangers to this condemnation; already, on September 7, 1662, Cartesian theses had been censured by the Faculty of Theology at Louvain at the instigation of the Jesuits. Clerselier therefore thought that he should no longer keep the letters exchanged between the philosopher and the <term>Reverend Fathers</term> <note>original: "RR. PP." (Révérends Pères), the standard honorific for members of the Society of Jesus.</note> private; to inform the public of the facts, he printed the dispute between Descartes and Father Bourdin, which is purely scientific. He judged it a clever move to show that, during Descartes’s lifetime, it was not the entire Society of Jesus that had declared against him, but only one Father, and regarding his *Dioptrics*, not his Philosophy; furthermore, this little quarrel had ended quickly enough with the reconciliation of the two adversaries and could be seen as a simple misunderstanding.

This dispute was of the same nature as the one sparked by <note>Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665), the famous French mathematician.</note> Fermat in 1637–1638, which was taken up again after Descartes’s death by Fermat himself, <note>Marin Cureau de la Chambre (1594–1669), a royal physician and scholar of optics.</note> Cureau de la Chambre, and Clerselier himself from 1657 to 1662. In his first two volumes, Clerselier had avoided publishing anything relating to another quarrel between Descartes and <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a mathematician known for his rivalry with Descartes over discovery priority.</note> Roberval: he always hoped that the latter would finally agree to share the original letters from Descartes to <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the Minim friar who served as the primary coordinator for the European scientific community.</note> Mersenne, which he had seized upon the death of the good friar in September 1648. But Roberval stubbornly refused, and Clerselier was forced to settle—for this part of the correspondence as for all the rest—for simply publishing the <term>minutes</term> <note>Drafts or archival copies kept by the sender before mailing the final letter.</note>. At the very least, he wished to clear himself of his responsibility as an editor and denounced Roberval’s entire conduct in this matter to the public. Then, as Roberval continued

He did so by printing, alongside the letters of the two adversaries, a letter of his own dated July 13, 1658, which he believed would settle the debate.

The third volume is therefore divided into several series:

I-XXVIII. *Disputes with the Jesuits.* — XXIX-XXXV. *Disputes with Hobbes.* — XXXVI-LXXIV. *Disputes with Fermat, Roberval, etc.* — LXXV-LXXXIV. *Letters to Carcavi, to Elizabeth, to Schooten, etc.* — LXXXV-XCVII. *New disputes with Roberval.* — XCVIII-CXXV. *Miscellaneous letters.*

The first series, I-XXVIII, begins with Descartes’s long apologetic letter to the <term>City Council of Utrecht</term> <note>original: "Corps de Ville d'Utrecht." <page-num>XXXIX</page-num>
<header>TO THE CORRESPONDENCE OF DESCARTES.</header>

Could Clerselier have done better than to print the drafts of these letters? Today we possess the original of one of them, dated July 29, 1640, and it is much more complete than the draft; it was rediscovered by chance in a book that came from the college of Louis-le-Grand—formerly the college of Clermont—where Father Bourdin had been a professor. But would Clerselier have been granted access to it? He, who cites Saint Augustine so willingly, just as Arnauld <note>Antoine Arnauld (1612–1694), a leading Jansenist theologian and philosopher who provided the "Fourth Objections" to Descartes's *Meditations*.</note> himself did, did he not appear perhaps a bit too much of a Jansenist <note>A follower of Jansenism, a Catholic theological movement emphasizing original sin and divine grace, which was often in fierce conflict with the Jesuits.</note> to be on very good terms with the Fathers of the Society of Jesus? He treats them with care, nonetheless: he softens the philosopher’s bitter words toward them; he takes care to always print *the Reverend Jesuit Fathers*, or at least *the Jesuit Fathers*, whereas in Descartes’s own autographs one finds simply *the Jesuits*.

As for the series XVII–XXV, Father Bourdin, having reconciled with the philosopher, took it upon himself to deliver several copies of the *Principles* <note>Descartes's *Principles of Philosophy* (*Principia Philosophiae*), published in 1644.</note> to their intended recipients. Descartes sent him, along with letter XXI for himself, letters XIX and XX for Fathers Charlet and Dinet. Then, these two Fathers having thanked their former pupil, Descartes wrote to them again (letters XXII and XXIII), still through the mediation of Father Bourdin (letter XXIV). — Regarding the first two letters, XVII and XVIII, one is addressed to an unknown Jesuit, the other likely to Father Vatier. Finally, the last, letter XXV, is to Father Mesland. This one should not stand alone: for Descartes had written at least two other letters to the same Father, and copies of them were circulating almost everywhere (several are found in the libraries of Paris and the provinces). But in these, the philosopher explained in his own way the transubstantiation <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> in the sacrament of the Eucharist, and Clerselier, overcome by scruples, had consulted the Archbishop of Paris on the matter, who dissuaded him from publishing them; forty years later, in 1701, Bossuet <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a powerful French bishop and theologian known for his orthodoxy.</note> still opposed their publication, and the two letters did not appear until 1811 through the efforts of a less timid priest, the Abbé Emery.

We do not have the originals for letters 56, 58, 60, 62, and 66. However, we have, in addition, three originals (numbers 63, 64, and 65) from La Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a mathematician and astronomer whose family held important scientific manuscripts.</note>, for which Clerselier did not possess the <term>minutes</term> <note>Drafts or rough copies kept by the sender for their own records.</note>: these are letters to Mersenne, dated September 7, October 5, and October 12; the same applies to three other numbers (67, 68, and 71), from November 2 and 23, 1646, and April 26, 1647. On the other hand, Clerselier provides us with several drafts whose originals were already missing in his time: these are letters LXXXVII, LXXXIX, XCI, and XCII. Thus, on four occasions, the series of drafts completes the series of originals; and six times, the text of the originals completes the series of drafts.

The 28 remaining letters (XCVIII-CXXV inclusive) are in an almost inextricable disorder, with the exception of the first five (XCVIII-CII) between Descartes and Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier, a skilled craftsman and lens-cutter whom Descartes hoped would help him create hyperbolic lenses.</note>, four of which are dated (June 18, October 8 and 26, November 13, 1629), while the last (CII) is from a much later date. But from the 103rd to the 125th (the latter, from Clerselier to La Forge <note>Louis de La Forge (1632–1666), a physician and philosopher who was one of the foremost proponents of Descartes’s occasionalism.</note> on December 4, 1660, does not actually belong to Descartes's correspondence), it is very difficult to find one's way. Let us first set aside a letter to Abbé Picot <note>Claude Picot (d. 1668), a close friend of Descartes who acted as his financial manager in France.</note> (CXV) from February 17, 1645, a letter from Schooten (CXVI) dated March 10, 1649, and Descartes's reply (CXVII) from April 9; we are still left with 19 letters, 8 of which are addressed to Mersenne (or rather 7, as numbers CXXI and CXXII represent only one, providing both the English translation of the original Latin text <note>original: "texte latin"</note> and the French version), and the other 11 to various correspondents.

Of the seven letters to Mersenne, we have four <term>autographs</term> <note>Manuscripts written in the author's own hand.</note>: CIX, CXIII, CXIV (March 18 and November 17, 1641, January 19, 1642), and CXVIII, which is undated (though it appears to be from 1648). There remain the drafts for CV (from the year 1642), CXXI and CXXII (objections, in both English translations of the original Latin and French <note>original: "en latin et en français"</note>, sent to Mersenne for Descartes on May 19, 1641), and CXXIII (Descartes’s response).

We are reasonably certain of the dates for letters CVI and CXXIV (April 8, 1642, and April 1648), although we do not know for sure to whom they are addressed; doubt remains for CIII, which appears to comprise two different letters.

Regarding the two letters CIV and CX (perhaps to Huygens), the enigma has not yet been resolved (the latter appears to be from January or February 1648).

Such is the old edition by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes’s literary executor, who played a crucial role in preserving his work but was often criticized for his editorial liberties.</note>, so precious in many respects, despite its shortcomings, which are, moreover, quite excusable. First, Clerselier desired—for the honor of Descartes and the glory of his philosophy—that these three volumes of letters be read, and he composed them accordingly: forgetting no category of readers, he first published a first volume for the use of society people <note>original: "personnes du monde," referring to the educated general public or high-society laypeople rather than specialized scholars.</note>, the only one that soon required a second edition; then a second volume for those curious about physics and metaphysics; and finally, the third for scholars and particularly for mathematicians. Furthermore, he limited himself to publishing what he possessed from Descartes's papers; restricting his task to that—laborious enough as it was—he did not concern himself with gathering what was scattered across Holland, perhaps Sweden, or England,

And in this, he could believe himself faithful enough to the philosopher’s thought: for after all, only what Descartes had judged worthy of being preserved was found in his papers, and all the rest, which was missing—whether letters received or letters sent—doubtless held no great importance in his eyes. If, moreover, the letters that Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes' friend and the primary editor of his posthumous works and correspondence.</note> published are themselves too sparse in indications regarding the events of the day or details about people, these <term>trifles</term> <note>original: "vétilles." Minor details or trivialities that 17th-century editors often omitted to focus on pure philosophy.</note> probably did not appear in the <term>minutes</term> <note>Drafts or preliminary copies kept by the author for his own records; see previous page.</note>: was it not enough to write them once in the letter actually sent? Furthermore, these deficiencies—to which our modern historical curiosity is all too sensitive—passed unnoticed in the 17th century, when people were primarily curious about a philosopher's ideas. Proof of this is that later, when Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), whose massive 1691 biography "La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes" remains a primary source for the philosopher's life.</note> would provide a voluminous history of Descartes, without sparing readers many small facts told with an abundance that would no longer be complained of today, there were critics in 1691 who reproached him for lingering and dwelling on uninteresting matters, and for having thus needlessly overburdened his thick book. But this meticulous concern for reality, which characterizes Baillet, is a sure guarantee for us that the new edition of the *Works of Descartes*, which his collaborator Jean-Baptiste Legrand <note>An Abbé who worked closely with Baillet and inherited the task of preparing a definitive edition of Descartes' works, though he died before its completion.</note> was preparing, would have better met the requirements not of his time, but of ours, as will be seen by examining what has survived of it.

The shortcomings of the Clerselier edition became apparent upon the death of Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a prominent mathematician and member of the Academy of Sciences who was often a bitter rival of Descartes.</note> in 1675. Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the Minim friar who acted as the central "mailbox" for the European scientific community; his cell in Paris was a hub for intellectual exchange.</note>, before his death (September 1, 1648), had entrusted him with the task of printing his *Treatises on Dioptrics and Catoptrics* <note>The study of the refraction and reflection of light, respectively.</note>; Roberval was thus able, as executor of the estate, to enter the monk’s cell. He took advantage of this to seize the letters from Descartes to Mersenne and consistently refused to share them. But "after his death" (Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes’ primary biographer.</note> tells us on page xxxiii of his Preface in 1691):
> "the packet of Mr. Descartes’ letters was found, by a stroke of good fortune,
> "in the hands of Mr. de La Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a renowned astronomer and mathematician.</note>, Royal Professor of
> "Mathematics, who felt it his duty to present them as a gift to the
> "Academy of Sciences."

La Hire’s initial thought, which was approved by the entire Academy, was to publish these letters separately; he possessed about thirty unpublished ones, and for many others, the original manuscripts would have provided a more complete text than that of the <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "minutes." These are the rough drafts or copies Descartes kept for himself, which Clerselier often used as his primary source when the final sent letters were unavailable.</note>. However, the plan for a partial publication was soon abandoned in favor of a much broader one: a new edition of the philosopher’s complete works.

After the three volumes of *Letters* (1657–1667), plus another volume, *Man by René Descartes and the Formation of the Fetus*, published first in 1664 and then a second time alongside *The World, or Treatise on Light* in 1677, there still remained enough material to produce another volume. This had been announced in the 1664 preface but was awaited in vain. Before his death, Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes' friend and the first major editor of his works.</note> wished to ensure the publication of this volume and entrusted the task to Abbé Jean-Baptiste Legrand, to whom he even bequeathed a sum of 500 livres <note>The *livre* was the currency of France until 1795; this bequest was intended to cover printing costs.</note> for the expenses. Legrand, instead of restricting himself to this final volume alone, conceived a project for a complete edition and set to work without delay: one finds the date 1684, written in his hand, in the margin of one of the letters shared by La Hire <note>Reference to the French National Library, new acquisitions, fr. n. a., 5160, folio 23.</note>. Legrand had also inherited Clerselier's numerous memoirs concerning Descartes, and it even appears he had begun to write a life of the philosopher; however, likely to devote himself entirely to his edition, he handed this part of his task over to Abbé Adrien Baillet, providing him with all his papers.

Baillet, who provides most of these details in his *Preface*, also informs us how he and Legrand understood their duties as biographer and editor: it was in a completely different, and far more satisfactory, manner than Clerselier. What the latter had neglected to do for various reasons, Baillet and Legrand did immediately, sparing no effort. Baillet wrote to Descartes' relatives in Brittany: his two brothers were dead, M. de Kerleau around 1660 and M. de Chavagne in 1680; but their eldest sons—both Councilors at the Parlement of Rennes <note>The sovereign court of justice for the province of Brittany, where the Descartes family held significant social standing.</note> and nephews of the philosopher—as well as his niece, Catherine Descartes <note>A poet and intellectual in her own right, known as "the third Grace" or "the tenth Muse."</note>, sent the most obliging responses. We likely owe to them the few fragments of family letters found here and there in Baillet’s work. Almost all of Descartes’ friends had also passed away: Baillet therefore reached out to their sons, and he provides a long list of them: M. l’abbé Chanut, son of the ambassador; M. Clerselier des Noyers, son of the editor of the *Letters*; M. le Vasseur,

A Counselor at the Grand Chamber <note>The primary judicial chamber of the Parlement of Paris.</note>, son of the Lord of Étioles—who was the relative, friend, and host of Descartes before his retirement to Holland—Abbé Mydorge, Canon of the Holy Sepulchre in Paris, also the son of a friend, and Mr. Hardy, Counselor at the Parlement, whose family included no fewer than three friends of the philosopher: his father, a former Master of Accounts <note>A high-ranking official in the chamber overseeing royal finances.</note>, a cousin of his father, Mr. Hardy, Counselor at the Châtelet <note>The seat of civil and criminal jurisdiction in Paris.</note>, and Abbé Picot, his maternal uncle, etc. — Baillet also gathered the testimony of Messrs. » Sir, that all the manuscripts of Mr. Descartes which have
» not yet been printed are in my possession, *besides*
» 120 letters that I have collected from various individuals.”

Legrand’s edition, had he finished it, would therefore have been much more complete than that of Clerselier. ...restored, which reconstruct the beginning, middle, or end of certain letters; and when it is only a matter of a few lines, these are found on strips of paper pasted in the appropriate places. The author, or rather the authors of these additions and corrections (for several hands can be distinguished, including Legrand’s for certain), carefully noted all the dates they found; they added, as much as possible, all the missing passages, whether it was a single sentence or even just a word. Chronological order would thus have been followed, and the authentic text scrupulously restored. This work, likely begun as early as 1684, or perhaps even earlier, lasted a long time; for the new edition was not yet ready when Legrand died in 1704. However, he entrusted the care of finishing his work to a Professor of Philosophy at the Collège des Grassins <note>A college within the University of Paris, known for its academic rigor.</note> named Marmion, leaving him the 500 livres from Clerselier <note>A sum of money left by Descartes' first editor, Claude Clerselier, to fund the publication of the philosopher's remaining papers.</note> for that purpose. Marmion died at the beginning of January 1705, and on his behalf, the sum of money, as well as the books and papers intended for the edition, were returned to Legrand’s mother. This entire history is recounted in the *News of the Republic of Letters* <note>original: *Nouvelles de la République des Lettres*, a major scholarly journal of the 17th and 18th centuries used to share intellectual developments across Europe.</note> in the month of June 1705. It is unknown what became of Legrand’s papers since then, specifically two notebooks that the Institute’s copy <note>Refers to a specific copy of Descartes' works held by the Institut de France.</note> identifies as: "the big notebook" and "the new notebook," referring to them to justify the dates.

Two documents remain, however, from this work on which three or four scholars collaborated. These are, first, the two volumes of the *Life of Descartes* published by Baillet in 1691, featuring so many original documents published on almost every page; and second, the copy of the three volumes of *Letters* which Legrand enriched with notes on almost every page, making use of the La Hire collection <note>The papers of Philippe de La Hire, a prominent mathematician and astronomer.</note>, and likely with the help of Baillet and Marmion as well. Let us examine these two documents.

Baillet tells us that Legrand had recovered the *manuscript letters of Regius* <note>Henricus Regius, a Dutch physician who was an early supporter, then later a rival, of Descartes.</note>. These letters were shared with him for the *Life of Descartes*: they are cited many times, with their

<page-num>L</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

...precise dates, and quite a few fragments of them have been translated into French. Thanks to these indicators, one can therefore reconstruct the chronological list of Regius's <note>Henricus Regius, or Hendrik de Roy, was a Dutch professor who was initially a staunch supporter of Descartes before a famous intellectual falling-out between the two.</note> letters (it includes 37 entries), which allows us to date Descartes' replies approximately; furthermore, we can restore the general meaning of this correspondence, which allows for a better understanding of these same replies.

Legrand also had in his hands *the letters to Abbot Picot* <note>Claude Picot, a close friend and financial manager for Descartes who also translated some of his works into French.</note>. Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, author of a massive 1691 biography of Descartes; his work is essential because he had access to many documents that are now lost.</note> cites them, in fact, giving the date in the margin and sometimes a fragment of the text. By gathering these new indicators, we can reconstruct—not, certainly, the entire correspondence with Picot, nor even a small part—but at least the chronological list (it counts 39 entries), which is so useful for classifying Descartes' letters, many passages of which are also explained by Baillet's excerpts.

Legrand had *some of the letters from Princess Elisabeth* <note>Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate, one of Descartes' most brilliant correspondents, whose questioning prompted him to write "The Passions of the Soul."</note>. We have better today: the publication by Foucher de Careil in 1879 gives us almost all of Elisabeth’s correspondence with Descartes. But one thing we would not have without Legrand is the list of letters from *Chanut* <note>Pierre Chanut, the French ambassador to Sweden and a key figure in inviting Descartes to the court of Queen Christina.</note> to Descartes, and the full text of some, which Baillet fortunately inserted into his large work. The same goes for several letters or fragments of letters to Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier, Descartes' first editor and brother-in-law to Chanut.</note>, and to "Mr. Tobias André" <note>original: "au sieur Tobie d'André"</note>, Professor at the University of Groningen. All this is no doubt incomplete, and Baillet often gives only a translation, which we cannot verify for lack of the Latin text; we are, however, forced to make do with it. Furthermore, Baillet has transmitted to us here and there documents of the first order, such as Descartes' petition to Servien <note>Abel Servien, a high-ranking French diplomat and negotiator of the Peace of Westphalia.</note>, the French ambassador in Holland, in May 1647, asking him to intervene on his behalf with the University of Leiden <note>original: "Leyde"</note>. Not all is lost, then, of Legrand’s enormous labor; and in the absence of the complete edition he was unable to give us, good materials remain, which will not be the least solid part of the new edition.

# TO THE CORRESPONDENCE OF DESCARTES.

<page-num>LI</page-num>

As for the copy of the *Letters of Descartes*, enriched with the notes of Legrand, Baillet, and undoubtedly Marmion <note>Jean-Baptiste Marmion, a priest who collaborated with Jean-Baptiste Legrand on the preparation of Descartes’ papers.</note>, it first belonged to Montempuis, Rector of the University of Paris (October 10, 1715 — October 10, 1717), whose books, bequeathed to the Library of that University, constituted its original core collection: the three volumes still bear the black stamp of "Montempuis, University of Paris." From there, they passed to the Library of the Institute <note>The Institut de France, the umbrella organization for France's national academies.</note> at the time of its founding; they also bear its red stamp, which dates from the First Republic <note>The period of French history from 1792 to 1804.</note>, and it is in this Library that they can still be consulted today.

Now, the Institute's copy teaches us that Mr. de La Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a prominent French mathematician and astronomer.</note> had organized a classification of the letters from Descartes to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a friar and mathematician who served as the central node of the 17th-century "Republic of Letters," facilitating communication between Descartes and other thinkers.</note>. Baillet recalled only this in his *Preface*, pages xxxiv-xxxv:
> "*the particular kindnesses of Mr. de La Hire, who had the*"
> "*patience*," he says, "*to be willing to read these letters with us, to*"
> "*point out to us their differences from those which are*"
> "*printed, and to share with us those which had not*"
> "*yet seen the light of day.*" <note>meaning: those that were previously unpublished.</note>
And in his work, he frequently cites the letters from Descartes to Mersenne, with their dates, without further indication. But in the Institute's copy, one finds, in addition to the same dates written by hand, numbers for most of them, and the indication is uniformly this: "*see the 21st (or the 35th, or the 50th, etc.) of Mr. de La Hire.*" The latter had therefore not only classified the letters to Mersenne according to chronological order, but he had also numbered them. And the numbering is even double: the first time, it begins with the most recent letters and moves backward against the chronological order; the second time, it follows that order, and goes downward, as is appropriate, starting from the oldest letter. The fairly numerous autographs that remain of this collection bear, at the bottom of the first page on the left, a number which is often that of the reverse classification. Thus, letter XV of volume III, page 100, Clerselier edition <note>Claude Clerselier was the first major editor of Descartes' correspondence (1657–1667).</note>, is indicated in the Institute's copy as

# INTRODUCTION

“the 82nd ms. letter of *Mr. de La Hire*,” and the autograph <note>A manuscript document written in the author's own hand.</note> of this same letter, which is also now held at the Library of the Institute <note>The library of the Institut de France in Paris.</note>, bears the number 2 in the indicated place. But often the Institute's copy gives both numbers at once in the following manner: the first was written initially, then crossed out, and the second was rewritten above it. Thus in vol. II, p. 209, we find: “*see the 72 of Mr. de la Hire*”; but the 7 was originally a 1, which was easily changed into a 7 with a single stroke; and this original number, 12, is indeed the one still read at the bottom of the ms. <note>Abbreviation for manuscript.</note> copy at the National Library (*fr., n. a., 5160, f. 65*) <note>Original: "français, nouvelles acquisitions" (French collection, new acquisitions), volume 5160, folio 65.</note>. Elsewhere, in vol. III, p. 157, the number 46—that is, the original number—was crossed out, and the number 38 rewritten above it; now, we find this number 46 on the autograph at the National Library (*f. 23*). In vol. III, p. 609, the number 39 was crossed out, and 45 rewritten in its place; the autograph of January 19, 1642, preserved at the Victor Cousin Library <note>A specialized philosophy library in Paris, originally based on the collection of the 19th-century thinker Victor Cousin.</note>, indeed gives 39 c., etc. The existence of these two lists, running in reverse order to one another, allows us to fix the total count of the numbers: as the two numbers for each letter always, when added together, give the total 84, it follows that the collection comprised 83 pieces <note>This is a mathematical proof of the collection size: if the $n$th item in a forward list is the $m$th item in a backward list, then $n + m = \text{Total} + 1$. Here $84 - 1 = 83$.</note>.

If one now draws up two lists of 83 numbers in parallel, running in opposite directions to each other, the two numbers that correspond are precisely those found written together—but with one of the two crossed out—on the copy at the Institute. This fact can be verified about thirty times, either on the copy alone when it provides the double numbering, or by comparing it with the autographs that we still possess. However, the backward numbering does not seem to have been followed from one end of the series to the other: it is found only for approximately the second half, more exactly starting from number 48 (the original figure) replaced by 36 following the natural order. Let us finally add that on the autographs, but not in the printed copy, the original figure—that of the backward classification—is usually followed by the letter *c*: for example,

48 c (*Victor Cousin Library, no. 17*), 46 c (*National Library, French collection, new acquisitions, 5160, folio 23*), 35 c (*Library of the Institute, 1st folder, 3rd letter*). It seems, therefore, that this rather strange reverse numbering was stopped halfway through, and for the remaining first half, the natural order was resumed. Thus, in the Institute's copy, up to number 36, one finds only a single number—the correct one—rather than two numbers with one crossed out. Furthermore, in the notebook of autographs <note>Documents written in the author's own hand.</note> and manuscript copies now returned to our National Library, if one arranges the various pieces according to chronological order, one first finds a series of letters bearing the numbers 2, 13, 15, 16, 19, 18 on the bottom left of the first page (*folios 43, 2, 4, 10, 15, 21*); these belong to the natural classification. Then, there is another series with the numbers 46, 41, 1, 31, 27, 21, 19, 17, 16, 13 (*folios 23, 27, 49, 29, 31, 37, 39, 40, 42, 44*), which belong to the reverse numbering system. The same numbers—13, 16, and 19—are found in both series, but they do not have the same meaning: in the second series, they must correspond to numbers 71, 68, and 65 of the natural classification. These details will be confirmed and completed by yet another document.

The work of Legrand <note>Albert Legrand, a priest who attempted to organize Descartes' papers in the late 17th century.</note> was used by no one during the 18th century. In 1724–1725, when Descartes’ correspondence was reprinted, the publishers were content to simply redistribute the three quarto <note>A large book size where the printing sheet is folded twice to form four leaves.</note> volumes of Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), Descartes' friend and first editor, who published the letters after the philosopher's death.</note> into six duodecimo <note>A smaller, more portable book size where the sheet is folded into twelve leaves.</note> volumes. However, the letters were published in the same order, and they did not even always include the few dates provided by the first editor. For the only changes, they added the French version of the Latin letters that had not previously been translated, as well as the Latin text for those where only the translation had been printed. But they did not take the trouble to consult the original autographs deposited by La Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), an astronomer who preserved many of Descartes' manuscripts.</note> at the Academy of Sciences. Still less did anyone think to take advantage of the notes written in the precious copy of the *Letters*, the very existence of which was perhaps not even suspected.

another list of the same letters from La Hire <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a French mathematician and astronomer who previously held these documents.</note> was drawn up, which, instead of 83 items, only includes 77. This time, the manuscript letters were divided into as many bundles as there were years, except for the undated letters and a few rejected pieces put into two bundles at the end. Who was responsible for this new classification? The National Library (*French Manuscript 20843, folios 122 and 123*) holds a draft <note>French: *minute*.</note> that provides the list in its entirety, and the draft is written in the hand of Dom Poirier. Mr. Léopold Delisle published it on pages 169–172 of the *Catalogue of the Libri and Barrois Collections* (Paris, 1888) <note>Original title: *Catalogue des fonds Libri et Barrois*.</note>. On the other hand, the National Library also (*French Ms., new acquisitions, 3280, folios 92–94*) holds a fragment of the same list, for the years 1638 and 1639 only, ranging from number 6 to number 21 inclusive. This fragment provides a cross-reference <note>French: *concordance*.</note> with La Hire’s numbers as well as with the letters published by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the primary editor of Descartes' posthumous works.</note>; this piece is in Arbogast’s hand. Mr. Paul Tannery, who pointed out this document (*Descartes' Correspondence in the Unpublished Works of the Libri Collection, Studied for the History of Mathematics*, Paris, Gauthier-Villars, 1893, p. 6) <note>Original title: *La Correspondance de Descartes dans les inédits du fonds Libri, étudiée pour l'histoire des mathématiques*.</note>, believes that the numbers in this second list, which appear on a good number of original manuscripts <note>French: *autographes*.</note>, are also in Arbogast's hand. This final reason might be decisive in attributing the second classification to Arbogast: it was he who held the originals in his hands, since he wrote a new number at the top right of the first page, always in parentheses, while the old number—the one from La Hire—is found at the bottom left, without parentheses. Furthermore, the new list, whether it is by Poirier or Arbogast, dates from the same period: Dom Poirier, a Benedictine of the Saint-Maur congregation, died on February 2, 1803, after having been the guardian of the Archives of the Abbey of Saint-Denis, then of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, whose library he reconstructed, as best he could, after it was destroyed by fire in August 1794; and the mathematician Arbogast died on April 8, 1803, after having been a member of the National Convention <note>The National Convention was the assembly that governed France during the most critical period of the French Revolution.</note> (it was likely during this time that he concerned himself with the manuscripts kept in the Archives of the Academy of Sciences). ### III.

## THE VICTOR COUSIN EDITION.

->(1824-1826.)<-

Between 1824 and 1826, a new edition of the *Works of Descartes* by Victor Cousin appeared in 11 octavo <term>octavo <note>A book size where each sheet of paper is folded into eight leaves, resulting in a medium-sized volume.</note></term> volumes (Paris, F.-G. Levrault). The correspondence is distributed across 5 volumes: VI, VII, VIII, IX, and X. Later, at the end of his life, Cousin judged his own work harshly: “*It is not worthy of Descartes*,” he wrote in 1866; “*I was too young when I undertook it.*” He was between thirty-two and thirty-four years old, and above all, he was occupied with other projects: a French translation of the *Works of Plato*, an edition of the *Works of Proclus*, etc. Furthermore, it was less a work of scholarly erudition than one of propaganda. He wanted, above all, to put Descartes into the hands of students and thinkers as quickly as possible to revive the philosophical spirit in France; and indeed, for three-quarters of a century, it was through the Cousin edition that Descartes was known in France and abroad; it is the Cousin edition that is cited by all works of philosophers and scholars. Finally, for its time (1824–1826), it could pass for a scholarly edition; with the notes Cousin added—thanks to the copy held at the Institute <note>The Institut de France, which held a crucial annotated copy of Descartes' letters.</note>—it appeared far superior, as indeed it is, to anything seen until then.

Victor Cousin therefore made use of the Institute's copy for the *Letters of Descartes* (which was the great innovation of his edition); however, he used it tentatively, as a document of which he was not certain, not knowing its provenance. We have seen that the text was improved and completed by annotations written in the margin, or on small strips of paper, sometimes even on entire sheets in- <note>The text likely continues "in-folio" or "in-quarto" on the following page, referring to the size of the paper inserts.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the 1824–1826 edition of Descartes' works by Victor Cousin, noting its historical importance as the standard reference for decades despite Cousin's own later self-criticism regarding its scholarly depth.</summary>
