serted into the volumes. Cousin reproduces these annotations, but at the bottom of the pages, in *italics*, and does not dare to incorporate them into the text; so much so that what originated from Descartes’ own originals finds itself relegated to the notes, as an accessory, while the incomplete drafts <term>drafts <note>The French "minutes" refers to the initial, often messy, versions of letters kept by the sender.</note></term> continue to hold a prominent place, occupying the major part of each page. Furthermore, he does not reproduce all of the annotations: as he sees them only as variants whose origin is unknown to him, he makes a choice among them—a choice that is necessarily arbitrary; at least he loyally warns the reader of this.

As for the actual order of the correspondence, Cousin proposes to re-establish the chronology, and he does indeed arrange the letters year by year. But there again, he does not dare to follow the indications of the Institute copy to the very end. For example, letter 103 <note>original: "CIII"</note>, vol. III, p. 584, is noted as a juxtaposition of two letters, perhaps even three: Cousin reproduces the note, but gives the three pieces all at once anyway, without separating them, vol. VI, p. 47-53. He similarly prints, vol. VI, p. 53, as a single letter, the 112th <note>original: "CXII^e"</note> letter of Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’ friend and the first major editor of his letters.</note>, vol. II, p. 529, even though a note warned him that there were two different pieces there, the second from September 7, 1646: Cousin nevertheless leaves it with the previous one, which is from October 8, 1629. This is only half as bad when the two letters joined into one are actually consecutive, as with the 111th <note>original: "CXI^e"</note> of Clerselier, vol. I, p. 498, which Cousin prints in vol. VI, p. 61: the first part is a letter from November 20, 1629, and the second belongs to a subsequent letter from December 18, 1629; still, it would be better if they were separated. But sometimes within the same year—1634, for example, where one finds only six letters (February, April, May 15, August 14 and 22, and September)—Cousin, instead of printing them in this order (which he nevertheless knew, since he provides it in a note), prints the one from August 14 (vol. VI, p. 247) before that of May 15 (*ibid.*, p. 257); that is to say, the 9th letter of La Hire before the 8th. Moreover, he keeps the fragment from February 1634 stitched to a letter from May 1637, although he re-

This edition was the standard for nearly three quarters of a century. More confidence was placed in it than Cousin himself had in the handwritten notes he reproduced; he followed his unknown guide only with hesitation, and he was followed blindly. How easy it would have been for him, however, to ensure the source of these notes, and what trouble he would have thus saved future editors! By consulting the Institute’s copy, instead of stopping at the stamp on the first page, where he read these words: *University of Paris, Montempuis* <note>Jean-Gabriel Petit de Montempuis (d. 1763) was a Rector of the University of Paris whose library was famous.</note>, which did not take him back further than the first half of the 18th century (Montempuis having been Rector from October 10, 1715, to October 10, 1717), why did he not instead focus on this name *La Hire*, which reappeared on so many pages, and why did he not read the *Preface* of Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes’ first major biographer.</note> in 1691, where he would have found this same name *La Hire*, joined to that of Father Legrand? There he would have seen that both of them, La Hire and Legrand, had held the originals of the letters to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), the mathematician and priest who served as the "post box" for the 17th-century scientific world.</note> in their hands, [which were] deposited at the *Academy of Sciences*. And no doubt he would have searched the Academy Archives for this La Hire collection, which was still there in its entirety. This time Cousin would have published them, thus saving them from the theft which fifteen years later

The famous Libri <note>Guglielmo Libri (1803–1869) was an Italian mathematician and a notorious book thief who stole thousands of rare manuscripts while serving as an inspector of French libraries.</note>, indeed, abusing his official duties which gave him access to all the public libraries, plundered them shamefully, especially from 1841 to 1847, and he succeeded in selling to Lord Ashburnham <note>Bertram Ashburnham, 4th Earl of Ashburnham (1797–1878), a famous English book collector who unknowingly purchased many of Libri's stolen items.</note>, in England, a considerable lot of manuscripts, which included twenty-three items from the old La Hire collection <note>The mathematician Philippe de La Hire had inherited many of Descartes' original papers.</note>. But many other items had been sold individually in previous years in private sales. Victor Cousin <note>Victor Cousin (1792–1867), the French philosopher and previous editor of Descartes mentioned on the preceding page.</note> bought back as many as he could, from 1840 until his death in 1867. Mr. Etienne Charavay <note>A famous French autograph expert and dealer.</note> has preserved the list of autographs sold by his firm: almost all those by Descartes are now found in the Victor Cousin Library at the Sorbonne. Thus, Cousin as a collector of autographs partially compensates for the shortcomings of Cousin as an editor of Descartes; we already owed him an edition, imperfect to be sure, though most useful; we further owe him an invaluable collection (17 letters by Descartes, plus 1 copy dating from the 17th century <note>original: "XVII^e siècle"</note>).

Since then, other efforts have contributed to reconstructing a large part of the old collection of letters to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was Descartes' "man in Paris" and his most frequent correspondent.</note>. On one hand, Mr. Ludovic Lalanne <note>A librarian and historian who worked at the Library of the Institute of France.</note> received at the Library of the Institute—and doubtless also solicited from generous donors—the autographs of Descartes that they happened to possess: 13 items were thus returned to the Library of the Institute, joining three others that had remained there. On the other hand, Mr. Léopold Delisle <note>Léopold Delisle (1826–1910) was the head of the National Library of France and a master of paleography who spent decades tracking down Libri's thefts.</note>, through feats of skill and tenacity, succeeded in recovering from England a good portion of the manuscripts sold by Libri to Lord Ashburnham, including a folder of 17 autographs by Descartes and 6 copies, which, upon entering the National Library <note>Bibliothèque Nationale</note> in 1888, was bound into a notebook. ### IV.

### AUTOGRAPHS AND MANUSCRIPT COPIES.

Under what conditions can Descartes’s Correspondence be published today? Let us first examine the publications which, during this century, have enriched this correspondence with new letters.

In 1811, Abbé Émery <note>Jacques-André Émery (1732–1811) was a French priest who sought to reconcile Cartesian philosophy with Catholic doctrine.</note> finally printed the two letters from *Descartes to Father Mesland* <note>Denis Mesland (1615–1672) was a Jesuit priest and mathematician who corresponded with Descartes on the theological implications of his physics, particularly regarding the Eucharist.</note> regarding the Eucharist, in a volume titled *Descartes’s Thoughts on Religion and Morality*. These same two letters were printed again, based on a better text, by Mr. Francisque Bouillier in his *History of Cartesian Philosophy* (3rd edition, vol. I, p. 454).

In 1827, Domela Nieuwenhuis printed—from manuscript copies preserved in the Huygens Collection at Leiden—two Latin letters: one from Plempius <note>Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius (1601–1671) was a physician and professor at Louvain who initially opposed but later respected Descartes's theories on the circulation of blood.</note> to Descartes and another from Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont (1587–1653) was a professor of theology at Louvain who critiqued Descartes's *Essays*.</note> to Plempius for Descartes, dated September 15 and 13, 1637 (*Commentary on R. Descartes’s dealings with Belgian philosophers* <note>original: "Commentatio de R. Cartesii commercio cum philosophis belgicis"</note>, small quarto, Louvain, p. 95–102).

In 1838, Victor Cousin, in the 3rd edition of his *Philosophical Fragments*, vol. II, p. 142, published two letters from Descartes to Colvius <note>Andreas Colvius (1594–1671) was a Dutch clergyman and scientist who sought Descartes's opinion on various mathematical and philosophical proofs.</note>, with a reply from Colvius between the two (April 23, June 9, and July 5, 1643); plus a short note from the philosopher to his watchmaker (July 18, 1643); and a letter to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a friar and polymath who served as the central hub for scientific and philosophical exchange in 17th-century Europe.</note> (March 31, 1641). In a subsequent edition, he added a letter to Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654) was a prominent French writer known for his influence on the French language and his correspondence with the intellectual elite.</note> dated June 14, 1637, which was found among the papers of Conrart <note>Valentin Conrart (1603–1675), a man of letters and a founding member of the Académie Française.</note> at the Arsenal Library.

<page-num>LXVII</page-num>
<header>TO THE CORRESPONDENCE OF DESCARTES. LXVII</header>

In 1839, in *The Scholars' Journal* <note>original: "Journal des Savants"</note>, p. 553-559, Libri <note>Guglielmo Libri (1803–1869) was a mathematician and historian of science famous both for his scholarship and for the high-profile theft of rare manuscripts.</note> corrected and completed, based on the original autograph manuscript, a letter to *Mersenne* <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a Minim friar, was the primary hub for scientific exchange in the 17th century, often called the "secretary of learned Europe."</note> dated March 23, 1643, which had already been published by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s literary executor and the first editor of his collected letters.</note> from a rough draft, vol. II, letter CXVI.

In 1860, in the second volume of the *Unpublished Works of Descartes* <note>original: "Œuvres inédites de Descartes"</note>, published by Foucher de Careil, twelve letters to Le Leu de Wilhem <note>David le Leu de Wilhem (1591–1658) was a Dutch counselor and brother-in-law to Constantin Huygens.</note> were included, plus a petition to *Mr. de la Thuillière* (*sic*, for *Thuillerie*) <note>Gaspard Coignet de la Thuillerie (1594–1653) was a French diplomat in the Netherlands.</note>, found in Holland, at The Hague and Leiden; as well as a letter to the *Reverend Father Oslier* (*sic*, for *Gibieuf*) <note>Guillaume Gibieuf (c. 1583–1650) was a priest of the Oratory and a close friend of Descartes.</note>, brought back from the British Museum in London; and one to *an unknown person* (*Golius*) <note>Jacobus Golius (1596–1667) was a celebrated mathematician and professor of Arabic at Leiden.</note>, brought back from the Imperial Library of Vienna; finally, two letters to *Constantin Huygens*, and two more to *Wilhem*.

In 1869, a Genevan, Mr. Eugène de Budé, published seventeen letters by Descartes, nearly all to Pollot <note>Alphonse Pollot (1602–1668) was a soldier and gentleman-in-waiting at the Dutch court who facilitated the correspondence between Descartes and Princess Elisabeth.</note>, based on a copy found in his private collection.

In 1879, Foucher de Careil again provided twenty-six letters from *Princess Elisabeth to Descartes*, based on a copy found at the home of Baron de Pallandt, at the Rosendaal castle near Arnhem <note>Princess Elisabeth of the Palatinate (1618–1680) was Descartes's most significant philosophical correspondent; her insightful questions prompted him to write "The Passions of the Soul."</note>.

In 1886, Abbé Georges Monchamp, in his *History of Cartesianism in Belgium* <note>original: "Histoire du cartésianisme en Belgique"</note>, revisited the discussion between Fromondus and Descartes, and completed the account of the exchange between Descartes and Plempius, by drawing attention to the full text of two letters from Descartes (February 15 and March 23, 1638), published by Plempius as early as the second edition of his *Foundations of Medicine* <note>original: "Fundamenta medicinæ"</note> (1644).

In 1887, Bierens de Haan studied, in his *Materials for the History of Mathematical and Physical Sciences in the Netherlands* <note>original: "Bouwstoffen voor de Geschiedenis der Wis- en Natuurkundige Wetenschappen in de Nederlanden"</note>, the quarrel between Stampioen and Waessenaer <note>Johan Stampioen and Jacobus van Waessenaer were rival mathematicians; Descartes supported Waessenaer in their dispute over algebraic methods.</note>, the latter of whom was supported by Descartes. And the following year, Mr. D.-J. Korteweg, in the *Netherlands Archives* <note>original: "Archives néerlandaises"</note>, added several documents, including a letter from Descartes, half-French and half-Flemish, dated February 1, 1640, the original autograph of which is in the British Museum.

<summary>This page lists the major 19th-century editorial contributions and archival discoveries that expanded the collection of Descartes's known correspondence, including letters to Princess Elisabeth and various Dutch scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Foucher de Careil, Princess Elisabeth, Libri, Mersenne, correspondence, Cartesianism, manuscripts, 19th-century bibliography</keywords>

<page-num>LXVIII</page-num>

# INTRODUCTION

The same Mr. Korteweg <note>Diederik Jacobus Korteweg (1848–1941) was a Dutch mathematician, best known for the Korteweg–De Vries equation, who also took a keen interest in the history of science.</note> found a *letter from Descartes to Colvius* <note>Andreas Colvius (1594–1671) was a Dutch clergyman and scientist who corresponded with many great thinkers of his time.</note>, dated June 14, 1637, at the Royal Library of Munich; and Father Monchamp published it in 1895 in a short work titled *Isaac Beeckman and Descartes*.

In 1890, the *Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original: "Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie"</note> (vol. III, p. 568) provided a letter from Descartes to a German gentleman, *Dozem*, dated March 25, 1642, which Ludwig Stein had found among the papers of Leibniz at the Royal Library of Hanover. In 1891 and 1892, Mr. Paul Tannery <note>Paul Tannery (1843–1904) was a preeminent historian of mathematics and a primary editor of the definitive edition of Descartes's works.</note> successively published, in the same journal (vol. IV, p. 442 and 529; vol. V, p. 217 and 469), *fourteen unpublished letters to Mersenne*, carefully selected from the fifty-seven manuscript pieces held between three institutions: the National Library, the Victor Cousin Library, and the Library of the Institute in Paris.

Finally, Mr. Korteweg had identified in the Collection of *Letters of Constantin Huygens* <note>Constantin Huygens (1596–1687) was a Dutch polymath and diplomat; his correspondence is a treasure trove for 17th-century intellectual history.</note>, at the Library of the Academy of Sciences in Amsterdam, copies of *seventeen letters to Descartes*; they were brought back to France and published in July 1895 in the *Burgundian Review of Higher Education* <note>original: "Revue bourguignonne de l’Enseignement supérieur"</note>. The same *Review* provided, in the following issue of January 1896, the text of a *Conversation between Descartes and Burman* <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679) was a Dutch theology student whose 1648 interview with Descartes provides crucial clarifications of the philosopher's later views.</note>, dated April 14, 1648, preserved in the manuscripts of the University of Göttingen Library.

However, in addition to these publications, a list has been drawn up over these last two years of all the autographs <note>The term "autograph" here refers to documents written in the author's own hand, which are highly valued by scholars for their accuracy compared to copies.</note> by Descartes known at the present time. No fewer than 93 have been counted, distributed as follows among various public libraries or private collections in France and abroad:

These 108 copies, almost all dated, joined with the 93 autographs, which are also nearly all dated, provide us with a total of 201 pieces for which the date is known. If we add the 23 letters for which we know the date through the list of Dom Poirier <note>Dom Poirier was a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur who inventoried Descartes's papers</note>—since these numbers have almost all been identified with the drafts <note>original: "minutes"</note> in the Clerselier edition <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes's letters and a devoted follower</note>—one can see that it is possible to securely re-establish the chronology almost everywhere.

Indeed, dated letters sometimes provide the dates for those that are not. For example, the drafts that Clerselier printed without a date, but which happen to be responses to Elizabeth <note>Princess Elizabeth of the Palatinate, a primary philosophical correspondent of Descartes</note> or to Huygens <note>Constantijn Huygens, a Dutch diplomat and polymath</note>, can be dated by approximation, now that we know the letters from Huygens and Elizabeth with their dates; and we will thus date more than fifty of them. The same applies to the letters or fragments of letters to Regius <note>Henricus Regius, a Dutch professor of medicine whose relationship with Descartes eventually soured</note>, since we know at least the date of the letters that the latter wrote to Descartes.

Or even, two letters are clearly from the same day, or a few days apart, and if only one of the two has its date, the other is also dated by extension. Thus, it had already been noted that a letter to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a monk who acted as the central hub of the 17th-century European scientific network</note> was from the same day as a letter to M. de Beaune <note>Florimond de Beaune, a mathematician who wrote the first major commentary on Descartes's *Geometry*</note>, even though they were printed in two different volumes (Clerselier, II, xcviii and III, lxxi); fortunately, the second was dated February 20, 1639: this, then, is also the date of the first.

Later, in an autograph to Mersenne dated October 5, 1646, Descartes speaks of three works: *Concerning the Purple Rain* <note>original Latin: "De pluvia purpurea"</note>, by Wendelin <note>Godefroy Wendelin, a Flemish astronomer</note>; *Foundations of Physics* <note>original Latin: "Fundamenta Physices"</note>, by Regius; plus a short work, printed in Paris, by a certain Jacques Bourgeois, *On the Grinding of Eyeglass Lenses* <note>original French: "Sur la taille des verres de lunette"</note>. Now, in another letter, without a date or a recipient's name (Clerselier, II, cxiii), Descartes speaks of these same three works which he has just received, and thanks his correspondent for them. It was Constantijn Huygens who received the packages of books addressed to Descartes and...

Another example: a letter to Mersenne (Clers., II, **LXXVII**) is now dated, *Amsterdam, August 14, 1634*, thanks to the autograph <note>A manuscript written in the author's own hand, rather than a copy</note>, which thus completes one of the first sentences:

> “Mr. *Beeckman* came here Saturday evening and lent me 
> ” the book by Galileo; but he took it back to *Dort* <note>Dort is the traditional English name for the Dutch city of Dordrecht</note> this morning. ”

Now, we find another letter from Descartes (Clers., II, **XVII**), printed this time with a date, *August 22, 1634*, and the name of the place, *Amsterdam*, but without the recipient's name. However, it is addressed to someone with whom he had just had a discussion in person for two days in a row: now, Beeckman <note>Isaac Beeckman (1588–1637), a Dutch philosopher and scientist who greatly influenced the young Descartes</note>, having arrived in Amsterdam from Dort on Saturday evening, had departed on August 14—that is, the Monday, two days later. Furthermore, Descartes's letter was written in Latin, as were the two other letters from him to Beeckman that we possess. It is therefore very likely a third letter to the same person, written in 1634, which serves as proof that he and Descartes had reconciled after their major quarrel of 1630 <note>This "great quarrel" concerned Beeckman's claims of influence over Descartes's early work on music and physics</note>.

Thus, the smallest detail becomes a precious piece of information, fixing not only the date of one letter but also several others that precede or follow it. In a letter (Clers., II, **LXVIII**) that was believed, without serious proof, to be from September 1632, we find this short sentence:

> “ *Mr. Reneri* <note>Henricus Reneri (1593–1639), the first professor to teach Cartesian philosophy at a university</note>
> ” *has gone to live in Deventer for five or six days now, and he is*
> ” *now the professor of philosophy.* ”

However, upon verification of the registers of the <term>Gymnasium Illustre <note>Latin for "Illustrious Gymnasium," a type of higher education academy in the Netherlands that ranked just below a university</note></term>, preserved in the Archives of Deventer, it appears that Reneri was appointed professor on October 4, 1631, and he delivered his inaugural lecture on November 28, 1631. Descartes's letter was therefore written between these two dates—that is, a year earlier than previously thought—and several other letters are moved forward by the same amount: the two following (Clers., II, **LXIX** and **LXX**) being from January 1632 and February 2, 1632, and those that come after (Clers., II, **LXXI** and **LXXII**) would also be from Eas... <note>The text likely continues "Easter 1632"</note>

Finally, as a last resort, we sometimes have the very position where Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes's collected letters; while his work was pioneering, it often lacked chronological precision</note> placed a particular undated letter; if it is found between two dated letters, and if not only these two but a good number before and after are also dated and follow one another, we indeed have a series in chronological order. In this case, we can leave the undated letter between the other two; that is likely its actual place, indeed, and all its duly dated neighbors guarantee the date it should itself possess.

If one dared to push approximation to the extreme (and why should one not?), Descartes provides us with the means to do so. He had his specific day for correspondence, which was the day the mail was dispatched. The mail left Leiden <note>Leyde</note> on Mondays, and from Amsterdam on Mondays as well; it is Descartes himself who informs us of this. Since the same courier who carried off his letters in the evening brought him those from his correspondents in the morning, he usually waited for its arrival to send off at least the most urgent replies on that same day; the others were deferred for a week <note>The original French "à huitaine" literally means "eight days," a common term for a week</note>, and sometimes written on Sunday—the day before the mail—to allow for more time. By marking every Monday of each year on a calendar between 1629 and 1650, we find that many dates, now known through autographs <note>Original manuscripts written in the author's own hand</note>, are indeed Mondays or Sundays. When we are nearly certain that an undated letter was written between two others that are well-dated, there is a strong chance it belongs to an intermediate Monday, and sometimes there is only one.

Such is the new edition of the *Letters of Descartes* that we propose to provide. It will not be perfect, for perfection is no longer possible due to the dispersal and destruction of so many of the philosopher’s papers. It will undoubtedly contain not only gaps but errors. However, we have made use of all previous efforts, the work of

[First] Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes's collected letters; while his work was pioneering, it often lacked chronological precision</note>, then the work of Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes's early and most significant biographer</note> and of Legrand, as well as the numerous contributions made in this century to the work now being prepared, and the goodwill encountered everywhere to facilitate this task. Nevertheless, the edition remains subject to the chance of new discoveries—which we hardly dare hope for, yet are not impossible. At least among the letters that may yet be found, not all will be entirely unknown: many will have their "waiting places" already marked in this edition at established dates. They will arrive not to fill empty pages left blank for them, but to complete fragments and give substance to placeholders <note>Original: "étiquette," literally a label or tag</note> set there in anticipation. Thus, thanks to this chronological order, the body of correspondence as a whole—by receiving all new additions into these pre-prepared frameworks—will remain solid and unshakable.

# REMARKS

## DESCARTES’S SPELLING

Descartes, if we are to believe what he himself says in several places, cared very little for spelling. In March 1636, as he was thinking of sending a copy of his manuscripts to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a Minim friar and mathematician who served as the central hub of the 17th-century "Republic of Letters," corresponding with almost every major thinker of his day</note>, he warned him in advance: “The only

> » difficulty in this is that my copy is no better written than this letter,
> » and that neither the spelling <note>Original: "ortographe"; Descartes often used simplified spellings</note> nor the commas are any better
> » observed...”

Later, when he was reproached for the spelling of the *Method* <note>The *Discourse on the Method* (1637), his most famous work</note> and the *Essays*, published in 1637, he responded as follows: “As for the spelling, it is for the printer to defend it; for

> » I desired nothing else of him in that regard, except that he follow
> » usage.” <note>By "usage," Descartes refers to the common practice of printers at the time, which was often inconsistent before the standardization by the Académie Française</note>

And in the same letter he adds, a few lines further down:

> “Furthermore, I have no intention of reforming French
> » spelling...; but if I must give my opinion here, I believe that
> » if pronunciation were followed exactly, it would bring
> » much more convenience to foreigners learning our
> » language...”

And again: “It is in speaking that languages are com-

> » posed, rather than in writing.” $^1$

# REMARKS

However, on November 15, 1638, he wrote to Mersenne: “I
> thank you for being pleased to correct the faults therein <gloss>this refers to the Dioptrics</gloss>, and if you would take the trouble to mark them all in your copy, so as to send it to us in the event that a second printing is made, you would oblige me; for in matters of language and spelling, I desire nothing so much as to follow common usage; but it has been so long since I have been out of France that I am ignorant of it in many things.” Finally, after having already said, regarding the *Method* and the *Essays*, that he would not advise anyone to learn French spelling “in a book printed in Leiden” <note>Leiden was a major center for printing in the Netherlands, but French expatriate authors often found the local compositors struggled with French orthography</note>, he repeated once more to Mersenne on February 9, 1639: “You oblige me by the trouble you take to correct the spelling errors, in which I desire nothing so much as to follow

> it seems that one would do better to use only the letters that must be pronounced, in order to conform writing to speech, just as speech conforms to thought: from this comes the fact that many are beginning to write as one speaks; for example, they put the letter *a* in all the places where *e* is pronounced like *a*, such as *annemy* <note>original: "annemy"; modern French "ennemi" (enemy)</note> and *Parlemant* <note>original: "Parlemant"; modern French "Parlement"</note>, instead of *ennemy* and *Parlement*, and they remove all the *b*’s, *c*’s, *s*’s, and *t*’s which are not pronounced.”

> “But those who wish for us to retain the origin of our language, and that we always remember that it comes from Latin, consider these people barbarians, and they willingly retain *dicts* and *faicts* <note>original: "dicts" and "faicts"; these versions retained the Latin "c" from "dictus" and "factus," which are silent in French "dits" and "faits"</note>, whereas others write *dis* and *fais*, etc. As for me, I consider it more appropriate to avoid all sorts of superfluity, and not to use 5 or 6 letters where only 3 or 4 are needed; just as one should not use 5 or 6 words where only one or two are needed, so as to imitate nature, which follows the shortest path when it acts. This I mean when it can be done conveniently, and when, in doing so, one offends no one: for it is certain that we pronounce many words which cannot be written as they are uttered; for example, one cannot write with our ordinary characters the third person plural of the imperfect tense of our verbs without putting in superfluous letters that are not pronounced, as one sees in these two words, *deuoient*, *rendoient* <note>These are older spellings of "devaient" (they owed) and "rendaient" (they rendered)</note>, in which the last six letters make only one syllable, so that it would be necessary to write them with a circumflex *ê* in this fashion, *deuêt*, *rendêt*, to pronounce them as one speaks now. This is what Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a poet of the Pléiade who attempted to introduce a phonetic system of spelling and "measured" verse to France</note> tried to remedy under Charles IX and Henry III, which has since been done by the Sieur de la Val in his Paraphrase of the Psalms, Father Monet in his Dictionary, and a few others.”

# ON THE SPELLING OF DESCARTES. LXXXI

> usage; and for a long time Maire <note>Joost Maire was a prominent printer in Leiden who handled Descartes’s works</note> (*his printer in Leiden*)
> had wanted me to ask you, but I would not have dared to send
> word of it to you, if it had not come from your own movement.” All these
passages are found in volume II of the *Letters of Mr. Descartes*, Clerselier edition <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’s literary executor and the first editor of his correspondence</note>, pages 527, 14, 420 and 446.

Descartes is therefore not as indifferent as he first appears to the spelling of his printed works; he desires that the public receive them well, and not be put off by too-strong peculiarities, nor especially by somewhat antiquated ways of writing, as could not fail to be the case for a Frenchman who retains abroad the habits he had when leaving his country and cannot follow the changes that occur there in his absence. Being unable to guess these changes, we shall see him, here as elsewhere, blazing his own trail and striving to write “clearly and distinctly,” just as he thought and expressed his thoughts.

We have in Paris three collections of Descartes’s autographs, which allow us to study his way of writing different words:

1st. The Victor Cousin Library, at the Sorbonne, possesses, gathered into one notebook, *seventeen* manuscript pieces by Descartes (not counting one copy).

2nd. The Library of the Institute possesses *sixteen*.

3rd. Finally, the National Library <note>The Bibliothèque Nationale de France (BnF) in Paris</note> possesses a rather large bound notebook, which contains *seventeen* letters by Descartes himself, plus six copies (*fr. n. a. 5160* <note>“fr. n. a.” stands for *français nouvelles acquisitions*, a cataloging designation for newly acquired French manuscripts</note>).

This last collection is by far the most considerable: several of the letters it contains are true treatises, and it includes in total, in Descartes’s own hand, 83 pages, some of which have up to 50 lines, and others 35 on average. Besides that, the seventeen autographs found there are of quite different dates:

Two letters, the oldest in this collection, are from November 1629 and from January or October 1631 (*f. 48, f. 46 and 47*).

Five others were written from June to October 1638, and fill 21 leaves, or 42 pages (*f. 2 to 23*).

The ten that remain are distributed as follows:

Three from 1641: March 4, June 23, and December 22 (*f. 23, 27 and 49*).

LXXXII
REMARKS

Only one from 1643, April 26 (*folio 29*).

Five from 1646, on March 30, September 7, October 12, November 2 and 23 (*folios 31, 37, 39, 40 and 42*).

One, finally, from 1647, April 26 (*folio 44*).

This collection thus offers the double advantage of allowing a comparison of Descartes’s spelling with that of his contemporaries, thanks to the six copies by other hands included within it, and also a comparison of Descartes with himself; his spelling changed from 1629 to 1650, as was first noted by Mr. Paul Tannery <note>Paul Tannery (1843–1904) was a distinguished historian of mathematics and science who co-edited the definitive *Oeuvres de Descartes*</note> in 1891 (*Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original: "Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie"</note>, IV, 529). We will therefore refer most often to the original manuscripts <term>autographes: documents written in the author's own hand</term> in the National Library, though we will not refrain from also referring—especially for the oldest ones—to the Victor Cousin Library <note>Victor Cousin (1792–1867) was a French philosopher and minister of education who collected many Cartesian papers</note> (April 3, 1622; August 14, 1634), to the Library of the Institute (December 18, 1629; April 15, 1630; May 15, 1634), as well as to the original manuscripts in Leiden, The Hague, and London.

In this study, we shall follow the order that seems suggested by the subject itself:

->I. Vowels (*u* and *v*, *i* and *y*; *y* in *ay* and *oy*).<-

### I. — VOWELS.

1. *u* and *v*. — It is well known that the 17th century did not make the same distinction as we do between the letters *u* and *v*, or, as was then said, between the vowel *u* and the consonant *u*, which has become our *v*. In accordance with the proper usage of his time, Descartes distinguished between them, but as signs used in writing, and according to the position the same letter occupied, whether at the beginning or in the middle of a word. At the beginning of a word, he always writes *v*, not only for the words we spell that way today,

The letters *u* and *v* are therefore quite distinct for Descartes, at least regarding their usage, and it is the same distinction as, for example, between σ and ς in Greek script <note>In Greek, the letter sigma is written as σ in the middle of a word but changes to ς at the end</note>: *u* in the body of words, *v* at the beginning. Let us add that, following this rule, there was then only one capital form, the *V*: for example, *Vtrecht*¹.

2. *i* and *y*. — It is also known that the 17th century was only just beginning to distinguish the vowel *i* from the consonant *i*, which has since become our *j*. Descartes does not yet distinguish them in his writing; everywhere he writes *i* where we today put *j*. Instead of *je* [I], *j'ai* [I have], *déjà* [already], *jamais* [never], *joint* [joined], *majeur* [major], etc., one finds in his original manuscripts <term>autographes: documents written in the author's own hand</term> *ie, i'ay, desia, iamais, ioint, maieur*, etc.

On the other hand, in many cases where we today put a simple *i*, Descartes often put a *y*. This is primarily at the end of pronouns like *cecy* [this], *celuy* [that], and adverbs like *voycy* [here is], *ainsy* [thus], *aussy* [also], *icy* [here], or *ny* [neither/nor] when repeated, etc. However, here the rule is not absolute, and one finds numerous examples of the simple *i*, often on the same page and within a few lines of each other: *ainsi* (folio 17 front, lines 30 and 33), *ainsy* (lines 35 and 36); *ny plan ni solide* [neither plane nor solid] (folio 17 front, line 17), etc. Adjectives and participles ending in *i* are written in both ways: *marry* and *marri* [upset], *demi* and *demy* [half] (more often *demi*), *vny* and *vni* [united or smooth], *failly* [failed], etc. We find *fini* [finite] and *infini* [infinite] (folio 21 back, lines 20 and 21). In nouns, the spelling is variable: Descartes writes *hyuer* [winter]; but he writes *stile* [style], rather than *style*, and always *pais* instead of *pays* [country]. A Latin word, *consyderare* <note>original Latin: "to consider"</note>, is written with a *y* (folio 48 back, line 18, November 1629); this was a frequent usage...

3. *Y in "ay" and "oy".* — Descartes most often writes *ay*, and not *ai*, at the end of words. While exceptions are numerous for *vray* [true], *gay* [cheerful], *vraye* [true—feminine], and *gays* [cheerful—plural], one also frequently finds *vrai*, *vraie*, and *vrais*. However, the first person of the present indicative of the verb "to have" <note>French: *avoir*</note> is always *i'ay* [I have], and consequently, the same applies to the first person of the future and the indefinite past <note>The "indefinite past" or *passé indéfini* is equivalent to the modern *passé composé* (e.g., I have spoken)</note> in all verbs: *ie m'arestray* [I will stop] (folio 18 front, line 8), *i'adioutay* [I added] (folio 17 back, lines 20 and 23), *ie manday* [I sent], etc. In the subjunctive, one likewise finds *qu'ils ayent* [that they may have], and even once *qu'il ayt* [that he may have] (folio 12 back, line 24), with the *y* rewritten over an *i* (unless it is an *i* rewritten over a *y*). — In the middle of words, Descartes also readily uses the *y*: *aymant* [loving], *aymer* [to love], *ayder* [to help], *aysé* [easy], *aygu* [sharp/acute], etc.; however, in the same letter—the oldest in the collection, from November 1629—one finds *aygu* (folio 48 back, line 39), and on the following line *aigu* (line 40), and again in a single letter from July 27, 1638, *aise* [ease] (folio 14 back, line 30), and *ayse* (line 40). Finally, one finds *raion* for *rayon* [ray/beam]. Descartes similarly writes *oy*, and not *oi*, first at the end of nouns like *foy* [faith], *roy* [king], etc., at the end of pronouns like *moy* [me], *soy* [oneself], *quoy* [what], and the adverb *pourquoy* [why], but especially at the end of the first person present indicative of verbs ending in *oir* and *oire*: *ie voy* [I see], *ie croy* [I believe], *ie conçoy* [I conceive]². ## II. — DIPHTHONGS.

1. Let us also note for the record *pleinement* <note>fully</note> (folio 2 back, line 6) and *plenement* (line 8), *la nege* <note>the snow</note>, *les venes* <note>the veins</note>, and conversely *seicher* <note>to dry</note>. But the most important diphthongs are *oi*, *eu*, and especially *an* and *en*.

Or else they are nouns like *cheute* <note>fall, modern: chute</note> or *relieure* <note>binding, modern: reliure</note>. But there is no fixed rule on this subject. The circumflex accent seems only to be a writing abbreviation, which one may or may not use ¹.

A very common word, *temps* <note>time</note>, was also changed by him. We find written *tans* in the autograph of November 1629, and also in an even older letter, from July 18, 1629, to Father Gibieuf. # REMARKS

...used without *s*. Let us first examine the first of these two functions of the letter *s*.

1. In the oldest original manuscripts <note>original: *autographes*</note> of the collection, those from November 1629 and January 1631, Descartes uses the same letter *s* for three types of cases where we today use *s*, *x*, or *z*. Then, he was gradually led to substitute, as we do, this *s* sometimes with *x* and sometimes with *z*.

For example, we read (folios 48, 46, and 47), not *those* <note>original: *ceux*</note>, *two* <note>original: *deux*</note>, *better* <note>original: *mieux*</note>, *cloudy* <note>original: *nebuleux*</note>, *rationals* <note>original: *rationaux*</note>, *I want* <note>original: *ie veux*</note>, etc., but *two* <note>original: *deus*</note>, *better* <note>original: *mieus*</note>, *cloudy* <note>original: *nebuleus*</note>, *rationals* <note>original: *rationaus*</note>, *I want* <note>original: *ie veus*</note>; and this is found again in two letters to Wilhem from February 7 (*happy* <note>original: *hureus*</note>, etc., for *heureux*) and December 12, 1633 (*advantageous* <note>original: *auantageus*</note>, etc.), in another to Mersenne from August 14, 1634, and one to Golius from May 9/19, 1635 (*eyes* <note>original: *yeus*</note>, *luminous* <note>original: *lumineus*</note>, etc.). But then in later texts, those from 1638, for example, and all subsequent ones, we find it written as it is today: *those* <note>original: *ceux*</note>, *two* <note>original: *deux*</note>, *better* <note>original: *mieux*</note>, *I want* <note>original: *ie veux*</note>, etc.—a significant new change that Descartes adopted in his spelling. His manuscripts, however, preserve here and there a few traces of the old habit: *choice* <note>original: *chois*</note> for *choix* (October 5, 1637), and *to which* <note>original: *ausquels*</note> for *auxquels*; this form *to which* <note>original: *ausquels*</note> is even the only one he ever employs. On the other hand, the *x* sometimes triumphs over the *s* in a very singular way: here are two examples, *the defects* <note>original: *les defaux*</note> for *les defauts* (folio 40 front, line 21, from November 2, 1646), and *twice* <note>original: *deux foix*</note> for *deux fois* (folio 42 back, line 19, from November 23, 1646); it is true that in this last case one can just as easily read *fois* as *foix*, the two letters *s* and *x* being written one over the other. Finally, a curious example: *of the flow and ebb* <note>original: *du flus et reflux*</note> (folio 29 front, lines 24–25, from April 26, 1643)¹.

The same letter *s*, as we have said, was also used by Descartes where we today place *z*, particularly in the second person plural of verbs: *you thought* <note>original: *vous pensiés*</note>, *you had* <note>original: *vous auiés*</note>, *you will be able* <note>original: *vous pourrés*</note>, *you ask* <note>original: *vous demandés*</note>, *you speak* <note>original: *vous parlés*</note>, *you propose* <note>original: *vous proposés*</note>, etc. (folio 48 front and back, folios 46 and 47). December 12, 1633, August 14, 1634, and May 9/19, 1635. Afterward, Descartes substituted ȥ (just like the ȥ mentioned a moment ago) for the *s* in the preceding cases; and the original manuscripts <note>original: *autographes*</note> from 1637 and 1638 show us quite clearly *you want* <note>original: *vous voulez*</note>, *you send word* <note>original: *vous mandez*</note>, etc. In reality, it is not only the letter ȥ being substituted for *s*; it is rather *ez* being used for *és* <note>The superscript 1 refers to the footnote at the bottom.</note>¹. And Descartes does not limit this reform (for it truly is a real one) to the second person plural of verbs: he extends it to the plural of past participles, *they have exercised* <note>original: *ils se sont exercez*</note>, *accustomed* <note>original: *accoustumez*</note>, *sent* <note>original: *enuoyez*</note>, *leaned* <note>original: *panchez*</note>, etc. (October 5, 1637)—not always, it is true, but in numerous cases. He even extends it quite frequently to the plural of nouns ending in *té* or *dé*, such as *difficulties* <note>original: *difficultez*</note>, *authorities* <note>original: *authoritez*</note>, *impieties* <note>original: *impietez*</note>, *truths* <note>original: *veritez*</note>, *proceedings* <note>original: *procedez*</note>, etc. Finally, this new habit goes so far as to make him write sometimes *they* <note>original: *ilz*</note>, *of which* <note>original: *desquelz*</note>, and even *son* <note>original: *filz*</note>, for *ils*, *desquels*, and *fils*.

2° *This addition of the s as a marker of the plural usually causes the t—which ends singular nouns and participles in "ent" and "ant"—to be dropped.* One presumably feels that, among three consecutive consonants, *nts* is one too many, and that two are sufficient: *ns* in the plural just as *nt* is used in the singular. Descartes therefore writes in the plural, like his contemporaries, *elements* <note>original: *elemens*</note>, *hindrances* <note>original: *empeschemens*</note>, *children* <note>original: *enfans*</note>, *heavy* <note>original: *pesans*</note>, *burning* <note>original: *bruslans*</note>, etc. This is not to say that one does not also find, on the same page, both *folding* <note>original: *pliants*</note> and *heavy* <note>original: *pesans*</note> (folio 8 front, lines 3 and 33). In the original manuscript of October 5, 1637, he twice writes *the teeth* <note>original: *les dents*</note>; but on the preceding page one reads *teeth* <note>original: *des dens*</note>, and on the same page, *two hundred* <note>original: *deux cens*</note>, *preceding* <note>original: *precedens*</note>, etc.

The endings *ant* and *ent* are not the only ones that lose their *t* in the plural. Descartes writes *the points* <note>original: *les poins*</note> more often than *the points* <note>original: *les points*</note>, although both are found (folio 48 front, lines 20 and 21); we even have an example of *joined* <note>original: *ioins*</note>, put for *ioints*. He once wrote *the healthiest* <note>original: *les plus sains*</note> (folio 13 front, line 11), where we would have put—if only to avoid ambiguity—*the holiest* <note>original: *les plus saints*</note>. Elsewhere he left this error, if it is one, always stemming from the same rule: *the shortest* <note>original: *les plus cours*</note> (folio 22 back, line 21), although he also writes *the shortest* <note>original: *les plus courts*</note> (October 5, 1637); once one even finds *parts* <note>original: *les pars*</note> for *parts*, and also *deserts* <note>original: *les desers*</note> (December 12, 1633) for *déserts*, and *offered* <note>original: *offers*</note> (October 5, 1640). XC

# REMARKS

...had not corrected *spirits* <note>original: *espris*</note>, written instead of *esprits*, as one of his readers complained (*Letters*, Clerselier edition, II, 4 and 14). This useless *t* displeased him so much that he had also suppressed it in a word that had long been printed as *nevertheless* <note>original: *neantmoins*</note>: Descartes usually wrote *nevertheless* <note>original: *neanmoins*</note>.

It is not only the letter *t* that the addition of an *s* causes to disappear at the end of words: in similar cases, the letter *d* disappears as well, and undoubtedly for the same reason—to avoid writing three consonants in a row (*nds*), the second of which is useless. Descartes once wrote *the greatest* <note>original: *les plus grans*</note>; but one also finds, in the same original manuscript from October 5, 1637, *the greatest* <note>original: *les plus grands*</note>. The rule is better observed—one might even say it is always followed—in the first person singular of the present indicative for verbs ending in *endre* or *ondre*: Descartes writes *I learn* <note>original: *i’apprens*</note>, *I descend* <note>original: *ie descens*</note>, *I respond* <note>original: *ie respons*</note>, etc. The reason for this appears to be what we have already stated: to avoid three consecutive consonants. In other cases where a *d* is followed by an *s* but there are only two consonants total, Descartes keeps the *d*. He writes *feet* <note>original: *pieds*</note> in the plural, just as he writes *foot* <note>original: *pied*</note> in the singular, and he writes *weight* <note>original: *poids*</note>, even though in the printed editions of the time, including his *Letters*, one finds *foot* <note>original: *pié*</note>, *feet* <note>original: *piés*</note>, and *weight* <note>original: *pois*</note>. On this subject, one can compare the printed and manuscript versions of the *Examination of the Geostatic Question* <note>This was a scientific treatise by Descartes concerning the weight of the Earth and the center of gravity.</note>, where these words *feet* and *weight* appear quite often (Clerselier edition, letter 73, vol. I, p. 327-347; and National Library, French collection, new acquisitions, 5160, f. 4-10).

Let us add the consonant *p* to the letters *t* and *d* that disappear before an *s* at the end of words. Descartes suppressed it in the word *time* <note>original: *temps*</note>, which he initially wrote as *tans*, and soon after as *tems*. He also suppressed it in the word *body* <note>original: *corps*</note>, though not consistently. After the publication of 1637, a reader complained about the spelling *body* <note>original: *cors*</note> because it was ambiguous—could it mean *body* <note>original: *corps*</note> or *hunting horns* <note>original: *cornets*</note>?—and Descartes seems to have hesitated between the two forms afterward, although *cors* remained his most frequent choice for a long time. For instance, in the *Examination of the Geostatic Question* (July 13, 1638), one finds *body* <note>original: *corps*</note> twice on the first page (one of which is in the title itself) and *body* <note>original: *cors*</note> five times (f. 4 recto, lines 2 and 30, etc.). Further on, *body* <note>original: *corps*</note> reappears a third time in a heading (f. 7 verso, line 17), then a fourth (f. 8 recto, line 21). In the last two original manuscripts of the same collection, which are both quite short, it is true...

XCI

# ON DESCARTES'S SPELLING.

one no longer finds anything but *body* <note>original: *corps* (f. 42 recto, l. 21, from November 23, 1646; and f. 44 recto, l. 15, verso, l. 3 and 11, from April 26, 1647)</note>; must we conclude that the spelling *corps* <note>with the silent 'p'</note> had in the long run prevailed over *cors*? — On the other hand, a case where Descartes never wrote either the *p*, or the *m* that precedes it, is that of *count* and *to count* <note>original: *conte* and *conter*</note>, *miscount* and *to miscount* <note>original: *mesconte* and *mesconter*</note>, which we write today, without being shocked by the three consecutive consonants, as *compte*, *compter*, *mécompte*, and *mécompter*.

3° To finish with this question of the letter *s* at the end of words, let us say that Descartes sometimes maintains it and sometimes suppresses it in certain adverbs, quite reasonably it seems. Thus, he constantly writes *always* <note>original: *tousiours*</note> and *already* <note>original: *desia*</note>: indeed, not having the letter *j* at his disposal <note>In the 17th century, 'i' was often used where we now use 'j'</note>, how else would he have written? He writes *however* using both *toutesfois* and *toutefois* (f. 48 recto, l. 3 and 19); but the first is rare, and he prefers the second, contrary to the printers of his time. He writes *sooner* <note>original: *plustost*</note>, which was commonly printed as *plustost*; and when he preserves the *s*, it is because he writes the two words separately, as in *the majority* <note>original: *la plus part*, literally "the most part"</note>. Finally, one finds *still* written as both *encores* and *encore* (f. 48 recto, l. 3 and 19, November 1629); but the second version soon prevails.

### IV. — CONSONANT S.

->(*Second function.*)<-

The consonant *s*, when joined to the vowels or diphthongs *a*, *ai*, *e*, *i*, *o*, *oi*, *u*, *ou*, gave them a particular sound, which we mark today with an accent while suppressing the *s*. Let us successively examine the cases that correspond to the circumflex accent, the acute accent, and the grave accent, which will lead us to speak of Descartes's use of accents.

1° Today, we primarily replace the *s* with a circumflex accent after the vowels *a*, *i*, *u* in the past definite <note>the *passé composé*'s more formal relative</note> (first and second person plural) and in the imperfect subjunctive of all verbs. Descartes therefore wrote, as one would expect, *you informed me* <note>original: *vous me mandastes*</note>, *you sent me* <note>original: *vous m'enuoyastes*</note> (f. 17 verso, l. 28 and 29), *that he might propose* <note>original: *qu'il proposast*</note>, etc.

XCII

# REMARKS

Next, Descartes writes *as* where we now write *â* in words such as *haste* and *to hasten* <note>original: *haste* and *haster*</note>, *task* and *to task* <note>original: *tasche* and *tascher*</note>, *blame* <note>original: *blasme*</note>, *sticks* <note>original: *bastons*</note>, *let us feel* <note>original: *tastons*</note>, etc. There are even cases where we have removed all accents from the *a*, although this vowel is found in his writing lengthened by an *s*, as in *travel* <note>original: *voyasge*</note>, *each* <note>original: *chasque*</note>, *everyone* <note>original: *chascun*</note>, etc. He writes *age* as *aage* <note>Modern French: *âge*</note>.

He writes *es* where we today put *ê* in the words *ready* <note>original: *prest*</note>, *arrest* <note>original: *arest*</note>, *same* <note>original: *mesme*</note>, *honest* <note>original: *honneste*</note>, *to be* <note>original: *estre*</note>, *to prevent* <note>original: *empescher*</note>, *to mix* <note>original: *mesler*</note>, etc. (and *mixture* <note>original: *meslange*</note>, where we now write *é*).

As for the vowel *i*, the issue is complex, as this letter is found in the diphthongs *ai* and *oi*. Descartes writes *master* <note>original: *maistre*</note> and *if you please* <note>original: *s'il vous plaist*</note>; he writes *to appear* <note>original: *paroistre*</note> and *it appears* <note>original: *il paroist*</note>, *to know* <note>original: *connoistre*</note>, etc. At first, he wrote *quick* and *speed* as *viste* and *vistesse* (folio 48 verso, lines 31 and 41, November 1629): later one finds *vite* and *vitesse*; however, *viste* reappears several more times (folio 24 verso, March 4, 1641). We find the word for *acts* <note>original: *agist*</note> four times in the same text from October 5, 1637, and even *he reduces* <note>original: *il reduist*</note>, which is likely a mistake, as Descartes elsewhere writes *he deduces* <note>original: *il deduit*</note>, etc.¹

XCIII

### ON THE ORTHOGRAPHY OF DESCARTES.

He writes *os* where we today use *ô*, in *our, your, soon, rather, coast, to remove* <note>original: *nostre, vostre, tost, plutost, coste, oster*</note>; and *ous* in words that we write with *ou*, such as *taste* <note>original: *goust*</note>. Sometimes we have even removed the accent entirely where he wrote *custom, to add* <note>original: *coustume, adiouster*</note>, etc.; he himself also writes, though rarely, *I added* <note>original: *i'adioutay*</note>, and once *I added* <note>original: *i'aioutay*</note> (folio 13 verso, lines 20 and 23). He willingly writes *to support* and *supported* <note>original: *soutenir* and *soutenu*</note>, although one also finds the versions with an 's' <note>original: *soustenir* and *soustenu*</note>: thus, in the space of only eight lines (folio 5 verso, lines 25-33), one finds *they support* <note>original: *soutienent*</note> once, *to support* <note>original: *soutenir*</note> twice, *supported* <note>original: *soustenu*</note> once, and *to support* <note>original: *soustenir*</note> twice; and further on, at a four-line interval (folio 6 verso and folio 7 recto), *supported* <note>original: *soustenu*</note> twice and *supported* <note>original: *soutenu*</note> once.

Finally, Descartes writes *us* where we today use *û*: for example, *to burn* <note>original: *brusler*</note>, etc. Let us note, however, that our *û* and even the unaccented *u* often correspond as much to the old form *eu* as to *us*, and that Descartes already uses it this way, as we have noted in *seen that, provided that, been able, known* <note>original: *vû que, pourvû que, pû, connû*</note>, etc. Sometimes the two old forms are found together: *that he should have* <note>original: *qu'il deust*</note>, *you read* <note>original: *vous-leustes*</note> (folio 25 verso, line 29). We have preserved one of the two in *that he had* <note>original: *qu'il eût*</note>, formerly written *that he had* <note>original: *qu'il eust*</note>.

2nd Our acute accent on the *e* (*é*) corresponds to the old form *es* (preserved, for example, in *to correspond* <note>original: *correspondre*</note>, but not in *to respond* <note>original: *répondre*</note>). Descartes usually employs *es*, though not always, for one also finds three forms for the same word:

> » which is in the optative forms, but that one pronounces it halfway, and that as
> » proof of this truth, it would be necessary to hear someone who had a
> » good pronunciation. »

Finally, pages 54-55: « If I am further reproached that there are terms from

> » pronounce it, such as *Master, to appear, to know* <note>original: *Maistre, parestre, connestre*</note>, and some

...es, é, e (just like the previous discussion regarding *eu, û, u*). Here, first, are the most frequent cases: *I was, been, to write, to testify, to be astonished, to clarify*, etc., *state, study*, etc. <note>original: *i'estois, esté, escrire, tesmoigner, s'estonner, esclaircir, estat, estude*</note>. But we also find *he answers* <note>original: *il repont*</note> and *he speaks of* <note>original: *il medit*</note>; we very often find *described* <note>original: *decrit* and *decrite*</note> (folio 15 recto, lines 4, 7, 9, and verso). In a letter from August 23, 1638, we find *they despise* <note>original: *ils mesprisent*</note> with an *s* rewritten above the word, which Descartes had initially written as *meprisent* (folio 20 recto, line 30). In this same letter, we find *I had miscalculated* <note>original: *ie m'estois meconté*</note> (folio 17 verso, line 27), and further on *I miscalculated* <note>original: *ie me suis mesconté*</note> (folio 20 verso, line 44), with an *s* rewritten above, Descartes having first written *meconté*. Finally, here are two last cases where his spelling fluctuates between *es, é*, and even *e* without an accent: we find on the same page and only a few lines apart, *distant* <note>original: *esloigné, éloigné* and *eloigné*</note> (folios 4, 5; notably folio 7 verso, lines 31 and 37), and again in the following letter from July 27, 1638 (folio 11 recto, lines 6, 28, 31, 32, 36); similarly, only four lines apart (folio 4 verso, lines 7 and 3 before the last), *distance* <note>original: *esloignement* and *éloignement*</note>.

The other case is that of the word *equal* <note>original: *égal*</note> and its derivatives: we find *esgal, égal,* and *egal*—that is to say, again the three forms *es, é,* and *e*. However, in the long letter of July 27, 1638 (folios 10 to 15, ten pages in total), the word *equal*, which appears so often, is written without an *s*. It seems that the words that appeared at every moment under Descartes’s pen—such as *equal* or *distant* in geometric demonstrations, or *describe* and *answer*—are also those where the *es* more easily becomes *é* or *e*. It is as if the letter wore out by force of being written so often, and was suppressed to save time. Furthermore, it is a matter of debate whether the mark found above this initial *é* is actually an acute accent, or rather a shorthand abbreviation for the *s* that he was avoiding writing in the body of the word: *égal* instead of *esgal*¹. Nevertheless, as we have seen, Descartes omits it entirely in *repont, medit, decrit*, etc.

-># ON DESCARTES' SPELLING.<-

an acute accent on the *e*; in the Clerselier edition (1657-1667), one often finds the word "this" printed as *cét*. Descartes, however, writes neither *cest* nor *cét*, but simply *cet*. <note>The author is comparing Descartes' 17th-century manuscript habits with the evolving standards of his early posthumous editors.</note>

3° There remains our grave accent. Sometimes it also corresponds to a separated letter, as in *quatrième* <note>fourth</note>, *etc.*, or *théorème* <note>theorem</note>, which Descartes wrote as *quatrième* and *theoresme*. At other times, it is a mark that corresponds to nothing in old French spelling: thus Descartes always writes *pere* <note>father</note>, *j'espere* <note>I hope</note>, *je considere* <note>I consider</note>, *diametre* <note>diameter</note>, etc. He is, however, acquainted with the grave accent, although he uses it very little; one can count the instances of the preposition *à* <note>to/at</note> with an accent (usually it is before the letter *a* when used as an algebraic symbol, to distinguish it from the latter); but most often he writes it like the verb *a* <note>has</note>, without an accent. One page is particularly remarkable in this regard (folio 11 recto); one finds there six instances of *à* with an accent, which is already rare, and perhaps more than twenty instances of the same preposition *a* without an accent. Descartes also did not accent the adverb of place *ou* <note>where</note>, leaving it the same as the conjunction *ou* <note>or</note>: only once or twice does one find *d'où il suit* <note>from where it follows</note>. — Let us note that, in the Clerselier edition (1657-1667), one finds an acute accent where we today place a grave accent: *troisième* <note>third</note>, *quatrième* <note>fourth</note>, etc. And later in the *Life of Mr. Des-Cartes* (1691), the syllables of the words *pere*, *espere*, etc., which were not yet accented in Clerselier, finally are, but with an acute accent: *pére*, *espére*, etc.

4° We can now speak of Descartes' accentuation. The acute accent is used on the *e* (*é*) at the end of words such as *vérité* <note>truth</note>, *extremité* <note>extremity</note>, *jeté* <note>thrown</note>, etc. Even then, this accent disappears in the plural when the form *és* is replaced by *ez*: *difficultez* <note>difficulties</note>, *procedez* <note>procedures/methods</note>, etc. It even disappears sometimes in the singular when a second *e* is added to the first to mark the feminine: *donnee* <note>given</note>, *nommee* <note>named</note>, *tiree* <note>drawn</note> (folio 48 recto, lines 15, 27).

The acute accent is also used at the beginning of words when the first syllable *es* is replaced by a simple *e*: *égal* <note>equal</note>, *éloigné* <note>distant</note>, etc. And even in this case, it does not always appear: one often finds *egal*, *eloigné*, *repondre* <note>to answer</note>, *medire* <note>to slander</note>, etc.

But this acute accent, which is found on the *é* as the first letter and on the *é* as the last letter of words, is always missing when the *e* is in the body of the words, such as *verité*, *procedé*, etc. (except for a few cases where *es* is replaced by *é*).

<summary>This page details René Descartes' specific orthographic habits regarding accents, noting his tendency to omit them in places where modern French or his early editors (like Clerselier) would require them.</summary>

<header>REMARKS</header>

The circumflex accent is not used on any of the vowels
*a, e, i, o* (Descartes writes *as, es, is, os*), but only on the
vowel *û*, when it is a contraction of *eu*, as in *vû* <note>seen</note>,
*pû* <note>been able</note>, *connû* <note>known</note>.

The grave accent is not used at all, except in very rare
exceptions, in *à* <note>to/at</note> as a preposition and *où* <note>where</note> as an adverb of place: even then, one most often finds this *a* and this *ou* without an accent.

But Descartes sometimes places a diaeresis (¨) over the *e* of the words
*rouë* <note>wheel</note>, *lieuë* <note>league</note>, *receuë* <note>received</note>. Yet one finds, in the same letter of
October 5, 1637, both *roue* and *rouë*; one also finds therein on two
occasions an *escrouë* <note>nut/scroll</note>. In the oldest autographs, this diaeresis
is placed on the last letter or on the penultimate indifferently
(*rouë* and *roüe*); later, it is found more often on the last¹.

As for the cedilla², Descartes uses it very irregularly: one
finds in his autographs both *façon* and *facon* <note>fashion/way</note>; *ie conçoy* and *ie concoy* <note>I conceive</note>.
He always writes *receu* <note>received</note>, and also always *scauoir, ie scauois* <note>to know, I knew</note>, etc.

When he elides the *a* or the *e* of the article, a pronoun, or a conjunction, sometimes he uses the apostrophe, sometimes he forgets to use it,
but in the latter case, he does not separate the article or the adjective from the following word. In
this last case, if the word begins with a *u*, this *u* no longer being
an initial letter, is not written as *v*: for example, *l'vn* and *lun* <note>the one</note>, *quelqu'vn* and
*quelquun* <note>someone</note>, etc.

The punctuation leaves much to be desired, much less so however in
the manuscripts than in the old editions, as is easy
to see in the letters, when one can compare the printed text
with an autograph; and this authorizes us to take some
liberties at least with the letters published by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the first editor of Descartes' letters</note>. Moreover,
Descartes himself expresses himself clearly on this subject, in a letter
of June 23, 1641: " *I pray you* ", he wrote to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk and mathematician who acted as a central hub for scientific correspondence in Europe</note>, " *to follow
» my copy, except that I may have omitted several periods and com-
» mas, which I would be very glad for someone to add; but the prin-
» ters have people who are accustomed to placing them, without it*

vowel from the *u* consonant. It is therefore on the *u* that it should have been regularly placed. (T).</margin>

2. <margin>The cedilla is an *e* written below the *c*, instead of being after it. By

## ON DESCARTES' SPELLING.

"there is no need for you to take the trouble." Let us say, finally, that in the three volumes edited by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes' primary editor and literary executor</note>, capital letters do not serve solely the same function as they do today. Thus, a capital was often placed on words like *For*, *But*, etc., after a semicolon, just as after a period; and in the middle of a sentence, nouns such as *Body*, *Animals*, *Stars*, *Salts*, etc., and even adjectives like *Geometric*, *Philosophical*, etc., very often have a capital letter, which was a way of drawing the reader's eye to a particular word. A significant fact: in the copy held by the Institute, whenever the words *Soul* and *Mind* <note>original: "Ame et Esprit"</note> happen to lack capitals, one of the annotators never fails to restore one in the margin—out of deference, no doubt, just as it is said that in conversation, Newton never pronounced the holy name of God without uncovering his head as a sign of respect. Nothing of the sort is found, moreover, except for rare exceptions, in Descartes' own autographs <note>term: autographs (original manuscripts written in the author's own hand)</note>.

### V. — OTHER SINGLE CONSONANTS.

1° At the end of words, the consonants *d* and *t* are sometimes used interchangeably; notably in the third person singular of the present indicative, Descartes writes *he sees* <note>original: "il void"</note>, *he concludes* <note>original: "il conclud"</note>. However, one also finds on the same page, *one takes* and *one hears* <note>original: "on prent" and "on entent"</note> (folio 2 recto), *he takes* and *he learns* (folio 17 recto, lines 3 and 35); ten lines apart, one finds *he learns* and *he depends* (folio 16 verso, lines 26 and 36); elsewhere *he answers* and *he answers*. One also finds *gallant* <note>original: "galand"</note>, with the plural *gallants*, and—a curious example—instead of *hot* <note>original: "chaud"</note>, once *hot* with an 'l' and 't' <note>original: "chault"</note> (folio 48 verso, line 24, November 1629), and another time, much later, *hot* with a 't' <note>original: "chaut"</note> (folio 44 verso, line 26, from April 26, 1647).

2° This last example shows us the very rare use of an *l*, in memory of the Latin <note>The Latin root for "hot" is "calidus," which explains the vestigial 'l' in older French spelling</note>. One also finds *thumb*, *high*, *it is necessary* <note>original: "poulce", "hault", "il fault"</note>, but only in the oldest autographs, those of November 1629 and January 1631 (folio 48 verso, line 27, and folios 46 and 47); even there, one finds both *high* <note>original: "hault"</note> and *high* <note>original: "hautes"</note> at the same time. But Descartes was not slow to discard this useless *l*; in the writing of October 5, 1637, one finds *thumb*, *high*, *it is necessary* <note>original: "pouce", "haut", "il faut"</note>.

3. Traces of Latin are less apparent in his writing than one might be inclined to believe: he does not write, as was common to write and print in his time, *double* <note>original: "doubte"</note>, *duty* <note>original: "debuoir"</note>, *written* <note>original: "escript"</note>, etc., but without the *b* or *p*: *doubt, duty, written* <note>original: "doute, deuoir, escrit"</note>, etc. He does, however, almost always write *to add* <note>original: "adiouster"</note>, except for one or two exceptions (folio 17 back, lines 23 and 38), *I added* and *added* <note>original: "i'aioutay" and "aiousté"</note>. But, instead of *to know, knowledge, known* <note>original: "cognoistre, cognoissance, cogneu"</note>, he writes *to know, knowledge* and even *known* without the *g*. — A remark, in passing, regarding the consonant *g*: Descartes preserves for it the same sound before *eu* as before *a, o, u*, and he writes *length* <note>original: "longueur"</note>, as well as *length* <note>The editor notes Descartes' consistent phonetic spelling here</note>.

4. The letter *h* is found not only in *method* and *philosophy, theorem, thesis, epithet, mathematics*, etc., but in *mechanics, author* and *authority, anger* <note>original: "cholere"</note>, *cord, school* and *scholar*. Once, however, we find *cord* <note>original: "corde"</note> (folio 24 back, line 28, from March 4, 1641), with *cords* <note>original: "chordes"</note> five lines lower (line 33), and another time *scholar* <note>original: "escolier"</note> (folio 18 back, line 31); but these two words without the *h* are rare. We also find *gibberish* <note>original: "galimathias"</note> (folio 20 front, line 34). Several times, however, Descartes writes *library* <note>original: "biblioteque"</note>, without the *h*; in a very old letter from January 1631, the *h* first written at the end of *Saint Elizabeth* is visibly crossed out; but later it reappears in *Her Highness* the Princess *Elizabeth*. Would one also find *Bohemia* <note>original: "Boëme"</note> without the *h*, as it actually appears in the copy of a letter from Descartes to Pollot, or is it the copyist who did not take the trouble to write the letter *h* here? The fact remains that Descartes suppresses it once more in *isochronous* <note>original: "isocrone"</note> (folio 33 front, line 12), once even in *parhelia* <note>original: "parelies" - an optical phenomenon of "mock suns"</note> (May 9/19, 1635), and in the Latin word *deluded* <note>original: "allucinatus"</note> (October 28, 1640)¹.

6th. Finally, the consonant *s* alternates with *z* in two or three singular cases. The word *base* (the base of a triangle) is found written by Descartes on the same page (folio 15 verso) four times as *baze*, twelve times as *base*, and three times with both *s* and *z*, where one is rewritten over the other. In the same letter, one usually finds *he weighs* <note>original: "il pese"</note>; once, however, Descartes writes *peze* (folio 7 verso, line 2), and a little further on a second time, but with an *s* rewritten over the *z* (line 30), and on the following page, a third time *peze*, without erasure (folio 8 recto, line 5). Already in a letter of February 2, 1632, one found *vase* once and *vaze* twice.

## VI. — DOUBLE CONSONANTS.

But one of the characteristic features of Descartes's spelling is the suppression or retention of double consonants, depending on the case and especially on the letters. Let us review the list of consonants from this point of view.

1. The cases where *b* is doubled are quite rare: once, however, Descartes writes *M. l'Abé de Launay* <note>Abbot de Launay; modern French: Abbé</note> (folio 27 verso, line 2, dated June 23, 1641).
On the other hand, he writes *accord* <note>agreement</note> and *accorder* <note>to grant/agree</note>, and even most often *deffendre* <note>to defend; modern: défendre</note>, and almost always *affîn que* <note>so that; modern: afin que</note>. He always writes *aggregat* <note>aggregate</note>, and once even he *exaggeroit* <note>was exaggerating</note>.

2. He also doubles, though not always, the letter *l*. We find *rouleau* <note>roll/roller</note> and *roller* <note>to roll</note> (October 5, 1637), and even later *poulle* <note>hen</note> in the same letter as *poulet* <note>chicken</note> (folio 41 recto, line 7, and verso, line 10). He writes *Claircellier* (folio 37 verso, line 26), and not *Clerselier* <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the editor of Descartes' letters</note>. He signs *vostre fidelle serviteur* <note>your faithful servant; modern: fidèle</note> (folio 38 recto and folio 43 recto). Once he even writes *immobille* <note>immobile</note>. But one finds on the same page *falloit* and *faloit* <note>it was necessary; modern: fallait</note> (folio 27 recto, lines 22 and 29). In the oldest letter one finds *on appelle* <note>one calls</note> (folio 48 recto, line 16, November 1629) for *appelle*, and elsewhere the two nouns *bale* <note>ball; modern: balle</note> (folio 12 verso, lines 8 and 14; and folio 19 verso, line 7) and *sale* <note>room; modern: salle</note> (folio 19 verso, line 9), for *balle* and *salle*, then *intervale* <note>interval</note> and *valée* <note>valley</note>.
Is this a mistake? Is it written intentionally? One reads once or twice *evidemment* <note>evidently</note> with *nm* instead of two *m*s (folio 22 verso, line 10). He writes *enflamé* <note>inflamed</note>, and usually one finds a single *m*, but by abbreviation, this *m* being topped with a macron <note>original: "tiret" (dash/line)</note> which indicates the other absent *m*: *coment* <note>how</note>, *home* <note>man</note>, *comode* <note>convenient</note>, *comun* <note>common</note>, etc.

3. But in many cases where we double the letter *n*, Descartes contents himself with a single *n*. For example, instead of writing *mienne* and *tienne* <note>mine and yours (feminine)</note>, he simply puts *miene* and *tiene*, as if it were enough for the feminine to add a silent *e* to the masculine *mien* and *tien*, without doubling the consonant *n*. In the third persons singular and plural of certain verbs, he writes *qu'il viene* <note>that he comes</note> and *qu'ils viennent* <note>that they come</note>, *tiene* and *tiennent*, *prene* and *prenent* <note>take</note>, etc.; likewise for all their derivatives. He similarly writes *Sorbone* <note>The Sorbonne university</note> with a single *n* (folio 25 recto, lines 14 and 26), and, although one most often finds *Mercenne*, one should not be surprised if one also encounters *Mercene* <note>Referring to Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), Descartes' main correspondent</note>.

4. The *p*, like the *l*, is sometimes doubled and sometimes not; let us add that most often it is. In the *Examination of the Geostatic Question* (July 13, 1638), one finds *l'apprens* <note>I learn it</note>, *nous supposerons* <note>we will suppose</note>, *il s'approche* <note>he approaches</note>, *rapporter* <note>to report/relate</note>, which is all the more remarkable as the same words are printed, in Volume I of the *Letters*, with a single *p*. 6° But the most remarkable case is that of the letter *t*. In the earliest autographs (from November 1629 and January 1631), this letter is doubled, it seems, more than is reasonable: *prattique* <note>practice</note>, *droitte* <note>straight/right</note>, *suitte* <note>sequel/result</note>, *ietté* <note>thrown</note>; this would still be the common spelling used by the annotators of the copy of the *Letters* kept at the Institute between 1684 and 1704.
