<page-num>102</page-num>
<header>REMARKS</header>

are always found in Descartes' original manuscripts not only without a *c*, but with a single *t*. — Let us conclude with a small word on which Descartes never varies: *cete*, the feminine form of the demonstrative adjective *cet* <note>modern French: "cette" (this/that)</note>; the addition of a silent *e* is sufficient to mark the feminine, without it being useful to double the preceding consonant *t* and write *cette*. Furthermore, the old form *cest* gave the feminine *ceste*, and as Descartes wrote *cet* in the masculine by removing the *s*, he likewise had to write the feminine *cete* for *ceste*.

->CONCLUSION.<-

Let us summarize all these remarks and outline the rules of Descartes' orthography. Here are the principal ones:
The equivalence of the letters *u* and *v*, each of the two having its designated place: *v* at the beginning and *u* in the body of words <note>This was a common printing convention in the 17th century where "v" and "u" were variants of the same letter.</note>.
Frequent use of *y* for *i*, either at the end of words (*moy* <note>me</note>, *soy* <note>oneself</note>, *ie voy* <note>I see</note>, *ie croy* <note>I believe</note>, *vny* <note>united</note>, *marry* <note>sorry/vexed</note>, etc.), or in the interior (*ayder* <note>to help</note>, *aymer* <note>to love</note>, *aysé* <note>easy</note>, *aygu* <note>sharp</note>, etc.), and always an *i* where we today place a *j*.
The diphthong *oi* for *ai* in the imperfect tense of verbs, and in certain nouns and adjectives <note>e.g., "disoit" instead of "disait".</note>.
The diphthong *an*, which was the only one used at first in endings, is soon reserved for present participles (*pliant* <note>bending</note>, *bruslant* <note>burning</note>, etc.) and for certain nouns and adjectives (*enfant* <note>child</note>, *grand* <note>tall/great</note>, etc.); it is replaced by *en* in most substantives and adverbs (*moment*, *clairement* <note>clearly</note>, etc.).
The consonant *s*, when added to the end of words, generally causes the preceding *t* to drop (*momens*, *enfans*), often also the *d* (*i'apprens* <note>I learn</note>) and the *t* (*les poins* <note>the points</note>), sometimes even the *p* (*tems* <note>time</note>).
Finally, the same letter *s*, joined to vowels or diphthongs in the body of words, indicates what was later replaced by an accent (grave, acute, or circumflex) <note>For example, "estre" became "être".</note>.
The use of other consonants is generally reduced to the strict minimum, except in two or three cases, such as *i'obmets* <note>I omit</note>, *adiouster* <note>to add</note>, *scauoir* <note>to know</note>, etc.

<summary>This page concludes a linguistic study of René Descartes' handwriting, detailing his specific spelling rules such as the use of 'y' for 'i' and the omission of silent consonants. It provides a concise summary of 17th-century orthographic conventions as practiced by the philosopher.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, orthography, French linguistics, 17th-century grammar, paleography, spelling conventions, etymology</keywords>

--- Page 109 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of René Descartes' orthography, specifically focusing on his simplification of consonant usage and his philosophical approach to language.</meta>

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>ON THE ORTHOGRAPHY OF DESCARTES.</header>

Finally, while it was common practice to double consonants in the feminine form and elsewhere, Descartes prefers the single letter, at least for *t* and *n*, and already for *l* and *p* as well, though not yet for *f, c, g*.

In short, despite many uncertainties and fluctuations, Descartes' spelling is most often in harmony with the very genius of the French language and the genius of the author himself. At times he abandons an excessive uniformity that gave rise to confusion (such as using *ant* everywhere as the ending for nouns, adjectives, and adverbs; or using the letter *s* as the sole and unique mark of the plural in all cases), and he introduces into word forms a variety favorable to "clarity" and "distinction"¹. <note>These are central terms in Cartesian philosophy: a "clear and distinct" idea is one that is so self-evident it cannot be doubted.</note> At other times he seeks simplicity, which also makes forms clearer and more distinct, either by removing superfluous consonants, such as *t, d, p*, before the *s* that joins them, or by avoiding the doubling of a *t* and an *n*, and sometimes also an *l* and a *p*, where nothing requires it—neither the need to mark the feminine gender nor the pronunciation. As for Latin etymology, one finds in Descartes no pedantic affectation to make it stand out by adding useless letters to French words; how often, on the contrary, does he remove a *b*, a *g*, or an *s* that his contemporaries maintained! However, he early on gave up the form *tans* <note>original: "tans" (an archaic spelling of 'temps' or time)</note> to write *tems*, but without inserting the *p* from the Latin *tempus* <note>original: "tempus" (time)</note>, even though he has a marked tendency to incorporate the *p* from *corpus* <note>original: "corpus" (body)</note> into the French *corps*; as for another word, *aer* <note>original: "aer" (air)</note> (which is found in his oldest autographs, folio 48 verso, lines 22 and 28, November 1629), he quickly gave it up to write *air*.

Descartes' orthography is therefore worth being exactly reproduced in a new edition of his works, not only for the greater joy of lovers of old language, and for the very legitimate satisfaction of philologists <note>scholars of historical language and literary texts</note>, but because one—

one finds even in the forms of the words the personal mark of the philosopher. Furthermore, this language is entirely embellished with old expressions, such as *once again* <note>original: "derechef"</note>, *remembrance* <note>original: "souuenance"</note> and *to remember* <note>original: "ressouuenir"</note>, *to hear* <note>original: "ouyr"</note>, etc., along with old phrasings, such as *the wherefores* <note>original: "les pour ce que"</note> and *the even-thoughs* <note>original: "les encore que"</note>, which he does not fear to overuse, in order to clearly show the solid framework of the sentences and to make their joints stand out; all of this also seems to require, it appears, an old orthography, especially if one prints with ancient characters and in the old format: our modern ways of writing would create the most shocking disparity with such a text. We will therefore scrupulously provide the spelling of Descartes, without omitting the slightest peculiarity (nor even the slightest error), whenever it is possible—that is to say, whenever we have the text written in his own hand.

For all the rest, we will follow the oldest editions, those which appeared during his lifetime and for which he himself corrected the text while it was being printed.

For the posthumous edition of the *Letters* (1657-1667), we will reproduce the text as it was given by Charles Angot, the printer of the three volumes, while taking some liberties, however—as he certainly took himself—regarding punctuation and capital letters. A difficulty arose, however: the first volume had three successive editions (1657, 1663, and 1667); now, the spelling varies from 1657 to 1663, and it is also not the same from 1663 to 1667. The question would become delicate if these changes constituted progress; but they seem due simply to the fact that the printer had changed typesetters. Thus the 2nd edition gave *grans* <note>great/large</note> (p. 34, l. 24), and the 3rd *grands*, which is perhaps more regular; but elsewhere the 2nd gives *jusques* <note>until</note> (p. 34, l. 23), *j’espère* <note>I hope</note> (p. 92, l. 12), *j’ay dit* <note>I have said</note> (p. 36, l. 24), *toû-jours* <note>always</note> (p. 46, 54, 128, 191, etc.), and the 3rd, on the same pages, *iusques*, *j’espere*, *j’ay dit*, *tousiours*, etc. It is also curious to note on the copy at the Institute the changes that the annotators from 1684 to 1704 would have brought to the text printed in 1667: *parce que* <note>because</note> substituted almost everywhere for *pource que* <note>for that/because</note>, and *dans* <note>in</note> for *en* <note>in/within</note> (e.g., *in the mind*, *in his letters*, etc.), so much so that more than one correction by their hands, which one would be tempted to take for a variation, is not in the least a return to the old text of Descartes, but a simple modernization of style. We will therefore stick to the...

<header>ON THE SPELLING OF DESCARTES.</header>

## ON THE SPELLING OF DESCARTES.

Letters, in the absence of an original autograph <note>A manuscript written in the author's own hand.</note> or a handwritten copy, follow the text of Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the primary editor and translator of Descartes' works after his death.</note> as it was printed by Charles Angot in 1667 for the first volume (third edition) and for the third, and in 1666 for the second (second edition).

Thus, one will find everywhere either the spelling of Descartes himself, or at the very least that of his time. And as this is a part—however small one may wish to consider it—of his habits and his character as a writer, we shall not allow ourselves to change anything, any more than one would change his costume or the slightest features of his face in an engraving where one intended to represent him as he truly was.

C. A. <note>Likely the initials of the editor or the publisher Charles Angot.</note>

## I.

### ->DESCARTES TO HIS ELDER BROTHER.<-

->April 3, 1622.<-

->AUTOGRAPH NO. 1, Victor Cousin Library.<-

The undersigned binds myself to Mr. Pierre Descartes, Counselor to the King in the Parliament of Brittany <note>The Parliament of Brittany was a sovereign judicial court; Pierre held a prestigious legal position there</note>, my brother, not to sell the properties included in the power of attorney <note>original: "procuration"</note> which he gave to me this day, for a price less than the sum of eight thousand crowns <note>original: "huict mil escus"; the écu was a high-value gold or silver coin</note>, namely: ten thousand livres <note>The livre was the standard unit of currency in France at the time</note> for the house and garden in the city of Poitiers, and fourteen thousand livres for the lands located at Availles, unless it be by his consent; and in the event that I sell the said things, to return the said sum, or a greater one if I am able to receive it from the sale of the said properties, to the total of the estates <note>original: "successions"</note> of the late Ladies Jeanne Sain, my grandmother, J. Brochard, my mother, and J. Brochard, Lady of Archangé, my aunt, coming to partition <note>This refers to the legal division of an inheritance among heirs</note>. Done at Rennes, this third day of April, one thousand six hundred twenty-two.

# CORRESPONDENCE.

This document, which Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes' first major biographer.</note> was aware of (see Letter II below), currently bears the following note:
"Autograph of my great-uncle the illustrious René Descartes. I am at this moment the sole descendant of Pierre, his eldest brother; my father's mother, Silvie Descartes, was the last of Pierre's line. July 17, 1834. H. de Châteaugiron."
When Descartes entered into this obligation, he had just returned to France, from which he had been absent since May 1617. He arrived in Rennes around the middle of March 1622, having given up his military career. He "was then twenty-six years old, and his father took the occasion of his reaching legal majority to put him in possession of his mother's estate, two-thirds of which he had already given to his elders: one to Mr. de la Bretaillière, his brother, and the other to Madame du Crevis, his sister." (BAILLET, *The Life of Mr. Des-Cartes*, vol. I, p. 106.) Regarding Descartes' share, see the following letter.

# CORRESPONDANCE.

perhaps Jean Silhon (See BAILLET, vol. I, p. 144), who himself presented these *Letters* in a preface to Cardinal Richelieu.

Clerselier *gives no date*. But D. Nisard, in his *History of French Literature* (Paris, Didot, 1844, vol. II, p. 6, *note preserved in subsequent editions*), mentions a *letter from Balzac dated March 30, 1628, thanking Descartes for his apology* <note>In this context, "apology" refers to a formal written defense of someone's character or ideas.</note>. We have been unable to find any other traces of this thank-you note.

The *Letters of the Lord of Balzac* had, in fact, sparked numerous criticisms from the moment of their appearance, such as: *The True Comic History of Francion*, by Charles Sorel (Paris, Billaine, 1624, octavo, privilege of August 5); *Response of the Lord Hydaspe to the Lord of Balzac*, by Father Garasse, 1624; *Letter from Théophile against Balzac to Eudoxus, 1624*; *Letter from M. de Croisilles to M. the Count of Cramail* (Paris, 1625, octavo), etc.

They were defended by François Ogier (*Apology for M. de Balzac*, Paris, Cl. Morlot, 1627, quarto, privilege of March 26; reprinted, vol. II, 2nd part, p. 105-159 of the Works of M. de Balzac, 1665), who added, as a supporting document, a *Conformity of the Eloquence of M. de Balzac with that of the greatest men of the past and present*, by *Brother André of St-Denis*. Descartes, in several places which will be pointed out hereafter, seems to have been inspired by *Ogier’s Apology*, of whom he remained a friend. The library of Carcassonne preserves a copy of the *Principles of Philosophy*, sent on September 18, 1644, with these words on the first page:
> "Descartes proposes [this work] to be judged by François Ogier, a senator of keen judgment." <note>original: "Fo Ogier acris iudicij senatori censenda proponit Des Cartes."</note>

But *Descartes’ letter* appears to respond particularly to a new attack directed against Balzac by *Father Goulu* (Dom Jean of St. Francis, General of the Feuillants <note>A reformed branch of the Cistercian Catholic religious order.</note>, died January 5, 1629): *Letters from Phylarchus to Aristus*, dealing with French eloquence, first part (Paris, Nicolas Buon, 1627, octavo, privilege of September 18). See EMILE ROY, *On Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac against Dom Jean Goulu, thesis*, Paris, Hachette, 1892.

According to Borel (See BAILLET, vol. I, p. 139 and following) Descartes had, as early as 1625, defended Balzac against Father Goulu before the Cardinal-Legate Barberini, whom he had met in Rome. However, the indication given by Nisard seems to better match the probable date of *Descartes’ letter*. The latter was in Brittany during the winter of 1628 (where, on January 22, he was godfather at Elven to a son of his eldest brother), then, in the autumn of the same year, at the camp before La Rochelle <note>Referring to the Siege of La Rochelle, a major military event in the struggle between the French royal forces and the Huguenots.</note>. *In the meantime, he undoubtedly came to Paris*.

### *To the Most Illustrious Gentleman \*\*\*\*\**
### *A Critique of certain Letters*
### *of Monsieur de Balzac.* <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654) was a founding member of the Académie Française, famous for his "Letters" which set new standards for French eloquence.</note>

## *Most Illustrious Sir,*

With whatever intention I read these Letters, whether to examine them seriously or rather to take delight in them, they satisfy me so greatly that I not only find nothing that ought to be criticized, but even among such excellent qualities, I cannot easily judge what should be especially praised. For there is in them a purity of expression, just as there is health in a human body—which is surely to be believed at its best when it leaves no conscious sensation of itself. <note>The author suggests that perfect style, like perfect health, is so natural that it does not draw attention to its own mechanics.</note> There is, moreover, an elegance and charm, like beauty in a perfectly formed woman; namely, a beauty which consists not in this or that single feature, but in such a harmony and temperament of all parts that no one part can be singled out as more eminent than the rest, lest at the same time the poorly preserved proportion of the others be accused of imperfection. <insert>as noted in the margin</insert> But just as the individual parts of beauty are easily distinguished among the blemishes and defects of the forms we are accustomed to seeing—and some of these are sometimes worthy of such great praise that we may best estimate from them how much greater would be the merits of a form perfect in every detail, if such a one were found—in a similar way, if I turn my mind to the writings of others, I often count many virtues of speech in them, specifically because they are marked by a mixture of certain faults. And since those virtues even there do not lack their own praise, I perceive from this all the more clearly how much more...

# CORRESPONDENCE. I. 463-464.

<page-num>8</page-num>

...of the choices to be made here, where they exist in their pure state. For among other writers, if perhaps some choice words, arranged in a careful order and poured forth in a generous style, satisfy the ears to no small degree, in that same place the meaning is for the most part lowly; and being scattered throughout a vast oration, it frustrates the attentive mind. If, on the other hand, highly significant expressions delight more capable minds with an abundance of noble thoughts, they more often weary those same minds with a compressed and somewhat obscure style. If there are some who, holding a middle ground between these extremes, more rigidly observe the true purpose of speech in expressing pure matters, they are so austere that they are not loved by those of delicate taste. If, finally, some exercise the gentler muses in wit and jokes, almost all of them misplace the beauty of their speech—either in the feigned majesty of obsolete words, or in the noise of foreign ones, or in the softness of new ones*, or in ridiculous ambiguities, or in poetic thoughts, false reasonings, and childish cleverness. <margin>a. Read: *atqui* [but/and yet] (?).</margin> And yet these trifles can no more please men of a more serious character than the follies of actors or the gestures of apes. In these Letters, however, the richness of the most elegant speech—which alone could suffice to fill the minds of readers—does not scatter or overwhelm the strength of the arguments; and the dignity of the sentiments, which could easily sustain itself by its own weight, is not oppressed by any poverty of expression. Instead, thoughts of the highest spirit, and removed from the common crowd, are expressed with the greatest accuracy in words frequent in the mouths of men and refined by long usage. And from such a happy harmony of matter and speech, certain easy graces arise*, no less different from those artificial ones by which the common people are accustomed to be deceived, than...

->...the natural complexion of a most beautiful girl differs from the red lead and white lead <note>minium and cerussa: toxic pigments used in early modern cosmetics</note> used by itching old women.<-

And let these things indeed be said concerning style, which would be almost the only thing to consider in this genre of writing, were it not that these letters possessed a deeper wisdom than those commonly sent to friends. Truly, because they frequently treat arguments no less significant than the very speeches delivered publicly by ancient orators*, something must be said regarding that extraordinary science of persuasion, which is usually required for the completion of eloquence. This science, moreover, has had its own virtues and its own vices among different peoples.

For in the first and uncultivated ages, before any discords yet existed in the world, and when the tongue followed the affections of a candid mind without reluctance, there was indeed in the greater spirits a certain divine force of eloquence. This force, flowing from a zeal for truth and an abundance of feeling, led rude men out of the forests, imposed laws, founded cities, and possessed the power of persuading and ruling simultaneously*. But a little later, among the Greeks and Romans, the contention of the forum and the frequency of public assemblies corrupted it while exercising it too much. For it passed down to common men who, despairing of conquering the minds of their listeners in open warfare <note>original: "aperto Marte"</note> and with the resources of truth alone, took refuge in sophisms and empty traps of words. Although they not infrequently deceived the unwary with these, they had no better right to compete for oratorical praise with their predecessors than traitors have to compete for true fortitude with courageous soldiers. And although they sometimes applied their painted reasons even to the patronage of truth, they nevertheless placed the chief glory of their art in sustaining the worse causes.

<meta>This page continues a discussion regarding the literary style and moral character of the French author Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac. The previous context likely compared him to ancient orators.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>
<header>CORRESPONDENCE. I, 464-465.</header>

I consider those men to have been most wretched in this regard: that they could not be the best orators without appearing to be evil men <note>original: "mali homines viderentur." This refers to the classical debate on whether a great orator must also be a "good man."</note>. Here, truly, Balzac explains whatever needs to be said with such powerful reasoning, and illustrates it with such grand examples, that I greatly admire how a certain vehemence in his style and a natural impulse are not broken by careful art. Instead, amidst the elegancies and ornamentation of the current age, he retains the strength and majesty of the eloquence of former times. For he does not take advantage of the reader's simplicity, but is accustomed to using those arguments which, although they are so clear that they easily find belief among the common people, are nonetheless so solid and true that the greater a person's talent <term>ingenium: innate intellectual ability or genius</term>, the more certainly he is convinced by them. This is especially true whenever he proves nothing other than what he has first persuaded himself to believe.

For although he is not unaware that paradoxes <note>original: "paradoxa." In this context, statements that seem self-contradictory but may express a truth.</note> can sometimes be adorned with true reasons, and although he declines dangerous truths in certain places with the most prudent art, there is nevertheless in his writings a certain noble liberty which sufficiently indicates that he endures nothing more reluctantly than to lie <note>original: "mentiri."</note>. Hence, if he ever undertakes to describe the vices of the nobility, he is not prevented from speaking the truth by a servile fear of power; if he describes virtues, he is not prevented by any malice of mind. If, however, he begins a discourse about himself, he dreads neither contempt by exposing the diseases of his body and the weakness of his nature, nor envy by not concealing the deserved praises of his own talent. I am not unaware that this can be taken in a worse sense by many at first sight; for vices are so frequent in this age, and virtues so rare, that whenever the same effect can be attributed to an honorable or a shameful cause, one does not doubt...

He defends Balzac's habit of speaking openly about his own strengths and physical ailments as a sign of noble sincerity rather than vanity.</summary>

<page-num>II</page-num>
<header>VI. — 1628.</header>
<sig>I, 465-466.</sig>

<margin>5</margin> mortals attempt to judge, according to what happens all too often. However, whoever notices that this same Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654), a foundational figure in French prose known for his published letters</note> freely declares in his writings not only the good, but also the bad—both his own and that of others—will surely never believe that such diverse habits exist in the same man: that he would at one moment disclose the disgraces of others through malignant recklessness, and at another, their good deeds through timid flattery; or that he would now describe his own infirmities through a certain baseness of soul, and then his excellent qualities through a desire for empty glory. Rather, one would believe that he is simply unable to conceal all these things—just as he perceives them to be—out of a love for truth and through an inherent nobility of spirit.

<margin>10</margin> Fair-minded posterity will recognize this <term>candor</term> <note>original: "candorem"; implies a shining honesty or purity of intent</note> and these ancient manners of a mind set above the common crowd, even if now, while the man is living, envious mortals refuse to admit so sublime a kind of virtue. For such is the depravity of the human race that, just as being chaste or sober is mocked in a gathering of corrupt youth, so it is that being high-minded and truthful is turned into a vice by almost everyone. False accusations are heard much more greedily than true praises, especially whenever excellent men wish to speak of themselves; for then, truth is most often attributed to pride, while concealment and lying are attributed to moderation.

<margin>15</margin> From this source, the infamous pamphlets against Balzac found such plausible material for accusation that they could join any other charges—no matter how unjust or ridiculous—to this "capital" offense. At the same time, the unskillful <term>common crowd</term> <note>original: "vulgus"</note> accepted them all as if they were validated by the popularity of this primary charge. And certainly, in this matter, it seems tragic to me that so many of those who consider themselves to be "Somebody" are included under the designation of the "Common Crowd."

The date and the recipient of this fragment are unknown. The Institute copy only provides conjectures in the margin drawn from the text:
<margin>“To one of Mr. D.’s friends in Paris, perhaps to Mr. Mydorge: it was written on October 20, 1629. See the reasons for this in the new notebook.”</margin>
*But Mydorge is excluded, because Descartes did not have to particularly recommend Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier, an instrument maker who worked with Descartes on lens-grinding</note> to him, and because, on the other hand, it clearly emerges from letter XIX hereafter (CLERSELIER, vol. II, p. 520) that, on March 4, 1630, Descartes had not yet written to Mydorge and that the latter still did not know his address in Holland, etc. I estimate that the letter, published by Clerselier from a draft <term>minute: a rough draft or original copy of a legal or formal document</term> which bore no heading (he likely added "Sir"), is the first that Descartes wrote from Holland to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a Minim friar and central figure in the 17th-century scientific "Republic of Letters"</note>. The latter, having obtained Descartes' address through Ferrier, seems to have asked him a question entirely analogous to the one he had posed to Beeckman shortly before (See letter X below); he likely supported Ferrier to help him obtain lodgings at the Louvre <note>The Louvre at this time housed various artists and craftsmen under royal protection</note>. The Minim <note>Mersenne, belonging to the Order of Minims</note> does not seem, moreover, to have preserved this first letter from Descartes; but perhaps he kept a continuation of it, which Descartes, conversely, had not written as a draft. The Lahire collection indeed included, under No. 1, an undated fragment prior to letter XIV below (from November 13, 1629), and it is not clear what this lost fragment could have contained, if not a request for information on the parhelia <note>parhelia: "sun dogs" or atmospheric optical phenomena</note> observed in Rome (See letter X). The present letter, under this hypothesis, would have left Amsterdam at the latest on September 25, 1629, but it may be earlier by one or several weeks. It is unknown, furthermore, if at the end of September, Descartes had already left Franeker; Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, Descartes' early biographer</note> indicates, but without precise proof—

### IX. — SEPTEMBER 1629.

...you deign to do something on my behalf; this gives me a better opinion of myself, and grants me such vanity that I dare to undertake recommending the same Mr. Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier was a skilled lens-grinder whom Descartes hoped would help him realize his optical theories</note> to you more particularly. There is a branch of Mathematics that I call the **science of miracles**, because it teaches one to use air and light so effectively that, by its means, one can display all the same illusions that they say Magicians make appear with the help of Demons. This science has never yet been practiced, as far as I know, and I know no one but him who is capable of it; but I maintain that he could achieve such things there that, even though I greatly despise such trifles, I will nonetheless not hide from you that if I could have drawn him away from Paris, I would have kept him here specifically to have him work on it, and to spend with him the hours I would otherwise waste in gambling or in useless conversations.

### X.
## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.
### October 8, 1629.

Text from the copy at the Institute, volume II, letter 112, pages 529-533.

*Variants according to the text by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the primary editor and translator of Descartes' posthumous works</note>. — The date is only provided on the Institute's copy, with the marginal note: <margin>I have the manuscript letter.</margin> This original by Descartes, like many other letters from him to Mersenne, was never part of the Lahire collection. It was likely written in Amsterdam, as Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, Descartes' early biographer</note> asserts (vol. I, p. 191).*

### My Reverend Father,

I do not think I have been so uncivil as to beg you not to propose any questions to me; it is too much honor you do me when it pleases you to take the trouble, and I learn more by this means than by any other kind of study. But I have no doubt requested you not to take it amiss if I do not strive to answer them as precisely as I would try to do if I were not entirely occupied with other thoughts: for I do not have a mind strong enough to employ it at the same time on several different things; and as I never find anything except by a long train of various considerations, I must give myself entirely to one subject when I wish to examine any part of it.

# II, 532. X. — 8 October 1629.

The Treble <note>original: "Deffus"; the highest part in a musical composition</note>, which is accustomed to moving by conjunct degrees <note>moving step-by-step along the scale</note>, suddenly makes a leap as far as a Fifth <term>Fifth: an interval encompassing five notes of the scale</term>, and the Bass, which is accustomed to moving by larger intervals, ascending only by a Third <term>Third: an interval encompassing three notes of the scale</term>, moves only in its ordinary manner; but in the latter case, it seems that both parts descend equally; for the leap of a Fifth in the Bass is hardly more than that of a Third in the Treble <note>original: "Superius"</note>; thus there is not much variety in this latter movement, which makes it sad and unpleasant. Add to this that, all things being equal, when the parts ascend, they awaken the attention much more than when they descend. This is all that comes to my pen regarding this.

<meta>This page continues a technical discussion regarding the physics of falling bodies and pendulums, likely from a letter by René Descartes. It follows a mathematical demonstration of how the length of a cord affects the time (measured in "moments") it takes for a weight to swing.</meta>

# CORRESPONDENCE. II, 532-533.

If the cord is 2 feet long, it will require 4/3 of a moment; if it is 4 feet, 16/9 of a moment; if 8 feet, 64/27; if 16 feet, 256/81, which is hardly more than 3 moments; and so on for the others. I am not telling you, however, exactly how long the cord must be for the weight to take precisely two moments to travel from C to B; for that would not result in such a simple number, and the <term>calculation</term><note>Descartes often found the extraction of roots or complex ratios "uneasy" or tedious compared to geometric proofs.</note> would be difficult for me to perform. But you can see, in proportion to the others, that it would have to be more than 5 times longer; thus, the fact that it is shorter is due to the <term>resistance of the air</term><note>original: "empefchement de l'air." This refers to air resistance or drag, which Descartes recognizes as a factor that slows the pendulum's motion compared to a theoretical vacuum.</note>, in which two things must be considered: namely, how much it hinders at the start of the movement, and how much thereafter. Now, one must compare both of these to the increase in the speed of the movement that would occur in a <term>vacuum</term><note>original: "efpace vuide." Descartes famously denied the existence of a true vacuum, but uses the concept here as a mathematical ideal.</note>, which is very difficult—and much more so in a circular motion than if you were to let the weight descend in a straight line.

As for what pertains to the motions and returns of the weight from C to <insert>D</insert> <note>original Latin: "Quod attinet ad motus et reditus ponderis a C ad..." This marks a transition from French to Latin in the manuscript.</note>

Page 23, line 2. — The phenomenon of *Parhelia* or "false suns," observed at Frascati on March 20, 1629, by Father Scheiner, a Jesuit; Cardinal Barberini had immediately sent a description of it to Peiresc. The latter made several copies which he distributed to scholars. Gassendi, who was then traveling in Holland with his friend Lullier, received one. In Amsterdam, he had made the acquaintance of two friends of Descartes: a physician, Waessenaer (whose son we will find in 1640 engaged in a mathematical quarrel), and Henry Reneri, who was primarily occupied with philosophy. He promised them both, upon leaving for Utrecht on July 10, a description of the phenomenon along with the discourse sent from Rome and his own explanation. Waessenaer and Reneri received the description first, and Reneri immediately sent it to Descartes, also asking for his explanation in order to compare it to the one he would receive from Gassendi. This latter explanation was sent from The Hague on July 14 (*Works of Gassendi*, Lyon, Laurent Anisson, 1658, vol. III, p. 651). Descartes took more time to provide his own (BAILLET, *Life of Mr. Descartes*, vol. I, p. 188). The first draft by Gassendi was first printed under this title: *A Rare Phenomenon Observed at Rome on March 20 and an Explanation of its Causes* (Amsterdam, Henrici Guerardi, 1629, in-quarto); then the following year, with additions and corrections, under this second title: *Parhelia, or Four False Suns which Appeared Around the True One at Rome on the Day of March 20, 1629, and a Letter Concerning Them to Henry Reneri* (Paris, Vitré, 1630, in-quarto).

Page 23, line 3. — The new reading accords better with the two dates of July 14 (when Gassendi sent his description) and October 8, 1629 (the date of this letter).

Page 23, line 17. — "It was possible that the good Father Mersenne had inadvertently taken the word *Tusculi* <note>The Latin name for Frascati, near Rome.</note>, which was in the original sent from Rome by Cardinal Barberini, for the city of Tivoli." Page 24, line 3. — An important new reading: Descartes, at this date, wrote primarily in Latin, especially on philosophical and scientific matters, as evidenced by the *Meditations* which were at least drafted during this same year, 1629.

Page 24, line 10. — Isaac Beeckman <note>A Dutch philosopher and scientist who was an early mentor to Descartes.</note>. Mersenne seems to have entered into a correspondence with him around the month of July 1629 by asking him the same question about music that he addressed a little later to Descartes (see letter IX). Beeckman replied to him, in a lost letter, as vaguely, it seems, as Descartes did, but already making allusion to the latter in terms that can be guessed from the following letter from Beeckman to Mersenne (National Library, French collection, new acquisitions 6206, folio 43), written around the month of August and responding to new questions. Here is the beginning of that letter, which Mersenne must have already had in his hands when he wrote to Descartes regarding Beeckman:

> "I am not surprised, most learned man, that a man so learned and devoted to the advancement of studies should seek assistance from all sides, even where there is none. It is the very same Mr. des Chartes <note>An older spelling of Descartes' name.</note> whom I had mentioned: whose genius you truly praise, and whom I conclude with absolute certainty from many circumstances to be the one called a noble mathematician by you in your *Optics* <note>original: "Opticis"</note>. It is *he*, I say, to whom ten years ago I communicated those things I had written concerning the causes of the sweetness of harmony, and who I thought had given you the occasion for these questions. He recently passed through here from your parts, and again (as he is fond of traveling) departed from here to return to you." This last sentence seems to indicate that Descartes had led Beeckman to believe he was returning to France.

Mersenne had also undoubtedly already received the following letter from Beeckman (same manuscript, folio 69) which ends as follows:

> "I have greeted Mr. des Chartes in your name by letter; for on the same day that I received yours, his letter was also delivered to me. He lives, he is well, and he is most friendly toward you."

Page 25, line 10. — Perhaps already Villiers, a physician from Sens, of whom we have 44 manuscript letters to Mersenne; some (though much later, in 1640) were shared with Descartes. (National Library, French collection, new acquisitions 6205, folios 365-437 and 308-356).

> "Regarding the transition in counterpoint <term>counterpoint: the relationship between two or more musical lines played at the same time</term> from a unison to a major third and vice versa,
> you seem to have satisfied yourself in Book I, theorem 21 of *Music*. For he who
> transitions from a unison to a major third, by your precepts, sins only against the 8th
> rule; but he who transitions from that third to a unison, sins
> against the 8th and 7th rules simultaneously. Mr. des Chartes <note>Descartes</note> (in <gloss>interlinear: our friend</gloss>) in his little book which he sent to me written about *Music*, writes about this matter
> as follows:
> *The reason why this is rather observed in the movement from imperfect consonances to <note>perfect ones, than in the</note>
> movement of perfect ones to imperfect ones, is because, while
> we hear an imperfect one, the ears long for a more perfect one, in which they may more
> rest, and are carried toward it by a natural impulse: whence it happens that the more neighboring
> one ought to be placed, since that is clearly the one they desire: on the other hand, while
> a perfect one is heard, we expect no imperfect one, and therefore it does not matter
> which one is placed.*" <note>original Latin: "De transitu in contrapuncto ab vnisono ad tertiam maiorem... vtra sit quæ ponatur."</note>

Page 33, line 26. — Compare *The Dioptrics, Tenth Discourse*, p. 142 and following of the 1637 edition. — The line *CD*, driven by the movement of the axis *AB*, describes a portion of a conical surface of revolution around this axis. The line *EF* (1st figure), linked to *CD*, remains parallel to *AB* and in the plane perpendicular to that of the figure. Each of its points therefore describes a hyperbolic arc <note>A curve formed by the intersection of a double cone and a plane</note>. In this first figure, the line *CD* is supposed to slide along itself (the piece it represents passing through the notched axis at *C*); in the second figure, on the contrary, *CD* is invariably fixed to *AB*, but the location of point *L*, where *CD* meets the plane perpendicular along *MN* to that of the figure, is always a hyperbolic arc.

### XII.

## FERRIER TO DESCARTES.

->Paris, October 26, 1629.<-

->Text from Clerselier, volume III, letter 100, p. 558-569.<-

Sir,

<margin>5</margin>Among so many obstacles that my ill fortune opposes at every hour to my designs, I could not receive a greater consolation than the testimonies you give me of the continuation of your goodwill, which I cherish beyond all that can be said. I will do everything in my power to make useful service of it, and will try to extract myself from where I am, if it is possible for me, in order to be able to devote myself more conveniently <note>Ferrier is likely referring to his financial or professional struggles in Paris</note>

# III, 558-559. XII. — 26 October 1629.

I am working diligently to prepare what is necessary for the work on the <term>glass lenses</term> <note>original: "verres"</note>, following your excellent instructions, which I believe I understand well enough.

And since it pleases you to order me to write to you about it, as if I were in a position to instruct you anew, I will tell you then that I remember very well the construction of the <term>machine</term> <note>a device designed for precision grinding</note> that you previously described to me, which consists of three main pieces: namely the <term>axle A B</term>, which turned in a circle; the <term>piece C D</term>, which moved across the <term>axle A B</term>; and the <term>cylinder E F</term>, which slid between the two <term>planks G H & I K</term>, and was meant to cut the glass with one of its ends, E or F. Now you desire that this machine serve only to cut <term>steel blades</term> <note>lames d'acier</note> of the shape <term>P N O M</term>, to serve like the iron of a <term>plane</term> <note>rabot; a woodworking tool used here as an analogy for a metal-shaving tool</note>, so that <term>P N O</term>, which must be the cutting edge, is carved according to the desired line. You want us to retain from the previous machine the <term>axle A B</term> and the <term>piece C D</term>, and that this piece remains fixed with the <term>axle A B</term>, so that there is only <term>circular motion</term> in the whole machine, and that we no longer use the <term>cylinder E F</term>; especially since when one turns the <term>axle A B</term>, the part of <term>C D</term> that meets between the two planks, namely <term>L</term>, describes exactly your—

For if the piece CD does not have free movement across the axis AB, it cannot happen that by turning the axis AB, this piece does not rise and fall, just as the cylinder of the first machine constrained it to do; and turning thus circularly, being firmly attached to the axis AB, it could only touch the plane of the boards at a single point in the middle, at the location of the axis of the required line, at point N, unless one raised the blade NM above the boards and the point L. For among the lines PNO, which can be made on the steel blades NM, opposite one another, those which are suitable for cutting the concave of the wheels Q, possess in themselves only the line of the convex; and those which can cut the convex of the wheels, possess in themselves only the line of the concave. # CORRESPONDENCE. III, 560-561.

I note further that, following your instructions, the wheels used to cut the **concave glasses** <note>original: "verres concaues"; these are lenses used to correct nearsightedness or for specific telescope components</note> must be smaller than the others; but it seems to me that this would be useless for your purpose, and that different machines would be required, according to the different sizes, to trace the two necessary lines.

**C** It also seems to me that it is not necessary to make two boards; it will be easier to adjust the blades **NM** to a single one, following the line **VX**, than if they were covered by another board; and these blades can be more easily secured by screws, or other inventions which are quite common for me to devise, than by boards.

I remark further, regarding the two figures of the wheel **Q** that you sent me, that in the first figure the blade **NM** should not be represented lying flat as it is; for you have represented this wheel in this first figure as being seen in its width, and not in its thickness; that is why one should only present to the view the thickness of the blade **NM**, and not the flat side or its width. But in the second figure, it is necessary to show the width of the blade, because the wheel appears there in its thickness.

**D** I find next another difficulty, namely, that to give a smooth edge to the blade **NM**, you

# XII. — 26 OCTOBER 1629.

III, 561-562.

...you wish for other similar pieces to be made like C D in length and thickness, but cut differently, in order to rough out and finish the necessary line. I find it very difficult to be able to make them so similar that they can fit one in the place of the other, to attach them to the axis A B, without taking on a new inclination <note>The angle or tilt of the component</note>, unless a means is found to be able to do it, and to rectify whatever might prevent it. And even by the friction that occurs in these things, where the hard rubs against the less hard, a path is made between the two by the filings <note>original: "limaille"; metal dust produced by abrasion</note> that come out of it, which prevents the required inclination from being preserved, unless these things are constantly brought closer to one another, in proportion to the resistance of the strong against the weak.

Moreover, instead of the small steel files that must be applied at point L of piece C D, it is necessary to apply whetstones <note>original: "pierres à éguiſer"</note> there to give the final sharp edge to the blades N M. Now, these stones must be soft, and consequently they diminish easily and wear down during the work when encountering things harder than themselves, such as these blades N M. For although these blades must be tempered <note>A heat-treatment process to increase the toughness of metal</note> after having received their first shape by these small files, they are nevertheless not in a state to cut; for after the tempering, the fire having dulled the keen edge <note>original: "vif-arreſte"</note> of the blade, it is necessary to give them a new one by means of the whetstones.

I beg of you, Sir, to give me your opinion on what can be done to rectify the inconveniences that I apprehend in these applications.

Afterward, you would wish that one choose some...

# CORRESPONDENCE. III, 562-563.

...a soft material that would be suitable for eating away at and polishing the glass, such as certain stones similar to slate, which are used to create a very delicate edge. You would like the <term>wheel Q</term> <note>referring to the grinding wheel in the diagram</note> to be made of this, like the wheels used by knife-grinders, and that by applying one or more <term>steel blades similar to NM</term> against it, one would give it—exactly around its entire thickness—the shape of the <term>line PNO</term> <note>the specific hyperbolic or parabolic curve required for the lens</note>, by turning the <term>wheel Q</term> on its center, as is marked in your two figures, which show them from two different directions.

<column-break/>

And once this wheel is thus carved, you would like it to be applied against the <term>glass R</term> placed on the <term>ordinary lathe S</term>, and that it should turn on its center, while at the same time the <term>wheel Q</term> would also turn on its own. This being the case, this wheel would hollow out the glass according to the <term>line PNO</term> very exactly, by means of these two different movements, and would eat away at the center of the glass as well as the edges.

And so that this wheel, which must be of soft material, might preserve its exact shape, you also desire that at the same time it turns to cut the glass, the <term>blade NM</term> (one or several) should remain always firm against it, to maintain it in its shape <note>this describes a self-truing mechanism where the template blade constantly corrects the wear on the grinding wheel</note>. You also say that the diameter of the <term>wheel Q</term> must not exceed a certain proportion (which you lead me to hope for), but that even if it were more...

# III, 563-564. XII. — 26 October 1629.

small, it does not matter. Finally, you say that it must also be observed that the line NM, which forms the middle of the blade PNOM, must be exactly parallel to the axis AB of the first machine, and that the perpendicular line falling from the axis AB onto the boards GH and IK must fall exactly upon this line MN. Furthermore, in the final figures, this same line NM, when extended, must pass exactly through the center of the wheel Q and meet to form a straight line with the axis RS, upon which the glass <note>original: "verre"; likely a lens or optical mirror</note> turns.

Now, Sir, since you give me the liberty to propose my difficulties to you in order to properly understand your design and to instruct myself, you will permit me to tell you my opinion on all the above, so that you may judge if I understand it; I even pray you to excuse me if I do not explain myself clearly enough. I say, then, that I believe I have clearly understood the invention of your machines, as well as that of the wheel Q, and the different manner in which the wheel and the glass attached to the lathe <term>RS (lathe/spindle): the rotating shaft used to hold the workpiece in place during grinding</term> move, in order to prevent the occurrence of the common defect of the "raised point" <note>original: "point en relief"; a common flaw in lens grinding where the center remains unground because the rotational velocity is zero at the exact axis</note>, which is formed in the center of glasses when turning the axis of the model upon the axis of the glass, because at this center there is no motion that can act, and which can eat away and wear it down, as the other parts further away are eaten and worn. All these inventions that you give me can only come from you. I say only that there is certain material that you believed could serve your works which is not suited to perfectly wear and eat away the glass.

<header>CORRESPONDENCE. III, 564.</header>

First, regarding the material of the wheel Q <note>In the accompanying diagrams, "Wheel Q" refers to the primary grinding tool</note>, there is no kind of stone, even if it were diamond itself, that can wear down the glass without placing between it and the glass a substance that grinds and crushes between the two, such as sandstone or emery <note>Emery is a dark granular rock used as an abrasive</note>; these substances would wear away much more of the wheel than the glass, as the wheel is softer, and for every glass lens one would use up an entire wheel. And whatever hardness the tempering might have given to the blades NM <note>The metal templates or "formers" used to guide the shape</note> which would be applied against the wheel, they would wear down even more, since glass is harder than all of that. Furthermore, these blades NM could not rub even slightly against any kind of whetstone, however soft it might be, without that stone’s movement promptly eating away the sharp edge of the shape that had been given to it; and thus it would be the wheel giving the shape to the iron tool, whereas the exact opposite is required.

I am also convinced that as the wheel Q decreases in its circumference as it wears down (even though it might preserve the necessary shape in its thickness), it would hollow out the glasses differently—the second ones more than the first, and so on—since the circles near their centers are smaller and more arched <margin>F</margin> than those further away. I do not know if there might be a defect in this regarding the effect of the lenses, since you told me that the smallness of the wheel does not matter; but for the size, you say there must be a proportion which you lead me to hope you will give me.

Notwithstanding all this, it seems to me that one can remedy a part of these difficulties by the means of which I...

# III, 564-565. XII. — 26 OCTOBER 1629.

I say then, in the first place, that the manner of using the second machine to give the desired curve <note>original: "ligne"</note> to the blades **N M** is very excellently invented, provided that a means is found to correct what is lost of the material through the friction of the movement, whether it is used to cut the blades or to cut the wheel **Q**. I would wish to make this wheel of brass <note>original: "laton"</note> or iron, so that it might preserve for a longer time the shape that the blade **N M** had given it; and when its shape becomes spoiled, it could be repaired with the same blade or another similar one. 

But this wheel **Q**, of brass or iron, must be positioned and have its movement above the glass, which must have its own movement from below; and I shall provide it as easily in this way as if it were on the side, by a method I have thought could be executed. This would make the wheel and the glass turn differently and equally at the same time by the movement of the foot, without the need for any toothed wheel or pinion, which create a trembling motion because of the teeth of the wheel engaging <note>original: "s'engrennent"</note> with those of the pinion.

For I find enough trouble in properly cutting the blades **N M**, which can warp or bend during the tempering process <note>Tempering is the process of heat-treating metal to increase its hardness, which often caused deformation in 17th-century metallurgy.</note>; besides, I believe it is very necessary to ensure that the plane **P N O** is perfectly straight along the cutting edge, otherwise errors would occur in the line.

I also remember that you never told me it was necessary to make large concaves <note>Concave lenses or surfaces.</note>, but rather that they must be small. This being the case, I find no difficulty in making the wheel (however small it may be) with its axle all in one piece, to give it a steady movement. This could not be done if the wheel were made of stone, because the wheel and the axle could then only be made of two separate pieces.

I did not understand that the shapes of the wheels **Q**, although arranged in two different directions, were intended for cutting convex glasses; for I believe that for that purpose they must be cut and hollowed out in the shape of a pulley, as shown in the attached figure. And the blades **N M**, which are to hollow them out, must be presented to the file **L D** on the side of **H I**, to receive from it their line or their shape; and the file **L D** must be tilted from **G** towards **I**. And this type of wheel could not wear down the convex glass at the same time as the other wears the concave; for it only rubs against it like a line crossing the diameter of the glass only. Nevertheless, it will always eat away better at the point made in the middle, by turn—

# III, 566-567. XII. — 26 OCTOBER 1629.

...aligning the axis of the glass against that of the concave model <note>A "model" refers to the metal tool or "lap" used to shape the lens</note>, as I have said previously, which will serve to prepare the glass to correct the defect of the wheel. But it may happen, if the convex glass is of a large extent, that the use of the wheel will be useless; for as the friction is greater toward that which is far from the center than toward that which is near it, the material <note>Abrasive slurry used for grinding</note> that one puts between the two to wear it down is dragged for a longer time by the circle *a a* than by *b b*, and consequently eats away more by making a large turn than by making a small one; and thus the glass and the model eat each other away and lose their shape, not being worn equally in a single rotation. It is also to be remarked that the material one puts between the two to wear the glass is carried away immediately by the movement of the wheel, and remains there less time than in the other wheel.

All these difficulties do not astonish me much, for with your assistance I hope to surmount them, and show that I will know better how to do than to say.

<margin>K</margin> There remains for me one more doubt that I could not leave behind, concerning the method required to find the necessary line by the triangles and my dial <note>likely a reference to a "sundial" or a specific measuring instrument used for calculating angles of refraction</note>, which is to know if two glass triangles of the same transparent material being different, and consequently making different refractions on the divided line which stops the ray at the said dial, one traced two models conforming to the different lines of the refractions; namely, I say, if the effect of the two glasses can be similar, such as for burning at a determined point following your rules.

You have taught me that the triangles can be constructed of whatever angle one wishes at discretion; I could not put this to the test, for the triangles I have at present are all similar; I beg you to resolve this point for me. I also know well that you told me that all small concave glasses <note>lenses</note> can serve for any large convex glass. I have lost a piece of paper on which you had traced for me the fashion of describing the required line with the ordinary compass, by seeking several points through which it must pass.

<page-num>III, 568</page-num>

# XII. — 26 OCTOBER 1629.

§1

is not unknown to you, and that the aforementioned gentleman knows only what you have taught him of it. If you judge that I might be able to understand it, you would greatly <note>original: "grandement"; later corrected to "beaucoup" (much)</note> oblige me by communicating it to me at your convenience. But he adds that one must provide him with a man who knows how to cut glass <term>verre</term> <note>Referring here to the precise grinding of optical lenses</note> exactly. I consider this last condition as difficult as all the rest, unless he trains new workmen made specifically for the task and by commission, as I do not believe he will find any of that caliber at present. He holds me in such low esteem that he does not believe I have enough wit to understand or undertake even lesser things, since he says as much in my presence. I admit my insufficiency, which ought to be excused, having never been instructed in anything whatsoever except by you, Sir, to whom I wish to owe everything. This contempt, nevertheless, could not so thoroughly rebuff me that I do not feel enough inclination within myself to taste and comprehend the true knowledge of the sciences which might be communicated to me by persons of your merit, so much ambition do I have to make myself known by something beyond the common; this gives me a certain kind of courage to seek the means to surmount many of the difficulties encountered in the operations of exquisite works. Do not, if you please, make the same judgment of me as Monsieur Mydorge <note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), a famous French mathematician and physicist known for his work on conic sections and optics</note> does; I hope so much from your affection that you will be pleased to know that you will have given me everything I shall possess; and if my bad fortune <term>fortune</term> <note>In this context, "fortune" refers to one's lot in life or external circumstances</note> robs me of the means to use it usefully—

And provided that on the entire surface of the wheel, there are more points that correspond to the true figure than there are others, it will give the exact figure to the glass without communicating any of its defects to it; whereas all the defects that are in the templates are communicated to the glass. This is also the reason why I had noted that one must have several blades N M <note>These blades are the metal templates used to shape the grinding wheel.</note> all similar, and not be satisfied with a single one to cut the wheel Q, so that if one fails in some points, the other compensates for the defect. And it is probable that, by using several blades all at once in this way, one can make the wheel Q in such a way that it will closely approach the true figure, and the glass will approach it even more closely. I am sending you this so that you may know in what the ingenuity and utility of all these movements consist, which is that even if there is something to find fault with in all your templates—that is to say, in the blades N M and the wheel Q—you will nonetheless be able to cut the glass exactly.

You can thus find an infinity of points: for by placing one foot of the compass again in B, and opening it a little wider than the first time, you take two other points equally distant from B, namely P and Q; then from center A drawing the circle X Q Y, and from center C the circle X P Y, the intersection of these two circles gives you again the two points X and Y, and so on to infinity. And I believe that this is the entire method used by Mr. Mydorge <note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), a French mathematician and friend of Descartes, known for his work on conic sections.</note>.

You can practice this by placing the foot of the compass only once in each of the points A, B, and C; namely, if having the foot of the compass in B, you take the points N O and P Q, and infinite others; then having the foot of the compass in A, you draw the circles T O V, X Q Y, and similar ones; and afterwards, placing the compass in C, you trace the other circles T N V, X P Y; this is the shortest way, but one must not make a mistake and mark the intersection of one circle instead of the other. Now, the line described in this way will burn <note>The "burning point" refers to the focal point where light rays converge to generate heat.</note> at the distance which is from A to B.

But if you wish to trace one that burns at a greater or lesser distance, for example, at the distance of D E, look for E F, which is to D E as B C is to A B, and having found it, use the points D E F to trace your line, just as you did with points A B C; that is to say, if you once have the proportion that exists between the lines A B and B C, by means of your quadrant <note>A mathematical instrument used for measuring angles and altitudes.</note>, it will serve you for

First volume of Mathematical Works, containing commentaries on Euclid's Elements of Geometry, etc., Mainz, at the expense of Antonius Hierat, printed by Reinhardus Elz, in the year 1611. — There were earlier editions: Rome, Accolti 1574; Rome, Grassi 1589; Cologne, Ciottus 1591; Rome, Zanetti 1603; Cologne 1607, etc.</margin>. I do not fail to highly esteem the invention of Mr. Gaudey, and I do not believe a better one can be found for the same purpose.

First, I suppose that motion, once imprinted in some body, remains there perpetually, unless it is removed by some other cause; that is to say, <term>that which is in a vacuum</term> <note>original Latin: "quod in vacuo"</note> moves forever.

Once it has begun to move, it always moves with an equal speed. Suppose, therefore, a weight existing at A is impelled by its own gravity <note>Latin: grauitas; here referring to the inherent force or "heaviness" pulling an object down</note> toward C. I say that as soon as it begins to move, if its gravity were to leave it <note>original: "illum", likely a typo for "illud" referring to the weight</note>, it would nevertheless continue in that same motion until it reached C; but then it would descend no slower or faster from A to B than from B to C. Because this is not actually the case, but rather gravity is present which presses it downward and adds new forces for descending at every single moment, it follows that it completes the distance BC much faster than AB. This is because, in traversing that latter part, it retains all the impetus <note>term: impetus - the momentum or "force" an object carries from its previous movement</note> with which it was moving through the space AB, and additionally, a new force grows within it because of the gravity which urges it anew at every moment. By what proportion this speed increases is demonstrated in the triangle ABCDE: namely, the first line denotes the force of speed impressed at the 1st moment, the 2nd line the force impressed at the 2nd moment, the 3rd the force imparted at the 3rd, and so on. From this is formed the triangle ACD, which represents the increase in the speed of motion in the descent of the weight from A all the way to C; and ABE, which represents the increase of speed in the first half of the space the weight traverses; and the trapezium <note>term: trapezium - a four-sided shape with at least one pair of parallel sides, used here to calculate the area of accumulated speed</note> BCDE, which represents the increase of speed in the latter half of the space the weight traverses, namely BC. And since the trapezium—

<meta>This page continues the editorial commentary on the correspondence between René Descartes and Marin Mersenne, specifically focusing on a letter dated November 13, 1629, regarding the laws of falling bodies.</meta>

# XIV. — NOVEMBER 13, 1629.

The Latin mathematical fragment contained in this letter must have been written much earlier, dating back to the period of Descartes' first stay in Holland (from 1617 to July 1619); it was, in fact, Beeckman <note>Isaac Beeckman (1588–1637), a Dutch philosopher and scientist who greatly influenced the young Descartes.</note> who posed the question to him regarding the mathematical law of the fall of heavy bodies in a vacuum <note>original: "la chute des graves dans le vide"</note> (cf. letter to Mersenne of December 18, 1629, Clerselier vol. II, p. 483, and the *Private Thoughts* <note>original: "Cogitationes privatæ"</note>, Foucher de Careil, vol. I, p. 16). At that time, Galileo had already been in possession of this law for at least fifteen years, but he was not to publish it until the *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* <note>original: "Massimi Sistemi"</note> in 1632.

In this *a priori* investigation, Descartes proceeds as Galileo also seems to have done, starting from the principle of the conservation of motion previously acquired (which Beeckman, moreover, already accepted), and employing a procedure entirely analogous to that of the method of indivisibles <note>A precursor to integral calculus used to calculate areas and volumes.</note> (thus well before Cavalieri <note>Bonaventura Cavalieri, an Italian mathematician known for his work on the geometry of indivisibles.</note>). But he commits a singular error in reasoning. On his diagram, the coordinate ABC ought to represent time, whereas he uses it equally to represent the distances traveled. The progression he follows, which is otherwise very ingenious, prevents him from immediately perceiving the contradictions to which this confusion on the diagram should have led him; he thus arrives at a relationship essentially different from that of Galileo, since it would amount to considering the distance traveled as proportional, not to the square of the time, but to a power of time where the exponent is the ratio of log 2 to log 4/3, which is to say approximately 2.4.

Having long since rejected the hypothesis of the possibility of a vacuum, Descartes never seriously revisited this attempt <note>original: "tentamen"</note>, and consequently never recognized his error. He even seems to have believed in good faith that Galileo's law did not differ from the one he himself had given to Beeckman as early as 1619. It is, on the contrary, possible that Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the first editor of Descartes' letters.</note>, noting the flaw in the reasoning developed in the present letter to Mersenne, deliberately set aside the draft (T).

<summary>This page analyzes a 1629 letter where Descartes attempts to mathematically define the law of falling bodies, revealing a significant geometric error that led him to a different conclusion than Galileo.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Isaac Beeckman, Galileo Galilei, Marin Mersenne, falling bodies, vacuum, method of indivisibles, mathematical physics, history of science</keywords>

### XV.

### DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

My Reverend Father,

This proposal for a new language seems more admirable at first glance than I find it to be upon looking closely; for there are only two things to learn in all languages, namely the meaning of words and the grammar. Regarding the meaning of words, he promises nothing special; for he says in the fourth proposition: *to interpret that language by means of a dictionary* <note>original: "linguam illam interpretari ex dictionario"</note>, which is what a man slightly versed in languages can do without him in any of the common languages. same language, that he will undertake to derive the meaning from it. What prevents everyone from being able to do this is the difficulty of grammar; and I suspect that this is the entire secret of your man. But it is nothing that is not very easy; for by creating a language where there is only one way to conjugate, to decline, and to construct words, and where there are no defective or irregular forms—which are all things resulting from the corruption of common usage—and even ensuring that the inflection of nouns or verbs and the construction are done by affixes <note>Particles added to the beginning or end of a word to change its meaning or function.</note>, either before or after the root words, which affixes would all be specified in the dictionary, it will be no wonder that ordinary minds could learn in less than six hours to compose in this language with the help of the dictionary, which is the subject of the first proposition.

As for the second, namely: *once this language is known, all others can be understood as its dialects* <note>original: "cognitâ hac linguâ cæteras omnes, vt eius dialectos, cognofcere"</note>, this is merely to talk up his wares <note>Descartes uses the metaphor of a merchant over-praising a "drug" or product to increase its perceived value.</note>; for he does not specify how much time it would take to know them, but only that one would consider them as dialects of this one. That is to say, since there are no grammatical irregularities in this language as there are in others, he takes it as their primitive source. Furthermore, it should be noted that in his dictionary, for the root words, he can use those that are in use in all languages as synonyms. For example, to signify love, he will take *to love* (French: *aymer*), *to love* (Latin: *amare*), *to love* (Greek: *φιλεῖν*) <note>original: "aymer, amare, φιλεῖν"</note>, etc. And a Frenchman, by adding the affix that marks the substantive noun to *aymer*, will make *amour* (love); a Greek will add the same to *φιλεῖν*, and so on for the others.

As a result of this, the sixth proposition is very easy to understand: *to discover a script, etc.* <note>original: "scripturam inuenire etc."</note>; for by placing in one's dictionary a single symbol which refers to *to love* <note>original: "aymer"</note>, *to love* <note>Latin: "amare"</note>, *to love* <note>Greek: "φιλεῖν"</note>, and all the synonyms, the book that is written with these characters could be interpreted by everyone who possesses this dictionary.

The fifth proposition is also, it seems, nothing more than a way to praise his own wares; as soon as I see the word *secret* <note>Latin: "arcanum"</note> in any proposition, I begin to have a poor opinion of it. However, I believe he means nothing more than this: because he has philosophized extensively on the grammars of all the languages he names in order to shorten his own, he could teach them more easily than the ordinary masters.

There remains the third proposition, which is a complete *secret* <note>Latin: "arcanum"</note> to me; for to say that he will explain the thoughts of the ancients by the words they used, by taking each word for the true definition of the thing, is properly to say that he will explain the thoughts of the ancients by taking their words in a different sense than they ever intended, which is contradictory; but perhaps he understands it differently.

Now, this idea of reforming grammar, or rather of creating a new one that could be learned in five or six hours, and which could be made common to all languages, would nonetheless be a useful invention for the public if all men would agree to put it into use—were it not for two inconveniences that I foresee. And what is most important, it would assist the judgment, representing all things to it so distinctly that it would be almost impossible for it to be deceived; whereas, quite to the contrary, the words we have possess almost nothing but confused meanings, to which the minds of men having been long accustomed, this is the reason they understand almost nothing perfectly. Now, I maintain that this language is possible, and that one can find the science upon which it depends, by means of which peasants could better judge the truth of things than <insert>learned</insert> men do now.

<note>The following section is a scholarly commentary by the original editor regarding the origins of the "universal language" project Descartes is critiquing.</note>
We have no indication regarding the project criticized by Descartes outside of this letter, and it does not seem possible to relate it to what Charles Sorel (in *On the Perfection of Man*, Paris, Robert de Nain, 1655, p. 346) says of the more or less analogous attempts of "a certain des Vallées" and of "Sieur le Maire." As for the ideas put forward by Descartes, they were—according to Baillet (vol. II, p. 475, based on a manuscript account by Poisson)—taken up by Christopher Wren, who gave "an essay of this universal language," and by several French scholars who conceived "similar designs." In this regard, one might mention Father Bernier (*The Reunion of Languages, or the Art of Learning Them All Through One*, 1674, quarto). Upon verification, Wren was only commissioned by the Royal Society of London, on May 18, 1668, to report on the work of a Dr. John Wilkins: *An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language*; Wilkins himself had been inspired by a Scotsman, George Dalgarno of Aberdeen, author of *The Art of Signs, commonly known as a Universal Character and Philosophical Language* <note>original: "Ars signorum, vulgo Character universalis et Lingua philosophica"</note>, octavo, London, 1661, which is conceived in a thoroughly Cartesian spirit.

# I, 503. XVI. — DECEMBER 18, 1629. 87

You ask next why equal things <note>Referring to musical intervals of the same size</note> awaken more attention when ascending than when descending: I no longer remember what I wrote to you about it; however, I will tell you that it is <margin>5</margin> not because they are equal or unequal, but generally because the sound which is more acute <term>acute</term><note>High-pitched; what we call "treble"</note> than the one preceding it (as happens when the parts ascend), awakens and strikes the ear more than the sound which is more grave <term>grave</term><note>Low-pitched; what we call "bass"</note>; and in a musical concert, if the <margin>10</margin> voices go almost always equally or if they lower and slow down little by little, that will put the listeners to sleep; but if on the contrary one raises the voice all of a sudden, that will be the means to awaken them.

According to various considerations, one can say that the <margin>15</margin> grave sound is "more sound" <note>original: "plus son"; implying it has more physical substance or presence</note> than the acute, for it is produced by bodies of greater extent, it can be heard from further away, etc. But it is called the foundation of music principally because it has movements that are slower and consequently can be divided into <margin>20</margin> more parts; for we call a "foundation" that which is, as it were, the most ample and the least diversified, and which can serve as the subject upon which one builds the rest: just as the first strokes of a pencil <note>Likely referring to a charcoal or graphite sketch</note> can be called the foundation of a portrait, even though they seem to <margin>25</margin> appear less than what one adds afterward with vivid colors.

<meta>This page continues René Descartes' letter to Marin Mersenne from December 18, 1629. Having previously discussed the perception of high and low pitches, Descartes now addresses Mersenne’s theories on harmony, the physics of fire, and the weight of the human body.</meta>

# CORRESPONDENCE. I, 503-504, II, 482.

Regarding your method for examining the quality <note>original: "bonté," literally "goodness"</note> of consonances <term>consonances</term><note>Musical intervals that sound pleasant or harmonious when played together.</note>, you have taught me what I ought to say: that it is too subtle—at least if I dare judge—to be distinguished by the ear, without which it is <margin>5</margin> impossible to judge the quality of any consonance; and when we judge them by reason, this reason must always assume the capacity of the ear. Regarding the transition from the major third to the unison, I hold to what the practitioners <note>Practical musicians and composers as opposed to abstract theorists.</note> say about it.

There is no doubt, in whatever way you <margin>15</margin> place a beam or a column, that it will always weigh or pull downwards; and our head weighs upon our shoulders, and our body upon our legs, even though we do not pay it any mind.
