# XVI. — DECEMBER 18, 1629.

<margin>11, 482.</margin> ...that speed is imprinted as one in the first moment by gravity, and as two in the second moment, etc. I respond, with all due respect <note>original Latin: "salua pace"</note>, that I did not understand it this way, but rather that speed is imprinted as one in the first moment by gravity, and again as one in the second moment <margin>5</margin> by that same gravity, and so on. Now, one from the first moment and one from the second make two, and one from the third makes three, and thus it increases in arithmetic proportion <term>arithmetic proportion</term><note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between any two consecutive terms is the same, such as 1, 2, 3, 4.</note>. Moreover, I thought this was sufficiently proven by the fact that gravity perpetually accompanies the <margin>10</margin> body in which it resides; for gravity cannot accompany a body unless it continually pushes it downward. For if we were to suppose, for example, a mass of lead falling downward by the force of gravity and, after it began to fall during the first moment, God were to remove all gravity from the lead—to the extent <margin>15</margin> that afterward the mass of lead were no heavier than if it were air or a feather—that mass would nevertheless continue to descend, at least in a vacuum <note>original Latin: "saltem in vacuo"</note>, since it has already begun to move and nothing can...

I have written what I knew of it in the previous [letter], *at least in a vacuum*, *but in the air*, what Mr. Beeckman sent to you is true, provided that you suppose that the faster the weight falls, the more the air resists it; for if that is the case—of which I am not yet entirely certain—eventually it will happen that the air will hinder it by exactly as much as gravity would add speed *in a vacuum* <note>original Latin: "in vacuo"</note>. This being so, the motion will thereafter remain uniform <note>original French: "demeurera tousiours égal," literally "will always remain equal."</note>; but this can only be determined through abstract thought, for in practice one should not hope for it. And as for your experiments, that a weight, falling from fifty

<column-break/>

feet, takes as much time to travel the last twenty-five as the first, *with all due respect* <note>original Latin: "saluâ pace"</note>, I cannot persuade myself that they are accurate: for *in a vacuum*, I find that it will take only a third of the time to travel the last twenty-five, and I cannot believe that the obstruction of the air is so significant that it makes that difference imperceptible. I am, etc. End of the Clerselier fragment <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes' letters.</note>, volume I, page 504. — Clerselier, volume II, pages 482-483, gives, on the contrary, first a French translation of the Latin passage (until *it is permitted to say*, p. 90, l. 7).

### CORRESPONDENCE. II, 482-483.

...a reason be given why it <note>Referring to the motion of the falling lead mentioned on the previous page.</note> should stop, but its speed will not increase. *He assumes, as I do, that what has once begun to move continues*

# II, 487-488. XVI. — DECEMBER 18, 1629.
<meta>CORRESPONDENCE. I.</meta>
->13<-

Regarding your experiments, I find iron certainly heavier than copper, but it is by so little that it is almost nothing more; and because I found a bit of rust on it, fearing that it might be this which has made it <margin>5</margin> heavier, I am letting it rust even more to see afterward if it will become even heavier.

Regarding the other experiments with the balances and the candle in the sun, I do not find it strange that they did not succeed, and there is no need to think <margin>10</margin> about it further.

I am now opening the third of your letters, which I received yesterday, in which I find once again the care you take with the experiments about which I had written to you, and I thank you for it; but there is no need to <margin>15</margin> trouble yourself further: even if the room were pierced all the way through, the ray would not fail to illuminate its sides.

What you say you have heard about crowns <term>crowns: optical halos or parhelia often seen around the sun or moon</term>, that the middle of them is green or blue, <margin>20</margin> one of the edges red and the other yellow, is without foundation and clearly false. I trust much more the experience of Mr. Gassendi <gloss>a. See above, page 84, l. 2.</gloss>, for I know by experience and by reason that in all the circles or rainbows <term>iris: Descartes uses the term "iris" to refer to rainbows or similar circular optical phenomena</term> that can exist, there is not...

...this, I do not know; and even though a thousand experiments could be conducted to find it more closely, nevertheless, because they cannot be justified by reason—at least as far as I can yet reach—I do not believe <margin>5</margin> one should take the trouble to perform them.

It is certain that the returns <term>returns: the vibrations or cycles of a string</term> of two strings that make the twelfth <note>a musical interval spanning an octave and a fifth</note> and relate to one another as 1 to 3, meet together twice as often as those which make the fifth and relate to one another <margin>10</margin> as 2 to 3. Within the last month, I have recovered the original of the little treatise where I explain this, an extract of which you have seen; it remained for eleven years in the hands of <gloss>Mr.</gloss> Beeckman<gloss>a</gloss>, and if that amount of time is sufficient for legal prescription <term>prescription: a legal principle where ownership of property is acquired through long-term possession</term>, he has the right to claim it as his own. Now, the matter of consonances <term>consonances: combinations of notes that sound pleasant or stable together</term> <margin>15</margin> is explained thus:

Let the strings A to B be as 3 to one, and A to C as 3 to 2; let A take one moment of time to make each turn or return, and consequently B 1/3

Regarding words that signify naturally, I
<margin>5</margin>find the reasoning sound for things that strike our senses so strongly that they oblige us to make a sound: just as, if someone hits us, it obliges us to cry out; if something pleasant happens, to laugh; and the sounds that are made, whether crying or laughing, are similar in all

Page 83, l. 7. — Descartes does not seem to have seen these crowns <note>atmospheric halos or rings around the sun or moon</note> until 1635; see his letter to Golius dated May 9/19, 1635.

Page 90, l. 18. — This opinion of Beeckman <note>Isaac Beeckman, a Dutch philosopher and scientist who influenced Descartes' early work</note> is found supported in the first three letters we possess from him to Mersenne (National Library, French collection, new acquisitions 6206, folio 43, p. 75 — folio 40 verso, p. 70 — folio 33 verso, p. 56), the last of which is dated October 1, 1629. He consistently maintains it in his later letters (April 30, 1630, ibid. folio 37, p. 63 — May 30, 1633, ibid. folio 42 verso, p. 73). He had already taught it to Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi, a French philosopher and mathematician</note>, during the latter's journey with Luillier in the Netherlands (from the end of 1628 to August 8, 1629), as is evident from the posthumous work published by Beeckman’s brother (*Century of Mathematico-Physical Meditations, Questions, and Solutions*, 1644, p. 45). "At that time I taught how to investigate the point of equality <note>original: 'æqualitatis'; referring to terminal velocity or a state of uniform motion</note> in falling."

## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

->Amsterdam, January 1630.<-

->Text from Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier, the first editor of Descartes' correspondence</note>, volume II, end of letter 105, p. 491-497.<-

*The copy at the Institute marks this second part of Clerselier’s letter II, 105 as forming a separate letter dated from Amsterdam on January 15, 1630. "See page 7 of the new notebook," adds the handwritten note. There is no doubt, indeed, that it is an intermediate between the letters of December 18, 1629, and February 25, 1630, and it does not seem that there were any others to Mersenne during this ten-week period, the midpoint of which falls on Monday, January 21, 1630.*

<margin>25</margin>a concert, etc.; just as one person prefers what is sweet, and another what is a bit tart or bitter, etc.

> <note>original: "Dices sextam minorem a tertia majore et tertiam minorem idem pati a sexta majore; verùm non tanta bonitatis differentia : 12e enim ictu quarta ter unitur, quinta quater, etc."</note> "You will say that the minor sixth suffers the same thing from the major third, and the minor third from the major sixth; but the difference in quality is not so great: for at the **12th stroke** <note>This refers to the frequency of vibrations in musical intervals</note> the fourth is united three times, the fifth four times, etc."

**Page 109, line 10.** — Beeckman (*ibid.* folio 33 verso) had written to Mersenne:
> <note>original: "Causa vocis auditæ est idem ille numero aer qui erat in ore loquentis, non, vt vulgo putatur, vicissitudo sphæralis motûs in aere quem circulis ex proiecto in aquam lapide factis assimilant."</note> "The cause of the voice being heard is that same numerical air that was in the speaker's mouth, and not, as is commonly thought, a sequence of spherical motion in the air, which they liken to the circles made by a stone thrown into water."
He had also maintained this same opinion before Gassendi, when the latter visited him in Dordrecht during the summer of 1629. See page 45 of Isaac Beeckman’s *Century of Mathematico-Physical Meditations, Questions, and Solutions*, Utrecht, 1644.

Scheiner’s great work on the spots of the Sun, his *Ursine Rose* <note>original: "Rosa Ursina"</note> (Bracciano), was not finished printing until June 13, 1630; some copies, however, bear the date October 25, 1629.

...words that they will invent, but which will be neither better nor more appropriate than ours; on the contrary, ours, having been thus invented at the beginning, have since been and are every <margin>5</margin> day corrected and softened by usage, which does more in such things than the understanding of a fine mind <note>original: *bon esprit*. 2. What makes you see two candles while lying down is that the <term>visual axes: the imaginary lines stretching from the center of each eye to the object being viewed</term> do not meet where the candle is. If you see <margin>10</margin> more than two, it is a dazzle of the sight.

3. I had already written to you <gloss>a</gloss> that it is one thing to say that one <term>consonance: a combination of notes that sound pleasant or "stable" together</term> is sweeter than another, and another thing to say that it is more pleasant. For everyone knows that honey is sweeter than <margin>15</margin> olives, and yet many people will prefer to eat olives than honey. Thus everyone knows that the <term>fifth: an interval such as C to G, considered very stable</term> is sweeter than the <term>fourth: an interval such as C to F</term>, the latter than the major third, and the major third than the minor; and yet there are places where the <margin>20</margin> minor third will please more than the fifth, even where a <term>dissonance: a clash of notes that creates tension</term> will be found more pleasant than a consonance.

4. I do not know of any qualities in consonances <margin>24</margin> that correspond to the passions <note>original: *passions*. In the 17th century, "passions" referred to emotions or mental states. Mersenne was likely asking if specific musical intervals naturally triggered specific emotions, like sadness or joy.</note>.

5. You prevent me as much from asking me by how much one consonance is more pleasant than another, as if you were to ask me by how much fruits are more pleasant for me to eat than <margin>30</margin> fish.

# II, 521. XIX. — MARCH 4, 1630.

6. Regarding the compositions of ratios, name them as you please, but you see clearly on your <term>monochord: an ancient scientific and musical instrument with a single string used to demonstrate the relationship between mathematical ratios and musical intervals</term> how a major tenth<sup>a</sup> can be divided into an octave<sup>b</sup> and a major third.

But throughout the rest of this winter, it has been so warm in this country <note>Descartes was living in the Netherlands at this time.</note> that neither ice nor snow was seen, and I had already thought of writing to you to complain that I had not been able to make any observations there regarding my <term>Meteors: a scientific treatise on atmospheric phenomena that Descartes eventually published in 1637 alongside his *Discourse on the Method*</term>. I pray you to keep me in your good graces.

*In the copy at the Institute, the beginning of a new letter is only indicated at the second paragraph, which is an obvious error. The assigned date is March 1630, which agrees well with Descartes' statement that it has been five or six months [since October 26, 1629] since he received news from Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier was an instrument maker whom Descartes hoped would help him cut hyperbolic lenses</note>, and with the reminder of this letter "written last March" regarding the said Ferrier—a reminder he makes in December 1630 (Clerselier, vol. II, p. 321). However, it is possible to be more precise. Indeed, in the following letter of April 15, 1630, Descartes says that it had only been eight days since he had written to Mersenne when he received, ten or twelve days after sending it, a letter from the <term>Minim: a member of the Order of Minims, a Catholic religious order to which Mersenne belonged</term> dated March 14. We can therefore fix the present letter to March 18, a Monday (the day the courier departs), as indicated in the first paragraph and confirmed by the fixed dates of Descartes' letters during this year.*

I replied to your previous letters on the very day that I received them; but you could not yet have had my letter when you wrote your most recent ones; for it always takes at least three <margin>5</margin> weeks to get a response, and the Messenger <note>The commercial postal carrier or courier</note> only arrives here on Saturday evening, or Sunday depending on the wind, and returns on Monday evening; and sometimes, on those trips when I am not expecting any letters from you, he is ready to depart before they are <margin>10</margin> brought to me.
Furthermore, you astonish me no less by telling me...

### II, 524-525. XX. — 18 MARCH 1630.

But generally, neither the **beautiful** nor the **pleasant** signifies anything other than a relationship between our judgment and the object; and because human judgments are so different, one cannot say that the beautiful or the pleasant have any fixed measure. And I could not explain it better than I did once before in my *Treatise on Music*<gloss>a</gloss> <note>Descartes refers here to his *Compendium Musicæ*, his first work, written in 1618 for Isaac Beeckman</note>; I will put the same words here, because I have the Book in my hands: *Among the objects of the senses, that which is most pleasing to the mind is not that which is most easily perceived by the sense, nor even that which is most difficult; but that which is not so easy as to leave the natural desire with which the senses are drawn toward objects completely unfulfilled, nor yet so difficult as to tire the sense*<gloss>b</gloss> <note>original: "Inter obiecta ſensus, illud non animo gratiſſimum eſt, quod facillimè ſenſu percipitur, neque etiam quod difficillimè; ſed quod non tam facilè, vt naturale deſiderium, quo ſenſus feruntur in obiecta, planè non impleat, neque etiam tam difficulter, vt ſenſum fatiget"</note>. I was explaining *that which is perceived by the sense easily or with difficulty*<gloss>b</gloss> <note>original: "id quod facilè, vel difficulter ſenſu percipitur"</note>, such as, for example, the sections of a garden bed, which, if they consist of only one or two kinds of shapes, always arranged in the same way, will be understood far more easily than if there were ten or twelve, and arranged diversely; but that is not to say that one can absolutely call one more beautiful than the other. ...that if **God did not exist, nonetheless these truths would be true** <note>original: "Deus non esset, nihilominus istæ veritates essent veræ"</note>; for the existence of God is the first and the most eternal of all truths that can be, and the only one from which all others proceed. But what makes it easy to be mistaken in this matter is that most <margin>5</margin> men do not consider God as an infinite and incomprehensible being, and as the sole Author upon whom all things depend; instead, they stop at the syllables of His name, and think it is enough to know Him if they know that **God** means the same as <margin>10</margin> what is called **Deus** in Latin, and who is worshiped by men. Those who have no higher thoughts than that can easily become atheists; and because they perfectly understand mathematical truths, but not that of the existence of God, it <margin>15</margin> is no wonder if they do not believe that these truths depend upon Him. But they should judge, on the contrary, that since God is a cause whose power surpasses the limits of human understanding, and since the necessity of these truths does not exceed our knowledge, <margin>20</margin> they are something lesser, and subject to this incomprehensible power. What you say about the **production of the Word** <note>original: "production du Verbe." In June, by contrast, we have a letter from Helmont to Mersenne, addressed to Brussels.*

*...the Latin [original] of this French version? The meaning is exactly the same on both sides, and when there is some difference, it is entirely to the advantage of the Latin—firstly for its conciseness, as the French version is a bit wordy, and sometimes even in terms of nuance of expression. The Dutch editors, Blaeu and Raei (especially the latter, who had known Descartes well), were indeed able to obtain a faithful copy of the Latin letters, if they did not specifically request it from Paris by asking Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes' friend and the primary editor of his posthumous letters.</note>, who was not the type of man to refuse it. Thus, later, the new edition published in Paris, in 12mo, in 1725, "where the Latin of several letters that had only been printed in French was joined," first published Blaeu's Latin text as the original (Epist. XI, vol. III, p. 138), and only then Clerselier's French version (p. 140). The recipient's name is missing in Clerselier and in the Latin edition.*

"This translation is not good," notes the copy from the Institute, referring back to Descartes himself, who, in Letter XXV hereafter (pp. 171-2), reproduces the first six lines of his Latin epistle, up to "had known" <note>original: "cognouisse"</note>. Now, this beginning is identical to that given by the Blaeu edition. We can conclude that the sequel is also the original text; we therefore provide it here, as we did for the previous letter, in preference to the French version by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier was Descartes' first editor and translator, though his versions are sometimes considered less precise than the original Latin</note>. The name of the recipient is missing from the two old editions, but it was already restored in the copy at the Institute. One even reads the proper name *Mersenno* (ll. 3-4), where there is only the initial M.

->Most Distinguished Sir,<-

You wander far from the truth and judge the kindness of a most religious man <note>Referring to Father Marin Mersenne, a monk and central figure in the 17th-century scientific "Republic of Letters."</note> with malice, if you suspect that anything about you was reported to me by Father Mersenne; but so that I

<margin>10</margin> could not make as much progress elsewhere as I could with you, and many other things of that kind, which you seemed to write familiarly and as a friend might write to one of your schoolboys <note>Beeckman was a rector of a Latin school; Descartes is mockingly suggesting Beeckman treats him like a child</note>; what else ought to have come to my mind, than that you had composed such letters so that, before sending them to me, you might
<margin>15</margin> boast to others by reading them aloud, claiming that I was frequently accustomed to being taught by you? <header>CORRESPONDENCE. II, 58-59.</header>

...I say, from those very ants and worms, I could never have suspected that I had learned anything or could ever learn anything. Do you not remember, when I was occupied with those studies* <note>Descartes is likely referring to his early mathematical and physical researches from 1618–1619, which he shared with Beeckman.</note> for which I declared you were not capable, and you desired to hear other things from me—things which I had long ago set aside as youthful exercises—<gloss>5</gloss> what a hindrance you were to me? You were so far from being a help, and I am now so far from giving you thanks ᵃ. Yet I clearly recognize from your last letters that you have sinned not out of malice, but out of a sickness <note>Descartes patronizingly suggests Beeckman's behavior is a result of a mental or temperamental "infirmity" rather than intentional evil.</note>; therefore, henceforth I shall pity you rather than scold you, and for the sake of <gloss>10</gloss> our old friendship, I will advise you here on the remedies by which I think you might be cured.

Consider first what kinds of things one person can teach another: namely, languages, history, experiments, and likewise certain and manifest demonstrations which <gloss>15</gloss> convince the intellect, such as those of the Geometers <note>term: Geometers. In the 17th century, this referred to mathematicians who used deductive proofs.</note>; these can be taught. However, the tenets and opinions of the Philosophers are not immediately "taught" simply by being spoken. Plato says one thing, Aristotle another, Epicurus another; Telesio, Campanella, Bruno, Basso, Vaninus <note>Descartes lists several "modern" or controversial philosophers: Bernardino Telesio, Tommaso Campanella, Giordano Bruno (burned at the stake in 1600), Sebastiano Basso, and Lucilio Vanini (executed in 1619). He uses them to illustrate the lack of certainty in non-mathematical philosophy.</note>, <gloss>20</gloss> and all the Innovators <note>term: Innovators. A label for contemporary thinkers who sought to overturn traditional Aristotelian philosophy.</note>—each says something different. Which of them "teaches"—I do not say me, but any student of wisdom? Only the first one who persuades with his reasons or at least with his authority. If, however, someone believes something without being moved by anyone's authority or reasons, <gloss>25</gloss> even if he has heard that very thing from many people, he is not to be thought of as having learned it from them. Indeed, it can happen that he *knows* it, because he is led to belief by true reasons; whereas others, although they previously held the same opinion, did not *know* it, since they deduced it from false principles. <gloss>30</gloss>

### II, 59-60. XXIV. — 17 OCTOBER 1630.

If you consider these things diligently, you will easily perceive that I have never learned anything more from that *Mathematical-Physics* <note>original: "Mathematico-Physica". This refers to the application of mathematical principles to physical problems, a cornerstone of the New Science that both men discussed in 1618.</note> of yours, which you dream about, than from the *Battle of the Frogs and Mice* <note>original: "Batrachomyomachia". This is an ancient Greek parody of the Iliad; Descartes uses it here to dismiss Beeckman’s work as a trivial joke.</note>; for was it your authority that moved me? Or did your reasons persuade me? But you said some things which, as soon as I understood them, I believed and approved. <margin>5</margin> Think, therefore, that because I immediately believed them, I did not learn them from you, but rather, since I already held the same opinion, I approved them. And do not feed your sickness <note>Descartes uses "sickness" (morbus) throughout this letter to describe Beeckman’s vanity and his obsessive need for intellectual credit.</note> by the fact that I confess to having sometimes <margin>10</margin> approved of what you said; for it happened so rarely that no one could discuss Philosophy <note>term: Philosophy. In this period, "Natural Philosophy" included what we now call science, such as physics and biology.</note> so unskillfully that they would not, by chance, say equally many things that agree with the truth. Indeed, many people can know the same thing, even if none has learned it from the other, and it is ridiculous <margin>15</margin> to distinguish so precisely, as you do, between what is yours and what belongs to another in the possession of the sciences, as if they were fields or money. If you know something, it is entirely yours, however much you may have learned it from another. But by what right, or rather by what sickness, if others know that same <margin>20</margin> thing, do you not allow it to be theirs as well? There is no longer any reason for me to pity you; your sickness has made you happy, and you possess no less wealth than that other man, who believed all the ships arriving at the port of his city were his own <note>A reference to Thrasyllus, a famous figure from classical antiquity who suffered from a delusion that he owned every ship that entered the harbor of Piraeus.</note>. But if I may say so, with your leave, <margin>25</margin> you use that fortune a little too insolently; for see how unjust you are; you wish to possess alone, and you forbid others to claim for themselves not only those things which they know and never learned from you, but even those very things which you confess to have learned from them. For you write that the *Algebra* <note>term: Algebra. Descartes refers here to his early developments in analytical geometry and algebraic notation, which he had shared with Beeckman years earlier.</note> which I gave you <margin>30</margin> is no longer mine; you have written the same about the *Music* <note>original: "Musica". This refers to the "Compendium Musicae," a short treatise on music theory that Descartes wrote for Beeckman as a New Year's gift in 1618.</note> elsewhere. You wish, then, I suppose, that these sciences be erased from my memory, because they are now yours:

### CORRESPONDENCE. II, 60-61.

For why would you ask for the original manuscripts <note>original: "autographa". Descartes refers to the papers he had written and shared with Beeckman years earlier.</note> (since you have copies <note>original: "exemplaria"</note> with you, whereas I have none), unless so that, with the lapse of time, I might be able to forget those things contained in them—on which I am no longer working—and you alone might possess them?
<margin>5</margin> But undoubtedly you wrote those things as a joke, for I know how elegant and witty you are; for you do not seriously wish it to be believed that anything is yours unless you stood forth as its first inventor <note>original: "inuentor"</note>. For that reason, you record the time in your manuscript <note>Descartes is mocking Beeckman’s "Journal," a diary where Beeckman meticulously recorded and dated every scientific thought or conversation.</note> when you thought of each thing, <margin>10</margin> lest anyone by chance be so impudent as to want to claim for themselves what they dreamed just one whole night later than you. In which matter, however, I do not judge you to be guarding your interests with enough prudence; for what if the reliability of that manuscript of yours is doubted? Would it not be safer to bring forth witnesses or to confirm it with public records? But <margin>15</margin> truly, to speak the truth, these "riches," which fear thieves <note>original: "fures". Descartes frequently uses the metaphor of "intellectual theft" to mock Beeckman’s anxiety over being credited.</note> and must be guarded with such anxiety, make you miserable rather than happy; nor, if you believe me, will you be sorry to lose them along with your sickness <note>Descartes refers again to Beeckman's perceived vanity and obsession with credit as a "morbus" or sickness.</note>.

<margin>20</margin> Consider within yourself, I pray, whether in your whole life you have found anything that is worthy of true praise. I will propose three types of inventions <note>original: "inuentorum"</note> to you. First, if you have anything of some importance that you were able to devise by the force of intellect <term>intellect: original "ingenij", referring to natural talent or mental power</term> and the guidance of <margin>25</margin> reason <note>original: "rationis"</note>, I admit you are to be praised; but I deny that you should therefore fear thieves. Water is very similar to water, but it always tastes different when it is drunk from the spring itself than when from a jug or a stream. Whatever is transferred from the place where it was born into another is sometimes improved, more often corrupted; but it <margin>30</margin> never retains all its native characteristics so well that it is not easy to recognize that it was translated from elsewhere. You write that you [have been robbed] by me...

Descartes argues that true intellectual discoveries are like spring water—they are inherently linked to their source—and that Beeckman’s anxiety over "intellectual thieves" only proves his own misery and vanity.</summary>

CORRESPONDENCE. I.

I truly deny that I have learned much [from you]; for if there are things I know, they are very few, not many; but whatever they may be, use them if you can, claim them as your own; as far as I am concerned, you may. I have inscribed them in no registers <note>original: "tabulis". Descartes is mocking Beeckman's habit of recording every thought in his diary or "ledger."</note>, <margin>5</margin> I have not recorded the time when they were discovered; yet I do not doubt that, if I ever wanted people to know the character of my own small store of talent <note>original: "fundulus ingenij mei". Literally "the little bottom" or "small foundation" of my mind.</note>, they would easily recognize that these fruits were harvested from that [talent], and not from some other source.
--- There is another kind of discovery <note>original: "inuentorum"</note> that does not come from talent <note>original: "ingenio"</note>, but from luck <note>original: "fortuna"</note>, and which I admit <margin>10</margin> must be guarded so that it remains safe from thieves. For if you have found something by chance, and another person hears of it from you by chance, he will possess it by the same right as you, and will be able to claim it for himself just as much. But I deny that any true praise is owed to such discoveries. <margin>15</margin> Since, however, the common people are so ignorant as to praise those in whom some gifts of luck stand out—thinking that Goddess <note>Descartes refers to the personified Goddess of Fortune (Fortuna), traditionally depicted as blind.</note> is not so blind as to bestow things on the completely undeserving—if she has happened to bestow something on you that stands out a little more, I shall judge you worthy of some praise. But only *what stands out a little* <margin>20</margin> *more*; for if a beggar <note>original: "mendicus"</note>, because he had collected a few coins by begging from door to door, believed that great honor was owed to him, he would be laughed at by everyone. Look, I pray you, carefully unroll your manuscript <note>original: "manuſcriptum"</note>; count everything. Either I am very much mistaken, or <margin>25</margin> you will find nothing in it of your own that is more precious than its binding <note>original: "integumento". Descartes is suggesting the physical cover is worth more than the intellectual content within.</note>. --- There is a third kind: those things which, although they are of no or very little value, are nonetheless esteemed as great matters by their inventors. These are so far from being worthy of any praise that, on the contrary, the more <margin>30</margin> highly they are valued by their owners and the more diligently they are guarded, the more they expose those owners to the laughter or pity of others. I set before your eyes a certain bli— <note>The word is cut off; it likely begins a metaphor about a "blind man" [caecum] which continues on the next page.</note>

->CORRESPONDENCE. II, 62-64.<-

Suppose there was someone so crazed with greed that he spent whole days searching for gems among the refuse of other people's houses. Whenever a small pebble or a fragment of glass fell into his hands, he immediately judged it to be a very precious 
<margin>5</margin> stone; and when he had finally found many such things and filled a little box with them, he would boast of being the wealthiest of men, showing off the box and despising others. Would you not say at first glance that a happy kind of madness had befallen him? But if afterward you saw him 
<margin>10</margin> hovering over the box, fearing thieves and miserably anguishing lest he lose those riches which he could not even use, would you not set aside your laughter and judge him worthy of pity? I do not wish, indeed, to compare your manuscript to that box; but I think there can be 
<margin>15</margin> hardly anything in it more solid than pebbles and fragments of glass.

Aristotle is the 
<margin>25</margin> thief; call him to court, let him restore your thought to you. But what did I do? When writing on music <note>Descartes refers to his *Compendium Musicae*, which he wrote for Beeckman in 1618.</note>, after I had explained something that did not depend on an accurate knowledge of sound, I added that the matter could be conceived in the same way, whether one says that sound 
<margin>30</margin> strikes the ears with many blows, or etc. <note>Descartes is citing his own phrasing to show he was merely using a common hypothesis, not claiming a discovery.</note> Did I steal that which I did not even claim for myself? Or was I obliged to praise what I did not even assert to be true? Or did I [attribute it] to you...

## II, 64-65. XXIV. — 17 OCTOBER 1630.

...assign it to you, something that all schoolmasters <note>original: "Ludimagistri." Beeckman was the rector of a school in Dordrecht; Descartes uses this title here as a slight, suggesting Beeckman is merely a local teacher rather than a profound philosopher.</note>, except for you, have learned from Aristotle? Truly, if I did not sympathize with your sickness <note>Descartes characterizes Beeckman's vanity and desire for credit as a mental "morbus" or disease.</note>, I would be unable to keep from laughing; for you did not even understand what a hyperbola was, unless perhaps as a grammarian <note>A play on words: "hyperbole" is a rhetorical figure of speech for exaggeration, whereas a "hyperbola" is a mathematical curve. I mentioned a certain property of it regarding the bending of rays <note>This refers to optics and how light refracts through lenses.</note>, the proof of which had slipped from my memory and—as sometimes happens with the easiest things—did not occur to me on the spot; but I demonstrated its converse to you in the <term>ellipse</term> <note>An oval-shaped geometric curve.</note>, and I explained several <term>theorems</term> <note>Logical statements in mathematics that have been proven.</note> from which it could be so easily deduced that it could escape no one who paid even the slightest attention. For this reason, I encouraged you to exercise your mind in seeking it out; which I certainly would not have done—since you admitted you knew nothing at all about <term>conics</term> <note>The branch of geometry dealing with the sections of a cone, such as circles, ellipses, and hyperbolas.</note>—unless I had judged it to be very easy. You indeed sought it, found it, and showed it to me; I was glad, and I said that I would use that proof if I were ever to write about that matter. Tell me: are you sane, since you reproach me for not showing enough honor and reverence to you as "my teacher"? If you had given one of your schoolboys, who had never before written a single poem, an <term>epigram</term> <note>A short, witty poem.</note> to compose; and you had dictated its meaning to him in such a way that the whole verse stood firm with only one or two words transposed, would you not be glad for his sake if he successfully transposed those words? Might you perhaps even add—to encourage him toward <term>poetry</term>—that you would use no other verses if you ever wanted to write an epigram on the same subject? But what if, because of that meager bit of praise, he were so puffed up that he [believed] himself to be a great poet...

# CORRESPONDENCE. II, 65-66.

...thought this, would you not laugh at him as if he were a child? And what if he actually believed that you envied him for that reason, and—calling himself your teacher—said seriously: *it is shameful for a teacher...* <note>original: "turpe est doctori &c." II, 66-67. XXIV. — 17 OCTOBER 1630.

I would wish for your infamy, but I fear I might lead you to Lycambes’s noose <note>original: "Lycambi laqueum." Literally "alienated" or "estranged," suggesting Beeckman is losing his sanity or has been driven mad by his "disease" (his vanity and anger).</note> that you actually believe it; yet, because I recognize <margin>15</margin> that the power of your "disease" can be very great, I will explain what gave you the occasion for that insult. It is the custom of Philosophers, and even of Theologians, whenever they wish to show that something is contrary to reason, to say that it cannot be done even by God; I do not deny that this way of speaking <margin>20</margin> seems a little too bold for my taste; and for that reason, to speak more modestly, if anything similar occurs to me (and it can occur more often in mathematical than in philosophical matters), that which others would say is impossible for God, I say only that it is impossible for an Angel <margin>25</margin> to do. But if for that reason I equate myself to an Angel, then by the same logic the wisest men in the world must be said to equate themselves to God; and I am indeed most unfortunate if I could not escape the suspicion of vanity in the very thing in which I was striving for a particular modesty. <margin>30</margin> Furthermore, I could write much more; but unless these things help you, more would not. And now I think I have abundantly...

A significant double gloss. For, first, Descartes did not need to teach the Rector of the college of Dordrecht that the reputed author of the *Batrachomyomachia* is Homer; that is information undoubtedly given, during the course of the translation, by Clerselier to his son, and which the latter will have inserted into his French text. Furthermore, Descartes would not have cited to a Dutchman (who was little acquainted with French literature, since their correspondence is in Latin) a popular book like the *Tales of the Stork* <note>original: "Contes de la Cigogne." A collection of popular stories or fables well-known in France at the time.</note>; this is again, undoubtedly, a word from Clerselier, to make the young boy understand into what category of works the *Batrachomyomachia* might fall. For this double reason, the Latin text, where these two pieces of information are missing, seems indeed to be the original by Descartes; for if

...if it were a translation of the French version, why would the translator have omitted these few words, which are nonetheless so curious?

Page 159, line 6. — French version:
> "But you will perhaps tell me" that you said certain things, which I no sooner heard <note>original: "entenduës." In the 17th century, this could mean both "heard" and "understood."</note> than I believed and approved them." (CLERSELIER, vol. II, p. 59).

The word "entendre" (to hear/understand), in 17th-century French, translated both the Latin *intelligere* (to understand) and *audire* (to hear). BAILLET (vol. I, p. 207), who undoubtedly did not consult the Latin text, understood it in the sense of *audire* (to hear):
> "Mr. Descartes might have approved" of things he had heard from Beeckman, as often happens in conversation."

But Descartes did not believe everything he heard so quickly; he wanted to understand it first: *intellexi* (I understood) is therefore more likely.

Page 159, line 23. — See Aelian, *Historical Miscellany* <note>original: "Variæ Historiæ." A 3rd-century Greek work often cited for its anecdotes.</note>, Book IV, chapter xxv.

Page 159, line 25. — *See how unjust you are* <note>original: "Vide quam iniustus es."</note>: A translator would have used the subjunctive *sis*, as is found twelve lines later: *for I know how elegant and witty you are* <note>original: "noui enim quàm sis elegans et facetus."</note>. The indicative *es* (you are) appears to be a grammatical error made intentionally to more strongly assert the fact.

Page 159, line 29. — Descartes to Mersenne, 1638 (CLERSELIER, vol. II, pp. 370-1):
> "I would find no difficulty in sending (to Mr. Mydorge) my old Algebra, except that it is a writing that does not seem to me to deserve to be seen; and because there is no one that I know of who has a copy of it, I shall be very glad if it no longer leaves my hands."

<margin>In the margin (BAILLET, vol. I, p. 320): "Mr. de la Barre and others have had it since."</margin> Mr. de la Barre, president of the Bureau of Finances of Tours, had conducted research in Touraine and Poitou for the *Life of Descartes* (BAILLET, vol. I, pp. XXIII-XXIV). This Algebra, which dated from 1618-1619, has not been found. The inventory of papers found in Descartes's trunks after his death mentions in Article D:
> "A small octavo register, containing one hundred and fifty-five pages, where he seems to have written for his own use an introduction containing the foundations of his Algebra."

Page 160, line 9. — A certain number of dates (only eight in total) are indeed found in the 1644 printed edition, with this warning from Beeckman's brother in the Preface:
> "I have compiled this century [collection of 100 items] from his many meditations, and I wished to present them in the order in which he had meditated upon them, occasionally even adding the time when these had occurred to him, lest anyone should think he had plundered the desks of other philosophers." <note>original: "Centuriam hanc ex multis ejus meditationibus compegi..." This note defends Beeckman against charges of plagiarism by providing a timeline of his thoughts.</note>

Compare below, Letter XXV, page 171, line 22.

Page 160, line 27. — French version, CLERSELIER (vol. II, p. 61):
> "Water is always similar to water, but it has quite another taste when it is drawn at its source than when one draws it from a pitcher or from its stream."

BAILLET already corrected this (vol. I, p. 208): "Than when one takes it in a pitcher or in a stream." The Latin text is infinitely preferable.

Indeed, he has just spoken of "turning" Latin verses (p. 163, l. 22).

**Page 165, l. 2.** — French version: "*I would rather fear making you despair, than giving you health*" (Clerselier, II, 66): *Making you despair* <note>original: "Vous desesperer"</note> is a free translation of *to lead to Lycambes's noose* <note>original Latin: "ad Lycambi laqueum perducere"</note>. Lycambes was a Theban who hanged himself out of despair, so badly had he been mocked in a satire by <term>Archilochus</term>. This is another of those Latinate elegances, like *cornea fibra*. **Page 167, l. 8.** — A hurtful allusion to Beeckman's country of origin. One of his compatriots, Paul of Middelburg, a predecessor of Galileo at the University of Padua, said: "*We give thanks to God, that being originated from Middelburg and the barbaric island of Zeeland in the icy Ocean, and if it may be said, born in a country of rams, or a region of cobblers, in which drunkenness*" <note>original Latin: "Gratias Deo agemus, quod Middelburgo oriundi et glacialis Oceani barbara Zelandiæ insula, et si fas sit dicere, vervecum in patria, aut cerdonum regione nati, in qua ebrietas..."</note>

### XXV.

## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

->[Amsterdam, 4 November 1630.]<-

->Text from Clerselier, volume II, letter 61, p. 311-315.<-

*Undated in Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier was the first editor of Descartes's correspondence, though he often removed dates and names</note>. The date we indicate is the lower limit, because the following Letter (see the fifth paragraph) is at least three weeks later, and the date, November 25, is almost certain. As for the upper limit, it is obviously October 21, 1630, the first Monday after the 17th, the date of the previous letter to Beeckman, the beginning of which is reproduced in this one. But Descartes likely only goes into the details of his quarrel with the rector of Dordrecht <note>Isaac Beeckman</note> because Mersenne asked him to, and Mersenne himself must have been informed of this quarrel only by Descartes himself, in a letter (now lost) written after the receipt of the second letter from Beeckman, cited below, which is to say probably October 14. The date of November 4, for the present letter XXV, seems more probable for this reason. The proper names in this letter were often replaced, in Clerselier's text, by an N.; we have restored them in parentheses.*

The beginning and the end of this passage are marked, on the copy at the Institute <note>The Institut de France, which holds many of these historical manuscripts.</note>, by the following annotations: "Another letter to Mersenne, 1630" — "here the fragment ends," written at the fourth and tenth paragraphs of a letter without a date or recipient's name. These determinations appear to be merely conjectural; however, the opening below allows us to place the present letter immediately after number XXV without any possible dispute. ## XXVII.

### DESCARTES TO FERRIER.

->[December 2, 1630.]<-

->Text from Clerselier, volume II, letter 62, pp. 316-319.<- <note>Claude Clerselier was Descartes' first major editor and a devoted follower who published his letters and unpublished papers after the philosopher's death.</note>

*This letter and the two following ones were written on the same day, as is evident from the first paragraph of Letter XXIX below. Descartes is replying to the "large packet" sent "this week" by Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier was a skilled craftsman and lens-maker; Descartes initially hoped he would move to the Netherlands to assist in manufacturing hyperbolic lenses for telescopes.</note>, which was accompanied by a letter from Gassendi to Renery <note>Pierre Gassendi was a contemporary philosopher and scientist, often a rival of Descartes; Henri Renery was one of Descartes' first disciples in the Netherlands.</note> (see the first note after Letter XXIX). We have the date (November 22, 1630) of this latter letter, published in the* Gassendi Opera <note>original: "Gassendi Opera," the collected works of Pierre Gassendi.</note>. *The packet must therefore have arrived in Amsterdam on Saturday, November 30. The letters that Descartes immediately wrote in response were sent on Monday, December 2, the day the mail departed. Apart from Gassendi and Mersenne, Ferrier had directly involved three other people in contacting Descartes (see Letter XXX below). We only have the response made to one of them, Father de Condren (Letter XXVIII); the other two were likely Father Gibieuf and Mydorge (if not Father de Sancy, as Mydorge seems to have written separately and earlier regarding Ferrier).*

[He] having been in Paris all through the year 1627 and also the year 1628 until December, had returned to Balzac <note>The family estate of Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac in Angoumois.</note>, where he remained all through the year 1629, except perhaps for a short trip to Paris: one of his letters, dated October 10, is from Paris, but perhaps by mistake; around that time he would have written to Descartes, who inquired about him in his letter to Ferrier, dated November 13, 1629 (p. 132, l. 10.) Throughout the year 1630, he still remained at Balzac, and did not come to Paris until 1631: a letter from January 6 is still dated from Balzac; another, from February 8, is dated from Paris, as well as those following until September 7 inclusive. From then on, the letters begin to be dated from Balzac again.

->Sir,<-

<margin>10</margin>hesitation <note>original: "scrupule"</note> about going to disturb your rest even in your desert <note>A common 17th-century term for a rural retreat or secluded estate, implying a place of quiet reflection.</note>, and believed it was better that I wait to write to you until you had left it; this is what has made me delay from one journey to the next, for the space of eighteen months, which I never intended to delay

### CORRESPONDANCE.

...I have not been tempted to return there <note>Descartes refers here to Paris, which he had left for the solitude of the Netherlands.</note> even once, except since I was informed that you were there. But this news has made me realize that I could now be happier somewhere else than I

<margin>15</margin> to tell you; I have become such a philosopher <note>original: "philosophe"; here meaning one who seeks wisdom through a quiet, detached lifestyle</note> that I despise most of the things that are usually valued, and value some others that people are not accustomed to caring about. However, because your feelings are so far removed from those of the
<margin>20</margin> common people, and because you have often shown me that you judge me more favorably than I deserve, I will not fail to speak with you about it more openly one day, if you would not find it disagreeable. For now, I will content myself with
<margin>25</margin> telling you that I am no longer in the mood to put anything into writing, as you once saw me inclined to do. It is not that I do not highly value reputation <term>reputation: social standing and fame resulting from published works</term>, when one is certain to acquire a good and great one, as you have done; but for a mediocre and uncertain one, such as I might hope for, I
<margin>30</margin> value it much less than the rest <term>repos: a state of quietude and seclusion from the world</term> and peace of mind <term>tranquillité d’esprit: mental calmness, often considered the ultimate goal of the philosophical life</term> that I possess. I sleep here ten hours every [night]...

## DESCARTES TO [RENERI].

### [Amsterdam], June 2, 1631.

->Text from Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier was the primary editor and translator of Descartes' posthumous works</note>, volume III, letter III, pp. 602-604.<-

*The recipient's name is missing in Clerselier; however, the end of the letter—"I will be able to tell you more about it this Thursday"—indicates that it is addressed to a correspondent living in the Netherlands, not far from Amsterdam, whom Descartes sees regularly. One might consider either Reneri, who since the end of 1629 was a tutor for a family in Leiden, or Golius, a professor of mathematics at the University in the same city, where Descartes had enrolled as a student on June 27, 1630. Furthermore, he wrote to both of them in French, and there is no reason to suppose that Clerselier provided a version of a Latin text. However, with Golius, Descartes specifically discusses mathematics (see Letters XXXIX and XL below), and he is far from having the same intimacy as with Reneri, who was, in fact, his first disciple and to whom he would later write on the same subject on July 2, 1634.*

->Sir,<-

To resolve your difficulties, imagine the air like wool, and the <term>ether [the "subtle matter" Descartes believed filled all space]</term> which is in its pores like <term>whirlwinds [tourbillons]</term> of wind, which move here and there <margin>5</margin> within this wool; and consider that this wind, which plays on all sides between the small threads of this wool, prevents them from pressing as hard against one another as they otherwise might. For <margin>10</margin> they are all heavy <note>original: "peſans"; in this context, it refers to having weight or being subject to gravity</note>, and they press upon one another as much as the agitation of this wind allows them, so much so that the wool against the earth is pressed by all that which is...

<summary>In this letter, Descartes uses a mechanical analogy of wool and wind to explain his theory of air and "ether," attempting to illustrate how atmospheric pressure and matter interact. The introductory note argues that the recipient is likely Henricus Reneri, Descartes' first devoted follower.</summary>

<keywords>physics, ether, vortices, atmospheric pressure, Henricus Reneri, mechanical philosophy, Amsterdam, Leiden</keywords>

Physical and Medical Meditations, Century I*, no. 77, p. 45, says this: "...Then I also showed

Cf. *ibid.*, no. 35, p. 13: "The 'flight from vacuum' is explained... It happens that air rests upon things in the manner of water, and compresses them according to the depth of the resting [air]. Certain things remain at rest, and are not constantly pushed away, because they are compressed equally on all sides by the resting air, just as happens to us when we dive <note>original: *urinantibus*; literally those swimming or diving underwater.</note> and are pressed by the water; however, they seek an empty space with great effort because of the immense depth of the resting air, and because of the mass resulting from it..."

estimate that the cause of this filling of air both above and below comes 
from the equilibrium that nature restores: for earth taken from caverns 
making a place for itself in the air, it drives it out and constrains it to descend

previously in the space occupied by the moved earth would have to be annihilated, or that it

> "...occupy the place of another air by penetration <note>In physics of this period, "penetration" referred to the impossible idea of two bodies occupying the same space at once.</note>, or that it should pass through or push an equal amount of air into imaginary spaces, or that it should suffer a perpetual condensation—something not seen in nature, which always makes up for its deficiencies by the shortest and easiest path."
> (*Essays of Jean Rey*, 1777 edition, pp. 109-111; cf. 124-128 and 142-143).

Rey responds on January 1, 1632: "People will tell me that the air filling the holes made high up in the beams of a floor must be called light, since it rises. But I will tell them that for the same reason they must say water is light, which rises into a boat through holes made in its planks, or (to make the comparison fit better) which rises into holes one might imagine made in the vaults of caves beneath the water. They will not grant me this, nor I them the rest. Certainly both instances of filling occur due to the weight of the higher parts, whether of air or water, which, sinking down upon the lower parts, force them to push those near the holes to fill them. Which you yourself confirm, without thinking of it, when you say that this comes from the equilibrium that nature restores." (*Ibid.*, pp. 124-5).

— Cf. the two small *Treatises on the Equilibrium of Liquids and the Weight of the Mass of Air*, published in 1663, a year after the death of Pascal, who had composed them "more than twelve years" [earlier] (Pascal and Descartes: the experiments on the vacuum, 1646-1651, by Ch. Adam, *Philosophical Review*, Dec. 1887 and Jan. 1888). — Around the same time (1631), Descartes was explaining the same ideas in his *The World* <note>original: *Le Monde*</note>, chapter IV of the fragments that remain to us: "What judgment should be made regarding the vacuum..."

## XXXV.

### VILLEBRESSIEU TO DESCARTES.

->[Summer of 1631.]<-

->[A. BAILLET,] *The Life of Monsieur Des-Cartes*, vol. I, pp. 257-261.<-

Baillet had in his hands several letters from Villebressieu to Descartes; what he says of them, regarding the year 1634, is not sufficient to distinguish these letters, so we gather hereafter the various citations made from them. The date indicated should naturally be seen as referring only to the oldest one, mentioned as follows:

...friend Beeckman, whom old age and illness seemed to threaten with death. A few days earlier, he had received news from Mr. de Ville-Bressieux, who had written to him from the borders of Denmark to send him the observations he had made there since their separation, and to give him an account of the time he had spent with a friend *with* whom he had left him. <margin>Manuscript letter from Est. de Ville-Bress. to Descartes.</margin> Having returned to Amsterdam, he wrote back to him in these terms: (Following is fragment F of letter XXXVI hereafter, a letter from which Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes's first major biographer, whose work is often the only source for lost letters.</note> must have drawn the beginning of this paragraph).

According to Baillet, moreover, Ville-Bressieu would have come to live with Descartes in 1632, and the journey both of them took to Denmark would not have taken place until 1634. In 1631, on the contrary, Descartes was supposedly in England. But we know that this trip to England, planned in 1630, was never carried out. On the other hand, in 1634, if Descartes—after his stay in Deventer from June 1632 to December 1633—did indeed return to Amsterdam, he resided (letter to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne, a monk and mathematician who served as the central "clearinghouse" for scientific correspondence in Europe.</note> of May 15, 1634) "at the house of Mr. Thomas Sergeant on Western Church Street" <note>original: *in den Westerkerck Straet*</note>; he had therefore abandoned the "Old Prince Lodging" <note>original: *logis du Vieux Prince*</note>, where he awaited Ville-Bressieu (letter XXXVI F). The following years being excluded (Descartes was in Utrecht in 1635, in Leiden in 1636, and Beeckman died on May 20, 1637), we must go back to 1631; we know, furthermore, from a letter from Beeckman dated October 7, 1631, that Descartes's reconciliation with him had already taken place.

As for the following excerpt, although Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet, Descartes’s biographer, who often struggled with the exact chronology of the philosopher's life.</note> provides it (vol. I, p. 257) before fragment D of letter XXXVI, as if the latter formed a reply, it seems instead to belong to a significantly later date; however, it is difficult to be precise:

<margin>D</margin>
> .... I cannot thank you worthily enough for the obligations I owe you. It is impossible for me to repay them, except by reminding you of the good you have done me in general and in detail. I studied you for so long when you did me the honor of liking me, and of making use of me during your journey to **Lower Germany** <note>Historically referring to the regions of the Netherlands and Northwest Germany.</note>, and in Paris for the execution of the **great elliptical mirror** <term>elliptical mirror: a curved mirror shaped like a section of an ellipse, designed to focus light or images in a specific way</term> that you had me make out of **artificial marble***. It was six feet high and two and a half feet wide. Being enclosed within a room, it received objects from the outside through a fairly small hole, and projected the image back outside through the same hole; and it made the image appear **upright**, contrary to the usual behavior of **concave mirrors**, which flip the object upside down as soon as it is beyond the focus or the burning point. I had been astonished by such an effect; but I have just learned that this happens because it can only receive the object through a hole entirely inverted; and its nature being to invert the images it has received upright, this is what causes such a miracle*.

# XXXVI. — SUMMER OF 1631.

...to warn then that the letter was written "some years since," from Amsterdam, to Villebressieu; it therefore seems he drew the whole from one and the same piece.

<margin>A</margin>
[IN THE MARGIN: Manuscript letter from Descartes to Ville-Bressieu] : "This means (of avoiding fallacies <note>original: "sophismes"</note>) was none other than his universal Rule, which he often called his natural Method, upon which he put to the test all sorts of propositions, of whatever nature and whatever kind they might be. The first fruit of this method was to show at once whether the proposition was possible or not, because it examined it and ensured it (to use his terms) with a knowledge and certainty equal to that which the rules of Arithmetic can produce. The other fruit consisted in making it solve the difficulty of the same proposition infallibly."

<margin>B</margin>
You have seen these two fruits of my fine rule or natural Method regarding what I was obliged to do during the conversation I had with the Papal Nuncio <note>Guillaume Guidi di Bagno, the Pope’s representative in Paris.</note>, Cardinal de Bérulle <note>Pierre de Bérulle (1575–1629), a powerful cleric who encouraged Descartes to dedicate his life to philosophy.</note>, Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), Descartes’s lifelong friend and the central coordinator of the 17th-century scientific community.</note>, and all <margin>5</margin> this great and learned company that had assembled at the home of the said Nuncio to hear the discourse of M. de Chandoux <note>Nicolas de Villers, Sieur de Chandoux, a chemist and philosopher later executed for counterfeiting; he argued for a philosophy based on probability rather than certainty.</note> regarding his new philosophy. It was there that I made the whole troop confess what the art of reasoning well can do upon the minds of those who are <margin>10</margin> moderately learned, and how much my principles are better established, more true, and more natural than any of the others that are already accepted among scholars. You remained convinced of it, as did all those who took the trouble to implore me to <margin>15</margin> write them down and teach them to the public.

<margin>C</margin>
[No. II of the manuscript letter to Ville-Bressieu. *Summary from Baillet, I, 260*] : "...to consider the cause by which all the things that appear simplest to us are made, as well as the clearest and least complex effects of nature. Great Mechanics <note>Descartes viewed the physical world as a vast machine governed by mathematical laws; "Mechanics" here refers to the underlying laws of physics.</note> being nothing else (according to him) than the order that God has imprinted upon the face of his..."

*...work, which we commonly call Nature, he estimated that it was better to look at this great model, and to focus on following this example, rather than the rules and maxims established by the caprice of several men of the study <note>original: "hommes de cabinet," referring to scholars who work only from books and abstract theory rather than practical observation</note>, whose imaginary principles produce no fruit, because they suit neither nature nor the person seeking to learn.*

<margin>D</margin>
*[*Manuscript letter from Descartes to Ville-Bressieu. Summary by Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes's first major biographer, who had access to many now-lost manuscripts.</note>, I, 257-8*] : "M. Descartes took the opportunity to give M. de Ville-Bressieu <note>Étienne de Villebressieu, a king's engineer and chemist who worked closely with Descartes on practical mechanics.</note> an account of his experiments and inventions. It was based on his precepts, and especially on his great maxim that the simplest things are usually the most excellent, that M. de Ville-Bressieu had found the proper Machine for raising water in large quantities and with great ease. Nevertheless, M. Descartes complimented him on it, as if he had invented and discovered this fine machine by his own pure genius. It must be admitted that he had been content to show him the reason <note>In this context, "reason" refers to the underlying physical or mathematical principle.</note> by which it should be done. Immediately, M. de Ville-Bressieu felt assured of the result, just as if he had tested it on a large and small scale, because M. Descartes had accustomed him early on to seek clarity on the cause of all the effects we observe in nature.*

*Among the other particular inventions that M. de Ville-Bressieu had devised alongside M. Descartes, we find:*

*1. The Double Spiral for descending from a tower without danger.*
*2. Wooden Pincers <note>likely a type of mechanical clamp or climbing aid</note> for climbing up by a slender rope.*
*3. The Lathe <note>or hoist</note> made with two sticks or pieces of wood for ascending and descending.*
*4. The Rolling Bridge for scaling a fortress that has a deep and wide moat.*
*5. The Boat for crossing rivers made of four wooden planks, which folded up and could be carried under the arm.*
*6. But above all, M. Descartes exhorted him to give the public his Sedan-Chair-Carriage <note>original: "Chariot-Chaise"</note>, judging this machine very useful for everyone, and particularly for wounded soldiers. The structure of it was neither difficult nor very expensive. It could be made wherever there were barrel hoops, and the two wheels could in no way inconvenience the person inside the carriage. Its principal convenience consisted in the fact that one could be transported in health and in sickness on all sorts of paths by a single man.*

He then, while praising the speaker’s delivery, did not praise the gathering, because they had been content only with the probable <note>original: "veriſimili." Descartes argues that "probable" or "likely" truths are not sufficient for science; only absolute, mathematical certainty will do.</note>, and he promised that he could prove any truth to be false by twelve probable arguments, and vice versa; having attempted this, they were amazed and remained stunned. Wherefore, asking whether some method of avoiding sophisms <note>Fallacious arguments intended to deceive.</note> existed, he asserted to them that truth could be mathematically demonstrated in all things according to his principles. He was then urged to make those principles public; having been forced to grant this to them, he withdrew to Holland so that he might publish them more clearly organized.” — Baillet (I, 161-164) first rectifies several facts: it was not at the siege of La Rochelle, but in Paris, where Descartes had returned as early as Saint Martin’s Day (Nov. 11, 1628), that the session took place at the home of the Pope’s nuncio, Mr. de Bagni or de Baigné, and not Barberini. Baillet then uses Borel's few lines as material for amplification, and reconstructs the entire scene by giving a role to everyone: “Cardinal de Bérulle, who was observing him particularly, noticed his silence. This was what forced him to...”

### XXXVII.

## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

->[Amsterdam, October 1631?]<-

->AUTOGRAPH, National Library, French Manuscript, new acquisitions, 5160, folios 46 and 47.<-

Variants based on the text by *Clerselier* <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes's letters and his brother-in-law; his editions are vital where originals are lost.</note>, volume II, letter 66, pages 325-328. — The original is on a large-format sheet, folded into two leaves: the first is entirely covered in writing on both the front and back (38 and 39 lines); the second is three-quarters torn away: only the top remains, which contains a table, plus 6 lines and a few still-legible words of the 7th line. These words (...I... why... that I...) are found in the printed version by *Clerselier* with 5 additional lines. Very little is therefore missing from the autograph (unless there was a post-scriptum), and the printed version can fill the gaps.
At the bottom left of the page: 6 c, which refers to the 6th letter in the classification by *La Hire* <note>Philippe de La Hire (1640–1718), a mathematician who organized Descartes's papers.</note>. At the top right, there is nothing, as *Dom Poirier* <note>Germain Poirier (1724–1803), a Benedictine monk and archivist.</note> did not include it in his new classification because the date is missing along with the end of the letter.
The indicated date is conjectural; *Baillet* <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), Descartes's early biographer.</note> (I, 223) marks this letter as being from February 1631, and a note from the *Institute’s Copy* <note>A reference to a specific archival copy held by the Institut de France.</note> marks it as January 13th; but the context, particularly the final sentence preserved by *Clerselier*, seems to show that it is more likely immediately prior to the following letter, XXXVIII; and that one is certainly from the final quarter of the year. However, a doubt remains, as it is surprising that *Mersenne* would have waited until October 1631 to send *Descartes* the book by *Father Gibieuf* <note>Guillaume Gibieuf, a priest of the Oratory whose work on liberty Descartes admired.</note> and the *Odes for the King*.

<header>II, 326-327. XXXVII. — OCTOBER 1631.</header>

Regarding the sweetness of consonances <term>consonance: the combination of two or more musical notes that sound stable or "sweet" together</term>, there are two things to distinguish: namely, what makes them more simple and concordant, and what makes them more pleasing to the ear. Now, as for what makes them more pleasing, <margin>5</margin> that depends on the places where they are used; and there are places where even false fifths <term>false fifth: a dissonant interval like the tritone or diminished fifth</term> and other dissonances are more pleasing than consonances, so that one cannot absolutely determine that one consonance is more pleasing than another. One <margin>10</margin> can say, however, that usually thirds and sixths are more pleasing than the fourth; that in happy songs, major thirds and sixths are more pleasing than minor ones, and the opposite in sad ones, etc., because there are more occasions <margin>15</margin> where they can be used pleasingly.

But one can say absolutely which consonances are the simplest and most concordant; for that depends only on the fact that their sounds unite more with one another, and that they more closely approach the <margin>20</margin> nature of unison <term>unison: the sounding of the same note by two voices or instruments</term>; so that one can say absolutely that the fourth is more concordant than the major third, even though it is usually not as pleasing—just as cassia <term>cassia: the sweet-tasting pulp of the "purging cassia" (Cassia fistula), used as a medicine</term> is much sweeter than olives, but not so pleasing to our taste. And to <margin>25</margin> understand this very clearly, one must suppose that sound is nothing other than a certain vibration of the air <note>original: "tremblement d'aer". Descartes is proposing a mechanical explanation for sound as physical motion rather than an abstract quality.</note>

Page 230, l. 20. — It is in his letter to Mersenne of November 13, 1629 (above, page 72) that Descartes treated the <term>descent of heavy bodies</term> <note>original: "descente des graves," a standard phrase in 17th-century physics for falling objects.</note> in a vacuum; if the numerical proportions he indicates here are not found in that letter, they might have appeared in the final portion which is now lost.

The denominators of these ratios are proportional, according to Descartes, to the time of fall during the traversal of the first space; the successive numerators are respectively proportional to the times of fall during the second space, the next two, the next four, then the eight, sixteen, etc. According to Galileo’s law, the ratio that Descartes thus supposes to be equal to 4^n / 3^(n+1) is (√2 - 1)√2^n; the difference, as one can see, is notable (T). <note>The editor "T" refers to Paul Tannery, who notes the discrepancy between Descartes' early calculations and the verified laws of acceleration established by Galileo.</note>

Page 232, l. 4. — This writing is clearly a solution to the problem of <term>Pappus</term> <note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290 – c. 350 AD), a Greek mathematician whose "Collection" preserved much of ancient geometry.</note>, which constitutes one of the main subjects of Descartes' *Geometry*, and can be stated as follows in modern language: given 2 *n* straight lines, find the locus of a point such that the product of its distances to *n* of these lines is in a fixed ratio to the product of the distances to the *n* other lines. One may also assume that in one or the other of the two groups, *p* lines coincide; then the corresponding distance appears in the product with the exponent *p*.

According to <term>Leibniz</term> <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), German polymath and co-inventor of calculus, who often commented on Descartes' legacy.</note> (*Remarks on the Abridgment of the Life of Monsieur des Cartes*, edited by Gerhardt, IV, 316), <term>Hardy</term> <note>Claude Hardy (1604–1678), French mathematician and translator of Euclid.</note> reportedly told him once [from 1673 to 1676] that <term>Golius</term> <note>Jacob Golius (1596–1667), a Dutch orientalist and mathematician who held the chair of mathematics at Leiden.</note>, "very well-versed in the profound Geometry of the ancients," had been the first to propose this problem to Descartes, to put to the test the method that the latter "touted quite loudly." Descartes reportedly spent six weeks on it, which, for that matter, is not surprising (as Leibniz notes against Boyle), given the complexity of the particular cases he had to investigate thoroughly and which he is far from having included all in his *Geometry*. Finally, still according to Leibniz, Descartes would have thus been disabused "of the low opinion he had held of the analysis of the ancients." (See hereafter p. 244, l. 6.)

The role of Golius is all the less doubtful since, according to Letter XLV below, he had previously proposed the same problem to <term>Mydorge</term> <note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), a French mathematician and close friend of Descartes.</note>. It is all the more singular that later (Letter CXII below, to <term>Mersenne</term> <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French priest and central figure in the 17th-century scientific community who facilitated correspondence between scholars.</note>, <term>Clerselier</term> <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the main editor and translator of Descartes' posthumous works.</note>, vol. III, p. 191), Descartes does not count him at all among those who, in the Netherlands, are in a position to understand his *Geometry*.

Page 239, l. 6. — The entirely different version that Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes’ letters; he often modified the text or diagrams to make them clearer to contemporary readers.</note> provides from this point onward relates to a different figure than the one in the autograph <note>The original manuscript written in Descartes' own hand.</note>. We restore it here, completing Clerselier’s version, where lines 3 G 3, E F, and I H are missing, and where the bottom line contains no numbers.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram used to illustrate light refraction. It shows a circle with a center point labeled G. A vertical line passes through the circle's center, containing points labeled H, B, G, D, and F. A horizontal segment I-H is at the top. To the right of the vertical axis, a point C is on the circle's circumference, and a point E is at the bottom right. Two slanted lines intersect the circle and the central vertical axis: one line is labeled with the digit '4' at its top and bottom extremities, and another line is labeled with '3' at its top and bottom. The line '3' passes through the center G. Points A and B are marked on the upper part of the circle.</image-desc>

The description of Vitellion’s instrument, which Descartes mentions later in his first draft, is found in Book II, Proposition 1, of that author. The essential part of it is a graduated circle, held vertically in the liquid which reaches up to its horizontal diameter. However, the accessory devices are very cumbersome to handle. Furthermore, this instrument is borrowed from Alhazen <note>A 10th-century Arab mathematician and physicist, often called "the father of optics."</note>, IV, 7 and VII, 1 (*Thesaurus of Optics* <note>original: "Opticæ thesaurus"</note>, edited by F. Risner, Basel, at the house of the Episcopii, 1572). Descartes says *Vitellion*, as do the Nuremberg editions of 1535 and 1541, and as does Kepler (*Additions to Vitellio* <note>original: "Paralipomena ad Vitellionem"</note>, Frankfurt, at the house of Claude Marne, 1604). Risner printed it as *Vitello*. The true form of the name is Witelo: this author, born in Poland, probably of a Thuringian father and a Polish mother (a "Thuringo-Pole" <note>original: "Thuringopolonus"</note>), had written his ten books toward the middle of the 13th century, in a monastery of the Premonstratensian order <note>An order of Roman Catholic canons regular founded in 1120.</note> near Valenciennes.

As for the glass, cut by Ferrier based on the design of Mydorge, and which had allowed Descartes to obtain the experimental verification of his law of refraction, it is discussed at length in Descartes’ letter to Constantijn Huygens of December 1635 (Clerselier, vol. II, pp. 364-365). It was then "eight or nine years" prior, which agrees with the present letter in indicating the course of the year 1627 as the date of the work in question.

Regarding the importance of this verification, which had exempted Descartes from any further experiments, one may consult P. <term>KRAMER</term> (*Descartes and the Law of Refraction of Light* <note>original: "Descartes und das Brechungsgesetz des Lichtes"</note>, in *Treatises on the History of Mathematics* <note>original: "Abhandlungen zur Geschichte der Mathematik"</note>, Issue 4, Leipzig, Teubner, 1882, pp. 235-278). See also D. J. <term>KORTEWEG</term> (*Descartes and Snellius, according to some...*

## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

->[Amsterdam, April 5, 1632.]<-

->Text from Clerselier, Volume II, Letter 71, pp. 339-340.<-

*Undated in Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes’ literary executor and the first editor of his letters.</note>. However, in letter XXXVIII to Mersenne, from Oct. or Nov. 1631, Descartes said: "I promise to send you something of my own before Easter" (p. 228, ll. 22-23). Now, we read in this one: "the Treatise that I had promised you for this Easter" (p. 242, ll. 6-7). This refers, therefore, to Easter 1632, which fell that year on April 11. The letter must be from April 5 at the latest, Mersenne having replied on the 15th to the last paragraph. (See the following letter.)*
