II, 344-345. XLV. — JUNE 1632.

...a clean copy to send to you; but I no longer dare to say when that will be, for I have already broken my promises so many times that I am ashamed of it.

Regarding your questions: first, I do not believe <margin>5</margin> that sound reflects to a single point, like light, since it is not communicated like light through rays that are entirely straight; instead, it always spreads <margin>10</margin> in a circle in every direction. 

<image-desc>A diagram showing a point 'A' emitting rays toward an opening 'B'. A solid straight line continues through 'B' to 'C'. Dashed or wavy lines representing sound waves spread out after passing through 'B' towards points 'D' (below) and 'E' (above).</image-desc>

For example, if body A emits light, the ray of this light that passes through the hole B can only be seen along the straight line BC; but if the same body A produces some sound, this <margin>15</margin> sound passing through hole B will be heard almost as well toward D and toward E as toward C.

2. The ratio of 5 to 8 <note>In music theory, this 5:8 ratio represents a minor sixth.</note> is a consonance, because when one hears the sound 8, one also hears its half, which is 4, which is not found in the ratio <margin>20</margin> of 5 to 7.

The refraction <term>Refraction|The bending of a wave (like light or sound) as it passes from one medium, such as air, into another, such as water.</term> of sound cannot be measured exactly, any more than its reflection; but as much as it can be observed, it is certain that it must occur *away from the perpendicular in water* <note>original Latin: "perpendiculari in aqua"</note>, quite the opposite of light. Regarding the method for measuring the refractions <margin>25</margin> of light, *I establish a comparison between the sines of the angles of incidence and the refracted angles* <note>original Latin: "instituo comparationem inter sinus angulorum incidentiæ & angulorum refractorum". This is a pivotal moment in science: Descartes's independent derivation of the Law of Refraction, now often called Snell's Law.</note>; but I would be very pleased if this were not yet made public, because the first part of my *Dioptrics* <term>Dioptrics|Descartes's major work on the science of light and vision.</term> will <margin>30</margin> contain nothing other than that alone. *It cannot easily be determined what figure a line seen at the bottom of the water might have* <note>original Latin: "Non poteſt facilè determinari qualem figuram linea viſa in fundo aquæ ſit"</note>...

<summary>Descartes explains the physical differences between sound and light propagation, arguing that sound waves spread spherically rather than in straight lines. He also privately shares his discovery of the Law of Refraction (Sines) while asking Mersenne to keep it confidential until his "Dioptrics" is published.</summary>

Galileo was famously skeptical of using astrology to prove physical or astronomical truths.</note> This aligns with Descartes' remark; it clearly targets the same work by Morin from 1631.

CORRESPONDENCE. II, 346-347.

<image-desc>A line drawing of a musical instrument or tool referred to in the text as a "Serpent". The instrument is shaped like a stylized S-curve with several small circular holes indicated along its length. A vertical line intersects the curves, and a horizontal line passes through one of the central holes, illustrating the geometric method described for measuring the distance between holes using perpendiculars falling onto a straight line drawn between the instrument's ends.</image-desc>

I believe that this great interval which is between the third and the fourth hole of a Serpent <note>The Serpent is a bass wind instrument, named for its curved shape, which was common in the 17th century.</note>, should only be attributed to the slant <note>original: "biais"</note> with which it is bent, and that the distance of these holes must be measured by the perpendiculars, which fall from the center of each hole, onto a straight line drawn from one of the ends of this instrument to the other.

What I had sent you regarding the ratio <note>original: "raiſon"</note> of 5 to 8 <sup>b</sup>, does not consist in being able to represent this same ratio by some other smaller or larger number; but in that when one hears some sound, one also naturally hears the resonance <note>original: "reſonance"</note> of another sound, which is higher by an octave <note>original: "octaue"</note> <sup>c</sup>, and thus when one hears the sound of two strings, of which one contains 8 parts and the other 5, and thus which make the minor sixth <note>original: "sexte mineure"</note>, one hears by the same means the resonance of half of the string of 8, which is 4 and which makes a major third <note>original: "tierce majeure"</note> <sup>d</sup> with the [other] string.

II, 349. XLVIII. — 22 JULY 1633.

...at the house of Mademoiselle Reyniers, near the Prince's Court,
in Amsterdam, since our messengers are unfaithful <note>In this context, "unfaithful" likely means unreliable or dishonest in delivering mail.</note>.

Page 268, l. 12. — Gassendi, in his *Life of Peiresc*, also speaks of a sunless clock, invented in Liège by a Jesuit named **Linus**, and provides a description of it under the year 1635; but he recalls that two years earlier, that is to say in 1633, Father Kircher had spoken to Peiresc of a clock based on another principle:

> "Peiresc... received word, among other things, that there was a religious and industrious man in Liège from the Society of Jesus named Linus, who had filled a vial with water of such a consistency that a small globe floated in the middle of it; inscribed around it were twenty-four hours, which, passing in order by a little fish or fixed pointer, marked the hours of the day, as if the globe were perfectly imitating the motion of the heavens.... He especially recalled to mind what Kircher had related two years before, that he had inserted grains of a certain Heliotrope <note>Heliotrope here refers to the "sunflower" or "turnsole" plant, which was believed to have a natural magnetic-like attraction to the sun.</note> into a piece of cork, which (like a flower) turned toward the Sun, causing the floating cork to turn and indicate the hours marked on a vessel with an attached pointer." <note>original: "Peireskius. . . accepit, inter cætera, versari Leodii religiosum... indiculoque apposito notatas in vase horas designarent."</note>

(*The Life of Peiresc*, The Hague, 1651, p. 435-436.) — In an unpublished letter from Wendelin to Mersenne (National Library, French new acquisitions 6205, p. 19-20), dated from Brussels on June 15, 1633, but responding to a letter written a year earlier, we read:

> "You added (I remember) a discovered method for making clocks which would provide every single minute and even smaller hourly parts most exquisitely, and yet would be prepared at no more than a three-obol expense <note>A "triobol" was a small ancient Greek coin of low value; Wendelin is emphasizing how cheaply the device could be made.</note>. Stirred by the novelty of the thing, and thinking to myself that something magnetic was undoubtedly hinted at here, I suspected that solar-following powers, the Heliotrope, were being called upon; and so, when I arrived in Liège a little later to see Mr. Woestenraet (whom you certainly know is quite full of your news), and when I discussed this matter, he told me to go to the English Jesuits. He said there was a certain Father there who constructed a globe of wax with such skill that, when placed in water, it would revolve of its own accord daily and reflect the solar motion, and as a consequence of this, represent the hours. I therefore met with the Father, and he confessed the same, saying that if I wished, he would provide this display <note>original: "ludum", meaning a demonstration or scientific curiosity.</note> within two days. It was not possible for me then, as I was heading to recently captured Maastricht <note>original: "Traiectum" refers to Maastricht here, which had been captured by the Dutch in 1632 during the Eighty Years' War.</note> on heavy business, to linger there. I only asked this: whether that wax globe, by its daily rotation, aligned itself with the axis of the world? Or did it choose for itself a vertical axis and make the rotation of its greatest circle horizontal? He replied horizontal, adding only this in these very words: 'all these bodies of the world are magnetic.' Thus far those matters, which I am now looking into somewhat more deeply after your letter of yesterday added mention of cork and nightshade <note>original: "solani", referring to plants of the Solanaceae family, which like the heliotrope, were being tested for solar-responsive properties.</note>." <note>original: "Addebas (memini) rationem inuentam horologiorum conficiendorum... postquam hesternæ tuæ literæ suberis ac solani mentionem adiecere."</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general context of Descartes' anxiety regarding Galileo’s trial to a specific letter addressed to David Le Leu de Wilhem. The introductory commentary provides the historical background of the 1633 condemnation that halted Descartes' publication of his own scientific work.</meta>

L. — DECEMBER 12, 1633.

[centrally] local; 2º <note>original: "Terra non est centrum mundi nec immobilis, sed secundum se totam movetur, etiam motu diurno"</note> *The Earth is not the center of the world nor is it immobile, but moves in its entirety, including a daily motion*; on March 5, the Congregation of the <term>Index: The *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, a list of books banned by the Catholic Church.</term> had suspended Copernicus's work <note>original: "donec corrigatur"</note> *until it is corrected*, and prohibited <note>original: "alios omnes libros pariter idem docentes"</note> *all other books teaching the same thing*. At the same time, Galileo was secretly admonished by Cardinal Bellarmine and a special injunction was made against him defending this suspect doctrine, whether verbally or in writing. Thus, in his famous dialogue of the *Chief World Systems* <note>Referring to the *Dialogo sopra i due massimi sistemi del mondo*, 1632.</note> of 1632, he took care to speak with the greatest respect of the decisions made, and not to establish any thesis dogmatically. These precautions were useless; summoned from Florence to Rome three times (Sept. 23, Dec. 9 and 30, 1632), he appeared before the <term>Holy Office: The Roman Inquisition.</term> on the first Sunday of Lent in 1633, underwent three interrogations (April 12, April 30, June 21) and heard his sentence on June 22. His book was burned; he himself was forced to recant and remained under the surveillance of the Holy Office. Initially relegated to Siena, where he was not permitted to leave the Archbishop's palace, he was authorized on December 1, 1633, to retire to his country villa in Arcetri, with orders not to leave it and to receive no visitors without special permission. (*Records of the Trial of Galileo*, by Henri de l'Epinois, Rome and Paris, Palmé, 1877.) — This condemnation caused a great stir, even reaching Holland, from where <term>Gassendi: Pierre Gassendi, a French philosopher and scientist who, like Descartes, sought to reconcile new science with philosophy.</term> wrote in July 1629, after having seen the scholars of that country: "Moreover, all those people there are for the movement of the earth." (*Letters of Peiresc*, IV, 202.)

<margin>5</margin>Page 276, l. 1. — It is difficult to reconstruct the statement of this question, as the equation to which it led Descartes is missing from the source text, and the relationship given further down cannot exist with the letters he presents. My corrections assume the following restitution, which, after various attempts, seemed to me the only admissible one:
*One proposes to construct a triangle ABC, right-angled at A, such that by inscribing a square within it, such as DEFG, the smallest side AC of the triangle is double the side of the square.*
The relationship indicated further on (lines 11-16, in the corrected text) is then easily verified, with MN being taken as the diameter of the circle inscribed in the triangle FEC. This relationship suggests that another condition was set to determine the absolute value of the sides of the triangle, for example, by giving the diameter MN. Descartes seems, moreover, to have complicated the said relationship at will, as he did for the statements of the questions that follow, with the goal of discouraging <term>Stampioen</term> <note>Jan Jansz de Jonge Stampioen (1610–1689), a Dutch mathematician who often engaged in public disputes and challenges with his contemporaries, including Descartes.</note>. (T). <note>The "(T)" likely refers to the editor Paul Tannery, who co-edited the definitive edition of Descartes' works.</note>

P. 276, l. 23. — <term>Binomial</term> <note>original: "Binome"</note>, in the mathematical language of the period, signifies the sum of a rational term and a square root (a radical of the second degree).

The four polyhedra that must first be inscribed in spheres are chosen from among the thirteen semi-regular solids of <term>Archimedes</term> <note>Also known as Archimedean solids; these are highly symmetrical, semi-regular convex polyhedra.</note>, enumerated by <term>Pappus</term>, book V, proposition 19 (p. 353 and following of the Hultsch edition, Berlin, Weidmann, 1876). They had, moreover, already been studied in 1633 by <term>Kepler</term> in his *The Harmony of the World* <note>original: "Harmonice Mundi" (1619). Page 277, l. 24. — The triangle in question is simply the equilateral triangle having one unit as its side. Descartes therefore proposes (cf. p. 278, l. 11-12) to take the unit for the side (edge) of three of the semi-regular polyhedra (the 5th, 8th, and 11th).

CORRESPONDENCE.

...a problem composed for his own pleasure and for which he obviously did not take the trouble to perform the actual calculations; he likely committed an oversight by substituting here the 7th semi-regular <term>polyhedron of Archimedes</term> <note>Also known as Archimedean solids, these are highly symmetrical geometric shapes. The 7th is usually identified as the icosidodecahedron, while the 9th is the truncated dodecahedron.</note> for the 9th, which he had initially chosen.

The statement continues to be enigmatic without offering true mathematical difficulties; $\frac{3 x^2 - x}{2}$ is the algebraic formula which, when one successively gives $x$ all integer values starting from one, generates the sequence of so-called <term>pentagonal numbers</term> <note>A type of "figured number" that can be represented as dots forming a regular pentagon.</note>. For example, by making $x = 4$, one obtains the pentagonal number 22. Inversely, from the equation $\frac{3 x^2 - x}{2} = 22$, one will derive 4 as the value of the root $x$ of the pentagon 22.

Highlighting the coefficient 1 of $x$ in the aforementioned formula, Descartes calculates the arithmetic sum of the coefficients of the numerator and the denominator. The task is to proceed in the same way for the "figured number" representing a solid having 20 triangles and 12 pentagons as faces, all with the same side or root $x$. The representation of this number can be done in different ways; but by following the principles established by the ancients for the representation of polygonal numbers, one easily finds the formula: $8 x^3 - 10 x^2 + 3 x$. The side of the polyhedron to be inscribed in the fourth sphere would therefore be $8 + 10 + 3 = 21$.

We thus have four spheres determined by the sides of the inscribed polyhedra; these four spheres must now be assumed to be in contact, each with the other three, and it remains to calculate the radius of the sphere that touches all four of them while enclosing them. This last question is the only one presenting a serious difficulty; Descartes, moreover, had already sent it to Mersenne (*see above, p. 139, l. 13*).

P. 282, l. 2. — The enmity between Father Scheiner and Galileo dates back to the time of the discovery of sunspots; Galileo had made it in 1610, and during a stay in Rome in the spring of 1611, he showed these spots through his telescope: Scheiner, then at Ingolstadt, was informed of this by Father Guldin, made observations, and published them at the beginning of 1612 under the pseudonym of *Apelles hiding behind the painting* <note>original: "Apelles latens post tabellam." Apelles was a famous painter of ancient Greece; the pseudonym implies a scholar hiding his identity.</note>, without a word about Galileo. The latter, in his *History and Demonstrations concerning Solar Spots* <note>original: "Istoria e dimostrazioni intorno alle Macchie Solari"</note>, 1613, loudly claimed priority. Though he did not then allow the suspicion to leak out that the "false Apelles" had knowingly tried to steal the glory of the discovery from him, he later had him accused of it by Mario Guiducci (*Discourse on Comets* <note>original: "Discorso delle Comete"</note>, 1619, and *Letter to Father Tarquinio Galluzzi* <note>original: "Lettera al P. Tarquinio Galluzzi"</note>, 1620: *Works of Galileo*, national edition, vol. VI, p. 48 and 188). Although Scheiner had not revealed his pseudonym, Galileo was undoubtedly enlightened on this matter, at least since the *Mathematical Investigations of Astronomical Controversies and Novelties* <note>original: "Disquisitiones mathematicae de controversiis et novitatibus astronomicis"</note>, published at Ingolstadt in 1614 as defended by Locher under the presidency of Scheiner.

->### LII. — FEBRUARY 1634.<-

The book mentioned by Descartes is the *Rosa Ursina, or the Sun diverse in the wonderful phenomenon of its torches and spots, and also its annual rotation around its center and fixed axis from west to east, and a nearly monthly conversion on its own poles around another movable axis from east to west, shown in four books as mobile* <note>original Latin: "Rosa Vrsina, sive Sol ex admirando facularum et macularum suarum phænomeno varius..."</note> by Father Christoph Scheiner, a Swabian German from the Society of Jesus, dedicated to Paolo Giordano II Orsini, Duke of Bracciano (Bracciano, at the press of Andrea Phaeus, printing begun in 1626, finished June 13, 1630).

At the time of Galileo's trial, Scheiner was in Rome, and on February 23, 1633, he wrote to Gassendi:

> "Four Dialogues by Galileo have recently appeared, written in Italian to establish the Copernican motion of the Earth against the common School of the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle, whose Earth-centered physics was the standard academic curriculum of the time.</note>: there he pulled apart my *Mathematical Disquisitions*, and also laid violent hands on the *Rosa Ursina*, and on the motion of solar spots and the Sun's annual motion. What do you think of these things? This writing displeases many. For my part, I am preparing a defense for myself and for the truth." (Gassendi, *Works*, VI, 408-9).

This clearly indicates the position he took at that moment; however, the work he announced did not appear until a year after his death, in 1651, under the title *Forerunner on behalf of the moving Sun and the stable Earth, against the Florentine Academician Galileo Galilei* <note>original: "Prodromus pro Sole mobili et terra stabili..."</note>.

Galileo had attracted another enemy among the Jesuits, Horazio Grassi; but the latter's colleagues had not supported him in the polemic he maintained against Galileo under the pseudonym of Lothario Sarsi; the Roman College, as a body, had affected neutrality.

P. 282, l. 7. — The full title of the *Rosa Ursina*, given in the preceding note, indicates the complexity of the hypotheses to which Scheiner had to resort and justifies on its own Descartes' remark, as does this passage from a letter from Gassendi to Scheiner, dated November 2, 1632:

> "As for the hypothesis by which you explain the matter, it is indeed most sharp; but perhaps a simpler one could be drawn from the annual motion of the Earth." (*Gassendi, Works*, VI, 54-55).

One reads similarly in a letter from Peiresc to Gassendi, dated September 6, 1633:

> "...however, the good Father Athanasius (Kircher), whom we saw pass through here in a great hurry, could not keep from admitting to us, in the presence of Father Ferrand, that Father Malapertius and Father Clavius themselves" (all Jesuits) "did not at all disapprove of Copernicus's opinion, but rather were not far from it, even though they had been pressured and forced to write in favor of the common assumptions of Aristotle; that Father Scheiner himself followed them only by force and out of obedience, as did he himself..." (*Letters of Peiresc*, IV, 354).

Kircher is unfortunately always a questionable source, and regarding Scheiner, his assertion deserves little credit. As for the illustrious Clavius, after Galileo's discoveries, he had in fact openly declared himself against the Ptolemaic system <note>The Ptolemaic system placed the Earth at the center of the universe; Clavius recognized that new observations made this model untenable, though he did not necessarily adopt the Copernican model before his death.</note>, but it must be observed that he died in 1612, before the condemnation of Copernicus's opinion.

# LIII.

## DESCARTES TO MERSENNE.

->[Amsterdam, April 1634.]<-

->*Text from Clerselier, volume II, letter 76, pp. 351-354.*<-

*This letter, which is undated in Clerselier’s collection, is certainly earlier than Letter LIV below, which is firmly dated May 15, 1634. This can be proven notably by comparing the proposal made here for an experiment involving a cannon fired toward the zenith <note>The point in the sky directly above an observer.</note> (page 287, lines 7-20) and the renewal of this proposal in the letter of May 15. It is clear that after receiving Letter LIII, Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a Minim friar and polymath who acted as the central "mailbox" for the European scientific community.</note> had an arquebus <note>An early type of long-gun or musket.</note> fired, the ball of which could not be found, and informed Descartes of this, who then replied with Letter LIV. The interval between the two letters seems, therefore, to have been at least a month; but it is difficult to accept that it was significantly longer, as the competition for the Ramus chair <note>A prestigious professorship at the Collège Royal, awarded via public competition.</note> (see page 288, line 25) usually took place around Easter, and the commission's decision regarding Morin’s proposal on longitudes <note>Jean-Baptiste Morin had proposed a method for finding longitude at sea using the moon, a major scientific challenge of the age.</note> (page 289, line 2) was made on March 30, 1634.*

*However, if the present letter was only written in April, its beginning presents a rather serious difficulty. Only one letter was lost in transit: that of November 1633. Descartes responds immediately to a letter from Mersenne informing him of this loss; but the Minim friar must have already received Letter LII, and while Descartes might have wanted to repeat what he had already written in the latter, it is difficult to understand why he expresses himself as if he had not sent it. Had he, in fact, held it back for some reason we cannot guess? Or had it suffered such a delay that Descartes must have believed, in April, that it was also lost? The ambiguity of the expression "the last ones" (line 2) does not allow for a definitive conclusion.*

I learn from your letters that the last ones I wrote to you have been lost, although I thought I had addressed them very securely. But I am not so in love with my thoughts as to want to use such exceptions in order to have the means to maintain them; and the desire I have <margin>30</margin>...

Page 288, l. 19. — Condemnation in 745 of Virgil, bishop of Salzburg, by Pope Zachary. <note>Virgil of Salzburg was an 8th-century Irish missionary and astronomer who was accused of heresy for suggesting the existence of the "antipodes"—people living on the opposite side of the Earth. In the 17th century, scientific thinkers often cited this case to show that the Church had previously made errors in judging cosmological theories.</note> One may see Boulliau's reflections on this subject in his letter to Gassendi dated June 21, 1633 (*Gassendi, Works, VI, 412*).

Page 288, l. 26. — According to the will of Ramus <note>Pierre de la Ramée, known as Ramus (1515–1572), was an influential humanist and mathematician whose legacy helped modernize the university curriculum.</note>, the chair of mathematics he had founded (at the Collège de France) was awarded every three years through a public competition. For seven consecutive days, the candidates had to deliver hour-long lectures; on the eighth day, they had to respond to objections, solve problems, or demonstrate theorems proposed by any attendee. In 1634, the chair was awarded to Gilles Personnier de Roberval <note>A famous French mathematician and physicist known for his work on the "method of indivisibles."</note>, who would hold it until his death in 1675.

Page 289, l. 2. — The problem of determining longitudes at sea <note>Longitudes are the east-west coordinates on a map. While latitude was easy to determine by the stars, finding longitude was the greatest navigational challenge of the era because it required a way to keep precise time while on a moving ship.</note>, which was only practically solved later by the construction of marine chronometers, had already been a priority for quite some time. The Spanish government, and then that of the Netherlands, had offered considerable rewards to anyone who could solve this problem. Richelieu <note>Cardinal Richelieu, the Chief Minister to King Louis XIII, who sought to expand French naval power.</note> imitated them, and J.-B. Morin, royal professor of mathematics (at the Collège de France), having proposed a system, a commission was appointed to examine it. On March 30, 1634, they issued an unfavorable decision. Morin's method, based on the observation of the Moon, was actually very satisfying in theory, but practically inapplicable due to the imperfection of the lunar tables <note>Data charts predicting the Moon's position; at the time, these were not accurate enough for sailors to use Morin's method for precise navigation.</note>; it had, moreover, already been proposed by Gemma Frisius and Kepler. Morin protested vigorously, first with a small quarto volume entitled: *Letters written to Mr. Morin by the most celebrated Astronomers of France approving his invention of longitudes, against the recent sentence rendered on this subject by Messrs. Pascal, Mydorge, Beaugra<unclear>nd</unclear>, Boulanger and Herigone, commissioners appointed to judge it, etc.* (Paris, Morin and Libert, 1635). It contains extracts from letters by Jacques de Valois, Gaultier (the prior of La Valette), and Gassendi. Morin was eventually compensated by Richelieu’s generosity, and he seems to have actually brought astrology into some high regard at the court of Louis XIII.

# LV.

## DESCARTES TO RENERI.

->[Amsterdam,] July 2, 163[4].<-

->MANUSCRIPT COPY, Hamburg, City Library.<-

*Taken from the Wolfs-Briefesammlung, vol. 28, p. 39, and published in the Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie, 1896, p. 327-329, with the date 1637. However, the final digit is missing in the manuscript, where only 163 is found. Reneri <note>Henricus Reneri (1593–1639) was a Dutch philosopher and one of Descartes’s earliest and most loyal supporters; he was the first to teach Cartesian ideas at Utrecht University.</note> is identified as a Professor of Philosophy at Utrecht; since his appointment dates to June 18, 1634, and he died in March 1639, we have a choice of dates from 1634 to 1638 inclusive. Perhaps it is appropriate to place this letter as close as possible to the similar letter of June 2, 1631 (Letter XXXIV above, p. 205), and date it July 2, 1634. Reneri, having just arrived in Utrecht, would have wanted to teach new ideas right away and would have written to Descartes to refresh his memory. In 1635, why would he have needed to write? Descartes was with him in Utrecht. In 1636, would he have disturbed him during his work in Leiden, where he was printing his books? In 1637, Descartes would likely have mentioned his recently published book. In 1638? Reneri would not have waited so long to inquire about a question of such importance. Finally, the same text, published by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier was the primary editor of Descartes’s posthumous works and correspondence.</note> without name or date, but with some variations (Volume II, letter 81, p. 362-363), is attached to a fragment forming another letter to Huygens from December 1635 (Letter LXV hereafter); the two drafts, found together, were likely written in 1634 and 1635.*

*The recipient's name is missing in Clerselier (vol. II, p. 139, letter 17, version) and in the Latin edition. However, it is clear that this concerns a very recent discussion: "controversies recently arisen between us" <note>original: "controuersiæ nuper inter nos exortæ"</note> (lines 1-2), and a verbal discussion: "recently, when we were together" <note>original: "nuper, cum una essemus"</note> (line 7), following which the adversary, having returned home, wrote a letter: "now... you set forth through letters" <note>original: "nunc... per literas exponis"</note> (p. 308, lines 7-9); Descartes responds to him. <margin>15</margin> you would consider your entire Philosophy as false if no sensible delay <note>original: "mora sensibilis"</note> intervened between the instant the motion was seen in the mirror and the instant it was felt by the hand. <margin>20</margin> overturned. <margin>30</margin> the eye.

Let ABC be a straight line; and so that we may reach the same conclusion whether it is the Sun or the Earth that moves, let A be the place where the Sun is located, B where the Earth is, and C where the Moon is sometimes found.

<image-desc>A simple geometrical diagram consisting of a horizontal straight line with three points marked above it: A on the left, B in the middle, and C on the right.</image-desc>

And let us now suppose that from Earth B, the Moon is seen undergoing an 
<margin>5</margin> eclipse at point C; now, according to what has been granted, this eclipse ought to be seen at the precise instant in which the light emitted by the Sun, while it was at point A, would have reached the eye after being reflected from the Moon—had it not been intercepted by the Earth. That is to say, again according to what has been granted, this would occur one hour later 
<margin>10</margin> than that light reaches Earth B; and therefore, the eclipse cannot be seen at C except one hour later than the Sun is seen at A—at least, if your concessions are true: namely, that the motion of a torch in a mirror a quarter-mile distant is seen a twenty-fourth part of a single 
<margin>15</margin> heartbeat <note>original: "pulsationis arteriae"; the pulse was a common measurement for small increments of time before the widespread use of pendulum clocks.</note> later than it is felt by the hand. 

Yet the constant and accurate observation of all astronomers, confirmed by countless experiments, testifies that if the Moon is seen at C from Earth B while undergoing an eclipse, the Sun must be seen at A not an hour earlier, but at that very same 
<margin>20</margin> instant. Moreover, a period of an hour is much more noticeable when observing the position of the Sun relative to the Earth and Moon than a twenty-fourth part of a single heartbeat is in your experiment. Therefore, your experiment is useless, and 
<margin>25</margin> mine—which is the experiment of all astronomers—shows far more clearly that light is seen in no perceptible amount of time. I maintained, therefore, that this argument was a demonstration; you, however, called it both a fallacy <note>original: "paralogismum"; a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> and a begging of the question <note>original: "petitionem principij"; a logical error where the premise of an argument assumes the truth of the conclusion it is meant to prove.</note>; but in your...

### II, 143-144. LVII. — 22 AUGUST 1634.

...it is quite clear from your response whether you spoke thus by right or rather injuriously. For you give only two answers, in the first of which an evident fallacy <note>original: "paralogismus"; a piece of illogical or circular reasoning.</note> appears, and in the second there is indeed no "begging of the question" <note>original: "petitio principii"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise.</note>, or the assumption of that <margin>5</margin> which was to be proven; but (what seems worse to me) it is a denial of that which had been granted. For when, having excluded the daily motion <note>original: "motu diurno"; the rotation of the Earth on its axis every 24 hours.</note>, you fall back on the slowness of the annual motion <note>original: "motus annui"; the Earth's orbit around the sun.</note> in a matter which depends entirely on the monthly motion of the Moon <note>original: "motu Lunae menstruo"</note>—which is more than twelve times faster than the annual motion—and furthermore, <margin>10</margin> in a matter where not only a difference of an hour (which I had shown to be sufficient), but even a difference of half a minute is usually observed quite conveniently, who would not recognize a fallacy? When you later say that the rays emitted from the Sun and Moon also move in a circle between the Sun and Moon together <margin>15</margin> with the Sun and Moon, so that, forsooth, they always appear in the places where they actually exist, although they are seen by means of the light that was emitted from them earlier, when they were in other places (for it cannot be understood otherwise), you clearly deny that very thing which you had <margin>20</margin> granted before, and upon which that whole part of my demonstration, which I had explained to you, depended; nor do you see that you fall into another part of it, which concerns the Eclipse of the Sun. ### CORRESPONDANCE. II, 144-145.

...at that moment when the Sun is at point A, it is seen by eyes located at point B, despite the intervening Moon—which is nevertheless also at point C, and would itself be seen there if it possessed its own light. For the Sun is seen there by the power of light <margin>5</margin> which departed from it twelve hours earlier <note>Descartes is using a hypothetical scenario where light takes twelve hours to travel from the Sun to the Earth to show how extreme the visual discrepancy would be.</note>, and which, having passed through the Moon's sphere half an hour ago, could not be blocked by her because she was not yet positioned between the Sun and the Earth. However, the light which is currently being blocked by her cannot reach point B until half an hour later; <margin>10</margin> and therefore, the loss of that light—that is, the Eclipse <note>original: "Eclipſis"; the temporary obscuring of one celestial body by another.</note>—could only be seen half an hour after the instant when the Sun, Moon, and Earth are in the same straight line. But it is evident from the experience of all astronomers <note>original: "Aſtronomorum"</note> that the exact opposite is true: namely, <margin>15</margin> that the Eclipse occurs at the moment when the Sun, Moon, and Earth are in a straight line. In this matter, not only an error of half an hour, but even half a minute would not go unnoticed.

Therefore, etc. Nor do I add innumerable other things by which this last position might be shown to be still more absurd <margin>20</margin> than the former; such as the fact that if it were posited, we ought always to see toward the East a black circle on the horizon between the earth and the sky, and toward the West, the Sun and stars below the mountains and similar objects. Nor do I ask by what force that circular motion of light, coming simultaneously <margin>25</margin> from different stars, is directed so that it always retains the unequal speeds of the stars from which it departed, etc. For unless the things I have already written convince you, I shall confess you to be plainly insurmountable. Farewell. Amsterdam <note>original: "Amſtelodami"</note>, 22 August 1634.

### LVIII.

## DESCARTES TO MORIN.

### [Amsterdam, Sept. or Oct. 1634.]

*Text from Clerselier, volume I, letter 57, pp. 184-185.*

Undated in *Clerselier* <note>Claude Clerselier was the primary editor of Descartes's posthumous letters, often working without exact dates from the originals.</note>. However, it concerns the following book: *The New and Hitherto Desired Science of Terrestrial and Celestial Longitudes, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Longitudinum terrestrium necnon coelestium nova et hactenus optata scientia, etc.*</note>, by the author Jean-Baptiste Morin (*Paris, at the house of Jean Libert, 1634.* License granted May 20, 1634, dedication to Cardinal Richelieu <note>The powerful chief minister to King Louis XIII of France.</note> dated July 26). Three other volumes appeared: the 2nd in 1636 (dedication Jan. 1); the 3rd in 1637 (printing finished Nov. 10); the 4th in 1639 (printing finished Jan. 3). The first volume does not provide a date for the completion of printing; but its progress can be traced in letters from Mersenne to Peiresc on May 14, July 2, and August 24, 1634; by the last date, it was finished (*Correspondents of Peiresc, volume XIX, Paris, Picard, 1894, pp. 82, 86, 106*). Furthermore, a letter of thanks from Gassendi to Morin for his book is printed between two others dated Sept. 6 and Oct. 30, 1634. Descartes’s letter is undoubtedly from roughly the same period, September or October 1634.
On the question of longitudes and Morin’s claims, see above, p. 289, line 2 and note, p. 291.

## LX.

### DESCARTES TO GOLIUS.

->Utrecht, 19 May 1635.<-

->*Autograph manuscript, Leiden, University Library, Huygens Collection.*<-

*A single sheet, large format, folded into two leaves: the first, front and back, contains the letter; on the back of the second is the address. The figure <note>A mathematical or optical diagram.</note> in the margin of the first page is in Descartes's hand, with this note: "I made this figure backwards by inadvertence" <note>original French: "i’ay fait cete figure a l’enuers par inaduertence"</note>; he had likely turned the sheet while drawing the circles, and the figure ended up reversed. — The printed version by Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the first editor of Descartes's letters.</note> (volume II, letter 102, pp. 462-464), without date or recipient's name, provides some variations.*

### Sir,

I was away from this city when your letters, with the observations that you did me the favor of sending, arrived here, and I only returned 7 or 8 days later; this is the reason why I have not written to you sooner to thank you for them. For I would have very much desired by the same means to be able

That evening, I had held my head resting on my right hand for quite a long time, with which I closed my right eye, and I meanwhile kept the other wide open; when, the air being quite dark, a candle was brought into the room where I was; and immediately, opening both eyes, I perceived two halos around this candle, more perfectly colored than I would have believed they could ever be, and such as you see them represented here. Page 318, line 16. — The autograph, signed and dated, allows us here to correct an error by Baillet <note>Adrien Baillet (1649–1706), an early and influential biographer of Descartes.</note>, reproduced twice in his *Life of Descartes*, page LI of the Chronological Table, and pages 268-271 of volume I. > “*And I saw a very clear experience of it this past summer.*

## LXI.

### DESCARTES TO ***.

->[Utrecht, autumn 1635.]<-

->Text from Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684), the editor who first published much of Descartes' correspondence.</note>, volume II, letter 103, pages 464-466.<-

This is the first part, in Clerselier, of a letter without a date or name of recipient, which continues with two segments certainly addressed to Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk and mathematician who served as a central correspondent for the European scientific community.</note> (previously Letters XXVI and XLV bis). Despite the heading “Sir,” which may have been added by Clerselier, this first part is probably also addressed to Mersenne; for Descartes seems never to have had any other correspondent posing a series of questions to which he responds as he does below. The end of the letter would sufficiently explain why the Minim friar <note>original: "le Minime"; referring to Mersenne's religious order.</note> might not have kept it; for he had probably only opened up to Descartes about his project to defend the opinion of Galileo <note>Galileo Galilei had been condemned by the Roman Inquisition in 1633, a fact that made Descartes very cautious about his own publications.</note>. — As for the date of the letter, besides the circumstance that it follows the previous one of May 19, 1635, in Clerselier, there are two clues: 1st, the *Dioptrics* <note>original: "la Dioptrique"</note> is now ready for printing; yet in April (Letter LIX, page 315, line 9), Descartes was already reading chapters of it to Constantijn Huygens who, on October 28 (Letter LXII following), gives advice for the edition; 2nd, Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654), a famous French writer.</note> is in Paris; yet we have, from 1635, a letter from him dated from that city on September 3 (1665 edition, vol. I, p. 373). We can therefore assume the autumn of 1635.

->Sir,<-

I thank you for the letters you did me the favor of sending, and I am very glad to learn that Monsieur de Balzac <note>Jean-Louis Guez de Balzac (1597–1654), a celebrated French author known for his influential prose style and correspondence.</note> still remembers me. I was almost of a mind to write to him during this journey, but I prefer to wait a little longer; meanwhile, if you happen to see him, you would oblige me by assuring him of my service. I also pray you to give my greetings to M. Sarrazin <note>Jean-François Sarasin (1614–1654), a French poet and man of letters.</note>, and tell him that I thank him most humbly for the book which he formerly intended to send me, and that I would not have failed to write to thank him for it, if the person to whom he had given it had taken care to deliver it to me.

Regarding the telescopes <note>original: "lunettes". In the 17th century, this term was used for both eyeglasses and spyglasses/telescopes.</note>, I will tell you that since the condemnation of Galileo <note>Galileo was condemned by the Roman Inquisition in June 1633. This event caused Descartes to suppress his own cosmological work, *The World*, fearing similar persecution.</note>, I have revised and entirely finished the Treatise <note>The *Dioptrics* (La Dioptrique), which was eventually published in 1637.</note> that I had formerly begun; and having entirely separated it from my *World* <note>original: "Monde"; referring to his treatise *Le Monde*, which he decided not to publish in its entirety during his lifetime.</note>, I propose to have it printed alone in a short time. However, because more than a year will perhaps still pass before it can be seen in print, if M. N.<gloss>a</gloss> desired to work on it before that time, I would consider it a favor, and I offer to have everything I have written concerning the practice transcribed and to send it to him whenever he pleases.

Firstly, I am not surprised that elderberry pith <note>The soft, spongy tissue found in the center of elderberry stems, often used in early physics experiments due to its extreme lightness.</note> weighs four or five hundred times less than gold; but I nevertheless thank you for communicating your experiment, and I shall always be very glad to know of those you have performed.

---

a. M. de Beaune <note>Florimond de Beaune (1601–1652), a mathematician and jurist who was an early follower of Descartes’ geometry.</note> (Copy from the Institute).

<summary>Descartes updates his correspondent on his literary social circle and discusses the status of his scientific writing following Galileo’s condemnation, specifically his decision to publish his work on optics separately from his suppressed cosmological treatise.</summary>

Secondly, I do not know if elder wood or "sapire" <gloss>Read fir?</gloss> <note>original: "sapire"; likely a transcription error for "sapin" (fir).</note> produce a higher-pitched sound than copper; but I believe generally that according as bodies are drier and stiffer—that is, more disposed to receive <margin>5</margin> within themselves a faster vibration—the higher their pitch will be.

3. And this sound is not produced by the division of the parts of the air, but only by its agitation, which accompanies that of the resonant body.

<margin>10</margin>4. It is one thing to consider the oscillations <note>original: "tours & retours"</note> of a string attached at both ends, and another for those of a string attached only at one end with a weight at the other <gloss>See above, Letters 10 and 14 (p. 28 and 29; p. 73 and 74).</gloss>: for the latter moves from bottom to top by the impetuosity <term>impetuosity: a term in 17th-century physics referring to the force or momentum of a moving object</term> or agitation within it, <margin>15</margin> and does not begin to return from top to bottom until this agitation has been entirely overcome by the weight <note>gravity</note> that makes it descend; this is why it moves very slowly when it finishes its ascent; and yet, for all that, I do not believe that it <margin>20</margin> stops for even a moment before descending again.

5. I also do not believe that the movement of a string attached at both ends always describes perfect circles or perfect ellipses; rather, all the inequalities of these strings, and the various <margin>25</margin> ways in which they can be struck, bring variety to the shape of their movement.

6. As for heat, I do not believe it to be the same thing as light, nor as the rarefaction of air <note>The 17th-century concept of a substance becoming less dense or expanding.</note>; but I conceive of it as a thing

If it is indeed to Mersenne that Descartes writes, the Minim <note>Mersenne belonged to the Order of Minims</note> left in any case to others the task he dreamed of undertaking. In France, after the condemnation of Galileo, Campanella was the first who published a book where the system of Copernicus was defended and declared not contrary to Scripture: *Tommaso Campanella of the Order of Preachers: Disputations on the four parts of his real philosophy, in four books... Volume II of his works* <note>original: "Thomæ Campanellæ ord. præd. Disputationum in quatuor partes suæ philosophiæ realis libri quatuor... Suorum operum Tomus II"</note> (Paris, Houssaye, 1637).

The editorial notes identify contemporary debates on heliocentrism and physics involving figures like Mersenne, Pascal, and Campanella.</summary>

<header>LXII. — 28 October 1635.</header>

### LXII.

## HUYGENS TO DESCARTES.

### Panderen, 28 Oct. 1635.

->Manuscript copy, Amsterdam, Academy of Sciences.<-
->*French letters of Constantin Huygens, volume I, page 643.*<-

Sir,

I shall always hold Jean Gillot <note>A student and assistant of Descartes who often acted as a messenger</note> in high esteem, for having seen in his youth the mystery of your incomparable instructions; and I shall always love him for the good <margin>5</margin> news he brought me: of the resolution you have made to present yourself to the ignorance of the world, by the publication of your *Dioptrics*. I beg you not to allow any imaginary consideration—of the kind that has kept you in doubt until <margin>10</margin> present—to further shake this plan. It is true that the *Elzeviers* <note>The Elzevirs were a renowned family of Dutch printers known for their high-quality editions</note> could have served you usefully; but in this public misfortune <note>likely referring to the disruptions caused by the Thirty Years' War or local outbreaks of plague</note> that turns you away from them, there will be some particular good fortune if you trust in *Willem Jansz Blaeu* <note>A famous Dutch cartographer and printer who had studied under Tycho Brahe</note>. <margin>15</margin> He is an industrious and exact man, well-versed in mathematics according to his ability, and who will be capable of overseeing the engravers of your diagrams <note>original: "figures"</note>. If I were to be believed, it would be by woodcut <term>woodcut: a relief printing technique where the image is carved into a block of wood</term>; copper plates print the marks of their edges and <margin>20</margin> clutter the text, or require more space than is suitable for books. For I presuppose that you will find it agreeable to accommodate the reader—

<summary>Constantin Huygens writes to Descartes, enthusiastically supporting his decision to publish "The Dioptrics" and recommending Willem Blaeu as a printer over the Elzeviers. Huygens also provides technical advice on using woodcuts instead of copper engravings for the book's scientific illustrations.</summary>
<keywords>Constantin Huygens, René Descartes, Jean Gillot, Dioptrics, publishing, Willem Blaeu, Elzeviers, woodcut vs copperplate, scientific illustration</keywords>

I will see to it that, through my efforts, you become known to one of the Princes of the earth <note>likely referring to the Prince of Orange, Huygens' employer</note>; if you prefer him to others, you will never repent it." #### Text from Clerselier, volume II, letter 81 end, pp. 363-366.

*Clerselier’s printed edition <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was Descartes' first editor and literary executor</note>, lacking a date or recipient’s name, combines two letters into one: the first (pp. 362-363), of which an old copy now exists, dated July 2, 1634, to Reneri; and this one, which is clearly a response to the previous letter from Huygens dated December 5, 1635.*

There was a little sunlight this morning, which gave me the opportunity to test your lens <term>lens: original "verre" (glass), referring here to a glass optical lens</term>. But you will forgive me, if you please, if I dare to assert that the turner <term>turner: a craftsman who shapes materials on a lathe</term> has not given it the shape that you prescribed; and you will see it easily, if you take
<margin>5</margin> the trouble to cover its flat side with that card in which there are various small holes, and, exposing it to the sun, you hold it behind the other card where there are several circles and lines marking the
<margin>10</margin> places where the sun’s rays, passing through these holes, should fall. For by moving it closer or further away, you will see that those [rays] which pass through the holes of the smallest circle converge at a distance of only five or six
<margin>15</margin> inches <note>original: "pouces"</note>, and those of the second circle much further away, at the point when those of the first are already beginning to spread out again; and those of the third and fourth even further away, when those of the first and second are

already very far apart, whereas they should have all converged together at a distance of fourteen inches <gloss>a</gloss> <note>a. See earlier, page 330, line 15, and page 326, line 26.</note>. And I would certainly tell you that I wanted to see if this did not proceed from the fact that, in tracing the hyperbola <term>hyperbola: a specific geometric curve that Descartes believed was the ideal shape for lenses to focus light perfectly</term>, you might have assumed the refraction <term>refraction: the bending of light as it passes from air into glass</term> of the glass to be greater or lesser than it actually is, because I did not know if you had taken the trouble to measure it beforehand. And if you had assumed it to be too large, it is true that those from the edges would converge further away than those from the middle, as they do; but these same rays [from the middle] would converge further away than fourteen inches, instead of converging much closer. And thus this glass cannot have the shape of a hyperbola, unless it were one where the exterior burning point <term>burning point: the focal point where the sun's rays converge with enough intensity to start a fire</term> was only six inches away, and the interior one much more than six. ### LXVII.

## DESCARTES TO [HUYGENS].

### Leiden, [31 March 1636].

->AUTOGRAPH, Saint Petersburg, Imperial Library.<-

*The address is missing, and the date the last of March 1636 <note>original: "Ult^a Martij 1636"</note> is in another hand. But Descartes is in Leiden, and he is writing to someone in a neighboring city, close enough that one can travel there in a few hours, since he himself will be there the next day after dinner. Now, Huygens was in The Hague (his Journal <note>original: "Dagboek"</note> notes a return to this city on 20 Dec. 1635, and mentions no departure before 8 May 1636); furthermore, another autograph from Descartes to Huygens (from 5 Oct. 1637) also bears, in Huygens’s hand, the indication in Latin of the day he received the letter; the date of 31 March 1636 thus confirms our conjecture, especially if one notices that 31 March was precisely a Monday this year, and that the letter would have been sent and received the same day, as is common between Leiden and The Hague.*

->Sir,<-

I admit that there is a major flaw in the writing that you have seen, as you point out, and that I have not sufficiently expanded upon the arguments by which I intend to prove that there is nothing in the world which is, in <margin>5</margin> itself, more self-evident and more certain than the existence of God and the human soul, so as to make them accessible to everyone. But I did not dare to attempt to do so, since I would have had to explain at great length the strongest arguments of the skeptics <note>The skeptics (or Pyrrhonists) argued that no certain knowledge was possible; Descartes used their doubt as a tool to find an indubitable truth.</note> <margin>10</margin> to show that there is no material thing whose existence one can be certain of, and by the same means, to accustom the reader to detach their thoughts from sensory things <note>Things perceived through the physical senses (sight, touch, etc.) rather than through pure reason.</note>; then to show that whoever doubts all material things in this way cannot, for all that, doubt their own <margin>15</margin> existence. From this it follows that this "self"—that is, the soul—is a being, or a substance, which is not at all corporeal, and that its nature is solely to think, and also that it is the first thing one can know with certainty. Indeed, by spending enough <margin>20</margin> time on this meditation, one gradually acquires a very clear and—if I may say so—intuitive knowledge of <term>intellectual nature</term> <note>The essence of a being that exists only as a mind or spirit, separate from physical matter.</note> in general; the idea of which, when considered without limitation, is that which represents God to us, and when limited, is that of an angel <margin>25</margin> or a human soul. Now, it is not possible to properly understand what I said afterward regarding the existence of God unless one starts from there, as I have sufficiently indicated on page 38 <note>Descartes is referring to a draft or proof sheet of his *Discourse on the Method*, which was published in June 1637.</note>. <meta>This page continues Fermat’s critical evaluation of the history of optics, specifically the study of refraction, as a prelude to his detailed critique of René Descartes’s "Dioptrique." This follows his introductory address to Father Mersenne on the previous page.</meta>

# CORRESPONDANCE. III, 169-170.

The knowledge of refractions has always been sought, but in vain. Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a pioneering Arab mathematician and physicist known as the "father of modern optics."</note> and Vitello <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1280/1314), a Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics was a standard text for centuries.</note> <gloss>a</gloss> worked on it without making much progress; and those who have come since have rightly noted that everything <margin>5</margin> reduced to establishing a certain proportion, by means of which, one refraction being known, all others could easily be found. So it is that all the foundations of <term>Dioptrics</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light, especially by lenses.</note> | must consist in this point; that is to say, in the correspondence and <margin>10</margin> ratio that one known refraction has to all others.

This being assumed, it was necessary for those who wished to establish the principles of Dioptrics to seek this correspondence and this ratio.

<margin>15</margin> Maurolico <note>Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575), an influential mathematician and astronomer from Sicily.</note>, Abbot of Messina, in his posthumous treatise *On Light and Shadow* <note>original: "De lumine & vmbrâ"</note> <gloss>b</gloss>, maintained that the angles he calls "of incidence" are proportional to those he names "of refraction." If this proposition were true, it would suffice to show us the true shapes <margin>20</margin> that <term>transparent bodies</term> <note>original: "corps diaphanes"; materials like glass or water through which light passes.</note> must have to produce such wonders. But because it was not well demonstrated by Maurolico, and because experience itself seems to prove it false, there remained enough for Monsieur Descartes to exercise his mind, and <margin>25</margin> to reveal new insights to us in these matters.

Photismi de lumine, et umbra... Diaphanorum partes... Problemata ad perspectivam, et Iridem pertinentia"</note> (Naples, from the printing house of Tarquinio Longo, 1611. ### III, 170-171. LXXII. — APRIL OR MAY 1637.

bodies, which, despite being the only ones capable of it, have nonetheless produced great obscurities until now.

His treatise on *Dioptrics* <note>René Descartes’s *La Dioptrique*, published in 1637 as one of the essays accompanying his *Discourse on the Method*.</note> is divided into several
<margin>5</margin>discourses, of which the principal ones are, it seems to me, the first two, which speak of Light and Refraction, because they contain the foundations of the science, from which one subsequently sees the beautiful conclusions and consequences he draws from them.

<margin>10</margin>Here is roughly his reasoning <gloss>a</gloss>. Light is nothing other than the inclination <note>Descartes theorized that light was not a moving particle, but an instantaneous pressure or "tendency to move" (inclination) transmitted through a medium.</note> that luminous bodies have to move. Now, this inclination to movement must probably follow the same laws as movement itself. And therefore we can regulate
<margin>15</margin>the effects of Light by the knowledge we can have of those of movement.

He then considers the movement of a ball in reflection and in refraction. And because it would be useless and tedious to copy all of his

"Written in April 1637. See the reasons for this in the new notebook." (Note from the copy at the Institute). Descartes is asking for the privilege <note>A "privilege" was a formal license granting exclusive rights to publish a book, a precursor to modern copyright</note> which was not signed until May 4 and likely did not arrive in Leiden until around the 16th. At the end of the second paragraph, the Institute copy contains a note in the margin, later erased: "This letter ends here." What follows (pp. 425-429) appears, in fact, to be later than another letter to Mersenne, which is certainly from the second half of May (Letter LXXVI hereafter); this is why we have moved it to June 1637 (Letter LXXXII hereafter).

<header>CORRESPONDENCE. I, 496-497.</header>

*...word, the fourth sentence of the previous letter (p. 364, l. 5-10), with the word "again" <note>original: "derechef"</note> added, as if Descartes were returning at the end to a recommendation he had already made at the beginning; these two fragments therefore seem to belong to the same letter, perhaps intentionally written on two separate sheets—one for Mersenne alone because of the few words on p. 364, l. 5, the other which could also be shown to the authors of the objections to which Descartes is responding.*

Regarding what you infer—that if the nature of man is only to think, he therefore has no will—I do not see the logical consequence; for willing, understanding, imagining, sensing, etc., are only 
<margin>5</margin> various ways of thinking, which all belong to the soul. You reject what I have said: that it is enough to judge well in order to do well; and yet it seems to me that the common doctrine of the Schools <note>Referring to Scholasticism, the traditional philosophy taught in universities based on Aristotle</note> is that *the will is not drawn toward evil, except insofar as it is represented to it by the intellect under some aspect of good* <note>original: "voluntas non fertur in malum, nisi quatenus ei sub aliqua ratione boni repræsentatur ab intellectu"</note>, from which comes this saying: 
<margin>10</margin> *every sinner is ignorant* <note>original: "omnis peccans est ignorans"</note>; so that if the understanding never represented anything to the will as good that was not actually so, the will could not fail in its choice. But it often represents various things to the will at the same

Page 383, line 5. — "Twenty-three or twenty-four years ago," says Descartes, which would bring us back to 1614 or 1613; and Father Noël was indeed, in fact, a tenured professor of Philosophy from the start of the October term in 1613; but Descartes had left the college in September 1612. Perhaps, in the draft, the numbers "23 and 24 years" were misread for **25 and 26**, which then brings us back to 1612 and 1611, when Descartes did indeed have Father Noël as a philosophy tutor <term>repetitor; a teaching assistant who reviewed lessons with students</term>.

Page 393, line 4. — Descartes did not lack for nieces at this date: in Brittany, there were three daughters of his elder brother, Pierre Descartes de Kerleau; and four daughters of his sister, Madame Rogier du Crévy. However, their parents would certainly not have sent these young children to the far reaches of Holland to entrust them to a bachelor uncle. It is more likely that Descartes is referring here, in coded language, to his own daughter, Francine, born in Deventer on July 19, 1635, and who was still, consequently, very much a child.

Page 394, line 5. — Evidently the same woman who appears in the register of baptismal acts in Deventer, dated July 28, 1635, as the mother of Francine (*Hijlena Ians* <note>original: "Hijlena Ians," Dutch for Hélène, daughter of Jan or John</note>), the father being our Descartes (*Reijner Iochems* <note>original: "Reijner Iochems," a pseudonym or variant for René, son of Joachim</note>).

Page 395, l. 5. — The Prince of Orange had laid siege to Breda on July 23. This stronghold, which belonged to the Dutch when Descartes stayed there in 1618 and 1619, had been captured by the Spanish on June 5, 1625, and was retaken from them on October 6, 1637.

Page 396, l. 23. — The *Compendium Musicæ* <note>Descartes' first work, a short treatise on the mathematical proportions of music theory.</note> addressed to Beeckman. A manuscript copy of it can still be found among the papers of the Huygens collection at the Leiden University Library, with this mention on the cover: *R. des Cartes to Isaac Beeckman* <note>original Latin: "R. des Cartes Isaaco Beckmanno"</note>, and this note at the end: *Breda in Brabant, on the day before the Calends of January, in the completed year 1618* <note>original Latin: "Bredæ Brabantinorum, pridie Calendas Ianuarias, Anno MDCXVIII completo." This date corresponds to December 31, 1618.</note>.

Page 396, l. 27. — Descartes will respond with a short treatise in French (see Letter LXXXIX, October 5, 1637, further on). However, on an attached paper, one finds—alongside figures drawn in his own hand—the Latin terms used by Huygens: the pulleys (*trochlea*), the lever (*vectis*), etc.

Page 397, l. 16. — A Spanish romance, written around 1465 by Garcia Ordoñez de Montalvo and published for the first time in 1508. A French translation by Herberay des Essarts appeared in 1540 (Paris, Denis Janot and Vincent Sertenas, folio). This comprised the essential part, in four books, which were frequently reprinted until 1577. The popularity of this romance was such that sequels were continuously produced throughout the 16th century and up until the time of Descartes. The first translator published four new books from 1544 to 1548. Others after him provided a 9th and 10th book in 1553, an 11th in 1554, and a 12th in 1556. These first twelve books formed the "folio" edition. Three more were added, bringing the number to 15 in a "quarto" edition. A "16mo" <note>Referring to the size of the book; 16mo or "sextodecimo" is a small, pocket-sized format.</note> edition contains 21—that is, all the previous ones plus 6 others (1576–1579). Three octavo volumes (books 22, 23, and 24) were added in 1615, followed by eight others from 1620 to 1625: the *History of the Knight of the Sun* and his brother *Rosiclair*, plus one more in 1625, the *History of Belianis of Greece*, and finally seven new volumes forming the conclusion under the title: *The Romance of Romances*. In total, about forty volumes. Was it these final books that Descartes amused himself by leafing through, or only the first four, or perhaps the collection entitled: *Treasury of all the books of Amadis de Gaule, containing the harangues, epistles, speeches, missive letters, requests, responses, replies, maxims, challenges, laments, and other most excellent things, very useful for instructing the French nobility in eloquence, virtue, grace, and generosity* (2 volumes, Lyon, published for Jean-Anth. Huguetan, 1582 and 1606)? See Eugène Baret, *On Amadis de Gaule and its influence in the 16th and 17th centuries* (Paris, Firmin-Didot, 1873).

### LXXXV.

### PLEMPIUS TO DESCARTES.

### Louvain, September 15, 1637.

*Manuscript copy, Leiden, University Library, Huygens Collection, 29 a.*

*Published by Domela Nieuwenhuis, "Commentary on R. Descartes' dealings with Belgian philosophers," p. 95-97 (quarto, Louvain, 1827). One can read the date on the manuscript as either September 19 or 15; however, the latter date is closer to the 13th, the date of the following letter from Fromondus (Froidmont), which was sent by Plempius (Plemp) to Descartes.*

->Most Noble Sir,<-

I received three copies of your commentaries <note>The *Discourse on the Method* and its accompanying scientific essays, published in June 1637.</note> about three weeks ago now: I am sorry that my people <note>original Latin: "parentes mei" — likely referring to his associates or intermediaries in the delivery</note> were a bit negligent in this matter, which caused the delay.
<margin>5</margin> I finally received them, then; I kept one for myself, gave the second to Master Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont, a professor of philosophy and theology at Louvain.</note>, and sent the third to Father Fournet on the same day I received them. Since then, Fromondus and I have been occupied with reading, turning the pages, and weighing the contents of the book. You ask what we think? First of all,
<margin>10</margin> the style in that language <note>The book was written in French rather than the traditional Latin, a bold move for a philosophical work at the time.</note> is so Attic <note>Refined, elegant, and clear, like the ancient Greek of Athens.</note> that I despair of anyone ever being able to translate the book into Latin quite so well. But this is a minor point and matters little to you. You ask about our thoughts on the ideas. Here are some notes Fromondus made and wrote to me, so that I might send them to you. These
<margin>15</margin> are a few small objections <note>original Latin: "Responsiunculæ"</note> which explain things differently according to our principles <note>The traditional Aristotelian-Scholastic philosophy taught at the University of Louvain.</note>. But, unless I am greatly mistaken, they do not undermine your philosophy in the slightest, and I believe there will be no one who will [be able to...]

Page 399, l. 4. — Plempius (Vopiscus-Fortunatus) was born in Amsterdam on December 23, 1601. He studied philosophy at Louvain, specifically under Libert Froidmont <note>Also known as Libertus Fromondus, a traditionalist theologian and scientist who famously critiqued Descartes.</note>, then completed his medical studies at Leiden, and later at Padua and Bologna. From 1623 to 1633, he practiced medicine in Amsterdam, where he became acquainted with Descartes through their mutual friend, the physician Elichmann, whom he asks about at the end of this letter. Since Descartes left Amsterdam for Deventer at the end of May 1632, and Plemp was appointed professor at the University of Louvain on August 3, 1633, their relationship dates to 1630, 1631, and the early months of 1632. On February 27, 1637, Plemp was elected Rector Magnificus <note>The titular head of the university.</note> for the second time. In the 3rd edition of his *Foundations of Medicine* (folio edition, Louvain, printed by Hieronymus Nempaeus; 1654), he published a letter as an appendix dated December 21, 1652, which reads on page 375:
> "I knew that man (Descartes) familiarly in Amsterdam,
> before I was called to the chair at Louvain by the most serene Isabella <note>Isabella Clara Eugenia, the Sovereign of the Spanish Netherlands.</note>,
> through the mediation of Johann Elichmann, a Silesian Doctor of Medicine,
> and I often discussed physical matters with him... Known to no one,
> he hid himself in the house of a cloth merchant, located on the street that
> takes its name from calves (still today *Kalverstraat*). There I visited him
> quite often: I always found a man neither reading books nor possessing
> them; intent only on meditations and committing them to paper;
> sometimes even dissecting animals, just as <term>HIPPOCRATES</term> <note>The ancient Greek 'Father of Medicine.'</note> found <term>DEMOCRITUS</term> <note>The 'Laughing Philosopher' of Abdera, often depicted as a solitary figure dissecting animals to find the seat of the soul or the cause of madness.</note> near Abdera."
A passage from the same letter informs us that Descartes had sent his book to Plempius following a visit that the latter had paid him at his new residence near Haarlem, presumably during the holidays:
> "Afterward, while returning from Louvain to my homeland, I saw him
> living on an estate near Haarlem; and thereafter we wrote several
> letters to one another, two of which appear in this work of mine." (See *Letters CVII and CXVII* below).

Page 400, l. 6. — Plempius was himself the author of an *Ophtalmographia, or concerning the structure, action, and use of the eye, contrary to the common opinion of physicians and philosophers* (Amsterdam, 1632). In the preface, Plempius congratulates himself on having been a pupil of Fromondus, and declares that it is to him that he owes everything new he teaches regarding Dioptrics <note>The study of light refraction and its effects on vision.</note>.

# LXXXVI.

## FROMONDUS TO PLEMPIUS.

->Louvain, September 13, 1637.<-

->*MS COPY, Leiden, University Library, Huygens Collection, 29 a.*<-

->*Printed like the preceding letter by Domela Nieuwenhuis, Commentary on the Correspondence of R. Descartes, etc., p. 97-102.*<-

->To the most distinguished Physician Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius, many greetings.<-

->Most Distinguished Sir,<-

I have run through many parts of that <term>French philosophy</term> <note>original: "philosophia gallica"; referring to Descartes' *Discourse on Method* and its accompanying essays.</note>. Please give the greatest thanks to our author on my behalf; I admire and embrace his genius in most matters. I seem to see a sort of Pythagoras or Democritus, who, as a self-imposed exile from his own country, travels among the Egyptians, the Brahmins, and the whole world to explore the nature of things and the universe. <margin>5</margin> However, although his genius is clear enough everywhere, the truth is obscured in places; and I fear that through love of his own invention he may flatter himself too much, and think he is embracing Juno, when, like Ixion, he only grasps a cloud. <margin>10</margin> <note>In Greek mythology, Ixion was tricked into embracing a cloud shaped like the goddess Juno; Fromondus is suggesting Descartes' theories might be illusions rather than reality.</note> Not infrequently, he falls back—unknowingly, I believe—into the physics of Epicurus <note>Epicurus was an ancient philosopher associated with atomism; Fromondus implies Descartes' mechanical explanations are too materialistic.</note>, which is crude and rather coarse, and not sufficiently refined, as most believe, by the file of exact truth. <margin>15</margin>

<summary>Libert Froidmont (Fromondus) writes to Plempius to acknowledge receipt of Descartes' new work, praising the author's genius while warning that his mechanical philosophy leans too heavily toward ancient atomism and may be illusory.</summary>
<keywords>Libert Froidmont, Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius, René Descartes, Louvain, mechanical philosophy, Epicureanism, scientific critique</keywords>

...only see here some notes as a sample; in which the truth is suspect to me <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "mihi"</note>, or at least I do not understand what that most learned man meant to say.

1. On pages 46–47, he seems to say that heat, such as that found in <term>heated hay</term> <note>original: "fœno calefacto"; Descartes used the example of damp hay fermenting and heating up to explain how biological heat could exist without a soul or fire.</note>, can perform all the operations of an animal in the human body, except for the actions proper to the rational soul. Therefore, the heat of hay, without any other <term>sensitive soul</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "sensitive soul" was the life principle responsible for sensation and movement in animals.</note>, could see, hear, etc. Such noble operations do not seem able to proceed from such an ignoble and brute cause.
<margin>10</margin>

2. Similarly, on page 56 he says that if an <term>automaton</term> <note>A self-operating machine; Descartes argued that animals were essentially complex biological robots.</note> had the internal organs and the outward shape of a beast, there would be no difference between a real beast and such a machine. Why then is it necessary to insert "substantial souls" into beasts, if the heat of hay suffices for the operations of all the internal and external senses and the appetite? <margin>15</margin> From this, perhaps, a path will be paved for atheists to attribute even the operations of the <term>rational soul</term> <note>The "rational soul" was considered the uniquely human, immortal part of the mind responsible for reason.</note> to a similar cause, and exclude it from the human body, or at least foist a material soul upon us in place of an immaterial one. <margin>20</margin> One ought not to attribute such lofty operations to such humble causes.

3. Nor does what he discusses on page 50 regarding the <term>systole</term> <note>The contraction of the heart.</note> and <term>diastole</term> <note>The relaxation and expansion of the heart.</note> of the heart seem plausible enough. I omit what you were just recently <margin>25</margin> discussing, which especially concerns you physicians. Truly, the <term>rarefaction</term> <note>The process of expanding in volume; Descartes believed blood expanded rapidly like steam when hitting the "heat" of the heart.</note> of a drop of blood cannot be completed and fill the cavity of the heart in such a short time as the heart's motion completes its expansion, unless the heat of the heart matched the glow of a furnace.

4. On page 4 of the <term>Dioptrics</term> <note>Descartes' *La Dioptrique*, an essay on optics published alongside his *Discourse on Method* in 1637.</note>, it does not seem to be correctly explained how a luminous body transmits its ray in an instant, by comparison with the staff of a blind man. This is because a ray emerging from the solar body should rather be compared to an arrow <margin>5</margin> shot from a bow, which crosses the air successively <note>Moving from one point to the next over time, rather than being everywhere at once.</note>, not in an instant. Furthermore, nothing is actually transmitted from the object being touched to the hand of the person holding the blind man’s staff; rather, since the staff is moved all at once, the hand immediately feels the resistance, as if warned by the part it <margin>10</margin> holds, which moves at the same moment in time as the far end that touches the object. This, however, cannot be applied to vision, since the eye does not see the sun by touching it through an intervening ray, just as the hand touches a stone through a staff.

<margin>15</margin> Next, he assumes everywhere that light is some thin body <note>original: "tenue quoddam corpus"</note>, insinuating itself through the pores of transparent objects <note>original: "diaphanorum"</note>. This was a view held by crude philosophy in the past, and it was excellently refuted by <term>Aristotle</term> <gloss>a</gloss>: otherwise, glass would not transmit rays with such <margin>20</margin> ease, since it is not at all porous. This is shown by a clear experiment: a person speaking from inside a glass room to someone else placed outside (if other <gloss>b</gloss> factors are exactly observed) is no more heard than if he were speaking through a steel wall. Finally, the sun would have long ago <margin>25</margin> exhausted its entire body if it had to illuminate by pouring out such a great flood of atoms from its very depths. But if he says that light is not the corpuscles themselves which are spread from the sun all the way to here, but rather some motion of those corpuscles (as he sometimes seems to say), that is far more improbable: for light to be transmitted...

Is it because the impulse of one color is greater than another? But even for one and the same color, a more intense or a weaker impulse would be greater or lesser <note>Froidmont is arguing that if color is just the strength of a "push," then a bright yellow and a dim yellow would look like different colors entirely.</note>.

9. On page 30, he seems to recognize no other sensation than that which is exercised in the brain. Does a part of an animal that is being burned, <margin>1</margin> therefore, not exercise any operation of touch by which it perceives the painful quality there? Yet we see this experienced just as much as we imagine it in the head.
