Therefore, one must necessarily admit some other <margin>2</margin> <term>integral union</term> <note>original: "vnio integralis." A philosophical term for a union where parts are joined into a whole naturally, rather than by mechanical fasteners like hooks.</note> between immediate parts, among which there is no heterogeneity or inequality of shapes.

...that the same small bodies <note>original: "corpuſcula." In Cartesian physics, these are the tiny particles of matter that make up all things.</note>, if they weakly strike the sense of touch, produce the sensation of cold, and if they strike more strongly, they produce heat! As if there were only a difference in that local impulse <note>original: "impulſu locali," meaning a physical push or motion.</note>, and not in the qualities themselves affecting the organ of touch in <margin>5</margin> various ways!

13. This is also a paradox, on page 164: that cold <term>rarefies</term> <note>original: "rarefacere." In physics, to make something less dense or take up more space.</note>; and the experience which moved him seems to have another cause, namely the air and "spirits" <note>original: "ſpiritus." In 17th-century science, these were highly refined, active substances or gases within a liquid.</note> which are squeezed out of the water when it is condensed by the cold. For these, by their exit, lift up the <margin>10</margin> top parts of the water enclosed in the vessel; hence it appears rarer there than the rest of the ice, simply because it is emptier and more porous, with large pores gaping open to the eye.

14. On page 165, he thinks that <term>exhalations</term> <note>original: "exhalationes." Dry or smoky vapors thought to rise from the earth.</note> are raised on high by the impact of the sun's rays, just like dust is raised by the <margin>15</margin> feet of those walking upon it. But the rays of the sun are not bodies that can press down upon the dust and force it upward; otherwise, we would also clearly feel such an impression of the rays upon us. And it does not seem probable that the fumes of exhalations or vapors are thrust upward in any way other than by their own <margin>20</margin> rarity or by the push of heavier things [displacing them]. This entire matter of the laws of equilibrium must be understood from Archimedes' book *On Floating Bodies* <note>original: "de inſidentibus humido." Archimedes’ foundational work on buoyancy and why things float.</note>, which the author [Descartes] seems never to have read.

15. Hence, on page 182, he does not touch upon the true cause of why <margin>25</margin> the top surface of water is smooth and uniformly round. For the genuine reason must be sought not from the friction of air particles, but from the doctrine of Archimedes in that book.

16. On pages 167–168, the cause of the rarity of vapors seems <margin>30</margin> false. For speed of motion does not cause rarity, because a body at rest can be extremely rare, nor [do] rays...

->Most Illustrious Sir,<-

I received your letter, along with the observations of Mr. Froidmont <note>original: "Domini Fromondi." Libert Froidmont was a professor at Louvain and a prominent critic of Descartes.</note>, and they were indeed most welcome to me, though (to confess the truth) not expected so soon. For several weeks ago I had heard that the book <note>Descartes' *Discourse on the Method*, published in June 1637.</note> had not yet been sent to you, and most of those to whom I offered it for reading here have testified to me that they could not sufficiently judge it until they had reread it several times. I owe you all the more thanks, certainly to you especially for such generous praise—more, I dare confess, than I deserve, but the greatest part of which I do not doubt should be attributed to your friendship toward me; and likewise to Mr. Froidmont, because he wished to be so diligent in reading my writing and so helpful in sending his thoughts about it. I truly seem to recognize, from the judgment of such a great man—and one so well-versed in these matters of which I treat<sup>a</sup>—the opinions of many others. But yet, because I notice that in many things he has not grasped my meaning, I cannot yet conclude from this what both he himself and others might say after a more accurate examination; nor do I fully agree with you | judging that my explanations can indeed be rejected and despised, but not refuted or disproven by reasons. Since I admit no principles unless they are very manifest <note>original: "valde manifesta"; a reference to Descartes' requirement for "clear and distinct" perceptions as the foundation of knowledge.</note>, and I consider nothing except magnitudes, shapes, and motions <term>magnitudes, shapes, and motions: In Cartesian physics, these are the only quantifiable properties of matter, as opposed to the "sensible qualities" like color or heat used in older Aristotelian science.</term>, in the manner of mathematicians, all the [arguments] of the philosophers...

I have blocked all loopholes <note>original: "subterfugia interclusi." <margin>5</margin>stration, will not, I hope, be despised with impunity—at least by those who teach. <margin>10</margin>festly destroyed that, if any nevertheless wish to defend them, they will not be able to respond easily—and perhaps not without the laughter of the audience—to those who have understood my work. *Observations of Mr. Froidmont on his Method, Dioptrics, and Meteors,* a title which seems translated word for word from Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier, Descartes' editor, who often titled letters for clarity rather than following the original manuscripts.</note>, instead of reproducing that of the manuscript copy. <margin>5, 10</margin>
It seems very timely to me that the most illustrious and learned man, Mr. Libert Froidmont <note>original: "D. Lib. Fromondus"</note>, recalled the fable of Ixion <note>In Greek mythology, Ixion attempted to seduce Hera but was tricked by Zeus into embracing a cloud (Nephele) in her shape. Froidmont suggests Descartes has embraced a "cloud" of illusion rather than the "goddess" of truth.</note> at the start of his objections against me, not only because he rightly warns me to be careful lest I embrace empty clouds of opinions in place of truth—which I profess to wish to do as much as is in my power, and to have always done until now—but also because he himself, while he thinks he is attacking my philosophy, refutes nothing except that empty philosophy composed of atoms and the void <note>original: "ex atomis & vacuo conflatam"</note> which is usually attributed to Democritus and Epicurus, and other similar things that have nothing to do with me.

<margin>15, 20</margin>
1. And first, regarding pages 46 and 47 <note>These page numbers refer to the first edition of the *Discourse on the Method* (1637).</note>, when he says that *such noble actions as vision and similar things cannot proceed from such an ignoble and brute cause as heat*, he supposes that I think beasts see exactly as we do, that is, by sensing or thinking that they see <note>original: "sentiendo siue cogitando se videre"</note>, which is believed to have been the opinion of Epicurus, and even now is the common view among almost everyone. However, throughout that entire part up to page 60, I show clearly enough that I do not think beasts see as we do when we sense that we are seeing, but only as we do when the mind is occupied elsewhere; for although images of external objects may be painted on the retinas of our eyes <note>original: "retinis oculorum nostrorum"</note>, and perhaps even their impressions in the nerves

<columns>2</columns>

images formed by optics determine our limbs to various movements, yet we feel nothing of them at all; in which case we move no differently than <term>automata</term> <note>Self-moving machines or mechanical devices. Descartes famously viewed the physical bodies of both animals and humans as complex machines governed by the laws of physics.</note>, for whose movements no one would say the force of heat is <margin>5</margin> insufficient.

2. Likewise, regarding page 56, when he asks what need there is to *attribute <term>substantial souls</term> to animals* <note>original: "animas substantiales brutis inferere." In the Scholastic tradition Froidmont followed, a "substantial soul" was a non-physical essence that gave a creature its life and form.</note>, and says that perhaps from here a path is paved for Atheists to also exclude the rational soul from the human body, this pertains to no one less than <margin>10</margin> to me. For I, with Holy Scripture, firmly believe and, unless I am mistaken, have clearly explained that the *souls of animals are nothing other than blood*—specifically that blood which, heated and thinned into <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritum." Descartes refers to "animal spirits," which he believed were the most subtle, agitated parts of the blood that acted like a hydraulic fluid to move the muscles.</note> by their heart, spreads from the arteries through <margin>15</margin> the brain into all the nerves and muscles. From this view, it follows that there is so great a difference between the souls of animals and our own, that no argument has yet been devised by anyone (as far as I know) more powerful for contradicting Atheists and persuading them that human minds *are not <margin>20</margin> drawn from the power of matter*. On the contrary, those who imagine I know not what "substantial souls"—distinct from blood, heat, and spirits—for animals, I first do not see what they would answer to Leviticus chapter 17, verse 14, where it is expressly said: *for the soul of all flesh is in the blood, and you shall not eat the blood of any flesh, because the soul of the flesh is in the blood*. And likewise Deuteronomy chapter 12, verse 23: *only take care not to <margin>27</margin> eat the blood, for their blood is as the soul, and therefore*

<summary>Descartes argues that animals are essentially biological machines (automata) powered by heat and blood, citing biblical passages to support his claim that animal "souls" are purely physical. <margin>15</margin> no falsehood; whereas the knowledge of reason is a little more complex and can be carried along through the winding paths of <term>syllogisms</term> <note>Logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal).</note>. Immediate, direct knowledge that does not require step-by-step logical reasoning.</note>, or
<margin>20</margin> merely apprehensive, and not bound by any entanglements of discourse; so much so that, according to them, if it is permitted to say so, the senses of animals come closer to the knowledge of God and the Angels than does human reasoning. Regarding page 50, when he says *that no less heat is required in the heart than in a furnace, so that drops of blood might be rarefied* <margin>5</margin> *quickly enough to inflate it* <note>original: "inflandum." To "rarefy" here means to expand rapidly through heat, which Descartes believed was the mechanism that moved the heart and circulated blood.</note>, he does not seem to have noticed how milk, oil, and almost all other liquids, when placed on a fire, expand very gradually and slowly at first; but when they have reached a certain degree of heat, they swell up in a moment of time. For if he had noticed these things, he would easily have judged that the blood contained in the <veins> <note>The word "veins" was missing in the original manuscript but added by later editors for clarity.</note> of any animal is as close as possible to that degree of heat which it must acquire in the heart, so that it might <margin>20</margin> rarefy there in a moment of time.

...blind: because, he says, a ray leaping forth from the solar body should rather be compared to an arrow shot from a bow, which passes through the air successively, and not in an instant, etc. Does he here see Leucippus in my place, or Epicurus, or certainly Lucretius, who somewhere (unless my memory fails me) spoke of the <term>darts of the sun</term> <note>original: "spicula solis." Indeed, since sound is the motion of air, or at least <margin>25</margin> depends on the motion of air, it should be a surprise to no one that those paths which are not open to a breeze—or to the whole body of air—do not admit sound either.

7. He will also understand <margin>10</margin> in what sense I said on page 23 that air impedes the passage of light more than water, nor will the experience of divers <note>original: "urinatorum." 9. Regarding page 30, he wonders why I do not acknowledge any other sensation than that which is carried out in the brain. But all <margin>5</margin> doctors and surgeons will, I hope, help me to persuade him of this: for they know that those whose limbs have recently been cut off often believe they still feel pain in those parts they lack. I once knew a young girl who, because she had a serious wound in her hand, <margin>10</margin> had her eyes covered whenever the surgeon approached, so that she might more easily allow herself to be treated by him. Her whole arm was amputated due to a spreading gangrene <term>gangrene: the death of body tissue, usually caused by a loss of blood supply or bacterial infection</term>, and cloths were substituted in its place in such a way that for several weeks afterward she remained unaware that she had been deprived of it. Meanwhile, however, <margin>15</margin> she complained that she felt various pains, now in her fingers, now in her metacarpus <term>metacarpus: the group of five bones in the palm of the hand</term>, now in her wrist <note>original: "brachiali"</note>, all of which she lacked. This was because those nerves in the arm, which previously descended from the brain to those parts, were still being affected. This would undoubtedly not have happened if the sense of pain—or, as <margin>20</margin> he calls it, the sensation—were performed outside the brain.

...to be praised, and in which I especially take pride and glory: namely, that I use a way of philosophizing in which there is no reasoning that is not mathematical and evident, and whose conclusions are confirmed by true experiments; <margin>5</margin> so much so that whatever can be concluded to be possible from its principles actually happens, whenever active things are applied to passive things in the proper way. I wonder that he does not notice that Mechanics, which has been in use until now, is nothing other than a small part of true Physics <term>Physics: the study of nature and the physical world</term>, which, since it found no place among the <margin>10</margin> followers of common Philosophy <note>Descartes refers here to Scholastic philosophy, based on Aristotle, which was the standard in universities at the time.</note>, retreated to the Mathematicians. However, this part of Philosophy remained more true and less corrupt than the others, because since it refers to use and practice, whoever errs in it is usually punished by a loss of expenses <note>original: "sumptuum iacturâ plecti solent." Descartes argues that engineers/mechanics have to be right, or they lose money, which keeps their science honest.</note>; so much so that if <margin>15</margin> he despises my way of philosophizing because it is similar to Mechanics, it seems to me the same as if he despised it because it is true. But if he does not want water and other bodies to be composed of some parts that are actually distinct, let him notice, I pray, that we perceive such parts with our sight in many things <margin>20</margin>: for thus we recognize dust particles in stones, fibers in wood, and, as he himself says, the warp and the woof <term>warp and woof: the vertical and horizontal threads in weaving, used here as a metaphor for the internal structure of muscle or flesh</term> in flesh, and similar things; and nothing is more consistent with reason than that we should judge those things which <margin>25</margin> we do not perceive with the senses because of their extreme smallness by the example and likeness of those which we do see. And let him remember that he himself even said in the objection to page 164 that the air and spirits enclosed in water lift its topmost parts by their exit, which certainly does not...

12. Regarding page 162, it seems like a paradox <note>original: "paradoxon"; a statement that contradicts common intuition</note> to him that a sluggish motion produces the sensation of cold, while a swifter motion produces heat. By this same logic, it must also seem a paradox to him that a light rubbing on the hand produces a sensation of tickling and pleasure, while a stronger rubbing produces pain; for pain and pleasure are no less different than heat and cold. Likewise this: if we apply one hand that is hot to a lukewarm body, that body seems cold to us; yet we think that same body is warm if we touch it with the other hand which is colder, etc.

13. Regarding page 164, it also seems a paradox to him that cold can cause rarefaction <note>term: rarefaction; the process of becoming less dense or occupying more space, the opposite of condensation</note>. And yet, he cannot explain away the experience that demonstrates it. For when he says that the air and spirits <note>term: spirits; in 17th-century physics, these were thought to be extremely subtle, active fluids within matter</note>, which are squeezed out of water condensed by cold, lift up the top parts of that water enclosed in a vessel, he is admitting that the air and spirits exit and lift the top parts, yet he does not suppose that anything succeeds into their place. Thus, by his own account, the water then occupies more space and simultaneously contains <insert>less</insert> matter within itself than before—which is certainly to be rarefied by cold, not condensed. For in whatever way it happens that a body occupies more space than before, this is called "being rarefied." However, one should not think that this cause he provides for the rising of the water is the true one; for, if air and spirits...

# II, 49. LXXXVIII. — 3 October 1637. 429

...does not admit an increase in quantity, nor do I understand any **rarefaction** <note>The process of a substance becoming less dense</note> except that which occurs when the parts of some **body** <note>In 17th-century physics, a "body" refers to any physical object or piece of matter</note> are moved away from one another, and its **pores** <note>Small gaps or channels within a substance</note> or the intervals cast between those parts are increased. <margin>5</margin> Nor do I say that the individual particles of a body, whose pores are thus increased, are themselves rarefied, but only the whole body. Nor, finally, do I deny that certain bodies, even if their parts are at rest, can be very rare: for in this way I call a **sponge** rare, not only when it is dry, but even <margin>10</margin> more so when it swells up, being soaked with water. For it is just the same whether air, or water, or any other matter is contained in its pores, since that matter does not belong to its own nature. And yet nothing is more evident than that the very rapid **motion** of the individual parts of some body <margin>15</margin> can also sometimes bring it about that those individual parts are moved further away from one another than if they were at rest; just as when a **firebrand** <note>original: "titio"; a burning piece of wood</note> is swung around somewhere, it prevents other firebrands from being able to be swung around in other ways in that space which it traverses; so much so that here <margin>20</margin> he seems to have **looked for a knot in a bulrush**. <note>original: "nodum in ſcirpo"; a Latin proverb meaning to find a difficulty where there is none, or to over-complicate a simple matter</note>

# LXXXIX.

## DESCARTES TO HUYGENS.

->October 5, 1637.<-

->*Autograph, Leiden, University Library, Huygens collection, 29 a.*<-

*The original manuscript fills two entire sheets, large format, folded in two—that is, four leaves, totaling eight pages—plus a quarter-sheet containing on both sides, in Descartes' own hand, the figures to which the text refers. Of these two sheets, the first includes the cover letter (p. 1 and 2), then the final third of the short Treatise on Mechanics or Explanation of Engines (p. 7 and 8); the first and second thirds are on the other sheet (p. 3 and 4, 5 and 6). The short Treatise should therefore not be separated from the letter, although Clerselier, volume II, letter 82, p. 366-368, provides the letter alone, based on a draft that offers some variations.*

*However, the Treatise was also found among Descartes' papers, as evidenced by the Stockholm inventory of February 14, 1650, item S. But, says Baillet (II, 400), "it was stolen or misplaced."*

Most Illustrious Sir, these are my responses to the objections of the most learned man, Mr. Froidmont; if he does not yet think himself to be fully
<column-break/>
satisfied by them, or if by chance, after a more accurate examination of the book, he should find many others, etc. <note>original Latin: "Clarissime Domine, quæ ad obiectiones..." This is the formal opening of Descartes' response to the theological critiques of his work.</note>

<meta>This page continues the editorial history and provenance of Descartes' short treatise on mechanics, following the discussion of its initial composition and circulation among his contemporaries.</meta>

# CORRESPONDENCE. II, 366.

However, *Pierre Borel* managed to obtain a copy of it which he even intended to publish; we read in his *Compendium of the Life of Descartes, 1653*: <note>original Latin: "Compendium Vitæ Cartesii"</note> "...and also a small treatise on mechanics, which I gave to the Booksellers along with two Letters from the most serene princess Elizabeth, so that they might be made public." <note>original Latin: "...ut et de mechanica tractatulum, quem Bibliopolæ cum duab. Epistolis serenissimæ principissæ Elizabethæ dedi, ut publici fiant juris."</note> (p. 42 of the 2nd edition, 1676). Was it from this copy of Borel's that Father Poisson became the editor of the little *Treatise* in Paris in 1668, or from another copy that he had sent for specifically from Stockholm through the efforts of Mr. de Loménie? Baillet says sometimes one, sometimes the other, *I, 317 and II, 400.*

Poisson's edition, from which we provide the variant readings, has as its title: *Treatise on Mechanics, composed by Monsieur Descartes: additionally the Abridgment of Music by the same author, translated into French with the necessary clarifications by N. P. P. D. L. <note>Nicolas Poisson, Prêtre de l'Oratoire (Priest of the Oratory)</note> (Paris, Charles Angot, 1668, in-quarto).* The *Treatise* (p. 7-15) is followed by *Remarks on the Mechanics of Mons. Descartes* (p. 16-52), by the same *Nicolas Poisson, Priest of the Oratory.*

In 1672, at Kiel, in Holstein, *Jean-Daniel Major*, unaware of this publication, produced a Latin version based on a text he had procured, with this title: *René Descartes' Explanation of Machines or Instruments, by the benefit of which a very heavy load can be lifted or moved with little force, translated from the French Language into Latin, and now published for the first time (Kiel, Holstein, Printed by Joachim Reumann, Academic Printer, in the year 1672).* <note>original Latin: "Ren. Des Cartes Explicatio Machinarum vel Instrumentorum, quorum beneficio parvâ vi elevari vel moveri potest gravissimum onus, ex Gallico Idiomate in Latinum versa, et nunc primùm edita"</note>

However, the original remained in the collection of *Constantin Huygens*, as his son, *Christiaan*, notes in one of his remarks on Baillet's work in 1691: "I have the treatise on Mechanics of which he speaks, in the hand of Mr. Descartes." (published by V. Cousin, *Philosophical Fragments, vol. II, p. 157, 3rd edition*). Attached to this autograph is a blank sheet which bears this title, in the hand of Constantin Huygens: "*The Mechanics of Mons^r Descartes, 1637*", and this note by the same hand: "R^a 24 Oct. 37" (R^a means *Received* <note>original Latin: "Recepta"</note>, see the letter from Huygens hereafter, p. 461, l. 9). This note, as well as the date of the autograph, corrects an error by Baillet (*I, 11, and 268*), who attributed this little treatise to the month of February 1636; it is true that he corrects himself in part, *I, 316.* — Descartes is responding here to Letter LXXXIV above, from Sept. 8, p. 395.

->Sir,<-

In whatever occupation your letters find me, they are always very dear and very welcome to me—

<summary>In this letter, Descartes explains his focus on theoretical mechanics over experimental data and introduces a short treatise on the principle of mechanical advantage in lifting heavy weights.</summary>

# CORRESPONDENCE.

A force capable of lifting a weight of 100 pounds to a height of two feet can also lift a weight of 200 pounds to a height of one foot, or one of 400 pounds to the height of half a foot, and so on, provided that the force is applied to it.

<margin>5</margin>And this principle cannot fail to be accepted if one considers that the effect must always be proportionate to the action necessary to produce it: so that if it is necessary to employ the action by which one can lift a weight of 100 pounds to the <margin>10</margin>height of two feet in order to lift a weight to the height of only one foot, this latter weight must weigh 200 pounds. For lifting 100 pounds to the height of one foot, and again another hundred to the height of one foot, is the same as lifting two hundred pounds to the height of one foot, <margin>15</margin>and also the same as lifting one hundred pounds to the height of two feet.

Now, the machines <note>The author uses "engins," referring to the simple machines of classical mechanics.</note> which serve to apply a force acting through a large space to a weight which it lifts through a smaller space are the pulley, the <margin>20</margin>inclined plane, the wedge, the windlass <note>original: "tour," a rotating drum or axle used for lifting.</note> or the wheel, the screw, the lever, and several others. For if one does not wish to relate them to one another, one can count more of them; and if one wishes to relate them, there is no need to include so many. <insert>a</insert>

### THE PULLEY.

Let A B C <note>original: "A B C^a"; the superscript 'a' refers to the author's original diagram legend.</note> be a cord passed around the pulley D, to which pulley the weight E is attached. And first, supposing that two men equally support or <margin>5</margin> raise each one of the ends of this cord, it is evident that if this weight weighs 200 pounds, each of these men will employ, to support or <margin>10</margin> lift it, only the force required to support or lift 100 pounds; for each carries only half of it. Let us suppose after this that A, one of the ends of this cord, being attached <margin>15</margin> firmly to some nail, the other end C is again supported by a man; and it is evident that this man, at C, will have no more need than before, to support the weight E, than the force required to support one hundred <margin>20</margin> pounds: because the nail which is at A performs the same office there as the man whom we previously supposed to be there. Finally, let us posit that this man who is at C pulls the cord to make the weight E rise; and it is evident that, if he employs the force required to <margin>25</margin> lift 100 pounds to the height of two feet, he will cause this weight E, which weighs 200, to rise to the height of one foot: for the cord A B C being doubled as it is

<margin>5</margin>
There is, however, one thing that prevents this calculation from being exact, namely the weight of the <term>pulley</term><note>A wheel with a grooved rim for a rope, used to change the direction of a force or provide mechanical advantage.</note>, and the difficulty one might have in making the rope slide and in carrying it. But that is very little in comparison to what is being lifted, and can only be estimated approximately.

<margin>10</margin>
Furthermore, it must be noted that it is not the pulley itself that causes this force, but only the doubling of the rope: for if one attaches another pulley toward A, through which the rope ABCH is passed, it will require no less force to pull H toward K, and <margin>15</margin> thus lift the weight E, than was required before to pull C toward G. But if to these two pulleys one adds yet another toward D, to which the weight is attached and through which the rope is passed, just as in the first one, then one will not <margin>20</margin> need more force to lift this weight of 200 pounds than to lift one of 50 without a pulley, because by pulling 4 feet of the rope, one will only raise it by one foot. And so by multiplying the pulleys, one can lift the greatest <term>burdens</term><note>original: "fardeaux"; refers to heavy loads or weights.</note> with the smallest <margin>25</margin> forces.

One should also note that a little more force is always required to lift a weight than to support it; which is why I have spoken here separately of the one and the other.

# LXXXIX. — OCTOBER 5, 1637.

## THE INCLINED PLANE.

If one has only enough strength to lift 100 pounds, but nevertheless wishes to lift the body F, which weighs 200, to the height of the line BA, one need only pull or <margin>5</margin> roll it along the inclined plane CA, which I suppose to be twice as long as the line AB; for, by this means, to make it reach point A, one will employ the force that is required to make 100 pounds rise twice as high. And the more one makes this plane CA inclined <note>meaning a shallower angle relative to the ground</note>, the less force one will need to lift the weight F by its means.

<margin>10</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of an inclined plane. It features a right-angled triangle with vertices labeled A (top left), B (bottom left), and C (bottom right). The vertical side is AB, and the horizontal base is BC. The hypotenuse is AC. A circular weight labeled F sits on the incline AC. A dashed horizontal line extends to the right from vertex A, parallel to the base BC.</image-desc>

<margin>15</margin> But there is still a deduction to be made from this calculation for the difficulty there would be in moving the body F along the plane AC if this plane were lying flat upon the line BC, all parts of which I suppose to be equally distant from the center of the earth <note>This refers to friction and the resistance of moving a mass even on a level surface</note>. It is true that, this impediment being <margin>20</margin> all the lesser as the plane is harder, more even, and more polished, it can again only be estimated approximately and is not very considerable. Nor is there any need to consider that, the line BC being a part of a circle that has the same center as the earth, the plane AC <margin>25</margin> must be ever so slightly arched and have the shape of a part of a spiral described between two circles which also have the center of the earth as their center; for that is in no way perceptible <note>The author acknowledges that on a planetary scale, "flat" surfaces are actually curved, but dismisses this as negligible for practical mechanics</note>.

## THE WEDGE.

The power of the wedge A B C D <gloss>original: "le coin, cuneus"</gloss> <gloss>a</gloss> is easily understood following what has just been said regarding the inclined plane: for the force with which one strikes it acts as if to make it

<margin>5</margin> move along the line B D, and the wood or other body that it splits does not open, or the load that it lifts does not rise, except along the line A C. In such a way <margin>10</margin> that the force with which one pushes or strikes this wedge must have the same proportion to the resistance of this wood, or of this load, as the line A C has to the line B D.

Where, however, to be exact once again, B D would have to be a part of a circle, and A D, C D, two portions of spirals that had the same center as the <margin>15</margin> earth, and the wedge would have to be of a material so perfectly hard and polished, and so light in weight, that no force would be required to move it. <note>The author is describing an idealized mathematical state where friction and gravity do not interfere with the mechanical advantage.</note>

And this difficulty is more noticeable in this device than in the preceding ones, insofar as it has more force.

Following this, one can easily resolve all the difficulties of the balance scale: and show that when it is supposed to be very exact—even imagining its center at O, by which it is supported, to be only an <margin>25</margin> indivisible point, just as I have here supposed for the lever—if its arms are tilted to one side or the other, the one that is lower must always be found to be the heaviest <insert>than the other</insert>. In such a way that the center of gravity is not fixed and <unclear>stable</unclear>.

My Reverend Father,

<margin>5, 10, 15</margin>
You inform me that one of your friends <note>Descartes refers here to Pierre de Fermat, though he does not name him initially.</note>, who has seen the *Dioptrics* <note>Descartes's treatise on optics, published in 1637.</note>, finds something therein to object to; and first, that he doubts whether the <term>inclination to movement</term> <note>The tendency or pressure toward motion, which Descartes uses to explain the instantaneous nature of light.</note> must follow the same laws as the movement itself, since there is as much difference between the one and the other as there is between <term>potentiality and act</term> <note>Aristotelian terms: 'potentiality' is the capacity to be, while 'act' is the actual realization of that capacity.</note>. But I am persuaded that he formed this doubt because he imagined that I doubted it myself; and because I placed these words on page 8, line 24: *For it is very easy to believe that the inclination to move must follow the same laws in this as the movement*, he thought that, by saying a thing is easy to believe, I meant to say it is only probable. In this, he has wandered far from my sentiment. For I repute as almost false everything that is only <term>verisimilar</term> <note>Likely or plausible, but not certain.</note>; and when I say that a thing is easy to believe, I do not mean to say that it is merely probable.

And he has committed a very manifest paralogism <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note> in that, assuming the line AF is not parallel to the surface CBE, he wanted one to be able, notwithstanding that, to imagine that this line designated the side to which this surface is not at all opposed; without considering that just as there are only the perpendiculars—not those drawn across this AF by his imagination, but those upon CBE—which mark in what sense this surface CBE is opposed to the movement of the ball, so also there are only the parallels to this same CBE which mark the sense in which it is not at all opposed to it.

I have also noticed much wit in your considerations regarding battle, notwithstanding that it is a matter where experience <margin>20</margin> and natural prudence, along with the presence of mind—which those who are afraid lose in such circumstances—serve more than precepts. And finally, I have found your Latin style so beautiful and so clear that I had never expected such from a man of your <margin>25</margin> profession <note>Likely referring to the correspondent's military career</note>. I advise you to continue to cultivate these fine qualities, and if I can contribute to them in any way, you will do me a favor by employing me. I am,

# CORRESPONDENCE. III, 182-183.

Consider a point A, which at the same time is pushed by two forces, one of which pushes it toward A O, and the other toward A D, such that the line of direction of the first movement is A O, and that of the second is A D. If there were only <margin>5</margin> the first force all alone, the heavy body <note>original: "le graue"; a term used in early modern physics to refer to any object with mass or weight</note> would always be found upon A O, and upon A D if there were only the second. But since these two forces hinder and resist one another mutually, let us suppose (& it must be remembered that we also suppose all these <margin>10</margin> movements to be uniform, for otherwise the composite movement would not occur along straight lines) that in one minute of an hour, | for example, the second force causes the heavy body to move away from its direction A O, along the length N B, which must be described parallel to A D: for <margin>15</margin> the heavy body which is carried toward A D by the second force, finding itself hindered by the first, will always carry it and advance from A toward D, along lines parallel to A D. Let us also suppose that in the same minute of an hour, the first force causes the heavy body to move away <margin>20</margin> from its direction A D, along the length C B, parallel—by the preceding reasoning—to the line A O. It is quite certain that in one minute of an hour the heavy body will be found at point B, which is the intersection of the two lines B N & B C. The composite movement will therefore occur along <margin>25</margin> the line A B, and we can say that the heavy body will traverse the line A B in one minute.

->Most Distinguished Sir,<-

I am glad that my response<sup>a</sup> to the objections of Master Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont, a professor at Louvain who criticized Descartes' theories on physics and the soul</note> has finally reached you. However, I am quite surprised that he judged from it that I was somewhat
<margin>5</margin>exasperated or irritated by his writing; for I was not so in any way, nor do I think a single word escaped me against him to which he had not first said something similar or harsher against me. Indeed, thinking that he delighted in that style, I somewhat forced my own nature—
<margin>10</margin>which is otherwise averse to all contention—lest perhaps, if I sustained his attack too softly and languidly, this "game" might please him less. Just as those who compete at <term>latrunculi</term> <note>An ancient Roman strategy game similar to chess</note> or chess are not usually any less friendly toward one another—and indeed, the very skill of playing is for some
<margin>15</margin>a cause and bond of friendship—so I have striven to earn his goodwill by my response.

Indeed, those things which I propose in the first chapters concerning the nature of light, the shape of the particles of salt and of fresh water, and similar matters, are not my "principles" <note>Descartes is defending himself against the charge that his initial assumptions are arbitrary</note>, as you yourself seem to object, but are rather conclusions which are demonstrated through everything that follows. <margin>15</margin> Furthermore, magnitudes, shapes, positions, and motions are to be taken as my formal object (to use the terms of the Philosophers <note>Referring to the Scholastic terminology used in universities at the time</note>), and the physical things which I explain are to be taken as the material object. But the principles or premises from which I deduce those conclusions are only those axioms upon <margin>20</margin> which the demonstrations of Geometers rely: such as, *the whole is greater than its part; if you take away equals from equals, the remainders will be equal;* etc. Yet these are not abstracted from all sensible matter, as they are with Geometers, but are applied to various experiments known and indubitable to the senses; as when from <margin>25</margin> the fact that the particles of salt are oblong and inflexible, I deduced the square shape of its grains, and many other things which are manifest to the senses. I wished to explain these things through that [cause] as an effect through its cause; but by no means to prove them, because they were already sufficiently known, but <margin>30</margin> on the contrary to demonstrate the cause through these *from the later* <term>à posteriori</term><note>Latin: à posteriori; reasoning from observed effects back to their underlying causes</note>, as...

The indication in the previous letter (p. 480, l. 1-2), that he found a copy of Vieta <note>François Vieta (1540–1603), the French mathematician whose work on algebra preceded Descartes.</note> "here by chance," might lead one to believe so; but it is too vague to allow for a certain conclusion, as *here* could simply mean in Holland. In any case, the next letter from Descartes to Paris with a fixed date will be that of March 31, 1638, a Wednesday (the mail day via Haarlem?), while we will subsequently have a letter from May 3, a Monday (via Amsterdam?). Furthermore, during the same period, Mersenne also seems to write by various routes (notably through the intermediary of Jan Maire, the bookseller in Leiden), and his letters seem to suffer very variable delays, either due to the season or because Descartes, being in the countryside, depended on more or less diligent intermediaries for his mail.

Subject to the reasons for doubt indicated above, we felt we could, in order to clarify matters, nevertheless maintain the hypothesis of Descartes' exclusive use of the Amsterdam mail, departing on Mondays, until March 31, 1638. Under these conditions, the determination of the date of the present letter and the following one, which was attached to it, rests on the following data: Descartes knows that the copies of his book <note>Referring to the *Discours de la Méthode*, published in 1637.</note> are finally on sale in Paris; this is the news from the final days of the year 1637 (see the note following the present letter). One could, strictly speaking, go back as far as December 20 or 27, 1637; but if the letter suffered no delay, it is at the earliest from January 4, and at the latest the 21st, for it appears from letter CXII below that Mersenne had not yet received it on January 8, but conversely had it in his hands by February 8.

In any case, Descartes announces having received, eight days prior, a writing by Fermat (*Method <note>original: "Methodus ad disquirendam maximam et minimam"</note> for investigating maximums and minimums*. *Works of Fermat*, vol. I, 1891, p. 133-136), while he does not yet have in his hands a packet sent at the same time which contained the *Introduction <note>original: "Isagoge ad locos planos et solidos"</note> to plane and solid loci* (*Works of Fermat*, vol. I, p. 91-110). It is, moreover, possible that the sending of the first writing had been announced by Mersenne in a previous letter. Finally, there is no doubt that it was only after having seen Descartes' *Geometry*, of which he previously only knew the *Dioptrics*, that Fermat asked Carcavi, the custodian of his writings, to deliver the two aforementioned short works to Mersenne to have them sent to Descartes. It is therefore indeed as early as December 1637, and not in January 1638,

### METHOD FOR INVESTIGATING THE MAXIMUM AND MINIMUM.
<note>original: "METHODUS AD DISQUIRENDAM MAXIMAM ET MINIMAM"</note>

The entire doctrine of finding the maximum and minimum rests upon two unknown positions and this single rule:
Let any term of the question be set as *A* (whether it be a plane, a solid, or a length, as is appropriate to satisfy the proposal) and, having found the maximum or minimum in terms involving the degree of *A*, as you please, let the same term as before be set again as *A + E*, and again let the maximum or minimum be found in terms with the degrees of *A* and *E* as coefficients, as you please. Let the two <term>homogeneous</term><note>Terms of the same dimension or degree.</note> expressions equal to the maximum or minimum be *adequated* <note>original: "Adæquentur"; a term used by Diophantus to describe a process of "near-equality" or comparison used in Fermat's method of tangents and maxima/minima.</note>, as Diophantus says, and, having removed the common terms (which being done, all the homogeneous terms on either side...

->XCIX. — JANUARY 1638.<-

Everything is divided by *E*: therefore *D* times *E* + *A-squared* will be equal to *D* times *A* twice <note>original Latin: "adæquabitur D in A bis." This refers to the method of "adequality," a proto-calculus technique for finding maxima and minima</note>. Let *D* times *E* be eliminated: therefore *A-squared* will equal *D* times *A* twice, and thus *A* will equal *D* twice. Therefore we have proved that *CE* is double that of *CD*, which is indeed the case.

Nor does this method ever fail; indeed, it can be extended to many most beautiful questions; for by its benefit we find the centers of gravity in figures comprised of curved and straight lines and in solids, and many other things, about which perhaps elsewhere, if leisure suffices.

Concerning the quadratures <note>The process of determining the area of a surface</note> of spaces contained under curved and straight lines, and even concerning the proportions of solids arising from them to cones of the same base and height, we have already dealt at length with Mr. de Roberval.

<keywords>Pierre de Fermat, René Descartes, Marin Mersenne, Vopiscus Fortunatus Plempius, blood circulation, Dioptrics, Étienne Pascal, Roberval, history of medicine, 17th-century mathematics</keywords>

--- Page 611 ---
<meta>This page continues the scientific correspondence regarding the mechanics of the heart, specifically addressing the debate between the Aristotelian view of heat-driven expansion and the Galenic view of vital faculty.</meta>

# I, 358-359. C. — JANUARY 1638.

Because you demand my objections against your opinion on the movement of the heart with such frequent and always eager entreaties, I am setting aside my other small tasks for a while and am proceeding to comply with you.

<margin>5</margin> First of all, as I see now, that opinion of yours is not new, but old, and indeed Aristotelian, set forth in the book *On Respiration*, chapter 20; his words are: *The pulsation of the heart is similar to boiling; for boiling occurs when fluid is refined by the work of heat; for the fluid raises itself because it rises into a larger mass. In the heart itself, the swelling of the fluid—which is always added from food—lifting the outermost membrane of the heart, creates the pulse: and this happens always without any intermission, for the fluid from which the nature of blood arises continually flows in. Pulsation, therefore, is the inflation of the warming fluid.* <note>original: "Pulsatio igitur est humoris concalescentis inflatio." This reflects the ancient theory that the heart acts like a boiler rather than a pump.</note> These are the words of Aristotle, which are explained by you more ingeniously and beautifully. Our Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note> taught on the contrary that the heart is moved by some faculty <note>term: faculty (facultas) — a natural power or "soul-force" believed by Galenists to govern specific bodily functions.</note>, and all we physicians teach that until now; the reasons why I still stand with them are as follows:

<margin>20</margin> 1. The heart, when removed from the body, still pulses for some time; indeed, when it is cut into minute parts, the individual small particles pulse for a good while, and in that state no blood flows in or out.

2. If someone inserts a reed or a bronze pipe into a cut artery so that the blood can pass through, and then binds the artery with a cord over the pipe, the artery will not pulse below the ligature. Therefore, the pulsation is not caused by the force of the inflowing blood, but by something else that flows through the membranes of the artery. That is an experiment of Galen's set forth in the book *Whether Blood is Contained in the Arteries*.

# CORRESPONDENCE. I, 359-360.

Chapter 1. Nor should it be said that this is impossible to perform because of the spurting out of arterial blood, for this can be avoided in the following manner. Place two ligatures <note>tightly tied cords or threads</note> on the artery, a palm's breadth or more apart from each other; then, with a sharp scalpel, cut into that same artery between the said two ligatures. No blood will flow out except for that which is contained between the bonds. Next, insert a pipe into the hole made there, and tie the artery again over the inserted pipe; then loosen the two original bonds. The blood will flow freely through the channel all the way to the furthest arteries, and yet those parts which are below the ligature will not pulse; loosen the ligature, and they will pulse again. To be sure, some blood will flow out through the wound, but what of it? Indeed, it will be possible to see what is intended.

3. If the dilation of the heart were caused by the rarefaction <note>the process of becoming less dense or expanding into vapor</note> of the blood, the diastole <note>the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood</note> of the heart would be much longer and more lasting than it currently is in animals. For a notable portion of blood flows into the heart, and for all of it to be converted into vapors, time is required; it cannot be rarefied as quickly or as suddenly as the diastole occurs. Even if we see oil and pitch immediately expand greatly when falling into a fire, that does not remove the difficulty: for there is not as much heat in the heart as there is in a fire; therefore, it is not capable of effecting what fire effects. On the contrary, in fish there is very little heat, and rather a coldness; yet their hearts pulse just as quickly as ours.

4. If the arteries are distended by the blood which the heart pours into them, only the part near the heart, which receives that blood most closely, would pulse; the remaining parts would not pulse at the same time. For that which is shaken out of the heart is not spread into all the arteries suddenly, because this

<summary>This page describes an experiment using ligatures and a pipe to study arterial pulse and argues against the theory that heart dilation is caused by the rapid heating and vaporization of blood.</summary>
<keywords>blood circulation, artery, heart, diastole, rarefaction, ligatures, pulse, animal heat, physiology</keywords>

--- Page 613 ---
<meta>This page continues a scientific debate regarding the circulatory system, specifically addressing objections raised against William Harvey's theories. It transitions from a list of anatomical doubts into a letter from René Descartes to Marin Mersenne.</meta>

...it resists the movement of such a thick body. And yet, all the arteries of the entire body pulse at the same time. This much regarding the cause of the heart's motion.

Against the **circulation of the blood**, which you support along with Harvey <note>William Harvey (1578–1657), the English physician who first described the systemic circulation of blood.</note>, I hold these points:

1. Arterial and venous blood would thus be clearly similar, indeed the same, which contradicts eyewitness observation <note>original: "autopsiæ"</note>. The former is more yellow and bright, while the latter is blacker and more somber.

2. Feverish matter residing elsewhere in the small veins far from the heart—which therefore only causes an intermittent fever—ought to produce several attacks per day; specifically, as many times as that blood, and the feverish fluid along with it, returns to the heart. However, you propose that this return happens a hundred, or even two hundred times a day.

3. In a living animal, if most of the veins <note>original: "plerisque"</note> leading to the leg are tied off while the arteries are left free, that leg ought to swell up in a wonderful manner in a short space of time, because the blood would continually flow in through the arteries <insert>but could not return</insert> through the veins. And yet, so far is this from happening that instead, if you leave the veins tied for a long time, the part is thinned out by a lack of nourishment.

I shall await your responses to these little doubts of mine as eagerly as you yourself demanded them from me.

## CII.

# Descartes to [Huygens].

### [January 25, 1638.]

->Text from Clerselier, volume II, letter 85, pp. 372-375.<-

*Without name or date in Clerselier <note>Claude Clerselier (1614–1684) was the first editor of Descartes' letters</note>. However, this letter (at least the second part) is clearly a response to letter XCV, dated November 23, 1637; it was therefore addressed to Huygens. The first part responds to another letter, likely written since then, which is lost (lines 4-5). The same fact is mentioned in this letter (p. 506, l. 11) and in the preceding one (p. 500-501); furthermore, Clerselier prints them one after the other, letters 84 and 85, as if he had found the drafts together in the same bundle. It appears from the following letter from Huygens, dated February 2, that he must have received this one. It would therefore be, like the preceding one, from January 25 or February 1 (C. A.) <note>C.A. refers to Charles Adam, the editor of the standard edition of Descartes' works</note>.*

*One may nevertheless be surprised: 1st, that Descartes delayed his response to Huygens' thanks for so long; 2nd, that the latter, in his letter of February 2, does not refer to the present one more explicitly. One might then wonder if Clerselier had combined two separate notes: the first, represented by the second paragraph of this letter, would be from the end of November 1637; the second (the first paragraph) would be from the beginning of February 1638, but Huygens would not yet have had it in his hands by the 2nd (P. T.) <note>P.T. refers to Paul Tannery, co-editor of the Adam-Tannery edition</note>.*

# II, 372-373. CII. — 25 January 1638.

->Sir,<-

I was very glad to see the Turner <note>The "Turner" refers to a craftsman, likely Jacques Tourneur, whom Descartes employed to realize his designs for lens-grinding machinery.</note>, for I judged from his conversation that he will be quite capable of making the Telescopes <note>original: "Lunettes"; in this context, it refers to long-range spyglasses or early telescopes.</note> succeed; and I am even more pleased to learn, from your last letter, that he is working on them with affection <margin>Lost letter. See p. 396, l. 4 and p. 433, l. 3.</margin>. He told me that he would first make a wooden model of the entire machine; I believe that is where he ought to begin, and as soon as he has done so, I shall very willingly go to Amsterdam expressly to see it. At that time, it will be easy for him to understand both the things that must be strictly observed and those to which it is not necessary to restrict himself. For instance, regarding the distance he places between the pillars A and B, it is entirely indifferent, as is the space that must be between the two boards. Furthermore, it is not necessary for the roller to touch these boards, as I previously described <margin>*Dioptrics*, Discourse X, p. 145.</margin>; for being well-joined to the two cubic pieces Y and Z, which must be at its two ends, it is sufficient that these two pieces touch them exactly on both sides. To this end, the boards do not need to be entirely polished, nor entirely made of copper; rather, I would only wish for their ends to be lined with copper on the inside, so that these two pieces Y and Z might slide upon them. And I believe that these pieces should, for this purpose, be made of iron, or lined with iron plates above and below; for experience teaches that copper and iron join <note>Descartes is referring to the "seizing" or friction of metals; he correctly notes that dissimilar metals often slide against each other with less friction than identical metals.</note> much better together than iron with iron, or copper with copper. I—

Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a central figure in the 17th-century scientific revolution who facilitated communication between scholars</note> has informed me that there was a desire to invite the Lord Cardinal <note>Likely Cardinal Richelieu</note> to have work begun on telescopes according to my *Dioptrics* <note>Descartes's treatise on optics, published in 1637</note>; but I fear they may not succeed easily without me, and if your turner <note>A craftsman who shapes materials on a lathe; here, the artisan building the machine</note> succeeds first, I offer to do my best to help him obtain a grant <note>original: "octroy"; a patent or exclusive privilege</note> so that he alone may sell them in France.

The three sheets that I had sent to you are not worth the least of the kind words contained in the letter you were pleased to write to me. I assure you that I felt more shame for having sent you so little than I expected in thanks; for indeed, the fear I had of involving myself in a treatise much longer than you had requested was the reason I omitted the finest parts of my subject. II. 374-375.          CII. — 25 January 1638.

...to add them there, I will satisfy here the final point of your letter, by telling you what I am occupying myself with. I have never had as much care for preserving myself as I do now; and whereas I formerly thought that death could only take thirty or forty years from me at most, it could no longer surprise me without taking away the hope of more than a century. For it seems to me very evident that if we only guarded ourselves against certain faults that we are accustomed to commit in the regimen of our lives <note>Descartes refers to "dietetics" or the "regimen of health," a major focus of his later years</note>, we could, without other inventions <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: "sans autres inventions." The variant note "a" indicates that the editor Clerselier read this as "without other inventions."</note> reach an old age much longer and happier than we currently do. But because I have need of much time and many experiments to examine everything that pertains to this subject, I am working now to compose an abridgment of Medicine, which I draw partly from books and partly from my own reasonings, from which I hope to be able to make use of as a provisional measure to obtain some delay from nature, and thus better pursue my design hereafter. I do not respond at all to what your courtesy wished to ask me regarding the sharing of the three sheets that you have; for besides the fact that I would be in a poor position to wish to dispose of a thing that is entirely yours—since I previously sent it to you without reserving any right to it—the inclination you show toward not sharing it, and the affection with which you oblige me, assure me | enough that you will do nothing in this matter that turns to my prejudice; and whatever you do, there is nothing that prevents me from being all my life,

# CIII.

## HUYGENS TO DESCARTES.

->The Hague, February 2, 1638.<-

->*MANUSCRIPT COPY, Amsterdam, Academy of Sciences.*<-
->*French Letters of Constantijn Huygens, volume I, page 817.*<-

Sir,

It happened that through the favor of Mr. Alphonse Polotti <note>An Italian equerry at the Dutch court and friend to both men.</note> I saw a flawed copy of what passed between you and the philosopher of Louvain<gloss>a</gloss>, that ill-advised reader of your book. I do not know if I shall forgive you for the fact <margin>5</margin> that I had to beg for this bread from a hand other than your own: but for the moment I am not resolved to interrupt my discourse, which tends toward informing you that, not finding courtesy to be free everywhere, I was forced to buy you with your own money <margin>10</margin> and to promise your *Mechanics* <note>Descartes' treatise on the explanation of machines and the laws of equilibrium.</note> in return to the aforementioned Mr. Polotti, who demands them of me, threatening a reproach of perfidy if I fail. The matter, therefore, as you see, remains unsettled; and it is still permissible for me to obey you, at the cost of being considered a rogue. <margin>15</margin> Let that not stand in the way. But in testifying to me, if you please, what your absolute and unreserved inclination is, I beg you to add whether you find out of place the proposal I make: to see these *Mechanics* entirely finished before opening to them <margin>20</margin>

---

<note>a. Libert Froidmont (or Fromondus), a professor at Louvain who had criticized Descartes' "Dioptrics" and "Meteors." See Letters LXXXVI and LXXXVIII, p. 402 and 412.</note>

# CORRESPONDENCE. II, I.

But Descartes, enumerating the objections sent to him from France or by foreigners in a letter to Mersenne dated June 29, 1638 (*Clerselier edition*, II, 381-382), would say, after citing Fromondus, Plempius, and a Jesuit from Louvain: "Finally, someone else from The Hague sent me some regarding various matters." On the other hand, we see (p. 515, l. 26) that the author of these objections was aware of Descartes' response to Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont, a theologian at Louvain who criticized Descartes' "Dioptrics" and "Meteors."</note>; now Huygens, in *Letter CIII above, from February 2, 1638 (p. 508, l. 2-5)*, informs us that Mr. de Pollot (*Alphonse*) had a copy of this response and had shared it with him specifically in The Hague. Finally, at the end of the letter, there is mention of "our French orthography," as if the author were French himself, or at least from a French-speaking country: now, the Pollot family had come to settle in Geneva. If the latter, as well as his brother, is excluded by the initial S <note>Referring to the signature or initial on the original manuscript</note>, it nonetheless seems that one should search within his circle. It is true that nothing in the letters from Huygens or Pollot to Descartes confirms that either was the intermediary to whom the author of the objections addressed himself.

As for the date, one can by conjecture fix it around February 1638 at the earliest, or perhaps in the month of March, as Descartes declares in his response (*Clerselier*, II, 8) that he is waiting for "a collection of everything that can be doubted on this subject" (the existence of God), doubtless the objections of Petit <note>Pierre Petit, a mathematician and physicist</note>, of which Mersenne had spoken to him in a letter of February 12 (*Clerselier*, III, 190) and which he would receive in March (*Clerselier*, III, 403). But if, on the contrary, this collection is the Writing of Father Gibieuf <note>Guillaume Gibieuf, a priest of the Oratory and friend of Descartes</note>, for which Descartes would acknowledge receipt only on May 24 (*Clerselier*, III, 391), the present letter might only be from April or May 1638.

->Sir,<-

Not daring to address myself directly to Mr. Descartes to propose my difficulties to him, I borrow your influence to pray you to present them to him, and to try to ensure that he takes them in good part, as coming from a person who has more desire to learn than to contradict.

# CORRESPONDENCE. II, 2-3.

those who have a diseased imagination <note>original: "fantaisie malade"; in 17th-century psychology, the 'fantasy' or imagination was the faculty that processed sensory images</note> do not think well; and if they had neither imagination nor memory, they would not think at all.

5. It does not follow from the fact that we doubt the <margin>5</margin> things that are around us, that there must be some being more perfect than our own. <note>A direct critique of Descartes' ontological argument where he moves from the imperfection of doubt to the perfection of God.</note> Most Philosophers have doubted many things, such as the Pyrrhonists <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis; ancient skeptics who argued that certain knowledge is impossible</note>, and they did not conclude from this that there was a Divinity; there are other proofs to <margin>10</margin> bring this thought to mind, and to prove it.

6. Experience shows that beasts make their affections and passions understood through their own kind of language, <margin>15</margin> and that through several signs they show their anger, their fear, their love, their pain, and their regret for having done wrong; witness what is read of certain horses who, having been employed to mate with <note>original: "couvrir"; literally 'to cover'</note> their mothers without knowing them, threw themselves into an abyss after having recognized them. <note>A reference to Aristotle's History of Animals regarding animal remorse.</note> One should not, in truth, | dwell upon these stories; but it is evident that animals <margin>20</margin> perform their operations by a principle more excellent than by the necessity arising from the disposition of their organs; namely, by an instinct, which will never be found in a machine, or in a clock, which have neither passion nor affection, as <margin>25</margin> animals do. <note>The author argues against the Cartesian view of "animal-machines," suggesting animals possess a sensitive soul or instinct beyond mere mechanics.</note>

7. The Author says that the soul must necessarily be created, but it would have been good to give the reason for it.

->II, 3. — CIV. — FEBRUARY 1638.<-

8. If light were extended like a staff <note>Descartes famously used the analogy of a blind man's stick to explain how light transmits force instantaneously</note>, it would not be a movement, but a pressing line; and if it were a movement traveling from the Sun to us, it would not happen in an instant, seeing as <margin>5</margin> all movement occurs over time; nor would it travel in a straight line if it must pass, like the must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> in a vat, through a space full of bodies larger than this <term>subtle matter</term> <note>a hypothetical fluid substance Descartes believed filled all space</note> which carries it, and which can break the straight line by their <margin>10</margin> agitation ᵃ.

9. Since the Author professes to write methodically, clearly, and distinctly, it seemed appropriate that he should show what this subtle matter is that he presupposes ᵇ: for one rightly asks, <margin>15</margin> firstly if it exists, 2nd if it is elementary or ethereal, and if, being elementary, it is specific or common to all the elements.

10. If water is only liquid because this subtle matter makes it so ᶜ, it would follow that ice <margin>20</margin> would melt no sooner before a fire than elsewhere; or it must be admitted that it is the fire, and not the subtle matter, which makes it liquid.

11. When I considered your learning, your genius, and your character, as well as the kindness with which you treat me, I knew that your remarks would be highly erudite, ingenious, and untainted by any prejudice of malice; and my judgment did not <margin>5</margin> deceive me. But I must thank you, both because you sent them and because you advised me on how I might support my opinion with the authority of Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), whose natural philosophy remained the standard authority in universities during this period.</note>. Indeed, since that man was so fortunate that whatever he once wrote—whether with care or without thinking—is today <margin>10</margin> regarded by most as oracles, I could wish for nothing more than to be able to follow in his footsteps in all things, provided I do not depart from the truth. But not even in this matter which we are discussing would I dare to boast that I have done so; for although, like him, I say that the beating of the heart arises from the swelling <note>original: "inflatione"</note> of the fluid <margin>15</margin> warming up within it, nevertheless by that "fluid" I understand nothing different from the blood. Nor do I speak, as he does, *of the swelling of the fluid, which always comes from food, lifting the outermost membrane of the heart.* For if I were to bring forward such things, I could be refuted <margin>20</margin> by many most evident reasons. And I would rightly be believed never to have attended to the structure of the heart of any animal if, by remaining silent about the ventricles <note><term>ventriculis</term>: the lower chambers of the heart that pump blood out.</note>, vessels, and valves, I were to affirm that only its outermost membrane was being lifted. Moreover, he who concludes the truth by chance from false premises (as the Logicians <margin>25</margin> say) seems to me to reason no better than if he were to deduce something false from them; nor, if two people reach the same place—one by wandering and the other by the right path—should it be thought that one followed in the footsteps of the other.

Regarding the first objection you raise—namely, that <margin>30</margin> individual particles of a heart removed from the body and dissected continue to beat for some time, even though no blood flows in or out—I res-

I respond that I once performed this experiment quite accurately, especially in fish, whose heart, when cut out, beats much longer than the heart of land animals; but I have always either judged, or, as often happens, seen with my very eyes <margin>5</margin> that some remnants of blood had slipped down from other upper parts into the section where the pulsation was occurring. I easily persuaded myself that a very small amount of blood <note>original: "pauxillulum sanguinis"</note> slipping from one part of the heart into another slightly warmer part is sufficient to produce this pulsation. For it must be noted <margin>10</margin> that the smaller the quantity of any liquid <term>humor|In 17th-century physiology, "humor" refers to any fluid in the body, such as blood or bile</term>, the more easily it can be rarefied <note>expanded or turned into vapor by heat</note>. And just as our hands become more ready to repeat a movement the more frequently they perform it, so also the heart—which from the first moment of its formation <margin>15</margin> has swollen and subsided in an incessant reciprocation—can be impelled to continue this very action by the slightest force. Finally, just as we see certain liquids grow hot and inflate simply by being mixed with others, so perhaps even in the recesses of the heart some liquid resides like a leaven <note>or ferment</note>, <margin>20</margin> by the mixing of which the incoming liquid swells up. Furthermore, this same objection seems to me to have much more force against the common opinion of others, who think that the motion of the heart proceeds from some faculty of the soul. For in what way, I ask, will that motion <margin>25</margin> depend on the human soul? That motion, I say, which is found even in the divided parts of the heart, since it is a matter of faith <note>a reference to theological doctrine</note> that the rational soul is indivisible, and has no other sensitive or vegetative soul joined to it.

You object secondly to that which Galen <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> put forward at <margin>30</margin> the end of the book *Whether Blood is Contained in the Arteries*, of which...

<summary>The author argues that the heart's beat is a mechanical process caused by the rapid expansion (rarefaction) of tiny amounts of blood, rather than being controlled by the soul. # CORRESPONDENCE. I, 363-364.

Indeed, I have never performed this experiment, nor is it convenient to do so now, but neither do I think it would be worth the effort. For, given that cause of the pulsation of the arteries which I propose, the laws of my Mechanics—that is, my Physics—teach that if a reed <note>original: "calamo"; a hollow tube or straw used in early physiological experiments</note> is inserted into the artery and the artery is tied over the reed itself, it ought not to pulse beyond the binding; however, once the ligature is loosened, it must pulse, exactly as Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential 2nd-century Roman physician</note> experienced. This holds provided that the reed is a little narrower than the artery, as he undoubtedly supposed; and I conclude that you yourself suppose the same from the fact that you say some blood will flow out through the wound once the ligature is loosened. For if the reed filled the entire capacity of the artery, since it would accurately plug the wound, not even the smallest amount of blood would slip out through it. However, with the reed floating within the capacity of the artery along with the blood, it is no wonder that it does not obstruct its motion.

For it must be noted that this motion does not occur because the blood exiting the heart is suddenly scattered through all the arteries, as you suppose in your fourth objection, but because, by occupying the part of the great artery <note>the aorta</note> closest to the heart, it expels and jolts all the other blood contained in that artery and its branches. This happens without delay—that is, as the Philosophers say, *in an instant*.

Let us assume, for the sake of example, that BCF is an artery full of blood (as they always are), and into which some new blood now enters from the heart A. In this way, we will easily understand that this new blood cannot fill the space B, which is at the orifice of this artery, without another part of the blood, which previously filled this same space B, receding toward C, and from there [moving] other parts of the blood...

# I, 364-365. CVII. — 15 FEBRUARY 1638.

...pushes toward D, and so on successively as far as E; so that at the very same instant in which the blood ascends from A to B, the artery must pulse at E. Nor will it be an obstacle if we imagine that there is contained within it a <margin>5</margin> reed <note>original: "calamus"; a hollow tube or straw used in early anatomical experiments</note> at D, or any other body, whether hollow or solid, provided that it floats freely in the blood, because such a body will be pushed toward E just as easily as the blood itself. <margin>10</margin> For the internal surface of the arteries is extremely smooth; and since they consist of membranes <term>tunics: the layers or walls of a blood vessel</term> that are quite tough, they do not contract themselves like the intestines or the veins to the measure of the body contained within them, but even when empty, and in <margin>15</margin> a dead animal, they are accustomed to being wide and gaping.

If, however, there is another reed placed into this artery at E, and over which it has been tied—as Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the influential Roman physician whose theories dominated medicine for centuries</note> maintains—although the blood can pass through this reed toward F, it will not, however, strike the sides of the artery there, at least not notably; because <margin>20</margin> in passing from a narrow place into a wider one, it will lose a great part of its force, and will exert the remainder along the length of the artery rather than according to its width. Consequently, it could indeed fill the artery by a continuous flow and make it more swollen, <margin>25</margin> but it could not agitate it with distinct throbs <note>original: "subsultibus"; the rhythmic jumping or leaping of the pulse</note>. Nor is there any other reason why the veins, joined to the arteries through various anastomoses <term>anastomoses: connections or openings between two vessels</term>, do not also pulse, other than because their extremities, through which the blood enters, are narrower than the channels into which it flows.

Nor should we be moved by the authority of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity, whose theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years.</note> affirming in various places <margin>a. *On whether blood is contained in the arteries*, chapter 9. *On the use of pulses*, chapter 5.</margin> that *the arteries are not distended like wineskins because they are filled, but are filled like bellows (and likewise like the throat, lungs, and the entire chest) because they are extended, and that once extended, they attract from any neighboring place through their extremities and openings whatever is suitable to fill their cavities.* For this is refuted by a most certain experiment, which I have not been reluctant to see several times before, and even today while writing. Namely, having opened the chest of a living rabbit and spread the ribs so that the heart and the trunk of the aorta appeared, I bound the aorta with a thread at a sufficient distance from the heart, and separated it from all those parts to which it adhered, so there could be no suspicion that any blood or spirit <note>original: "spiritûs". In early modern medicine, "spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids that animated the body.</note> would flow into it from anywhere else but the heart: then I cut into the same vessel with a scalpel between the heart and the ligature, and I saw most clearly...
