# I, 366-367 CVII. — FEBRUARY 15, 1638.

At the time when the artery was being extended <note>The expansion phase, or diastole</note>, I observed the blood leaping out from the incision; however, when it was being contracted <note>The systolic phase</note>, it did not flow out. On the contrary, if the opinion of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), whose medical theories dominated for over a millennium</note> were true, that artery ought to have drawn in air through the incision at every moment of its expansion <margin>5</margin>, and should never have emitted blood except during the time of its contraction; thus, it seems to me that no one can remain in doubt.

Continuing, moreover, in this dissection of a living animal, I cut off the middle part of the heart—specifically that which is called its point <note>The apex of the heart</note>—but from the moment it was separated from the base, I noticed that it did not pulse even once. I mention this here in connection with the preceding objection so that you may observe that the parts of the heart near its base do pulse for some time, because <margin>15</margin> some new blood flows into them from the vessels and the auricles <note>The atria</note> attached to them, but the parts at the tip do not. Furthermore, after the point of the heart was cut off, its base, remaining still attached to the vessels, pulsed for quite a long time; and in it, I very conveniently observed <margin>20</margin> those two cavities, which are called the ventricles of the heart, becoming larger during expansion <term>diastole: the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood</term>, and narrower during contraction <term>systole: the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle contracts and pumps blood from the chambers into the arteries</term>. By this experiment, the opinion of Harvey <note>William Harvey (1578–1657), who first correctly described the systemic circulation of blood</note> regarding the motion of the heart is refuted <margin>25</margin>: for he says the exact opposite, namely that the ventricles are dilated during contraction to receive blood, and are constricted during expansion to thrust it out into the arteries. I have added these things here in passing so that you may see that no opinion different from mine can be imagined which certain experiments do not contradict.

# CORRESPONDENCE. I, 367-368.

You object thirdly: if the dilation of the heart were caused by the expansion <note>original: "rarefacto," referring to the process of a substance increasing in volume, often through heat</note> of the blood, its diastole <note>the phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and the chambers fill with blood</note> would be much longer and more lasting than it currently is. You perhaps persuade yourself of this because you imagine that expansion to be <margin>5</margin> similar to what occurs in Aeolipiles <note>an early steam engine or "wind ball" that demonstrates gas expansion</note>, when the water within them is turned into vapor. But various types of expansion must be distinguished; for it happens one way when a liquid turns entirely into smoke or air and changes its form, as in Aeolipiles; and another way when the liquid retains its form and only <margin>10</margin> increases in volume. Now, it is clear that the first method does not suit the blood in the heart for any reason: first, because that does not happen to the whole liquid at once, but only to those parts which, rising from its surface, extend themselves into the neighboring air, as I have explained at length in the *Meteorology* <note>referring to Descartes' published work *Météores*, chapters 2 and 4</note>, chapters 2 and 4. Indeed, <margin>15</margin> there is no such air in the heart, nor any surface bordering the air, but its cavities in living animals, however large they may be, are entirely filled with blood. Furthermore, if this were the case, not blood, but only steamy air would be contained in the arteries. Now, however, no one <margin>20</margin> doubts that they are full of blood; and here, in passing, one may marvel at how barren of truth the ancients were, among whom there was such doubt on this matter that Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD)</note> wrote an entire book to prove that blood is contained in the arteries.

# CVII. — 15 February 1638.

...contained by nature, he has deigned to write. The other mode of **rarefaction** <note>The process by which a substance becomes less dense and increases in volume</note>, by which a liquid increases in mass, must again be distinguished: for it happens either gradually, or in an instant. <margin>5</margin> Gradually, of course, when the parts of the liquid step by step acquire some new motion, or shape, or position, by reason of which they leave more or larger intervals around themselves than before. And in my *Meteorology* <note>original: "Meteoris"; referring to Descartes' published work on atmospheric phenomena</note>, I explained how such rarefaction can arise not only from heat, but also from intense cold and other causes. <margin>10</margin> Finally, rarefaction occurs in an instant, according to the foundations of my **Philosophy**, whenever the particles of a liquid—either all of them or certainly the majority, dispersed here and there through its mass—simultaneously acquire some change, by reason of which they require a notably larger space. <margin>15</margin> The matter itself indicates that this last mode is the one by which the **blood** is rarefied in the **heart**; for its **diastole** <note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes and allows the chambers to fill with blood</note> occurs in an instant. And if we attend to all those things which I wrote in the 5th part of the *Discourse on Method* <note>original: "libelli de Methodo"</note>, we will no more be permitted to doubt this matter <margin>20</margin> than we doubt whether oil and other liquids are so rarefied when we see them rise in a pot with sudden leaps. For the entire structure of the heart, its **heat**, and the very nature of the blood itself conspire toward this, so that we perceive nothing with our senses that seems more certain to me. <margin>25</margin> For as far as heat is concerned, even if not much is felt in fish, it is nevertheless much greater in their hearts than in any other members.

But you deny that it is the nature of blood to be suddenly rarefied, because, of course, it is not similar to oil or pitch, but...

...more watery and earthy in nature. As if this property belonged only to fatty substances! Does not water itself, if only fish or something else is cooked in it, usually swell up in this way? # CVII. — 15 FEBRUARY 1638.

Leaven <note>original: "fermentum"; here used to describe the chemical-mechanical process of fermentation</note> is usually made from a portion of dough already fermented, wine leaven from the remains of grapes, and beer leaven from a certain dregs of the same. Nor is a very intense degree of heat required here, but rather a varying one according to
<margin>5</margin> the varying nature of the blood of individual animals. I remember that I have already written this in my response to the third objection of Mr. Fromondus <note>Libert Froidmont, a theologian and scientist at Louvain who challenged Descartes' theories</note>. Just as neither beer, nor wine, nor bread—from which a large part of our blood arises—require intense heat to be fermented,
<margin>10</margin> but they grow warm even of their own accord.

To your fourth objection, I think I have already responded sufficiently above, since I have shown in what manner all the arteries pulse at the same time. Therefore, it remains for me to respond to those things which you have brought forward against the circulation of the blood.
<margin>15</margin> The first is: the difference between arterial and venous blood, which I myself indicated on page 52 of the *Discourse on Method* <note>Descartes' famous 1637 work</note> could be raised as an objection against Harvey <note>William Harvey, the English physician who first correctly described the systemic circulation of blood</note>, because by his opinion no change in the blood is understood to occur in the heart. But for me, who describes its sudden inflation and
<margin>20</margin> a kind of boiling <note>original: "ebullitionem"; Descartes believed the heart acted like a heat engine or boiler rather than a pump</note>, I did not fear that the same would be objected. For, I ask you, what thing can be the cause of a greater and more sudden change in any body than that boiling and simultaneous fermentation? But you will say that the blood flowing from the arteries through their extremities into the veins
<margin>25</margin> suffers no change there, and therefore that the blood in the veins ought not to be different from that which is in the arteries. To respond accurately to this objection, I would first wish for you to notice that not a single drop of blood is contained in the arteries which [did not pass] through the heart shortly before...

# CORRESPONDENCE. I, 371-372.

...has not passed through, but that there are always some [fluids] in the veins which did not flow from the arteries, because, of course, some amount of humor <note>The term "humor" refers to bodily fluids in early modern medicine, believed to determine health and temperament.</note> is always gliding into them from the intestines; and likewise, all the veins, together with the liver, are to be regarded as a single vessel.
<margin>5</margin>

With these points established, it is easily understood that the blood must retain in all the arteries those same qualities which it acquires in the heart. So much so, that if we imagined it became white while passing through the heart—just as it becomes red in the liver—plainly nothing but white blood would be contained in the arteries, and nothing but red in the veins. For the white blood, which would continually flow into them from the arteries, | once mixed with the other already red blood, would immediately take on its color, not otherwise than water poured into wine. Furthermore, it should be noted that there are many things which, after they have been heated, acquire very different qualities solely from the fact that they are cooled either slowly or quickly. Thus glass, unless it cools slowly, becomes so fragile that it cannot even withstand the air; and the same material can turn now into iron, now into steel <note>original: "chalybem"</note>, according to the different method of smelting. Indeed, the blood which flows out of an artery can be compared with glass that has been drawn glowing from the furnace; while that which comes from a vein can be compared with glass that has been annealed <note>original: "recoctum," referring to the process of slow cooling to strengthen material</note> by a slow fire. And the most intense fire of the furnaces does not seem to have as much power over steel or glass as the moderate heat of the heart has over the blood, which is surely a fluid so ready for change that the air alone corrupts it as soon as it has been drawn from the vein.

Regarding what you add concerning the matter of intermittent fevers, I have nothing else to say than that I do not have even the slightest suspicion that it resides in the veins,

# I, 372-373. CVII. — 15 February 1638.

And I marvel that this opinion, supported by no probable reason, has had many followers; nevertheless, Fernel <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a highly influential French physician who systematized medicine</note> disputes against them at length in his *Pathology*, book 4, chapter 9, so that I may even repel authority with authority. But furthermore, he <margin>5</margin> conquers them with reasons, and among others he has one which seems sufficient to me. Namely, if the matter of intermittent fevers <note>original: "febrium intermittentium"</note> proceeded from the veins, either there would never be a double tertian fever <note>A fever where paroxysms occur daily, caused by two overlapping cycles</note>, or every very violent tertian fever would be double; and the same applies to the quartan fever. <margin>10</margin> However, I add no reasons of my own here, nor do I say what I think about fevers, nor will I allow myself to be dragged from one set of difficulties into others.

There remains the experiment concerning the tying of most of the veins leading to the leg, while leaving the arteries free; once this is done, <margin>15</margin> you say that the leg does not swell, but rather gradually wastes away from a lack of nourishment. Here, certainly, a distinction must be made; for as soon as the veins are so tied, they will undoubtedly swell somewhat, and if you open any of them below the ligature, all or nearly all of the body's <margin>20</margin> blood will be able to flow out through it, as surgeons experience daily. And this, unless I am mistaken, does not merely persuade one of the circulation of the blood <note>original: "sanguinis circulationem"</note> with probability, but evidently demonstrates it. If, however, the veins are left tied in this way for a long time, I am easily <margin>25</margin> persuaded that what you write will be true, although I have never tested it; this is because the blood stagnating in the tied veins will in a short time become very thick and poorly suited for nourishing the body. Moreover, new blood will not continually flow into that part through the arteries, because in all the other small branches and passages, both of the arteries and the veins—

# CORRESPONDENCE.

In this chapter, we read on page 265: <note>original: "Hæ rationes pondus mihi habere videbantur..."</note> "These reasons seemed to me to have weight: wherefore I decided to send them to Mr. Descartes so that I might understand what he would respond against them: which I had already been asked to do many times through letters by Descartes himself, a most friendly man and very familiar to me. On that account, however, one or two babblers <note>Latin: *blatero*; a derogatory term for a windbag or idle talker</note> have recently attacked me in public writings, claiming that I recounted the responses not only as a summary (as I say), but with a loss of truth and without sufficient good faith: and that I partly mutilated and perverted them, and partly passed over them with a certain artifice. Adding another lie: *that these letters, transcribed by many, were circulating in the hands of many two years before my book was published*, when they were written in the same year the book was published, indeed in the same month this chapter was being printed. Furthermore, to confess the truth, they are worthy of being read even by those who do not approve of the doctrine itself, because of the sharp contemplation and wonderful exercise of genius which they betray: I, however, thought I had satisfied the matter abundantly by bringing forward only the substance of the responses, so as not to delay the beginners. Now, because I see this is taken so poorly by malicious men, I must yield to the occasion. Therefore, may it be done with your peace, *René*, Most Noble Man, I produce your letters in their entirety, transcribed word for word."

(p. 172, col. 1-2, of the 3rd edition, 1654, conforming here to the second). There follow the two letters of February 15 and March 23, 1638. The "babbler" of whom Plempius speaks is none other than Regius <note>Henricus Regius, a Dutch physician and early disciple of Descartes who later fell out with him</note>, and it concerns the theses that the latter had his students defend at Utrecht (see Letter 10 from Regius to Descartes, January 1640).

# CVIII. — 22 FEBRUARY 1638.

*...that there was nothing to change in Morin's text, as he had personally delivered it to Clerselier for printing (see our introduction and Clerselier, Volume I, preface). — Baillet (Volume I, page 356) provides this indication: "Father Mersenne <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a monk and central figure in the 17th-century scientific revolution who acted as a clearinghouse for ideas.</note> seemed to have joined some of his own difficulties with the objections of Mr. Morin." (See Letter CXXXIV below, dated 1 August 1638). Descartes' response was not sent until 13 July (Letter CXXVII below).*

->Sir,<-

From the moment I had the honor of seeing you and knowing you in Paris, I judged that you possessed a mind capable of leaving something rare and excellent to posterity; and I have greatly rejoiced to see my judgment succeed through the beautiful book you have brought to light on subjects of Mathematics and Physics, which are also the two primary objects of my natural speculations. But just as, regarding Mathematics, you will find only people to admire the sublimity of your mind, so too, regarding Physics, I believe you will not be surprised if there are persons who contradict you. For, since you have reserved for yourself the knowledge of the principles and universal notions of your new Physics (the publication of which is passionately desired by all the learned) and since you base your reasoning only on comparisons or suppositions, the truth of which is at the very least in doubt, it would be to sin against the first precept of your method—which is very good, and which is familiar to me—to acquiesce <note>Morin is critiquing Descartes' "Discourse on Method," specifically the rule to never accept anything as true without clear evidence.</note>

And although, according to page 76 of your *Method* <note>Referring to Descartes' *Discours de la méthode*, published in 1637.</note>, experience renders most of the effects you treat very certain, nevertheless you know very well that the appearance of celestial movements <margin>5</margin> is derived just as certainly from the supposition of the stability of the earth as from the supposition of its mobility; and therefore, that the experience of this appearance is not sufficient to prove which of the two aforementioned causes is the true one. the relationship of their Tables with the Heavens. And I believe I have been the first in the world who, in my book on Longitudes<margin>a</margin> <note>original: "Longitudes"; likely referring to Jean-Baptiste Morin's work on determining longitude at sea</note>, has given to Astronomers the true means of avoiding henceforth all these false suppositions and all the Logical Circles <note>A "logical circle" or circular reasoning occurs when the proof assumes the very thing it seeks to demonstrate.</note> that can be committed in this matter. But Astronomers, through their false suppositions, usually only fail in the "more or less" regarding the movement of the Planets, whereas a Physicist <note>term: Physicist (Phyſicien); in the 17th century, this referred to a "natural philosopher" who studied the underlying nature and causes of the physical world.</note> can err in the very nature of the thing he treats. There is nothing so easy as to adjust some cause to an effect; and you know that this is familiar to Astronomers, who by means of various hypotheses, of circles or ellipses, concur toward the same goal; and the same is very well known to you in your Geometry. But to prove that the cause of a given effect is its true and unique cause, one must at the very least prove that such an effect cannot be produced by any other cause.

Now I believe that, being who you are, you will not have failed, according to page 69 of your *Method* <note>Referring to Descartes' "Discourse on the Method," published in 1637.</note>, to well foresee all that one could object to you; but that, still reserving for yourself the particular knowledge of your principles of Physics, from which all the rest is deduced, you wished to amuse yourself, not only by making fine minds desire the publication of your *Physics*, but also by exercising them in the difficulties that you have left in your new doctrine: indeed, you even invite them to it on page 75 of your—

# I, 187-188. CVIII. — 22 FEBRUARY 1638.

you can: and I assure you that I will not hide it under a bushel <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 5:15, meaning the author will not keep the recipient's ideas secret</note>, but that I will make it known to your honor.

I do not know, however, what I should expect from you; <margin>5</margin> for some have tried to make me believe that, if I were to address you even slightly in the terminology of the School <note>The "School" refers to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian philosophy taught in universities</note>, you would instantly judge me more worthy of contempt than of a response. But by reading your discourses, I do not recognize you to be such an enemy of the School as they claim, and I <margin>10</margin> hold this good opinion of your mind: that it will easily grant that every well-demonstrated truth can withstand all the terms of the School; and that any proposition which cannot withstand this test is at the very least doubtful, if not entirely false. For if someone <margin>15</margin> wished to pass off a fiction as a truth, an accident <term>accident: in Aristotelian terms, a quality that exists only within a substance, like color or heat</term> as a substance, a motion without a mover, etc., I make you the judge yourself of what he would deserve. The School seems to me to have failed only in <margin>20</margin> that it occupied itself more with speculation in the search for terms which must be used to discuss things, than in the search for the actual truth of things through sound experiments <note>The French "experiences" here carries the dual meaning of observations and controlled experiments</note>; thus it is poor in the latter, and rich in the former; that is why <margin>25</margin> I am like you: I seek the truth of things only in Nature, and no longer trust the School, which serves me only for its terminology.

Now I shall begin with the views you hold on the nature of Light, so that they may serve me as a foundation, and so that we may see if they are everywhere the <margin>30</margin> same, or if they are different, and in what way.

### CIX.

## DESCARTES TO [FATHER VATIER].

### [February 22, 1638.]

->Text from Clerselier, volume I, letter 114, p. 513-518.<-

"To a Reverend Jesuit Father," without name or date. But Descartes informs us in two later letters that this is a Jesuit from *La Flèche* <note>The prestigious Jesuit college where Descartes himself was educated.</note> (Letter CXIV hereafter; Clerselier, II, 378), namely *Father Vatier* (Letter CXII; Clerselier, III, 189). As for the date, Descartes states (*p. 561, l. 24*) that he received "only eight days ago" the objections of a physician from Louvain—that is to say, those of *Plempius*—to which he responded, it seems, immediately, on *February 15* (Letter CVII above): this letter would therefore be from Monday, *February 22*.

->My Reverend Father,<-

I am delighted by the favor you have done me, by looking so carefully at the book of my Essays <note>Referring to the 1637 publication of the *Discourse on the Method* along with the essays *Dioptrics*, *Meteors*, and *Geometry*.</note>, and by sending me your feelings on them with so many testimonies of goodwill. I would have accompanied the book with a letter in <margin>5</margin> sending it to you, and would have taken that opportunity to assure you of my very humble service, had it not been that I hoped to let it pass through the world without the name of its author being known; but since this plan was unable to succeed, I must believe that it is rather the affection <margin>10</margin> you have had for the father, than the merit of the child <note>Descartes uses a common 17th-century metaphor, referring to himself as the "father" and his book as his "child."</note>, which is the cause of the favorable reception it has received at your house, and I am very particularly obliged to thank you for it. I do not know if it is that I flatter myself...

<summary>Descartes writes to the Jesuit Father Antoine Vatier to thank him for his positive feedback on the "Essays." He reveals that although he originally intended to publish the work anonymously, he is pleased that it has been well-received by his former teachers at La Flèche.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, Father Vatier, La Flèche, Jesuit education, anonymity, Discourse on Method, Plempius, 17th-century philosophy</keywords>

<margin>5, 10</margin>
The first person to propose that the Moon receives its light from the Sun undoubtedly gave no other proof than that, by assuming this, one can very easily explain all the different faces<gloss>Read *phases*?</gloss> of its light: which has been sufficient to ensure that, since then, this opinion has passed through the world without contradiction. And the connection between my thoughts is such that I dare to hope that my principles will be found just as well proven by the consequences that I draw from them—once they have been noted enough to become familiar and considered all together—as the fact that the Moon borrows its light is proven by its waxing and waning.

<margin>15, 20, 25, 30</margin>

### VI bis.

### BALZAC TO DESCARTES.

->Paris, March 30, 1628.<-

*The Christian Socrates <note>original: "Socrate Chrestien"</note>, by the Lord of Balzac, and other Works by the same Author.*
*(Paris, Augustin Courbé, in-duodecimo, 1657, p. 345; 1661, p. 239, etc.)*

*This letter is the one that D. Nisard <note>Désiré Nisard (1806–1888) was a prominent French literary critic</note> had pointed out (see above, p. 6, lines 3-7), as a thank-you addressed to Descartes for the Apology <note>In this context, an "Apology" is a formal written defense of someone's character or work</note> he had composed in Balzac's favor. The page preceding it, in the editions indicated above of "The Christian Socrates" (p. 343 or p. 237), provides the half-title: "Three Discourses sent to Monsieur Descartes." Indeed, this letter—which is missing from the large edition of Balzac's Works, 2 volumes in-folio, 1665—is found attached, in the specific editions of "The Christian Socrates," to the three Discourses or Dissertations: "The Quibbling Sophist," "The Quibbler Convicted of Forgery," and "The Quibbler's Final Objection Refuted." <note>original titles: "Le Sophiste Chicaneur," "Le Chicaneur convaincu de faux," and "La derniere objection du Chicaneur refutée"</note> It thus serves to date by approximation not only Letter VI (of which it acknowledges receipt), as we have seen, but also these three Dissertations; it confirms and clarifies a conjecture that we had proposed on page 12, in the final explanatory note.*

->Sir,<-

I have received the Latin Discourse <note>original: "Discours Latin"</note> that you have written. I would not dare call it your Judgment on my Writings,

### LETTER XIII, PAGE 69, LINES 3-5.

Compare this promise or hope with what Pierre Borel, in his *Summary of the Life of René Descartes* <note>original: "Compendium Vitæ R. Cartesii"</note>, 1653, reports of Descartes, on the authority of Villebressieu: "and I heard from Mr. Bressieu that Ferrier <note>Jean Ferrier, a craftsman who worked with Descartes on grinding lenses</note>, under his (meaning Descartes’) guidance, had made an excellent hyperbolic telescope, by which even the leaves of small plants appeared large from three leagues <note>A league was roughly 2.5 to 3 miles</note> away." (p. 31 of the 2nd edition, 1676).

The first part of this letter is explained and completed by three documents printed some time later:

1° In a work written against Stampioen, under the inspiration of Descartes and even with his collaboration (see a letter to Huygens(?) from October 1639, Clerselier, III, 417), *Remarks on the New Algebraic Rule of Johan Stampioen the Younger* <note>original Dutch: "Aenmerckingen op den Nieuwen Stel-Regel van Iohan Stampioen d'Jonge"</note> (Leiden, Jan Maire, 1639), the mathematician Waessenaer recalls a question proposed many years ago (*many years long*) by Stampioen; he reproduces the statement in its entirety along with the diagram, and adds to it, without explanation or demonstration, the solution given, he says, six years ago (*over six years*), which brings us back to the end of 1633.

Moriaen soude wit maken." This is a reference to the "labor in vain" proverb, suggesting that finding whole-number solutions for this specific geometric problem is impossible.</note>

Thus, the statement of the question proposed by Stampioen <note>Jan Jansz de Jonge Stampioen (1610–1689), a Dutch mathematician who challenged Descartes.</note> was as follows:
*In the right-angled triangle ABC, the square DEFG is inscribed, and in the partial triangles DGB and EFC are inscribed the circles KL and MN, which, on the secants DC and EB, intercept given lengths, namely KL = 7 and MN = 5. One is asked to construct the triangle ABC.*
Descartes took as his unknown the ratio of AB to AC (or the tangent of angle C). He arrived at the sixth-degree equation given above (p. 575, lines 5-6), which must be substituted for the one we had tried to reconstruct by conjecture on p. 276, line 7.
For the general case ($KL = a$, $MN = b$, $a > b$), the equation is given in the analysis above by Waessenaer <note>Jacob van Waessenaer, a student used by Descartes to publish his mathematical solutions during his rivalry with Stampioen.</note> (by setting $y = 1$).
This equation has only two positive roots, which are always real; as long as $a$ differs from $b$, they are unequal, and one is greater while the other is less than one. This is why Descartes says "*one of the two roots*," meaning the one that is greater than one.
Furthermore, on p. 276, lines 15-16, it is now necessary to restore $BC + BF$ instead of $BC + 2\ GF$, as the relationship indicated by Descartes (*see the figure on page 276*) is:

-> $4\ GF^2 \times HD = \overline{MN}^2 \times (BC + BF)$. <-

### LETTER LXI, PAGE 324, LINE 11.

Twice Mersenne defended or wished to defend Galileo; the first time was in one of the three small treatises published together in Paris in 1634 (see page 303 above, note *a*). He even had a specific copy of this treatise made, with different pages substituted, so that he could send it to one of his friends in Rome, J.-B. Doni, who helped him obtain licenses or permissions from the ecclesiastical authority to read books on the Index <note>The *Index Librorum Prohibitorum*, the Catholic Church's list of banned books.</note>, and who later became secretary of the College of Cardinals. Not content with this first defense of the theory of the earth's movement, Mersenne planned to defend Galileo himself against his detractors in the large work he soon put to press, which did not appear until 1636: *The Instruments of Harmony, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Harmonicorum Instrumentorum, etc.*</note> (Paris <note>original: *Lutetiæ Parisiorum*</note>, at the expense of Guillaume Baudry, 1636; dedication, Ides of November <note>November 13th</note> 1635). But this second project was abandoned. The letters that follow, from July 26, Dec. 4, 1634, and May 25, 1635, provide all these details. It appears that our letter LXI is perhaps not from the autumn, but from the spring of 1635 (the project of Mersenne to which Descartes seems to allude having been abandoned since May 25), unless it concerns another project, that of responding

# ADDITIONS.

...to Morin, for example, Mersenne having avoided telling Descartes that he was openly taking up the defense of Galileo, seeing his friend so fearful in this regard. <note>Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583–1656) was a French mathematician and astrologer; Descartes was notoriously cautious about publishing his own scientific views after hearing of Galileo's trial.</note>

> "Sir," wrote Mersenne to Peiresc on July 26, 1634, "I am sending you the 3 small treatises I have made... I beg you to send to Mr. Doni, when you find the opportunity, those where his name is, of which the *Questions on Morals, Mathematics, etc.* are different from yours, because there are reasons for the movement of the earth, without refutation; for which I had put the sentence of the cardinals (**the condemnation of Galileo, pronounced on June 22, 1633**) as medicine as you will see; but because I was told that there had been some noise among the doctors of the Sorbonne <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris.</note> because of the reasons that I did not refute, I have removed all the questions they could take offense at, and have put others in that you will see in the book for Mr. Doni, which will be more appropriate for Rome. Nevertheless, if you are not satisfied with having seen them in there, I will send them to you separately. Furthermore, I am not sending any to Mr. Gassendi, because being always with you, he will be able to read them..." (p. 89-90 of *Peiresc's Correspondents, published by Tamizey de Larroque, fasc. XIX, Paris, Picard, 1894*).

On Dec. 4, 1634, he asks Peiresc to request information for him from Galileo:

> "...which he will do all the more quickly if he knows that I am working to answer for him all his envious critics whose books I have seen, by destroying their reasons and strengthening his own, when I find them to be true after having examined them *at the touchstone* <note>original Latin: *ad lapidem Lydium* — a reference to the Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold, here meaning a rigorous or definitive test</note>; but I cannot finish until I have seen what Scheiner <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit astronomer and rival of Galileo.</note> will write against him, assuming that he writes, as we were told a year ago (see *previously p. 283, second paragraph*). Now, you must not fear that what I say will ever be censored, insofar as it will be perpetually supported by experience..." (*Ibid., p. 108-109*).

Same letter, at the end:

> "If you know of anyone who has written against Galileo, besides Bérigard, Inchofer, and Roca, I pray you indicate it to me; for since I have undertaken to defend the truth that shall be known to me, it is necessary that I see them all. I am still waiting for Claramontius (**Chiaramonti**) of Florence, which I do not yet have, against him; I estimate that he will be the most clever, for he has already written against Tycho and Kepler, and I will be very happy to receive your advice and your aid both on that and on the other things concerning my labor." (*Ibid., p. 110*).

But, on May 25, 1635, he announces to Peiresc that he is abandoning this project:

> "I have been careful to bring from Italy all those who have written against him (*Galileo*)...; but I have found that they are almost not worthy of being named in regard to this great man, and not trusting myself alone, I had my friends read them who found the same thing; so that I am content to act nobly with him by speaking of his experiments and mine, as you will see, God willing." (*Ibid., p. 114*).

### LETTER LXII, PAGES 325-328.

Huygens corresponded with Descartes through their mutual friend, Reneri, who lived in Utrecht. Huygens's letter was accompanied by this note: "covered to Reneri for Descartes <note>In the hand of a secretary of Huygens; 'covered' means sealed, the opposite of 'open'.</note>. Oct 29, 1635." <note>original Latin: "Rogo te, vir doctissime, ut has incomparabili amico nostro tradas : si quid responsi dabit, quotidie equis dispositis ad nos commeatur, neque defuturi sunt, qui perferant..."</note> (*Amsterdam, Academy of Sciences, Latin letters manuscript of Constantijn Huygens, no. 223*).

<header>ADDITIONS. 581</header>

A geometric diagram illustrating the physical theory of atoms and pores within a bent blade (lamina). Two concentric dashed arcs represent the curved blade, labeled 'A' at the top and 'B' at the bottom. Between these arcs, circles represent 'pores'. An outer pore is labeled 'C' at the top and 'D' at the bottom. Two inner pores closer to the center of the arc are labeled 'E'.

> » It had escaped my memory to ask you for your opinion, to be sent to me immediately, regarding the recoil of bows and the bending of steel blades—specifically, why they return to their shape. Is it because atoms, flowing through the pores in perpetual motion, force the pores (which have been changed from a circular shape to an elliptical or narrower one) to return to their original circular form? <note>original Latin: "an quia atomi, perpetuo motu poros tranantes, cogunt poros e circulari figurâ ad ellipticam aut aliam angustiorem conuersos, redire ad figuram pristinam circularem?"</note> Let the bent blade be A B, and let pores C D be wider, and E E narrower: could it be that the atoms passing through C D force the rest of the depth of the pore to resume that shape? But why would atoms move from C toward E, rather than from E toward C? I ask, therefore, whether they move from east to west (let D be the east, and E E the west), or from west to east, or in every direction? Unless you can prove this, I would like you to assign a cause for that return of A B to its original straight line. But since the blade A B itself consists of atoms, then new atoms rushing here and there from C to E will force the curved pores E E to return to straightness and restore the small round spaces, or circular pores. Since I am greatly troubled by this difficulty, I urge you to provide its solution. » <note>This excerpt is from Pierre Gassendi, a philosopher and scientist who tried to reconcile the ancient theory of atoms with 17th-century physics.</note> (*Gassendi's Works*, VI, 430).

### LETTER LXXXIII, PAGES 393-395.

Here is a conjecture on the unknown recipient of this letter:

1º <term>Descartes</term> mentions the <term>Feast of Saint-Victor</term> <note>The feast of Saint Victor of Marseilles, observed on July 21st.</note>: might we not think he is addressing a Catholic, rather than a Protestant?

2º He has just received books and is going to begin studying medicine: might we not think these were medical books sent by a doctor?

3º Finally, he seems surprised that these books took so long to arrive: they remained for two nights on the water. These books therefore arrived by boat, undoubtedly the boat that transported goods via the canal from <term>Leiden</term> to <term>Amsterdam</term>, then from Amsterdam to <term>Haarlem</term>; <term>Leiden</term> being the great warehouse of books for all of <term>Holland</term>.

Now <term>Descartes</term> had a Catholic friend in <term>Leiden</term> who was involved in medicine, <term>Cornelis van Hooghelande</term>. It was to him specifically that he would have <term>Waessenaer</term> address letters on February 1, 1640, as a person of trust, for <term>Golius</term>, <term>Schooten</term>, etc. A little later, in June 1640, we find him again with <term>Hooghelande</term> at the bedside of a sick child, the daughter of their friend, <term>Van Zurck</term>. Finally, before leaving for <term>Sweden</term>, it was to <term>Hooghelande</term> again that he gave instructions for his private affairs (letter of August 30, 1649), and to whom he entrusted a chest full of manuscripts for safekeeping.

## POSTSCRIPT.

*May we be permitted, in concluding this first volume, to address a double appeal to those who will read it.*

*It is a legitimate hope to see the recovery, before the completion of our edition, of original letters (or early copies) to or from Descartes, not included in the list on pages 68–74 of the Introduction. In particular, regarding the items dispersed by Libri <note>Guglielmo Libri (1803–1869), a famous mathematician and book thief who stole numerous manuscripts from French public libraries.</note>, it is hard to believe they are gone forever; one should expect much less to discover even one of the letters once collected by Legrand <note>Albert Legrand, a 17th-century biographer whose collection of Descartes’ papers was largely lost or scattered.</note>; conversely, such a discovery would be all the more precious as it might put us on the trail of unexpected finds.*

*The reception given to the project for this edition allows us to hope that the publication of the first Volume will redouble the zeal of the goodwill of which we have already had so many proofs, and that we will see an increase in the sharing of documents that could expand the materials at our disposal for the Correspondence of Des-*

maps. But we ask our readers to kindly point out to us any errors or mistakes, *which human nature has failed to avoid* <note>original: "quas humana parum cavit natura." This is a variation of a line from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, acknowledging that despite best intentions, human nature is prone to oversight.</note>.

We have made every *effort*, and the publisher has spared no expense, to provide an irreproachable text of Descartes. Conversely, in our introduction <term>prolegomena: a formal introductory essay or preliminary remarks to a scholarly work</term>, notes, etc., we admit that several errors of detail will be found; in particular, there remain some that are easy to recognize in the cross-references for variant readings <note>Differences found between various early copies or editions of the same letter.</note> and those for clarifications. However, we believe it will be more convenient for the reader to find all the corrections to be made to our work gathered together following the Correspondence, rather than having to search for them across the various volumes, as is the usual practice for publications of this kind.

It is in order to prepare this general revision, and to perfect the undertaken work as much as possible, that we request the assistance of everyone interested in Descartes.

*Paris, October 22, 1897.*

**PAUL TANNERY.**

->*Finished printing*<- <note>original: "Achevé d'imprimer." This is a traditional bibliographical statement indicating when the physical production of the book was completed.</note>
->*by* LÉOPOLD CERF<- <note>Léopold Cerf was a significant Parisian printer and publisher of the late 19th century, known for producing historical and academic works.</note>
->*12 Sainte-Anne Street, in Paris*<-
->*on October 26, 1897*<-

<summary>This page acts as the official colophon for the work, crediting the Parisian printer Léopold Cerf and providing the exact date the printing was finished in 1897.</summary>
